items.title: ZEMBA concludes inaugural tender with Hapag-Lloyd
items.original_title: ZEMBA concludes inaugural tender with Hapag-Lloyd
items.summary: The Zero Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance (ZEMBA) has delivered 82,000 mtCO2-equivalent (mtCO2e) in emissions reductions in 2025 and 2026 under its first low-emission shipping tender with Hapag-Lloyd, which concluded this month. The reductions were achieved through the use of liquefied biomethane (LBM) across eight international shipping voyages under 17 contracts between Hapag-Lloyd and ZEMBA members. The German container liner secured ZEMBA’s inaugural tender to replace conventional bunker fuels with lower-emission alternatives. It then allocated environmental attribute certificates representing the emissions reductions achieved during these voyages to ZEMBA members through a book-and-claim mechanism. ZEMBA members include major cargo owners such as Amazon, Nike, IKEA and Patagonia. Second tender moves to e-fuels ZEMBA has awarded its second tender to Hapag-Lloyd and Norwegian shipping company North Sea Container Line (NCL), with fuel deliveries scheduled to begin in 2027. Hapag-Lloyd will use e-methanol on a trans-oceanic trade route, while NCL will deploy green ammonia on a northern European route. Both fuels will be produced using green hydrogen generated with renewable energy and are expected to deliver lifecycle emissions reductions of at least 90% compared with conventional marine fuels. ZEMBA expects the two companies to collectively deliver around 120,000 mtCO2e in emissions reductions over three years from 2027.

items.title: Asia’s search for long-term, lower-carbon LNG supply puts Canada in focus but competition is intensifying
items.original_title: Asia’s search for long-term, lower-carbon LNG supply puts Canada in focus but competition is intensifying
items.summary: Asia’s long-term energy security will increasingly depend on diversified, reliable and lower-carbon LNG supply. As buyers look beyond traditional sources, Canada is emerging as a compelling long-term supplier due to its proximity to the Asian market, as well as its lower carbon intensity. Canada’s LNG sector is entering a new phase of growth. For LNG exporters, competitiveness on delivered cost is becoming just as important as supply reliability and emissions performance. Canada’s momentum and the competition it faces The FID for LNG Canada Phase 2 represents an important milestone in Canada’s efforts to expand its LNG export capacity, while Ksi Lisims LNG continues to advance toward a final investment decision and build commercial momentum. However, Canada is competing for both investment capital and access to a rapidly growing, yet very price-sensitive, Asian LNG market. Competition is intensifying as buyers evaluate long-term LNG offtake opportunities across a growing range of global supply options. The contracting and investment decisions made over the next three to five years will help shape Asia’s LNG supply landscape for decades to come.

items.title: US Natgas Prices Fall Back to 2-Month Low
items.original_title: US Natgas Prices Fall Back to 2-Month Low
items.summary: US natural gas prices fell back to $2.76 per MMBtu on Friday, their lowest level in two months, as mild weather forecasts weighed on expected heating demand. Above-average temperatures are expected across the Midwest and East through November 5, according to Commodity Weather Group, likely limiting gas consumption. This outweighed support from a smaller-than-usual storage build, strong LNG feedgas demand, and lower production. EIA data showed that energy companies added 77 bcf of natural gas to storage in the week ended October 16, below the 86 bcf injected during the same week last year and the five-year average of 87 bcf. Meanwhile, average gas flows to the nine major US LNG export facilities rose to 18.2 bcfd in October, up from 17.9 bcfd in September. On the supply side, natural gas production across the Lower 48 states averaged 111.4 bcfd this month, down from record highs of 113.3 bcfd in August and September. Source: Trading Economics

items.title: Soybeans Rebound on Strong Export Demand
items.original_title: Soybeans Rebound on Strong Export Demand
items.summary: Soybean futures rose toward $12.6 per bushel, rebounding from a two-month low reached on October 21, as strong export demand led by China helped end an eight-session losing streak. The USDA reported 2.84 million metric tons of net US soybean export sales for the 2026/27 marketing year in the week ended October 15, sharply above 574,900 tons a week earlier. China accounted for 2.18 million tons, while export shipments climbed 75% week over week to 2.02 million tons, up 88% from the four-week average. A separate USDA announcement also confirmed a sale of 202,000 tons to China. Still, futures remained on track for a second consecutive weekly loss as the advancing US harvest and expectations for a large crop continued to weigh on prices. The USDA projects US soybean production at 4.56 billion bushels for the 2026/27 marketing year. However, analysts suggested harvest-related pressure was easing as fieldwork neared completion. Source: Trading Economics

items.title: Diesel arbitrage: why freight has shut the Europe import window
items.original_title: Diesel arbitrage: why freight has shut the Europe import window
items.summary: Freight, not relative diesel prices, has closed the US arbitrage into Europe. Rates for prompt US Gulf Coast cargoes have climbed from around 250 to over 400 worldscale, closing the arbs, before settling lower in recent sessions to come closer to an equilibrium. Key insights Freight closed the window the market opened From about 20 September to early October, buyers could pay almost any freight rate for US Gulf Coast diesel into Europe and still profit. For freight traders, that gives a reference level: • TC14 was near 400 worldscale at the end of last week. Red arbitrages do not stop diesel moving Refiners keep running because they earn the crack, and the diesel has to go somewhere. The flow data supports the point: • India to Europe diesel flows were suppressed from March to June, when the economics pointed east. The supply picture is a Russia and US story, not only a Middle East story The US Gulf Coast supplied almost half of North West Europe’s diesel imports over the past 12 months, a much larger share than a year earlier. For new routes without published prices, such as Russian diesel into the US, use proxies and override the inputs: a worldscale assumption for freight and an assumed differential for the cargo.

items.title: OEG books three more offshore wind CTVs at Diverse Marine
items.original_title: OEG books three more offshore wind CTVs at Diverse Marine
items.summary: UK offshore services player OEG Marine Services has ordered three crew transfer vessels (CTVs) from Isle of Wight shipbuilder Diverse Marine as part of its offshore wind fleet expansion and renewal programme. The vessels, based on Chartwell Marine’s Brevity SL class design, are scheduled for delivery throughout 2027. Each vessel will measure 26 m in length, with a load line length of less than 24 m, and will be built at Diverse Marine’s Cowes facility. The first vessel will feature quad Volvo Penta IPS propulsion compliant with IMO Tier III emissions standards, alongside Hull Vane transom foils designed to improve fuel efficiency at cruising speeds. All three newbuilds will share the same specification, be classed by Bureau Veritas and operate under the UK flag. The vessels are expected to support construction activities at an offshore wind project off the UK’s east coast in 2027, working alongside OEG’s existing Chartwell-designed Fulmar and Furioso . The order marks the second collaboration between OEG and Diverse Marine following the delivery of the Fulmar in 2025. That vessel has since supported construction work at Scotland’s Inch Cape offshore wind farm. OEG director Leif Cooper said the Chartwell design performed better than expected, prompting the company to return to Diverse Marine for additional vessels.

items.title: Rio Tinto targets larger capesizes in $1.9bn Australian bauxite push
items.original_title: Rio Tinto targets larger capesizes in $1.9bn Australian bauxite push
items.summary: Mining giant Rio Tinto has approved a $1.9bn investment in a major bauxite expansion in Australia’s Queensland state, including an upgrade of its export facilities to accommodate larger capesize bulk carriers. The Kangwinan project on the western Cape York Peninsula will add 20m tonnes of annual bauxite production capacity, with first output targeted for 2029 and full production expected by 2032. The development will replace production from the ageing Andoom mine near Weipa, which is expected to reach the end of its life this decade, while also helping offset the planned closure of the Gove operation in the Northern Territory in 2029. Once fully operational, Kangwinan will lift annual capacity at Rio Tinto’s Weipa operations to around 44m tonnes, compared with current production of approximately 38m tonnes. The new mining centre will be located about 15 km southeast of Rio Tinto’s existing Amrun mine. A 15 km conveyor system will transport bauxite to expanded stockyards and the Amrun export wharf, which will be upgraded to handle larger capesize vessels. SEB further pointed out that shipments from Australia to China involve voyages roughly 3.3 times shorter than those from Guinea, where surging bauxite exports have been a major driver of capesize tonne-mile demand.

items.title: Taylor Maritime agrees final owned bulker sale ahead of London exit
items.original_title: Taylor Maritime agrees final owned bulker sale ahead of London exit
items.summary: London-listed Taylor Maritime has agreed to sell its last owned bulk carrier for $15.1m, taking its fleet disposal programme to 56 vessels and putting total proceeds on course to reach almost $933m. The Ed Buttery-led company said the final sale is expected to complete in December, bringing to an end a three-year selling campaign that has steadily dismantled one of the largest geared dry bulk fleets in the market. Since the beginning of 2023, Taylor Maritime has executed 55 vessel disposals with expected gross proceeds of $917.7m, at an average discount of 3.5% to fair market value. The move follows the completion of three handysize disposals announced earlier this month, which generated $48.6m. While the latest agreement covers Taylor Maritime’s last owned ship, one vessel remains on charter under a sale-and-leaseback arrangement with a purchase option. That contract expires in April 2027, and the company is assessing the most efficient way to exit the arrangement. Taylor Maritime expects to cease all commercial shipping operations by the end of 2026, with the wind-down now moving towards its final shareholder distributions. The company has confirmed a fourth compulsory capital return of $45m in November, taking the amount returned to investors since January to $263.4m.

items.summary: US investment firm Wildcat Equity Partners has struck an agreement to acquire Fraser Industries, the Wisconsin-based shipbuilding and repair group, with plans to invest $350m in expanding its facilities and workforce. Wildcat Defense, the investment firm’s maritime and defence arm said the transaction covers Fraser Shipyards, Lake Assault Boats, Northern Engineering and Fraser Terminal. Financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. The $350m represents Wildcat’s planned investment in the business rather than the purchase price. The companies expect to complete the transaction in approximately three months, with Fraser co-owner and chief executive Patrick Kelly remaining in his position. The company is targeting a threefold increase in production, with the expansion expected to take place over five years. Established in 1888, Fraser Shipyards provides maintenance, repair and overhaul services to the Great Lakes merchant fleet, alongside commercial newbuilding work. Announced in July, that partnership involves yard design, production systems, automation, artificial intelligence and workforce development. The companies identified Fraser as a potential demonstration site for modernising shipbuilding operations across the US.

items.title: Icon Energy faces shareholder revolt over dilution
items.original_title: Icon Energy faces shareholder revolt over dilution
items.summary: Nasdaq-listed Greek dry bulk owner Icon Energy is facing pressure from a significant shareholder to overhaul its capital structure and board, following accusations that repeated equity issuances have heavily diluted ordinary investors. Canada’s Hampton Financial, which holds 325,000 Icon shares representing approximately 9% of the company, has disclosed a letter sent to Icon’s management demanding changes to its preferred shares, dividend arrangements and corporate governance. Hampton, led by chairman and chief executive Peter Deeb, claims Icon has raised approximately $25m through common share issuances since its 2024 flotation, while ordinary shareholders have suffered substantial losses. The Canadian investment firm has also questioned the treatment of preferred shares held by Icon’s controlling shareholder and chief executive, Ismini Panagiotidi. Hampton is proposing that Icon exchange its outstanding Series A preferred shares for a new instrument with a $20m face value, a fixed 6% cash dividend and conversion rights priced at $5 per ordinary share. The investor argues that these measures would address dilution concerns while preserving Panagiotidi’s control of the business. Icon, established in 2023, operates three bulk carriers. The company entered the Nasdaq market in July 2024 and subsequently expanded its fleet through secondhand acquisitions.

items.title: Lila Global doubles up on vintage LNG carriers
items.original_title: Lila Global doubles up on vintage LNG carriers
items.summary: Lila Global is expanding its presence in the ageing LNG carrier market, adding a second steam-powered vessel to its fleet as the global LNG trade undergoes major disruption. Earlier this month, Splash reported that the 18-year-old, steam-powered LNG carrier Tangguh Batur (145,700 cu m) had been sold for $30m and renamed Eagle M, with market chatter linking the purchase to Lila Global’s parent company, GMS, controlled by Anil Sharma (pictured). That deal has now been confirmed, with the vessel listed on Lila Global’s website, marking the company’s entry into the LNG segment. The vessel’s value has already increased since the acquisition, with VesselsValue now assessing Eagle M at $32.75m. Meanwhile, Lila Global has emerged as the buyer of another vintage LNG carrier, the 2003-built Castillo de Villalba renamed Carla, a vessel that is five years older than the Eagle M. The former Elcano-owned vessel has been sold for $24.5m, well above its VesselsValue market valuation of just under $18m. items.title: Sierra Leone launches Chinese-backed national shipping company
items.original_title: Sierra Leone launches Chinese-backed national shipping company
items.summary: Sierra Leone has launched a new national shipping company backed by China’s Zhejiang Xiehai Group, with ambitions to develop a fleet of 50 vessels and capture a greater share of the country’s international cargo trade. President Julius Maada Bio inaugurated Sierra Leone Ocean Shipping Company (SLOSCO) at Queen Elizabeth II Quay in Freetown earlier this week. The venture is 70% owned by Zhejiang Xiehai Group, with the remaining 30% held by the state-owned Sierra Leone National Shipping Agency (SLNSA). The company plans to establish a fleet of 50 ships, with an initial phase involving 30 vessels, targeting dry bulk, liquid bulk and other cargoes. Its principal markets include Sierra Leone’s substantial iron ore and bauxite exports, alongside imports of petroleum products, grain and other essential commodities. The new venture follows the restructuring of Sierra Leone’s longstanding national shipping company into SLNSA last year. Legislation provides the national carrier with rights covering 40% of the value of the country’s import and export cargoes. SLOSCO is headed by chief executive Sui Xiao, with former BRS Shipbrokers executive Laurent Debart serving as chief operating officer. The venture represents another expansion of Chinese shipping interests in West Africa, with Freetown seeking to retain more of the freight revenue generated by its international trade.

items.summary: Oslo-listed 2020 Bulkers has appointed offshore industry veteran Tom Babinski as group chief executive, replacing Lars-Christian Svensen following its transformation from a dry bulk owner into a major anchor-handling vessel player. The company said Svensen has resigned with immediate effect, with Babinski taking over the top job after previously being lined up to lead its newly acquired AHTS AS business. Babinski brings experience from Aurora Offshore Management, Viking Supply Ships, Westshore Shipbrokers, Framar and Sevnor. The management reshuffle comes just weeks after 2020 Bulkers completed the bulk of its offshore fleet consolidation, following a deal unveiled in September to acquire companies controlling up to 15 large anchor-handling tug supply (AHTS) vessels. The expansion has been backed by a $175m private placement completed in September, with the underlying fleet transactions initially carrying an aggregate agreed vessel value of approximately $407m on a debt-free, cash-free basis. For 2020 Bulkers, the move marks a complete change of direction after the company disposed of its entire newcastlemax fleet earlier this year. Following the disposal of its remaining six ships, the company returned approximately $316m to shareholders through a special distribution in April.

items.title: Seatrium bags five-vessel Karpowership conversion deal
items.original_title: Seatrium bags five-vessel Karpowership conversion deal
items.summary: Singapore-based offshore and marine engineering group Seatrium has secured a contract from Turkey’s Karpowership to convert and integrate five hydrogen-ready floating power plants. The deal covers Karpowership’s third-generation Whale Class powerships, with Seatrium responsible for major conversion work, equipment integration, mechanical completion, and pre-commissioning. Engineering activities are already underway, with the first vessel scheduled to arrive at Seatrium’s Tuas Boulevard yard in Singapore in December 2027. The Whale Class represents Karpowership’s largest floating power plant design, capable of delivering up to 600MW of electricity per vessel. The ships will feature hydrogen-ready multi-fuel generation systems and integrated onboard substations, allowing them to connect directly to national electricity grids. Karpowership said the vessels could begin supplying electricity within 30 days of deployment. The award follows a letter of intent signed in August 2025 covering three FSRU conversions and the potential integration of up to six new-generation powerships. The two companies established their partnership in 2018, with Seatrium having since completed seven FSRU conversion projects for Karpowership. The Singapore group also secured the eighth and ninth FSRU conversion projects earlier this year.

items.summary: Norwegian engineering and construction specialist Aibel has secured a front-end engineering and design (FEED) contract for the topsides of the planned Wisting FPSO vessel in the Barents Sea. Equinor and its partners awarded the contract following a competitive tender, and it covers engineering and further development of the topsides design ahead of a potential final investment decision. The contract also includes an option for engineering, procurement, and project management, while fabrication of the topsides modules will be awarded separately. Aibel said around 250 employees at its Asker offices, supported by personnel in Haugesund, will work on the project. The partners plan to complete concept selection and decide whether to advance the project by the end of 2026, with a final investment decision targeted for late 2027. Located around 310 km north of Hammerfest in water depths of approximately 400 m, Wisting is Norway’s largest undeveloped oil discovery, with estimated recoverable resources of just under 500m barrels of oil equivalent. The current development concept centres on a newbuild FPSO with onboard power generation using energy-efficient gas turbines, while carbon capture and storage remains under consideration. Equinor operates Wisting alongside Aker BP, Petoro, and Inpex. If sanctioned, the field is expected to remain in production for around 30 years.

items.title: New report reveals China’s key strengths across green shipping corridor building blocks
items.original_title: New report reveals China’s key strengths across green shipping corridor building blocks
items.summary: A new report from the Global Maritime Forum reveals that China has quickly become a global leader in green shipping corridors, with nearly one-fifth of the world’s corridor initiatives connecting to a Chinese port. Launched today at the Global Maritime Forum’s Annual Summit 2026 in Shanghai, ‘Green shipping corridors: How China is re-energising the global movement’ measures China’s progress against the four key building blocks considered crucial to successfully starting up a green corridor. The report finds that China is one of the strongest actors globally in this space, holding strategic advantages in three of the four building blocks. “The Global Maritime Forum has been measuring global progress on green corridors since 2022, when China was involved in three announced initiatives—now, that number has risen to more than 20,” said Jesse Fahnestock, director of decarbonisation at the Global Maritime Forum. “China’s advancements on green fuel development and efforts around international collaboration could be success factors for these initiatives.” First introduced in a 2021 report for the Getting to Zero Coalition, the concept of the four building blocks remains a useful tool for benchmarking corridor viability: • Viable zero-emission fuel and technology pathways: Availability of zero-emission fuels, technologies, and bunkering infrastructure to service zero-emission vessels.

items.title: The Port of Riga to become a testbed for resilient maritime connectivity, as LVR Flote and HARDMODE sign MoU
items.original_title: The Port of Riga to become a testbed for resilient maritime connectivity, as LVR Flote and HARDMODE sign MoU
items.summary: LVR Flote, a provider of technical port services, and connectivity technology company HARDMODE have partnered to develop and test secure communications technologies for ports and the wider maritime sector as a crucial part of critical infrastructure. The Port of Riga will serve as a real-world testing environment for new connectivity solutions designed to remain reliable in challenging conditions, where connectivity is a must for mission-critical operations. The result is one solution rather than a set of systems someone has to integrate on site, and the Port of Riga is the right place to prove that in real operations.” The Baltic Sea region has experienced repeated GNSS interference affecting shipping and port operations in recent years. As a developer of dual-use connectivity solutions for defence, critical infrastructure, first responders and maritime environments, HARDMODE, together with LVR Flote, will research how different communication technologies, such as mobile, non-terrestrial, tactical and narrowband, can support port operations in a single joint ecosystem. LVR Flote brings direct operational expertise and real service requirements, helping technology companies pilot new solutions for ports and the wider maritime sector in a real port environment and see how different systems work together. In return, LVR Flote gains access to solutions that could improve the efficiency, resilience and quality of port technical services.

The IRGC added that three more vessels collided with mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, and warned the US military that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases. The announcement comes amid mounting tensions over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has stepped up attacks on vessels and sought to exert greater control since the United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28. In an October 14 report, Reuters cited two senior Iranian officials as saying Tehran had adopted new tactics to target ships it considered to be violating its restrictions, in an effort to keep oil prices high and increase pressure on Washington ahead of the US midterm elections in November. A US military official told Reuters that Iran had begun using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets after US strikes destroyed much of its radar capabilities. The official said US forces had recently confronted and destroyed a dhow being used by Iranian spotters, with no casualties.

items.title: Hapag-Lloyd expects more shipping services to return to Suez Canal
items.original_title: Hapag-Lloyd expects more shipping services to return to Suez Canal
items.summary: Hamburg-based shipping company Hapag-Lloyd expects additional services to resume transits through the Suez Canal, joining two services already operating to and from Asia, according to a statement from the Suez Canal Authority (SCA). The anticipated return was discussed during a meeting between Ossama Rabiee, Chairman and Managing Director of the SCA, and Juan Pablo Richards, Hapag-Lloyd’s Senior Managing Director for Region South Europe. Held at the SCA’s headquarters in the Irshad Building in Ismailia, the meeting explored cooperation to increase traffic through the canal. Richards explained that Hapag-Lloyd is closely monitoring developments in the Red Sea and maritime safety indicators to guide changes to its sailing schedules as transits gradually resume through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Suez Canal. Rabiee affirmed the canal’s readiness to accommodate returning shipping services, pointing to the SCA’s ongoing development of maritime services and modernization of its fleet to meet customers’ changing requirements. He expressed hope for the full resumption of Hapag-Lloyd’s services through the canal, emphasizing the waterway’s importance to maintaining global supply chains amid geopolitical challenges and rapid changes in the shipping industry. Richards identified an opportunity for the SCA’s Maritime Training and Simulation Academy to work with the Damietta Alliance Container Terminal, also known as Tahya Misr 1, at Damietta Port on training for Ship Captains.

items.title: The soaring cost of shipping is lifting the price of oil for consumers
items.original_title: The soaring cost of shipping is lifting the price of oil for consumers
items.summary: D isruptions in the Middle East are pushing tanker rates to historic highs The price of oil is only part of what determines the cost to supply the world with fuel. Crude oil and the products refined from it must travel – often thousands of kilometres by specialised marine tankers – from producing regions and refining centres to the places where they are consumed. Typically, transport makes up a small proportion of the overall price of oil, but when shipping becomes more expensive, costs can mount across the supply chain. By mid-October, the cost of shipping crude from the Middle East Gulf to Asia on a large tanker had climbed to over $37 per barrel, more than five times its level before the war began. The temporary suspension of pipeline flows coincided with a ramp-up in Chinese buying, resulting in more Saudi oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz and pushing up demand for tankers. In the third quarter of 2026, demand for these two tanker classes, measured on a tonne-mile basis – which accounts for both the volume of cargo transported and the distance it travels – was around 20% higher than a year earlier.

items.original_title: Dual-Fuel Ship Fleet Tops 500 as Industry Investment Passes $200 Billion
items.summary: Jane McAllister works a ZIM containership at the Port of Virginia. Photo courtesy McAllister Towing The global fleet of dual-fuel containerships and vehicle carriers has surpassed 500 vessels, with shipowners committing more than $200 billion to ships capable of running on alternative fuels, according to new figures from the World Shipping Council (WSC). The latest WSC Dual-Fuel Fleet Dashboard shows 503 dual-fuel vessels in service as of September 2026, a 41% increase from 358 a year earlier. The figures highlight the scale of investment underway as container lines and vehicle carriers prepare for a transition to lower-emission fuels, even as uncertainty over future environmental regulations continues to cloud the industry’s outlook. “The container ship and vehicle carrier industry have committed more than $200 billion to ships that can run on cleaner fuels, with more than 500 already sailing and hundreds more on the way,” said WSC President and CEO Joe Kramek. “The investment is happening, but these ships need commercially competitive alternative fuels to deliver their full potential to reduce emissions.” Dual-fuel vessels are designed to operate on conventional marine fuels as well as alternative fuels, giving operators flexibility as new fuel supplies and infrastructure develop. Shipping companies and fuel producers need certainty to make the investments that will shape the future fleet and its fuel supply,” Kramek said.

REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo QatarEnergy has signed two long-term agreements to purchase up to 4 million tonnes of U.S. liquefied natural gas annually from Cheniere Energy through 2054, as the Gulf producer continues to grapple with damage to its own export facilities from the war with Iran. Under the contracts, QatarEnergy will purchase the LNG on a free-on-board (FOB) basis, taking responsibility for transporting cargoes from the U.S. The deal comes as QatarEnergy faces significant disruptions to its own LNG production following Iranian missile strikes on its Ras Laffan Industrial City in March. QatarEnergy has warned that repairs could take three to five years, potentially costing $20 billion annually in lost revenue and disrupting long-term supply commitments to customers in Europe and Asia. QatarEnergy described the agreements as part of its broader strategy to diversify its global LNG portfolio. “This major long-term purchase will expand and diversify our global LNG portfolio and advance our ability to meet the evolving requirements of the market,” said Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, Qatar’s minister of state for energy affairs and CEO of QatarEnergy. items.title: Marco Polo Marine expands Korean offshore push with new JV
items.original_title: Marco Polo Marine expands Korean offshore push with new JV
items.summary: Singapore-listed offshore vessel owner and shipyard group Marco Polo Marine has established a joint venture in South Korea with local partner NSEL, strengthening its presence in the country’s offshore vessel market. The new company, Baramgil Offshore, will focus on vessel operations, management and chartering, with NSEL holding a 51% stake and Baramgil Corporation taking the remaining 49%. Baramgil Corporation is 90% owned by Marco Polo Marine’s Taiwan-based affiliate PKR Offshore, in which the Singapore group holds an indirect 49% interest. The venture has been established with an initial paid-up capital of about $107,000, with Marco Polo Marine funding its investment through internal resources. The latest move builds on an existing partnership between PKR Offshore and NSEL, established in 2023 to pursue opportunities in South Korea’s offshore wind sector. The partners made their first move into the Korean market in 2024, deploying a Korean-flagged crew transfer vessel (CTV) for offshore wind work. Marco Polo Marine has also been expanding its offshore wind support fleet across Asia. In July, the company secured a multi-year framework agreement with Siemens Gamesa covering two commissioning service operation vessels (CSOVs), primarily for projects in Taiwan, with potential deployments in South Korea and Japan. The agreement is scheduled to begin in 2029, with provisions for an earlier start in 2028.

items.title: Another typhoon threatens recovery of East Asian ports from congestion
items.original_title: Another typhoon threatens recovery of East Asian ports from congestion
items.summary: Congestion may be easing in eastern China, but with Typhoon Champi set to sweep across the north-east coast of Taiwan tomorrow there are concerns that disruption to vessel movements could undo benefits carriers are seeing in China. Maersk told customers waiting times at ports along the east China coast were showing a continued week-on-week decline, with its wider east Asian network stabilising following disruption from earlier typhoons., The carrier said: “Recovery efforts across East Asia continue to progress, although strong export demand is putting pressure on congested ports. Operational conditions at East China ports have improved. “While the direct impact of recent typhoon activity has largely subsided, recovery across the wider regional network remains ongoing. Furthermore, there have been restrictions on vessel movements at some ports, with anticipated closures affecting Zhejiang, Fujian, and surrounding areas if the typhoon matches forecast severity, raising the prospect of renewed delays. The extent of any typhoon-induced disruption will depend on how long restrictions remain in place, the number of vessels affected and how quickly terminals can clear backlogs once operations resume. And, if the threat of a typhoon was not enough, Maersk noted it was likely intermittent delays would continue along its East Asia network, adding that it was “monitoring conditions and contacting customers whose shipments might be affected” to discuss available options.

items.title: Intra-Asia rates soften as congestion at major ports begins to ease
items.original_title: Intra-Asia rates soften as congestion at major ports begins to ease
items.summary: Intra-Asia rates are receding from their recent highs as bottlenecks in major Chinese and other Asian ports subside. On 15 October, Drewry’s Intra-Asia Container Index dipped 3%, to an average of $1,453 per 40ft. Rates from Shanghai to key destinations, including Busan in South Korea, Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam, and Jawaharlal Nehru Port in India, softened as vessel waiting times declined. Rates from Shanghai to Nhava Sheva fell 11%, to $3,370 per 40ft, while those to Busan declined 8% to $1,000 per 40ft. Shanghai–Singapore rates dropped 7% to $1,973 per 40ft. Port congestion eased during Week 41, with average vessel waiting times at Busan at 23 hours, from 26 hours a week earlier. At Jawaharlal Nehru Port, waiting times declined to 24 hours, from 42, and Singapore recorded a decrease to 34 hours, from 50. However, the deteriorating situation in the Middle East continued to support freight rates on the Shanghai–Jebel Ali route, which remained elevated, at $8,416 per 40ft. Freight rates from Busan to Shanghai rose 4%, to $159 per 40ft, with Yokohama to Shanghai up 4%, to $120 per 40ft.

items.title: Eastern Pacific takes wraps off first ammonia dual-fuel VLAC
items.original_title: Eastern Pacific takes wraps off first ammonia dual-fuel VLAC
items.summary: Idan Ofer’s Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) has named its first ammonia dual-fuel very large ammonia carrier (VLAC) at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in South Korea, bringing the 93,000 cu m vessel closer to its commercial debut. The Singapore-based owner christened the vessel Terra Clove at the Ulsan yard, with delivery scheduled for November following sea trials. The newbuilding is the first ammonia dual-fuel commercial vessel to be registered under the Singapore flag and the first of two such ships being built by HD Hyundai for EPS. Designed to transport ammonia as cargo and burn it as propulsion fuel, the 230 m long vessel is fitted with Everllence’s 6G60ME-LGIA two-stroke engine, which completed factory acceptance testing in April and passed type approval testing in June. The two will collaborate on alternative fuels, dual-fuel propulsion, energy efficiency and ammonia safety, including research into methane and ammonia emissions. The development adds to EPS’s expanding position in the ammonia carrier market. Earlier this year, the company returned to China’s Jiangnan Shipyard for two additional 90,000 cu m VLACs, scheduled for delivery in the first half of 2028. Those vessels will feature LPG dual-fuel propulsion, rather than engines designed to burn ammonia.

items.original_title: Copper Prices Slide to 5-Week Low
items.summary: Copper futures fell toward $6.40 per pound on Thursday, reaching their lowest level in five weeks as a global selloff in artificial intelligence stocks dampened sentiment toward the metal. Copper remains a key beneficiary of AI expansion due to its essential role in data centers and power infrastructure. Prices also faced pressure this week amid speculation that the US may abandon proposed tariffs on refined copper imports. Markets increasingly expect the Trump administration to reconsider the measures ahead of the midterm elections, as global supplies tighten and inflationary pressures persist. Copper prices hit record highs last month after traders redirected shipments to US warehouses in anticipation of potential tariffs, reducing availability in other major markets. Meanwhile, supply concerns remain elevated amid the risk of labor strikes at major mining companies due to ongoing labor disputes. Source: Trading Economics

items.title: Panama Canal Reports Growth in Transits and Tonnage in Fiscal Year 2026
items.original_title: Panama Canal Reports Growth in Transits and Tonnage in Fiscal Year 2026
items.summary: The Panama Canal recorded growth in both vessel transits and tonnage in Fiscal Year 2026, which ran from October 2025 through September 2026. The Panama Canal presented its FY2026 results today during a call hosted by Anna Milne, Managing Director of Emerging Markets Corporate Research at Bank of America Merrill Lynch. Panama Canal Administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta, Deputy Administrator Miguel Lorenzo, and Vice President of Finance Juan Mojica discussed the canal’s water management strategy and progress on initiatives under its Vision 2025–2035, including the Río Indio Lake Project. The Panama Canal handled 13,951 transits in FY2026, up 4.1% from 13,404 in FY2025. Tonnage reached 521 million Panama Canal Universal Measurement System (PC/UMS) tons, an increase of 6.5% from 489.2 million PC/UMS tons the previous fiscal year. “Far from restricting trade flows, the Panama Canal facilitates international maritime trade by providing its customers with a reliable and safe route,” Administrator Espino de Marotta said during the call. Results from FY2026 also highlight the performance and dedication of the canal’s workforce and its ability to deliver strong results in a complex global environment.

items.title: Gulf producers stand to gain as China replaces Iranian loss
items.original_title: Gulf producers stand to gain as China replaces Iranian loss
items.summary: China’s non-Iranian Middle Eastern crude arrivals are set to reach their highest level since the war began, despite VLCC tightness and Hormuz ship-to-ship (STS) bottlenecks delaying cargo deliveries. As Iranian supplies dwindle, Gulf producers — particularly Saudi Arabia and Iraq — are well positioned to capture more of China’s crude demand. Meanwhile, Beijing’s fuel export policy remains closely tied to Middle Eastern crude availability, with tighter quotas limiting the scope for China to expand seaborne product exports in Q4. China’s Middle Eastern crude arrivals recover despite Hormuz bottlenecks Recent Middle Eastern crude arrivals into China have come entirely from the Middle East Gulf (MEG), rather than the Red Sea or Mediterranean, as China-bound loadings have shifted fully back to the MEG since late July. Replacing Iranian crude is critical to China’s fuel balance China’s total seaborne crude imports are expected to strengthen to around 8.8mbd in October, up from a Q3 average of 7.5mbd, although still well below the 2025 average of 10.6mbd. China imported nearly 1.4mbd of Iranian crude and condensate on average through 2025 and the first half of 2026. Resilient Hormuz transit and ongoing STS activity point to the potential for another strong month, as additional cargoes may signal China once STS transfers are completed.

items.summary: European natural gas prices held above €87/MWh on Thursday, hovering just below their highest levels in nearly four years, as constrained Middle Eastern LNG supplies and low storage levels heightened concerns over winter availability. Continued attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have raised doubts about how quickly regional gas shipments can recover, with LNG exports running around 80% below year-ago levels. Alternative suppliers have limited capacity to rapidly compensate for the loss of Gulf exports, increasing the risk of tight market conditions persisting into 2027. European gas storage stood at 74.58% capacity as of October 21, the lowest level for this time of year since records began in 2009, leaving the region with a limited supply buffer as winter approaches. items.title: Shipowners warn fuel transition could slip beyond 2030 as methanol demand remains uncertain
items.original_title: Shipowners warn fuel transition could slip beyond 2030 as methanol demand remains uncertain
items.summary: Regulatory uncertainty and limited shipbuilding capacity could delay the wider adoption of alternative marine fuels beyond 2030, shipping executives said, while orders for methanol-capable vessels may not translate directly into demand for the fuel. Speaking at the tenth Annual International Shipping Forum in Pudong, Shanghai, Safe Bulkers president Loukas Barmparis said ambiguity over decarbonization rules and heavily booked shipyards would delay the transition, pointing to a period after 2030 toward 2035. He described maritime decarbonization as “somehow stalled,” with progress currently concentrated on improving the energy efficiency of existing ships and newer vessel designs. “That’s something shipowners can very well do, very much in their control.” Orders may not translate to demand Meanwhile, dual-fuel vessels, such as new methanol-capable orders, may not ensure that a new ship will operate entirely on methanol, Bocchetti added. Fuel costs and logistics would determine actual use, while producers need demand from more than a handful of owners to support supply growth. DNV said more than 294 methanol-capable vessels were on order globally as of August 2026, making methanol the second-largest alternative-fuel technology in the orderbook after LNG, based on its latest Maritime Forecast to 2050, released in August. The forecast puts shipping’s low-greenhouse-gas fuel demand, covering low-GHG fuels collectively, at 4 million–22 million mt of oil equivalent in 2030, depending on regulatory outcomes.

items.title: Goldman Sachs sees crude freight rates surge to $20 per barrel
items.original_title: Goldman Sachs sees crude freight rates surge to $20 per barrel
items.summary: Global average crude freight rates have climbed above $20 per barrel from $3 per barrel a year ago, according to Goldman Sachs analysis released Wednesday. The increase initially started in the very large crude carrier segment and on Middle Eastern routes before spreading to all major crude trading routes, particularly affecting long-haul voyages. The bank identified five main drivers behind the $20 per barrel year-over-year surge in the average global crude freight rate. A war risk premium in Hormuz accounts for $7 per barrel, representing one-third of the increase in the global average crude freight rate. Inefficient tanker allocation and increased tanker redirections account for $3 per barrel, and the blockage of the Iranian fleet adds $2 per barrel by boosting demand for non-sanctioned crude tankers. Goldman Sachs expects these factors to continue supporting global freight rates as long as the conflict in the Middle East persists. The bank noted that high freight rates may reduce refiners’ overall demand for crude or shift it towards more closely located crude suppliers. Goldman Sachs sees high freight rates widening crude price differentials by changing crude trading patterns and supporting refined product prices while suppressing refiners’ net margins.

items.original_title: MMI Daily Iron Ore Index Report October 22 2026
items.summary: Today’s decline extended across domestic futures, port spot and seaborne markets, testing the earlier recovery again. DCE most-traded closed at 669.0 yuan/mt, down 1.83%, and all eight Qingdao products fell 9 yuan/wmt. The seaborne 61% index eased to USD 88.60/dmt and the 65% to 106.25, with all 12 brands lower. Surveyed daily hot metal output was 2.3584 million mt on Oct 21, up 6,400 mt from the previous period, alongside a modest increase in the blast furnace operating rate. Higher output is not the same as discretionary restocking: mill stocks, end-user orders and margins still shape purchasing schedules. Lower arrival flows may ease future supply pressure, but existing inventory still requires transactions and collections for absorption. The near-term question is whether lower prices generate persistent demand. Buying restricted to current consumption could leave prices soft and range-bound, while sustained trading and restocking would help translate production improvement into price support. Higher freight adds a cost variable, making selling prices, procurement contracts and exchange rates important to margin assessment rather than extrapolating one day’s production or price move into a trend reversal.

items.summary: Luxembourg-incorporated shipowner Seven Yield has secured five-year time charters for two LNG-powered car carriers with a major Chinese automobile manufacturer, extending employment for the vessels into the next decade. The agreements cover the 2020-built, 7,500 ceu sisterships Siem Confucius and Siem Aristotle , with the new charters scheduled to start in 2027 and 2028, respectively. Seven Yield has not identified the carmaker or disclosed the charter rates and overall contract value. The ships entered service in 2020 under arrangements involving Seven Yield, Siem Car Carriers and Volkswagen, replacing conventionally fuelled vessels on the manufacturer’s transatlantic logistics network. The latest charter agreements will give Seven Yield another five years of contracted employment for each ship. The company operates a diversified maritime leasing portfolio of 18 vessels, including eight car carriers, six roros, two bulk carriers and two other vessels. Its most recent published portfolio figures from September showed approximately $700m in contracted revenue backlog. The fixtures come as Chinese vehicle manufacturers increasingly seek greater control over their overseas shipping arrangements.BYD, in particular, has been building up dedicated car-carrier capacity to support its international expansion. The company recently confirmed that it had secured another 10 vessels, although their contractual arrangements have not been fully disclosed.

items.title: Maersk Tankers lines up EU backing for four VLAC ammonia conversions
items.original_title: Maersk Tankers lines up EU backing for four VLAC ammonia conversions
items.summary: Danish shipowner Maersk Tankers has moved closer to converting four very large ammonia carriers to run on the cargo they transport after its retrofit proposal was selected for support under the European Union’s Innovation Fund. The project, known as RIPPLE, involves installing dual-fuel, two-stroke ammonia engines on four vessels in the company’s expanding gas carrier fleet. The European Commission has invited the project to begin grant agreement preparations, although the amount of funding has not yet been finalised. Crucially, Maersk Tankers said any decision to proceed would depend on securing commercial commitments from customers. The proposed conversions would allow the vessels to use ammonia as propulsion fuel rather than relying solely on conventional marine fuels. The project is expected to avoid more than 1.2m tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions over ten years, assuming the conversions and planned operations go ahead. Maersk Tankers is building up a fleet of ten 93,000 cu m VLACs at South Korea’s HD Hyundai Samho. The vessels were specified with the possibility of converting to ammonia propulsion, although installation of the necessary engines has always depended on commercial and regulatory conditions. The Commission selected 77 projects under its latest Innovation Fund round, with final grant agreements expected to be determined during the first quarter of 2027.

items.title: China’s green corridor push hits commercial reality check
items.original_title: China’s green corridor push hits commercial reality check
items.summary: China has emerged as a major player in the global green shipping corridor movement, with at least 21 initiatives linked to the country, although most remain in their early stages and only one has progressed towards commercial operation, according to a new report from the Global Maritime Forum. The study, released during the organisation’s annual summit in Shanghai, shows that China accounts for nearly a fifth of the world’s green shipping corridor initiatives, having added ten new projects in 2025 alone. However, of the 21 initiatives identified by the end of June this year, 12 were still at the initiation stage, five were exploring feasibility, three had reached preparation and just one had entered the realisation phase. Chinese projects under development are targeting annual production of 30m tonnes of green methanol and 15m tonnes of green ammonia by the early 2030s, although the report cautions that not all announced capacity will reach the investment stage. The report found that green methanol and ammonia still cost two to three times as much as conventional marine fuels, even with China’s competitive production costs. The findings come as China begins turning some of its green shipping plans into commercial operations.

items.summary: London-listed Tufton Assets has secured higher-paying employment across its tanker and dry bulk fleet, with two MR product tankers extended for another year and further charter renewals in the pipeline. The charterer of the 2016-built Catherine Grace and Madelyn Grace exercised options in October to extend both vessels’ employment by 12 months at rates above their previous firm periods, the ship investment company said in its third-quarter update. The latest extensions add to a string of chartering moves during the third quarter, when the company secured improved terms for three vessels and fixed two handysize bulkers on new arrangements. The company also secured more than $15,000 per day for handysize bulker Amilyn and converted the index-linked charter of sistership Staithes to a fixed $19,000 per day for the fourth quarter. The wider chartering activity comes as Tufton benefits from stronger tanker and dry bulk markets. The company said disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with reduced availability of compliant tankers, had helped lift freight rates, while grain, iron ore and bauxite demand supported dry bulk earnings. Tufton’s fleet currently comprises 21 vessels, including eight product tankers, two chemical tankers and 11 bulk carriers. Earlier this year, Tufton expanded its dry bulk exposure with the $33m acquisition of two Japanese-built handysize vessels, which entered the fleet in April.

items.title: China adds new state-owned shipbuilding player in Guangzhou
items.original_title: China adds new state-owned shipbuilding player in Guangzhou
items.summary: Guangzhou has formally launched a new state-owned maritime industrial group as the southern Chinese shipbuilding hub looks to expand its manufacturing capacity and bring more of the industry’s supply chain under local ownership. Guangzhou Marine Equipment Group, established with registered capital of RMB2bn ($300m), has begun operations following an unveiling ceremony this week. The company is wholly owned by Guangzhou Industrial Investment Holding Group, with the municipal government as its ultimate shareholder. The new group has joined forces with China State Shipbuilding Corporation-controlled Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) and Huangpu Wenchong, as well as COSCO Shipping Specialized Carriers, marine technology company SEAHI Robotics and the Guangzhou branch of China Classification Society. Guangzhou Marine Equipment Group has set a target of reaching about $3.9bn in business scale by 2030, according to local government-backed reporting. Guangzhou is developing a new marine equipment manufacturing and shipbuilding base at Longxue North in Nansha, involving investment of approximately $1.09bn. Guangzhou Marine Equipment Group is also lined up to participate in the development, although its financial commitment has not been disclosed. GSI recently signed an agreement with China Railway Shanhaiguan Bridge Group to outsource hull block production, adding manufacturing capacity outside the traditional shipbuilding supply chain.

items.title: A new world order emerges in LNG shipping
items.original_title: A new world order emerges in LNG shipping
items.summary: The world’s LNG trading map is undergoing its biggest upheaval in years, with the near-paralysis of Gulf exports redirecting cargoes across oceans, forcing Asian buyers towards alternative suppliers and pushing European gas prices to their highest levels since 2022. While gas prices approach $30 per million British thermal units, LNG carrier spot earnings remain remarkably weak, with the Baltic Exchange assessing the US Gulf-Europe route at just $21,200 a day last week. Vortexa recorded just five confirmed LNG carrier transits of Hormuz last week, against a four-week average of 12. The Al Kharsaah, carrying Qatari LNG towards Poland via the Red Sea, came under fire from a small boat in the Gulf of Aden on October 17. S&P Global data shows Europe and Turkey received 76 of the 143 US LNG cargoes delivered in September. Indian LNG imports were 7% higher year-on-year in September despite elevated prices. Japan’s major utilities held 2.64m tonnes of LNG in inventory earlier this month, their highest stockpile since December 2023. A cold winter would intensify competition for Atlantic cargoes, particularly as the EU prepares to end remaining Russian LNG imports from January 1. LNG Canada’s September investment decision to double capacity to 28m tonnes annually reinforces the emergence of a Pacific export corridor offering Asian customers shorter voyages than traditional Atlantic suppliers.

items.title: US sanctions net widens to shipping agents and lawyers
items.original_title: US sanctions net widens to shipping agents and lawyers
items.summary: Washington has widened its crackdown on Iran’s shadow fleet, sanctioning a Greek-Panamanian law firm, shipping agents in Singapore and Dubai, and nine vessels in a move targeting the service providers behind Tehran’s commodity exports. Announcing the measures yesterday, the US Treasury said Karnakis and Karnakis had established corporate structures for shipowners moving hundreds of millions of dollars worth of Iranian oil, LPG, petrochemicals and steel. Five individuals linked to the practice have also been designated. The group’s other designated ships are Destiny, Flamingo 1, Harmony and Prince. Singapore-based Amigoz Singapore was sanctioned for acting as port agent for a shipment of Iranian light crude and providing bunkering services to the shadow fleet tanker Zixuan. Treasury also linked the company to networks associated with Iranian shipping figure Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani. Dubai-based Whales Shipping Line was designated for supporting Amigoz and acting as shipping agent for a company accused of arranging Iranian petrochemical purchases. The action forms part of Operation Economic Outcast, launched in August, which is intended to cut Iran off from international financial and shipping services. US authorities are simultaneously investigating a Greek bank’s possible links with Iran, underlining the campaign’s extension from ships and owners to lawyers, agents and financiers.

items.title: Iran claims seven vessels hit in new wave of Hormuz attacks
items.original_title: Iran claims seven vessels hit in new wave of Hormuz attacks
items.summary: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed today that seven vessels had been attacked or struck mines across the Persian Gulf over the past 24 hours, including four conducting ship-to-ship oil transfers. The IRGC Navy said it had tracked four vessels that previously used a route Tehran considers unauthorised, before striking them simultaneously as they transferred oil in the north-central Gulf. It claimed all four were burning. Three more vessels reportedly struck naval mines west of the Strait of Hormuz overnight, catching fire and becoming immobilised. Iran has supplied no vessel names, flag details, casualty figures or independently verifiable evidence supporting the seven claims. The latest UK Maritime Trade Operations warning concerns an incident early yesterday, when an unidentified tanker was struck by a projectile 11 nautical miles west of Bukha, Oman. Another tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile 30 nautical miles southeast of Iraq’s Al Faw on Tuesday evening. The organisation identified the tanker Al Dasma as having suffered a second attack on October 20. Tehran has meanwhile warned Washington that continued attempts to move vessels through routes it considers prohibited could provoke attacks against American military bases across the region.

items.title: DOF secures deepwater installation job in Africa
items.original_title: DOF secures deepwater installation job in Africa
items.summary: Norwegian offshore vessel owner DOF has secured a subsea installation contract worth for deepwater field developments offshore Africa. The Skandi Acergy vessel will execute the contract, with operations scheduled to begin early in the first quarter of 2027 and expected to last around 100 days. Under the agreement, DOF will provide project management, engineering, logistics, and offshore execution services, including transporting and installing various subsea production systems (SPS). DOF’s Norwegian and UK engineering teams will support the offshore execution phase. The company’s Atlantic region teams in Bergen and Aberdeen will handle engineering, planning, and project management activities, while the offshore installation work will be carried out during a dedicated campaign. DOF did not disclose the client’s identity or the precise contract value. However, the company classified the deal as significant, a category covering contracts valued between $15m and $25m. “Deepwater SPS installation is a critical phase in the development of any field and requires careful planning, strong engineering and proven execution capability,” said Mons Aase, DOF chief executive.

Integrated into HarborLab’s DA evaluation page, DEX reviews Proforma and Final Disbursement Accounts for commercial port calls. It brings HarborLab’s existing AI tools for DA evaluation together in one guided flow, drawing on the same tariff data and historical Final DAs that already underpin the platform’s port cost checks. Operators using HarborLab’s platform recover an average of $700 per port call, with savings that compound significantly across larger fleets. DEX is designed for DA teams on commercial port calls at ship owners, commercial traders, and charterers. Teams can book a live demo from today, and HarborLab is onboarding customers in phases, starting this year.

items.title: India’s crude import bill surges 46% to $90.6 billion in April-September on elevated oil prices
items.original_title: India’s crude import bill surges 46% to $90.6 billion in April-September on elevated oil prices
items.summary: India’s crude oil import bill surged 46.3 percent to $90.6 billion during April–September on higher global prices even as volumes remained largely flat from the year-ago period, data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) shows. On October 21, Brent crude was trading higher at around $110 a barrel on supply concerns, with traders wary of Red Sea shipping risks and threats to oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia from Iran-backed Houthi rebels. India imported 122.7 million tonnes of oil during April-September, largely unchanged from 121.8 million tonnes in the previous year. In September, the import bill jumped 46.6 percent to $15.4 billion, while volumes were up 6.8 percent at 21.7 million tonnes. The average price of Indian crude basket has risen to $121.25 a barrel in October from $65.08 from last year. The bigger risk for India is not the availability of crude but persistently higher landed prices that can inflate the import bill, widen the current account deficit and weigh on the broader economy, analysts say. The country imports around 1.8-2 billion barrels of crude annually and every $1-a-barrel increase in price raises the country’s import bill by up to $2 billion a year.

items.title: US sanctions relief could lift tanker rates in Russia, inject capacity to Gulf shuttles: analysts
items.original_title: US sanctions relief could lift tanker rates in Russia, inject capacity to Gulf shuttles: analysts
items.summary: US sanctions relief on shadow-fleet tankers could redirect ships from Russian oil trades toward the Middle East, potentially raising Russian freight costs while easing some of the tanker shortages around the Strait of Hormuz, shipping analysts said. In recent public remarks, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the US will allow legitimate businesses to acquire sanctioned tankers for non-sanctioned trades to reduce shipping costs, though Washington has yet to announce a detailed relief proposal. The number of oil and LPG tankers sanctioned by Western authorities amounted to 1,226 as of the end of August, with the US having been particularly targeting VLCCs, according to S&P Global Energy Horizons research. But BRS Shipbrokers estimated only 148 tankers in deepsea trades, equivalent to 2.5% of the global total by vessel count, were sanctioned solely by the US Office of Foreign Assets Control as of Oct. That means sanctions relief could redistribute existing tanker capacity rather than simply release large amounts of idle tonnage. BRS said some shadow fleet operators could also use sanctions relief to sell their tankers into the current strong secondhand market, provided Washington gave buyers sufficient assurances that they would not face sanctions risks over the vessels’ previous trading histories.

items.title: Panama Canal Traffic and Tonnage Rise Despite El Niño Challenges
items.original_title: Panama Canal Traffic and Tonnage Rise Despite El Niño Challenges
items.summary: The Panama Canal reported growth in vessel traffic, tonnage and revenue in fiscal year 2026, as stronger demand from energy carriers and containerships helped lift volumes despite ongoing concerns over water availability. The waterway handled 13,951 vessel transits during the fiscal year ended September 30, up 4.1% from 13,404 the previous year, according to results released Wednesday by the Panama Canal Authority. Total tonnage climbed 6.5% to 521 million Panama Canal Universal Measurement System (PC/UMS) tons, compared with 489.2 million tons in fiscal 2025. The results come as the canal continues to balance growing shipping demand with water conservation measures designed to protect operations during the developing El Niño weather pattern. Despite the challenges, the canal maintained a maximum authorized draft of 50 feet throughout the fiscal year’s dry season, providing relatively stable operating conditions for shipping customers. “Far from restricting trade flows, the Panama Canal facilitates international maritime trade by providing its customers with a reliable and safe route,” Panama Canal Administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta said during a conference call hosted by Bank of America Merrill Lynch. The canal has warned that a continuing water deficit could require further operational adjustments, particularly if El Niño conditions intensify.

Army Photo By Chris Servello (OpEd) After years of testing and debating how unmanned surface vessels fit into the fleet, the Navy is starting to show what these systems can do. And senior leaders in the Department of War and Department of the Navy are talking less about the promise of unmanned warfare and more about making it part of everyday operations. The Navy needs to decide how it intends to fight with unmanned vessels, what missions they’ll perform and how it will organize, train and sustain the forces operating them. It’s time to move from proving these systems work to making them a routine part of fleet operations. For years, Task Force 59 worked with industry and regional partners to introduce unmanned systems into one of the world’s toughest maritime environments. The deployment of the Leidos-built Seahawk medium unmanned surface vessel with the Theodore Roosevelt strike group is another important step.

items.title: Follow the money or follow the flag? Politics clouds port investment
items.original_title: Follow the money or follow the flag? Politics clouds port investment
items.summary: In the seven years since TOC Americas last took place in Cartagena, global laden container volumes have slipped about 10% below where they would have been without the multiple disruptions that have hit the industry since 2018, according to Dinesh Sharma, director at Drewry Maritime Advisors. Sharma’s research measured growth from 2018 against forecasts of where the industry had imagined it would be today last time they met in Cartagena. Predicting the future, he said, was and is not easy. Transshipment hubs grew by about 6% a year on average over that period, against roughly 3% for gateway ports and 1.5% for the underlying economies they serve. The inefficiency, he said, is no longer contained at the big transshipment hubs: it is flowing through to gateways too, leaving Latin America’s overall throughput an estimated 2–3% below his 2018 projection. Washington’s growing interest in the region’s infrastructure raises the odds that port decisions get caught up in politics rather than commercial logic.

items.original_title: Imported iron ore margins narrow to 9.62 yuan/mt on higher brand premiums
items.summary: The average margin on imported iron ore narrowed to 9.62 yuan/mt today from 11.52 yuan/mt, driven mainly by higher premiums on some brands alongside weaker spot prices. On the supply side, BHP’s Q1 FY2027 report showed Western Australia Iron Ore (WAIO) production at 71.91 million mt on a 100% basis, up 2.4% year-on-year, with full-year guidance unchanged at 286-298 million mt. Lump accounted for 27.9% of WAIO sales, the lowest in five quarters. On freight, SMM data showed the Australia-China route up 0.49/mt week-on-week at 11.91/mt on 19 October, while the Brazil-China route eased to 30.46/mt. The net change in CFR costs was limited. On the demand side, mills remain lossmaking and restocking is still on a just-in-need basis, with port inventories building again last week. items.title: European gas rallies on Persian gulf disruption pressure; Hot UK Inflation dents
items.original_title: European gas rallies on Persian gulf disruption pressure; Hot UK Inflation dents
items.summary: European wholesale natural gas prices surged on Wednesday, with both major regional benchmarks gaining over 3% as hotter-than-expected British inflation data and ongoing Persian Gulf energy disruptions heightened anxieties over winter fuel adequacy. The benchmark Dutch TTF front-month contract rose 3.1% to trade at 87.95 euros per megawatt-hour (MWh). In Great Britain, the equivalent NBP natural gas futures contract similarly advanced 3.2% to 216.57 pence per therm, with both contracts holding near their highest levels since late 2022. Wednesday’s gas rally coincided with fresh macroeconomic data highlighting the acute economic toll of elevated energy import costs on the British economy. Official figures showed Britain’s annual consumer price inflation accelerated to 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August and exceeding market consensus. Lacking large-scale long-term gas storage infrastructure, the UK relies heavily on real-time imports of pipeline gas and Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) cargoes to meet domestic power generation and home heating needs. The European benchmark remains up approximately 210% year-to-date. With maritime strikes and transit friction restricting LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz – keeping Middle Eastern deliveries to Europe nearly 80% below year-ago levels—European utilities face intense competition from Asian buyers for uncommitted Atlantic basin cargoes.

items.title: IEA: Gulf Oil Shipping Costs Top $37 Per Barrel, Five Times Pre-War Levels
items.original_title: IEA: Gulf Oil Shipping Costs Top $37 Per Barrel, Five Times Pre-War Levels
items.summary: FILE PHOTO: Crude oil tanker Odessa, carrying UAE crude after passing through the Strait of Hormuz with its Automatic Identification System transponder turned off, navigates the waters at Daesan port, where it is expected to discharge crude oil, in Seosan, South Korea, May 8, 2026. REUTERS/Kim Soo-hyeon/File Photo The cost of shipping crude oil from the Middle East Gulf to Asia has surged to more than $37 per barrel, over five times prewar levels, as an increasingly complex shipping network keeps oil flowing despite escalating Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the International Energy Agency. The extraordinary increase comes as Persian Gulf oil exports have actually surpassed prewar levels, highlighting the steep price of maintaining energy flows through one of the world’s most dangerous shipping corridors. According to The Wall Street Journal , citing vessel-tracking data from Kpler, Middle East oil shipments averaged more than 24 million barrels per day in the week ending October 18, exceeding the prewar average of 23.3 million barrels per day. In a separate analysis published Wednesday , the IEA said tanker rates reached historic highs in September and continued climbing into October, with the cost of transporting crude from the Middle East Gulf to Asia exceeding $37 per barrel by mid-month.

items.title: Nearly two-thirds of Far East-Europe capacity now back to Suez Canal
items.original_title: Nearly two-thirds of Far East-Europe capacity now back to Suez Canal
items.summary: Some 63% of the ocean capacity deployed between the Far East and Europe has returned to the Red Sea, following three years of detours, but some operators are hedging against renewed disruption by maintaining several Cape of Good Hope routes. Having surveyed the 10 largest carrier networks over the past month, Alphaliner found vessels on 24 of the 46 direct Far East–Europe services were transiting the Red Sea, accounting for 70% of deployed capacity on Far East-Mediterranean routes. On the Far East-North Europe trades, the number was a little lower, 58%, with containers moving between the Far East and Europe via Suez now topping 5.5m teu, of the possible 8.7m teu available to the trades – CMA CGM alone accounting for 1.3m of this. However, the Suez return remains something of a mixed bag, with multiple services opting to transit the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait on outbound routes to Europe, but electing to sail around the Cape on return journeys. Of the 10 carriers surveyed, five confirmed they had resumed Red Sea transits over the past month, that number set to climb to eight after Premier Alliance partners HMM, ONE, and Yang Ming all announced a return to the waterway.

items.title: Airfreight in Africa booming, thanks to disrupted ocean shipping services
items.original_title: Airfreight in Africa booming, thanks to disrupted ocean shipping services
items.summary: African airfreight is seeing something of a boom from the disruption in ocean freight across the Middle East, but forwarders remain sceptical as to whether it will provoke long-term structural benefits. Hennie Heymans, CEO of DHL Express’s Sub-Saharan Africa operations, told The Loadstar the shift from ocean services had left airfreight the only viable alternative to keep goods moving. “When people run into trouble from a seafreight point of view, the alternative becomes airfreight, becomes express, and that is a notable trend across African airfreight’s growth momentum at the moment,” Mr Heymans told The Loadstar . For DHL Express, the timing has proved particularly useful, coinciding with the launch of its Heavy Weight Express service, allowing its customers to ship consignments of up to 3,000kg, with individual pieces of up to 1,000kg. Expanding beyond smaller parcels, the new service is designed for automotive, energy, engineering, machinery, and pharmaceuticals, Mr Heymans noting the significant cost implications delays place on these sectors. “The timing of the launch worked out quite well, which makes the conversation a lot easier, and a lot more comfortable for those customers seeking these sorts of services,” explained Mr Heymans.

items.summary: AG Seville Shipyard has won the competition to continue operating the ship repair facilities at Spain’s Port of Seville, clearing an important hurdle for a proposed €10m ($11.2m) investment programme. Seville Port Authority’s board approved the selection of AG Seville Shipyard on October 20, allowing the company to retain its position at the former Astilleros del Guadalquivir facilities. The operator’s existing concession expires in December.The new concession will cover approximately 22,000 sq m of port land and infrastructure, including the dry dock, the southern section of the Muelle de Armamento and a disused slipway. The concession can run for up to 25 years, although final administrative approval is still required before the new agreement becomes effective. AG Seville Shipyard faced competition for the facilities from Spanish maritime group Boluda, which had also expressed interest in taking over the site. The successful operator has controlled part of the former Seville shipyard since 2017, developing ship repair and maintenance operations at facilities that had suffered years of decline following the collapse of the former public shipyard. The larger €10m programme is AG Seville’s proposed investment plan, rather than an amount separately confirmed as contractually committed in the latest announcement. The port authority also approved an additional €4.2m ($4.7m) for improvements to Seville’s port free zone.

items.summary: Revised rules on the transport of live animals by sea are being negotiated in the EU. EU Member States are making progress in negotiations on new rules for the transport of live animals. The aim should be to improve animal welfare, prevent accidents, ensure fair competition and help raise international standards for the transport of live animals. Three years on, the European Commission’s proposal for new rules on the transport of live animals is still under consideration in the European Parliament and the Council. This will improve animal welfare and increase safety for the seafarers working on board Nina Porst, Executive Director of Sustainable Ships and Skills at Danish Shipping A 2025 study by the European Parliamentary Research Service highlights, among other things, persistent problems that may affect animal welfare. A central demand is that all ships authorised to transport live animals from the EU should meet high and comparable standards for both the vessel itself and its arrangements for carrying animals, regardless of the flag they fly. This will improve animal welfare and increase safety for the seafarers working on board.

items.summary: US natural gas prices edged up to $2.97 per MMBtu on Wednesday, attempting to rebound from a four-week low hit in the previous session, as improving LNG export activity and reduced output partly offset weak demand due to mild weather. Average gas flows to the nine major US LNG export terminals rose to 18.2 bcfd so far in October from 17.9 bcfd in September. Meanwhile, gas production across the Lower 48 states averaged 111.4 bcfd this month, down from record highs of 113.3 bcfd in August and September. The storage surplus also continued to shrink, with inventories as of October 9 standing 3.9% below year-earlier levels and just 1.3% above the five-year average. Meanwhile, mild temperatures are expected to persist through late October, curbing both heating and cooling demand, while expectations of a “Super El Niño” further weigh on the winter demand outlook. items.original_title: Key auto shipping hub scores green milestone
items.summary: A roll-on/roll-off (Ro-Ro) vessel loaded with over 4,000 new energy vehicles for export to Europe departed on Friday from an automobile terminal in Guangzhou, capital of Guangdong province, after completing its refueling with 2,300 metric tons of methanol. This marked the first green methanol refueling operation for a Ro-Ro vessel in Guangdong, signifying a key step forward for the Nansha Automobile Terminal of Guangzhou Port in upgrading its green and low-carbon shipping services and in building a global export channel for domestic automobiles. The operation helps establish the Guangzhou-based port as the world’s first port to achieve green methanol refueling operations for three types of clean energy-powered vessels — container ships, bulk carriers and automobile Ro-Ro ships, according to the port operator. The CM Guangzhou vessel, with a design capacity of 7,800 standard car units, is a new generation of large green Ro-Ro ships and the first methanol dual-fuel Ro-Ro ship to dock at the Nansha Automobile Terminal. items.title: Australian fund takes control of UK ports giant in £10bn deal
items.original_title: Australian fund takes control of UK ports giant in £10bn deal
items.summary: Australian infrastructure investor IFM Investors has agreed to acquire a controlling stake in Associated British Ports (ABP), Britain’s largest port operator, in a deal valuing the business at more than £10bn ($13.4bn). The transaction will see Canadian pension giants CPP Investments and OMERS sell their combined 63.88% stake in ABP to Global Infraco Haven Bidco, an indirect subsidiary of the IFM Global Infrastructure Fund. ABP confirmed the binding agreement in a London Stock Exchange announcement today. ABP operates 21 ports across Britain, including Southampton, Immingham and the Humber complex, handling around a quarter of the country’s seaborne trade. The deal brings an end to two decades of Canadian involvement in the port operator. OMERS was part of the consortium that took ABP private in 2006 for £2.8bn, while CPP Investments acquired its interest in 2015. IFM is owned by Australian and British pension funds and manages around $96bn in infrastructure assets globally. As Splash reported in August, the company is advancing a £500m development at Port Talbot in Wales to establish a major floating offshore wind manufacturing and assembly hub. Completion of the transaction remains subject to regulatory approvals and mandatory national security filings in the UK.
