items.title: Gestion Maritime makes ultramax debut with China order
items.original_title: Gestion Maritime makes ultramax debut with China order
items.summary: Monaco-based shipowner Gestion Maritime is moving into the ultramax segment with an order for three 64,000 dwt bulk carriers at China’s Nantong Xiangyu Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering. The Danilo Fumarola-led company has booked the trio for delivery between late 2028 and early 2029, expanding beyond its traditional panamax and kamsarmax fleet. The vessels are costing in the low $30m range apiece, putting the overall investment at more than $90m. Gestion Maritime currently operates six panamax and kamsarmax bulkers and has recently trimmed its fleet through asset sales. The latest investment will bring smaller and more modern tonnage into a portfolio built largely around Japanese- and South Korean-built ships. The company, whose roots date back to 1908 and the Corrado shipping family, has traditionally pursued an asset trading strategy, buying ships when values ease and disposing of tonnage during stronger markets. In 2019, it exited the product tanker sector by selling two 2015-built MR tankers to Hafnia interests for $31m each, returning its focus to dry bulk. The newbuilding deal adds another international owner to Nantong Xiangyu’s growing customer base. The Chinese shipbuilder marked the delivery of its 100th ultramax bulker in July and has continued to attract orders for the 63,500 to 64,000 dwt segment.

items.title: Danaos linked to $218m boxship order in China
items.original_title: Danaos linked to $218m boxship order in China
items.summary: Greek owner Danaos has been linked to another $218m newbuilding investment in China, with brokers placing the John Coustas-led company behind a pair of 9,200 teu boxships at Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding (SWS). According to Xclusiv Shipbrokers, the New York-listed owner has lined up two ships at the CSSC-controlled yard, priced at around $109m each, with delivery scheduled for 2029. Neither Danaos nor the shipbuilder has publicly confirmed the deal. Danaos has been a regular customer of Chinese shipyards in recent years, spreading orders across several builders as it renews and expands its containership fleet. The company already has seven 9,200 teu vessels under construction at other Chinese yards under contracts placed in 2024, with deliveries scheduled between 2027 and 2028. Its more recent investments include six 1,800 teu feeder vessels booked in November last year for delivery through 2029, followed by four 5,300 teu ships at CSSC Huangpu Wenchong, disclosed in February. Beyond containers, Danaos has also been building a sizeable position in dry bulk. The group had been exploring a separate Oslo listing for its 15-ship bulker business, including a potential minority stake sale, as part of efforts to unlock value from the fleet. The company had warned in its October 9 US securities filing that there was no guarantee the proposed listing would proceed.

items.title: Iraqi Line returns to Gulf container trade after 50 years
items.original_title: Iraqi Line returns to Gulf container trade after 50 years
items.summary: Iraq’s national shipping line is returning to scheduled container services in the Gulf after more than half a century, as the country seeks to rebuild maritime connections disrupted by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. According to Alphaliner, Iraqi Maritime Line is deploying the 902 teu Basrah on an eight-day shuttle linking Jebel Ali in Dubai with Umm Qasr, Iraq’s principal container gateway. The first sailing was scheduled to depart Jebel Ali yesterday, arriving in Umm Qasr two days later. Iraq’s transport ministry has described the initiative as the national carrier’s first regular Gulf operation since the mid-1960s. The relaunch comes as Iraqi container supply chains have been radically reshaped since the Hormuz shipping crisis erupted at the end of February. According to the Jordan Shipping Association, Aqaba handled 37,182 Iraq-bound transit containers during the first seven months of 2026, compared with just 3,599 during the corresponding period last year, a 933% increase. Hapag-Lloyd outlined a routing in July whereby containers are discharged at Khorfakkan, outside the Strait of Hormuz, before being trucked across the UAE to Sharjah or Jebel Ali and transferred onto third-party feeder vessels serving Iraq and other upper Gulf destinations.

items.title: Alpha Gas turns to China for VLGC pair
items.original_title: Alpha Gas turns to China for VLGC pair
items.summary: Greek shipowner Alpha Gas has moved into Chinese gas carrier construction, contracting two very large gas carriers at Hengli Heavy Industries as Anna Angelicoussis continues expanding her group’s fleet. Shipbroking and market sources have linked the Athens-based company to a pair of 88,000 cu m VLGCs capable of carrying ammonia, with the vessels scheduled for completion by 2029. The deal is understood to have been concluded in September, although details only emerged this week. items.title: Disconnected systems and AI hype are driving digital fatigue in shipping, warns OrbitMI
items.original_title: Disconnected systems and AI hype are driving digital fatigue in shipping, warns OrbitMI
items.summary: Shipping’s drive to digitalise risks slowing itself down as fragmented software, weak digital training and growing pressure to adopt artificial intelligence add complexity to operational and commercial decisions, according to OrbitMI. OrbitMI warns that the sector is entering a period of ‘digital fatigue’: growing scepticism and frustration when technology fails to deliver the promised simplicity or measurable productivity and performance improvement gains. After years of adding platforms and bolt-on applications, many teams still transfer data manually, work across separate dashboards and adapt established processes to generic interfaces. Research by Thetius and Marcura found that 82% of maritime professionals believe AI can improve efficiency and 81% are running pilots, but only 11% have the policies and governance needed to scale it. Two-thirds are concerned that overreliance on AI could erode human judgement, while 69% worry it may miss critical red flags in contracts or voyage planning. What users need are tools that are truly collaborative and are fully integrated in their workflows; always present but never intrusive. OrbitMI has been investing in this approach through the acquisition of AI specialist AuQub and maritime advisory and voyage optimisation business Gale Force, alongside the expansion of its maritime, product and technology leadership over the past 18 months.

items.title: MARPOWER Advances Key Technologies For Maritime Decarbonization
items.original_title: MARPOWER Advances Key Technologies For Maritime Decarbonization
items.summary: Maritime transport remains one of the most challenging sectors to decarbonize due to its high energy requirements, reliance on fossil fuels and the long operational lifetime of vessels. Against this backdrop, the EU-funded MARPOWER project (Efficient zero-emissions gas turbine POWER system for MARitime transport) is developing an advanced gas turbine-based energy conversion system for power generation and cogeneration on board ships, designed to operate with different sustainable fuels while improving overall efficiency. Two years into the project, the overall cycle and system design has been completed and detailed designs have been developed for its main components. Next steps: from individual technologies to maritime integration During the second half of the MARPOWER project, work will increasingly move towards further experimental testing, integration and validation under more representative conditions. The vessel studies will also be relevant to the potential integration of MARPOWER technologies into existing ships. Together with the vessel studies and technical validation, these activities will provide a broader basis for assessing the integration, safety, environmental performance and economic implications of the complete MARPOWER system. Technical advances from the project have already been presented at relevant international events, including ASME Turbo Expo and IFToMM Rotordynamics 2026.

Since 2023, MPA and CCS have worked with local research and industry partners on projects ranging from the use of B100 biofuel on harbour craft to the evaluation, testing and verification for smart ships. items.title: ESI 2.0 prompts ports to rethink environmental incentive schemes

items.summary: The updated Environmental Ship Index (ESI 2.0) is prompting ports to review how they reward better environmental performance, as the new methodology brings vessel scoring more closely in line with the environmental priorities shaping shipping today. Developed and owned by IAPH and administered globally by OceanScore, ESI provides ports with a framework for identifying and incentivising vessels that perform beyond environmental standards. ESI 2.0 updates this framework to reflect developments in regulation, technology and vessel operations, with increased recognition of areas including energy use, greenhouse gas performance, innovation and electrification. ESI 2.0 reflects the priorities of shipping today As shipping adopts cleaner fuels, electrification and new emissions-reduction technologies, the way environmental performance is measured also needs to evolve. Port of Aarhus turns the new methodology into action To understand the impact of ESI 2.0, OceanScore analysed Port of Aarhus’ 2025 vessel calls and how its existing incentive scheme would perform under the updated methodology. Keeping incentives effective as shipping evolves The Aarhus example demonstrates how ports can respond to changes in environmental performance measurement while keeping their incentive schemes relevant to the vessels they serve. “ESI 2.0 reflects how environmental priorities in shipping are evolving, and the Aarhus example shows how ports can translate that into practical incentives,” says Thomas Smith, Head of Cargo Solutions at OceanScore.

items.title: Ports Are Scaling AI. Here’s How to Make It Deliver
items.original_title: Ports Are Scaling AI. Here’s How to Make It Deliver
items.summary: Ports and terminals are no strangers to reinvention. Over the past 50 years, the industry has managed and adapted to the shift to containerization and ever-larger vessels, the move from paper manifests to electronic messaging and transactions, and the subsequent evolution to system-to-system integration with other parties in the shipping industries. But many port functions still run on clipboards, radio calls, or the gut instincts of a planner, who has watched the yard fill up and empty thousands of times. To assess how far the industry has come, BCG and TIC4.0 (an international nonprofit association of terminal operators and equipment and solution providers dedicated to the creation and promotion of digital standards for the cargo-handling industry) surveyed more than 100 leaders from across the container ports and terminals ecosystem. On average, those we surveyed are already using or exploring the top 16 of the 43 use cases we assessed, from extracting data from shipping documents (62%) to predicting when a crane or straddle carrier will fail (48%). Survey Demographics In August 2026, BCG and the Terminal Industry Committee 4.0 (TIC4.0) surveyed the port and terminal ecosystem on the adoption of AI and generative AI, to establish where the industry sees the opportunity and where it sees the risk.

items.title: HarborLab: Why shipping’s husbandry bills are still stuck in Excel
items.original_title: HarborLab: Why shipping’s husbandry bills are still stuck in Excel
items.summary: Shipping has spent years tightening voyage costs, bunker procurement and commercial port expenses, but one sizeable part of the bill remains comparatively untouched: husbandry. For Antonis Malaxianakis, founder and CEO of Athens-based port cost management platform HarborLab, that blind spot is particularly evident around bunkering, crew changes and stores, where technical departments can still be managing substantial sums through spreadsheets and email. “Husbandry calls have never carried the same profit and loss visibility as commercial port calls,” Malaxianakis tells Maritime CEO. For Malaxianakis, who worked in disbursement departments at Thenamaris and Product Shipping & Trading before founding HarborLab in 2020, the problem is less about a lack of attention from technical managers than the tools available to them. “One data point from our analysis makes the structural difference concrete: 75% of technical managers in APAC still manage husbandry bills in Excel today, compared with 40% in EMEA,” he says. The HarborLab-managed vessels generated $220,000 in savings compared with $70,000 on the other half. The system also picks up incorrect and duplicated charges, with the company then taking discrepancies back to agents in an effort to turn the finding into a credit. Behind that sits a database built from more than 40,000 port calls across over 1,400 ports.

items.title: South Korean Oil Tanker Takes Red Sea Detour
items.original_title: South Korean Oil Tanker Takes Red Sea Detour
items.summary: Amid the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a 19th South Korean oil tanker is transporting crude oil to South Korea via a Red Sea detour. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries announced that as of 10 a.m. on Oct. 20, one South Korean vessel had loaded crude oil at Yanbu Port in Saudi Arabia and was heading to South Korea after passing through the Suez Canal. This shipment is the 19th case of crude transport via the Red Sea since the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz began at the end of February. South Korean oil tankers had originally, from April, loaded crude at Yanbu Port on the Red Sea and entered South Korea via the southern Bab el-Mandeb Strait. As the closure of the Strait of Hormuz becomes prolonged, detour shipments to secure domestic energy supply are expected to continue for the time being. So far, a total of 19 South Korean vessels have transported crude oil through the Red Sea. The government said it is continuously monitoring the safe operation of vessels and managing the situation to prevent disruptions in crude oil supply.

items.title: Blue Autonomy opens an online academy for ship performance professionals
items.original_title: Blue Autonomy opens an online academy for ship performance professionals
items.summary: Blue Autonomy today opened the Blue Autonomy Academy (academy.blueautonomy.gr), an online school of 39 self-paced courses on vessel performance, maritime data and the regulations that price them. The courses are written for technical superintendents, performance analysts, technical and fleet managers, naval architects, marine engineers, and the chartering and operations staff who meet performance figures in charter parties. They are grouped into nine specialisations, from ship resistance and propulsion to hull and propeller performance under ISO 19030, speed trials under ISO 15016, bunker quantity and quality, speed and consumption claims, and the CII, EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime regimes. Each paid course ends in a graded examination and a certificate that anyone, an employer included, can verify online. “Behind every number a ship reports there is a calculation someone made,” said Christos Papandreou, CEO and Founder of Blue Autonomy. The Academy teaches the people who sign for these numbers to take them apart, check each input and stand behind the result, whether the question comes from a charterer, a verifier or the office.” Courses are bought once, with no subscription. Until 20 November 2026, the early-bird code ACADEMY25 gives 25% off every course and specialisation. Companies buying for several people receive a single offer and invoice on request. Source: Blue Autonomy

Wärtsilä 20 engines will power two new inland waterway pusher tugs being built by Estaleiro Rio Maguari for LHG Mining in Brazil. The Wärtsilä equipment is scheduled for delivery during 2027.

items.title: Trump’s Plan to Revive Sanctioned Tankers Faces Tough Sell
items.original_title: Trump’s Plan to Revive Sanctioned Tankers Faces Tough Sell
items.summary: Russia's shadow fleet vessels wait in the unofficial anchorage area in the Gulf of Finland near Vaindloo, Estonia April 10, 2026. REUTERS/Ints Kalnins (Bloomberg) — A US plan to rehabilitate sanctioned tankers to boost oil supply may attract only a sliver of the dark fleet , as existing contracts, complex compliance checks and sky-high freight rates reduce incentives for would-be sellers. The measure — detailed on Monday, just weeks ahead of the US midterm elections — is the latest in a string of efforts by the Trump administration to cool crude and fuel prices driven higher by months of war in the Persian Gulf and the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine. But with limited numbers of sanctioned supertankers actually available and would-be sellers unwilling to forgo lucrative crossings in the Middle East, industry analysts say the effort to revive so-called dark vessels may struggle to gain traction. “The number of vessels that could realistically migrate back into mainstream trading would likely be materially smaller than the overall sanctioned fleet.” Under the US proposal, blacklisted vessels can be sold and rejoin the legitimate fleet, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Monday, adding the government would “convert” tankers to expand global availability but would not lift existing sanctions.

items.title: Kpler Expands ‘Dark Fleet’ Tracking With Airbus Satellite Deal
items.original_title: Kpler Expands ‘Dark Fleet’ Tracking With Airbus Satellite Deal
items.summary: A satellite image of side-by-side ships at sea, off the coast of Sohar, Oman, June 9, 2026. SPOT © CNES 2026, Distribution Airbus DS/Handout via REUTERS Maritime data provider Kpler has reached an agreement with Airbus to expand its ability to track vessels that disappear from conventional ship-tracking systems, adding daily satellite imagery to help identify ships operating without reliable Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals. The agreement, announced Tuesday , will integrate imagery from Airbus’s SPOT Earth observation satellites with Kpler’s existing vessel-tracking network, allowing analysts to detect ships independently of their reported AIS positions. The service will use high-resolution satellite imagery, with a resolution of 1.5 meters and a 60-kilometer swath, combined with artificial intelligence to identify vessels at sea and in port. The technology is intended to address a growing challenge for maritime tracking: determining whether a vessel has deliberately switched off or manipulated its AIS signal, or whether its reported position has been affected by interference with satellite navigation systems. By comparing AIS data with independently captured satellite imagery, Kpler says it can better distinguish between the two. Gordon said combining AIS information with satellite imagery and other independent sources would give shipping companies and governments a clearer picture of maritime activity, particularly when vessels disappear from electronic tracking systems.

items.title: EU Puts Icebreakers, Shipping Security at Center of New Arctic Strategy
items.original_title: EU Puts Icebreakers, Shipping Security at Center of New Arctic Strategy
items.summary: The European Union unveiled a new Arctic strategy Tuesday aimed at strengthening maritime security, expanding icebreaker capacity and protecting critical infrastructure as melting sea ice opens new shipping routes and geopolitical competition intensifies across the region. The strategy , the EU’s first major update since 2021, marks a shift toward security and economic interests in a region increasingly important to global shipping, trade and energy supplies. At the center of the plan is a proposed Maritime Security Hub designed to improve surveillance and information sharing across the Arctic, including the monitoring and protection of critical undersea infrastructure. Von der Leyen pointed to Russia’s growing military presence in the Arctic, increasing pressure on regional security and the emergence of new shipping routes as reasons for Europe to take a more active role. The EU also plans to expand its use of satellite monitoring and data sharing, including a dedicated Arctic surveillance pilot scheduled for 2027 to improve maritime domain awareness. New shipping routes could create opportunities for ports, logistics providers and shipbuilders, but Arctic operations remain constrained by ice conditions, limited infrastructure, environmental risks and the availability of emergency response capabilities.

items.title: New mining operations unearth opportunities for logistics in Africa
items.original_title: New mining operations unearth opportunities for logistics in Africa
items.summary: Mining developments in sub-Saharan Africa are boosting the continent’s infrastructure, which supply chain operators have been crying out for, but significant gaps remain. Data from the OECD shows more than $155bn will be required for upgrades in port, rail, and road infrastructure over the next decade if the sub-Sahara region “is to meet its potential”, but with multiple projects already under way, there are positive signs. DHL Express Sub-Saharan Africa CEO Hennie Heymans told The Loadstar : “We’ve seen enormous improvement. If you go to Kenya, there’s an incredibly smooth new highway, which is partly what’s driving the growth in that economy. “If you look at Ethiopia, it is building €15bn airport in Addis Ababa. Rwanda, one of the smallest countries, is building a €4bn airport. We see fantastic improvements in infrastructure.” And this investment is having real world logistics implications, with journeys between Nairobi and Addis Ababa, that previously took upwards of a week, down to 24 hours; while an eight-lane highway has dropped domestic journeys from four hours to mere minutes. Much of the spur behind this has been new mining operations, necessitating the development of roads, port improvements, and services to support them.

items.summary: Airlines are strengthening freighter links between Asia, Europe, and the Americas for winter, adding transatlantic flights, connections to Latin American manufacturing and distribution hubs, and capacity serving Asia’s technology exports. Air Canada Cargo’s new 767-30F services to Amsterdam, Monterrey, and Panama City join selected US frequency increases from Lufthansa Cargo, a new Cairo link from Air France, and additional transpacific options from JAL and Cathay Cargo. The additions come as forwarders renegotiate allocations ahead of the winter passenger timetable, when fewer flights on some routes reduce available belly capacity. Elsewhere, Lufthansa Cargo’s winter schedule, effective 25 October, offers 88 freighter routes serving 40 destinations, including up to 46 weekly rotations to 17 Asia-Pacific destinations. Its own 767 freighter timetable adds a weekly Narita-Dalian service. Cathay Cargo has also linked additional Americas freighter capacity for the peak to growth in semiconductor and data-centre equipment shipments from Asia. It expects a leased A330 converted freighter in the fourth quarter, operated on its behalf by Air Hong Kong, to support regional general cargo demand. IATA reported global cargo demand up 4.4% year on year in August, while capacity fell 0.1%. Asia-North America cargo capacity demand increased 13.2%.

items.title: Port of Singapore faces new challenges – but also new opportunities
items.original_title: Port of Singapore faces new challenges – but also new opportunities
items.summary: Singapore’s position as a global container transhipment hub depends on its ability to remain competitive within international liner shipping networks, as rival ports accelerate investment in digitalisation and automation. At the Singapore Port Workers Union’s 80th anniversary dinner on Sunday, senior minister Lee Hsien Loong (pictured) said Singapore’s port competitiveness could not be taken for granted, and warned that complacency at PSA International risked losing business to competing ports. Unlike major Chinese gateways such as Shanghai and Ningbo-Zhoushan, which benefit from substantial domestic volumes, Singapore relies heavily on transhipment traffic and its role as a connecting hub for global shipping lines. Mr Lee, who was Singapore’s prime minister from 2004 to 2024, cited Shanghai’s Yangshan port as an example of a competitor making significant advances in automation and digitalisation. The new port is expected to have an annual handling capacity of 65m teu by the 2040s, with technology playing a central role in increasing throughput and maximising productivity, amid the country’s land constraints. Singapore handled almost 45m teu in 2025, while throughput in the first half of this year was up 4.7% year on year, to 22.7m teu.

items.title: UK shipowners warn against copying FuelEU red tape
items.original_title: UK shipowners warn against copying FuelEU red tape
items.summary: The UK Chamber of Shipping has urged the British government to avoid repeating the compliance problems encountered under FuelEU Maritime as it prepares to introduce its own maritime fuel standard. In a policy paper published this week, the industry body warned that the EU regime, which came into force in January 2025, had imposed a substantially greater administrative workload on shipowners and regulators than initially anticipated. The 22-page report identifies difficulties with reporting deadlines, fuel certification, emissions calculations and compliance pooling arrangements. The Chamber wants the UK government to establish a fully tested ship-level monitoring and reporting system before introducing compliance obligations. Peter Aylott, the Chamber’s director of policy, said the government had an opportunity to learn from the EU’s experience rather than create another regulatory system that increased costs and complexity. The paper also calls for close alignment with emerging International Maritime Organization requirements to avoid duplicate certification, reporting and verification obligations. The intervention comes as the Department for Transport prepares to consult on a domestic maritime fuel standard, with the consultation expected later this year. Britain’s maritime decarbonisation strategy, unveiled in March 2025, targets a 30% reduction in domestic shipping’s lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by 2030, rising to 80% by 2040 and zero by 2050, against a 2008 baseline.

items.summary: Greek shipowner Capital Tankers has lined up $930.3m in financing for 11 VLCC newbuildings under construction in China and South Korea, making further headway in funding its expanding crude tanker fleet. The Evangelos Marinakis-backed company has signed four financing arrangements since late September, covering vessels booked at Hanwha Ocean, Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Co (DSIC) and Hengli Shipbuilding. The largest portion, totalling $450.6m, covers five 307,000 dwt VLCCs at DSIC. Capital Tankers has also arranged $241.8m for three 320,000 dwt LNG dual-fuel-ready VLCCs at South Korea’s Hanwha Ocean, alongside $237.9m for three 306,000 dwt vessels at Hengli in China. Separately, Capital Tankers has disclosed a $64.5m sale-and-leaseback arrangement for its newly delivered 155,348 dwt LNG dual-fuel suezmax Amor , built at New Times Shipbuilding in China. The latest financing commitments follow Capital Tankers’ $500m Oslo private placement earlier this year, which was upsized after strong investor demand as the Marinakis group brought its crude tanker business to the public market. In June, it acquired three VLCC newbuilding contracts at Hengli from parent Capital Maritime & Trading at $122m apiece, with deliveries scheduled for the second half of 2027. Seventeen vessels are trading, with another 16 due for delivery through mid-2028. The company also retains options for 13 additional crude tankers.

items.title: Euroseas seals bumper charter and $26m boxship sale
items.original_title: Euroseas seals bumper charter and $26m boxship sale
items.summary: Nasdaq-listed Greek containership owner Euroseas has secured a $62,500-a-day charter for a 25-year-old feeder vessel while agreeing to sell its sistership for $26m, capitalising on continued strength in the smaller boxship market. The Aristides Pittas-led company said its 2001-built, 2,556 teu EM Corfu has been fixed for a minimum of 12 and maximum of 14 months at the charterer’s option. The new contract will begin in mid-December, following a scheduled drydocking, and represents a sharp increase from the vessel’s previous employment at $28,000 per day. Euroseas expects the minimum charter period to generate approximately $17.8m in EBITDA. The vessel is expected to change hands at the end of October, once its current charter expires. Both vessels were previously fixed in November 2024, with EM Corfu securing $28,000 per day and Evridiki G $29,500 per day. The latest charter more than doubles EM Corfu’s previous daily rate, while the sale allows Euroseas to realise a substantial gain from its sistership without undertaking another costly drydocking. Following the disposal, Euroseas will operate 20 containerships with a combined capacity of approximately 58,600 teu. The company also has 12 vessels under construction in China, ranging from 1,800 teu feeders to 4,484 teu intermediate containerships, with deliveries scheduled between 2027 and 2029.

items.title: Dutch inland shipping duo expands into Belgium with new chartering venture
items.original_title: Dutch inland shipping duo expands into Belgium with new chartering venture
items.summary: Dutch inland shipping companies Amer Shipping and Van de Graaf & Meeusen have joined forces to establish a new chartering business in Antwerp, backed by a fresh dry cargo newbuilding order at Concordia Damen. The two family-owned operators have launched TriBarge to target Belgian and French shippers, combining their existing networks and vessel capacity with plans for joint fleet investment. The new company will handle dry cargo, general cargo and breakbulk movements across the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) region, German canals, the Moselle and inland waterways reaching Basel. Through its partnership with Stream Shipping, an existing venture between Amer Shipping and German cooperative MSG eG, TriBarge will also be able to serve destinations as far as the Black Sea. The newbuilding, to be named Porta Sud , is scheduled to enter service in the second half of 2027 and will be designed to access smaller inland ports, tributaries and canals as well as major rivers. The move comes just weeks after Amer Shipping returned to Concordia Damen for another two 110 m CDS Dry Cargo newbuildings, lifting its programme of shallow-draught vessels to six. Amer Shipping operates a network of close to 60 vessels, transporting around 9m tonnes of cargo annually across the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Germany and Switzerland.

items.title: South Asia LNG demand growth derailed as Middle East conflict exposes critical supply vulnerabilities
items.original_title: South Asia LNG demand growth derailed as Middle East conflict exposes critical supply vulnerabilities
items.summary: South Asian LNG markets have absorbed one of the most severe supply shocks in the history of the global gas trade, as the war in the Middle East and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz cut off Qatari and UAE LNG flows to a region that had made itself critically dependent on them. LNG demand across South Asia, which had been projected to grow by 2.7 million tonnes (Mt), or 7%, in 2026, is now expected to decline by around 6 Mt and the outlook beyond 2026 has been materially downgraded, according to Wood Mackenzie’s latest analysis. In 2025, nearly 90% of Qatari and UAE LNG shipments through the Strait were destined for Asia, making the region the most affected. The resulting spike in spot prices compared to contracted LNG prices caused fiscal crises and reduced gas demand by over 3 Mt in Bangladesh and approximately 1.5 Mt in both India and Pakistan. “The Middle East conflict has exposed the structural vulnerabilities of South Asian LNG markets in stark terms,” said Johnson Quadros, Head of Gas and LNG research at Wood Mackenzie.

items.title: European stocks extend slide as French unrest triggers de-risking
items.original_title: European stocks extend slide as French unrest triggers de-risking
items.summary: European shares traded lower on Tuesday, as investors continued to trim exposure to continental equities and sovereign debt following severe civil unrest across France, while an escalation in Middle East geopolitical tensions drove crude oil prices to five-month peaks. The pan-European Stoxx 600 index fell 0.3%, surrendering recent gains as cross-asset trading desks digested the widening financial and political fallout from France’s worst social stability crisis in decades. France’s CAC 40 fell 0.1% after falling over 1% in the previous session, while Germany’s DAX was down 0.4%. London’s FTSE 100 and Italy’s FTSE MIB fell 0.2% each. Following days of widespread rioting, looting, and violent clashes over elevated living costs and declining public services, the French government imposed mandatory nighttime curfews across major urban centers, including Paris and Nice. French sovereign debt suffered its worst daily sell-off in nearly a month on Monday, widening the credit default swap (CDS) risk premium required by international investors to hold French paper over benchmark German Bunds. While Monday’s bond rout was acute, Tuesday’s equity sell-off remained relatively contained as institutional investors balanced domestic political risks against upcoming mega-cap earnings catalysts.

items.original_title: Copper Prices Decline as US Tariff Concerns Ease
items.summary: Copper futures fell toward $6.50 per pound on Tuesday, nearing one-month lows as expectations grew that the US may abandon proposed tariffs on refined copper imports. Markets increasingly anticipate that the Trump administration could shelve the tariff plans ahead of the midterm elections amid tightening global supplies and persistent inflationary pressures. Copper prices reached record highs last month as traders redirected shipments to US warehouses in anticipation of potential tariffs, tightening availability in other major markets. Additional support came from labor strikes and adverse weather conditions that disrupted mining operations in Chile, the world’s largest copper producer. On the demand side, copper continued to benefit from strong growth prospects in data center infrastructure, semiconductor manufacturing and battery energy storage systems. Source: Trading Economics

items.original_title: China unexpectedly increases its purchases of Brazilian oil
items.summary: According to the South China Morning Post , amidst the turmoil in the global energy supply chain due to the conflict in the Gulf region, the Brazilian economy has seized a golden opportunity. A quarterly analysis based on official government data shows that the financial situation of this South American economy is very positive. Energy Information Administration (EIA) shows that China aggressively purchased oil from Brazil, even as its total crude oil imports fell by 32% in the second quarter. Reports show that oil now accounts for nearly 26% of the country’s total exports to China, up 6.3 percentage points from the previous year, and second only to its main export item, soybeans (which account for over 35%). This was due to Brazil reaching its annual quota of 1.1 million tons under protectionist regulations from the Chinese market. According to the report, China dropped to fifth place among countries buying Brazilian beef in September, accounting for only 5.6% of total consumption, behind the US with a market share of 21.5%.

items.title: Supply Constraints Keep Asian Coal Prices High
items.original_title: Supply Constraints Keep Asian Coal Prices High
items.summary: Asian thermal coal prices are likely to stay elevated in the near term as Indonesian supply uncertainty and lower Chinese production limit supply, says Fitch Ratings. Demand from gas-to-coal switching in Japan and Korea is likely to stay firm, driven by the Middle East conflict, pushing regional prices higher – particularly for high- Calorific Value (CV) coal. Firmer prices will support miners’ near-term cash flow and debt-servicing capacity, but not reverse longer-term pressure from declining Chinese and Indian import requirements and the energy transition. Indonesian export supply is likely to remain difficult to predict despite the government easing its (initially) much lower 2026 production coal output target of 600 million tonnes (2025: actual output 790 million). Chinese coal supply should recover as tighter safety inspections following May’s Shanxi mine accident ease gradually. Chinese demand, which accounted for over one-third of Asian seaborne thermal-coal imports in 2025, should provide limited support once domestic production normalises. High gas prices should have limited implications for Chinese coal demand because gas-fired generation accounts for only a small share of the power mix. S&SEA coal demand remains robust, supported by 5%-7% power demand growth, weaker hydropower output, and transmission constraints on renewable additions. Qinhuangdao 5,500 kcal/kg thermal coal exceeded CNY1,000/tonne in early October despite seasonally weak demand.

items.title: Blue Autonomy takes vessel performance training online
items.original_title: Blue Autonomy takes vessel performance training online
items.summary: Athens-based maritime technology outfit Blue Autonomy has launched an online academy aimed at the growing number of shipping professionals expected to understand, challenge and defend vessel performance data. The Blue Autonomy Academy opens with 39 self-paced courses covering vessel performance, maritime data and the regulations increasingly putting a price on those numbers. The courses are arranged across nine specialisations and aimed at technical superintendents, performance analysts, fleet and technical managers, naval architects and marine engineers, as well as chartering and operations teams dealing with performance figures in charterparties. Topics range from ship resistance and propulsion to hull and propeller performance under ISO 19030, speed trials under ISO 15016, bunker quantity and quality, speed and consumption claims, and shipping’s CII, EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime regimes. Blue Autonomy says seven courses are being offered free in full, including its maritime decarbonisation and compliance specialisation. The certificates are private professional training and are not presented as state-recognised qualifications. “Behind every number a ship reports there is a calculation someone made,” said Christos Papandreou, founder and chief executive of Blue Autonomy. “The Academy teaches the people who sign for these numbers to take them apart, check each input and stand behind the result.” Papandreou is a naval architect and marine engineer with around 15 years in fleet performance and operational data.

items.title: Eastern Pacific links wind propulsion repayments to fuel savings
items.original_title: Eastern Pacific links wind propulsion repayments to fuel savings
items.summary: Singapore-based Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) has secured financing for wind-assisted propulsion systems on two vessels through a fund linking repayments to independently verified fuel savings. The Fund for Energy Efficiency Technologies (FEET), managed by AIM Horizon Investments with the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) as decarbonisation adviser, is making its first deployment with the EPS projects. The vessels, Pacific Sentinel and Pacific Sunstone , have each been fitted with three 22-metre suction sails, making them the first ships in the EPS fleet to adopt wind-assisted propulsion. FEET offers up to 100% upfront financing for energy efficiency technologies, with shipowners making payments based on verified fuel and regulatory savings. The financing model builds on earlier trials involving GCMD and EPS aboard Pacific Sentinel , during which researchers collected 276m data points over four months of trading in the Americas between May and September 2025. The analysis examined 203 valid sail on-off transitions to isolate the technology’s impact on fuel consumption from changing operating conditions. The methodology has undergone independent review, with future project savings subject to verification before payments are calculated. “Decarbonisation moves faster when the technology, the data, and the financing come together,” said EPS chief executive Cyril Ducau.

items.title: US moves to legitimise shadow tanker fleet
items.original_title: US moves to legitimise shadow tanker fleet
items.summary: The Trump administration is authorising the sale of sanctioned oil tankers to approved investors who would refurbish the vessels and return them to legitimate crude trades, US energy secretary Chris Wright revealed yesterday, as Washington scrambles to contain soaring freight costs amid the Hormuz crisis. Speaking at a Citadel Securities event in New York, Wright said the government was developing an approval process for formerly blacklisted vessels to trade under recognised owners, carrying only non-sanctioned oil. “We’re going to move some of the ships from what I call the ‘bad-guy fleet’ to the ‘good-guy fleet,’” he said. Kpler estimates only 24 of roughly 160 OFAC-sanctioned VLCCs could realistically return to mainstream trading after ownership and age restrictions are considered. It argued yesterday that war risk around the Middle East Gulf, rather than vessel numbers alone, is driving freight costs, and that loosening sanctions could weaken geopolitical leverage without delivering meaningful relief.\ Braemar put the potential increase even lower at just 19 VLCCs once vessels tied to Iran and European sanctions are excluded. BRS, meanwhile, has identified 148 deepsea tankers sanctioned by the US alone, representing just 2.5% of the global deepsea fleet. Only 14 appear to have been idle for more than three months.

items.title: MSC tipped for another 20 megamaxes in China
items.original_title: MSC tipped for another 20 megamaxes in China
items.summary: Mediterranean Shipping Co (MSC) has reportedly added another 20 megamax containerships at China’s Hengli Heavy Industries, further expanding its already massive orderbook as global newbuilding commitments climb to their highest level in more than a decade. According to liner consultancy Linerlytica, Gianluigi Aponte’s carrier has booked 20 additional 24,000 teu vessels at the Dalian-based shipbuilder, representing another 480,000 teu of future capacity. The latest deal takes MSC’s programme of vessels exceeding 20,000 teu at Hengli to 62 ships, Linerlytica said in its latest weekly market report. MSC has built up a substantial pipeline at Hengli since the two companies signed a strategic cooperation agreement in 2024. The liner giant initially contracted ten 21,000 teu and ten 24,000 teu LNG dual-fuel newbuildings, before returning for six 22,000 teu ships last year. At the end of September, Alphaliner data cited by Splash put MSC’s operated fleet at around 7.4m teu, representing 21.5% of global liner capacity, with another 2.94m teu on order. South Korea’s HMM is also pressing ahead with its fleet expansion, confirming contracts worth about KRW1.92trn ($1.44bn) for eight 13,000 teu LNG dual-fuel containerships at HD Hyundai. Six vessels will be built at HD Hyundai Samho and two at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, with deliveries starting in 2029.

items.title: Navigator sets course for UK domicile
items.original_title: Navigator sets course for UK domicile
items.summary: New York-listed gas carrier owner Navigator Gas is moving to shift its corporate domicile from the Marshall Islands to Britain, putting the proposed restructuring to shareholders next month. The London-headquartered company said it had entered into a merger agreement with its wholly owned British subsidiary, Navigator Gas plc, which would become the group’s new listed parent company. Under the proposed transaction, Navigator Holdings shareholders would receive one share in Navigator Gas plc for every existing share held, with the new parent retaining the group’s New York Stock Exchange listing. Navigator pointed to Britain’s tax treaty network, corporate governance framework and established shipping tonnage tax regime among the reasons for the move. Navigator operates 48 semi- or fully refrigerated gas carriers, including 18 capable of transporting ethylene and ethane. It also holds a 50% stake in an ethylene export terminal at Morgan’s Point, Texas. Earlier this year, Navigator agreed to sell eight smaller gas carriers and its stake in the Unigas joint venture to an investor group involving Bernhard Schulte and Sloman Neptun. The transaction was valued at approximately $183m and formed part of the company’s move to concentrate on higher-specification gas tonnage. Navigator said the proposed change of domicile is not expected to materially affect employees, vessel operations or customer services.

items.title: Bulker officer missing after rescuing 28 from burning boxship
items.original_title: Bulker officer missing after rescuing 28 from burning boxship
items.summary: The chief officer of a Portuguese-flagged bulk carrier is missing after being swept overboard during a dramatic operation that rescued all 28 seafarers from a burning 11,800 teu containership in the South Atlantic. Portuguese maritime accident investigators have opened an investigation into the casualty aboard the Aeolian Arrow , which responded to a distress call from the Singapore-flagged Espirito Santo Express on October 15. The Seaspan-owned, Hapag-Lloyd-chartered containership had suffered a serious fire while sailing from Singapore towards Santos, Brazil. The Aeolian Arrow launched its rescue boat in heavy seas, recovering 19 crew members from a lifeboat and another nine from a life raft. However, as the bulker’s rescue boat was being recovered, its chief officer fell into the sea. Portugal’s Maritime Accident Investigation Office (GAMA) said the officer was initially spotted alive, but repeated attempts to recover him were unsuccessful before he disappeared from sight. The 330 m Espirito Santo Express , built in 2018 and capable of carrying approximately 11,900 teu, was subsequently left abandoned and drifting in the South Atlantic. Hapag-Lloyd and fellow service operator Ocean Network Express have confirmed the containership’s crew survived, while warning that the impact on cargo and vessel operations remains under assessment.

items.title: Spodumene shipments triple as battery boom creates new dry bulk trades
items.original_title: Spodumene shipments triple as battery boom creates new dry bulk trades
items.summary: The seaborne trade in spodumene, a lithium-bearing mineral essential for battery production, is emerging as one of dry bulk shipping’s fastest-growing niche cargoes, with volumes more than tripling over the past five years. New research from Greek shipbroker Ursa Shipbrokers shows global shipments reached 4.04m tonnes in the first nine months of 2026, up 11.9% year-on-year and a record for the period. Annual shipments have climbed from just 1.58m tonnes in 2020 to 5.08m tonnes last year, reflecting the rapid expansion of lithium mining and growing demand from electric vehicle manufacturers and battery storage projects. Australia dominates the trade, accounting for 81% of shipments during the first nine months of this year, equivalent to 3.26m tonnes. China remains overwhelmingly the principal destination, receiving 88% of global seaborne spodumene cargoes, equivalent to 3.56m tonnes, reflecting its dominant position in lithium refining and battery manufacturing. Ultramaxes accounted for 39.6% of vessel deadweight employed in spodumene shipments this year, with handysizes representing a further 46%. New trading routes are also developing as African lithium production expands. Last week, Kodal Minerals confirmed that a fifth shipment of approximately 17,400 tonnes of spodumene concentrate had departed the Ivory Coast’s port of San Pedro in September, carrying material from its Bougouni mine in Mali to China.

items.title: Northern Sea Route smashes shipping records again
items.original_title: Northern Sea Route smashes shipping records again
items.summary: Shipping along Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) has already broken last year’s transit record. New figures from Norway’s Centre for High North Logistics (CHNL) show 104 confirmed transits by September 30, surpassing the 103 recorded during the whole of 2025 and 97 in 2024. Estimated transit cargo reached 3.7m tonnes, up 15% on the whole of last year, while the combined deadweight of vessels using the route increased 26% to 7.8m dwt. CHNL identified another 45 potential transits already underway or within the route at the end of September, suggesting the season could approach 150 voyages and more than 4.5m tonnes of cargo. Four direct Asia-Europe voyages had been completed by September 30, compared with just one during the whole of last year. Russian oil exports through the NSR have climbed nearly 50% this year, with approximately 20m barrels shipped to Asia between July and mid-October. Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, Suez Canal and Black Sea has made the expensive and potentially hazardous Arctic passage increasingly attractive. Russian LNG shipments are also contributing to traffic growth, with CHNL recording four eastbound LNG cargoes totalling approximately 300,000 tonnes.

items.title: NGM Energy back in the asset game with suezmax flip
items.original_title: NGM Energy back in the asset game with suezmax flip
items.summary: Asset plays have been the name of the game in shipping circles in recent weeks, with a string of relatively new Middle Eastern players flipping tankers to Chinese buyers at eye-catching profits. But one familiar Greek name, long associated with remarkable timing in the sale-and-purchase market, has been conspicuously absent from the headlines. Now NGM Energy, controlled by the Moundreas family, is back in the S&P charts, with a reported deal that sees the Greek owner pocket a staggering $57.1m gross gain on a 16-year-old suezmax acquired less than a year ago. In November last year, NGM Energy returned to the buoyant secondhand crude tanker market, picking up the 156,527 dwt Advantage Summer (built 2010) for $40.4m. Now the Jiangsu Rongsheng-built tanker is reported sold for a remarkable $97.5m, with delivery to its new owners scheduled for January 2027, a $57.1m uplift in the vessel’s value, equivalent to a gain of more than 141% on NGM’s purchase price. Several other 2010-built ships in the same segments have changed hands over the past week, with price tags just under $100m. This week sales chatter suggest that the $100m barrier has just been broken, with unconfirmed reports noting a 2010-built suezmax tanker has just been sold for $103m.

items.title: The AI forwarder of the future
items.original_title: The AI forwarder of the future
items.summary: “Innovation and productivity are at the core of what we do.” That was the slogan by a global TMS provider in 2016. In the rear-view mirror, most of the innovation has barely moved the needle from a top-down perspective. Productivity of 40 to 60 files remains a common market result. Based on our own experience from building Forto and working with many of the leading global forwarders, we reviewed end-to-end processes of up to 100 steps each: the time each requires, its automation potential, and the time that remains manual: the automation estimates came out up to 82%. We see an evolution of the sources of AI automation over time currently (see graphic). Coordinating activities that carry their own process knowledge and, hence, deliver customer value beyond (month 18 and beyond): These build on the first two, but they also need an understanding of the process itself, plus the judgment to run it. In a tender where $10 on a submitted rate card decides on the actual nomination, a cost advantage of $50, $70 or $100 per file changes the ability to price Profitability . We found in a recent analysis that up to 30% of relevant customer information comes from the customer’s context, such as SOPs, the actual eMail or documents.

items.title: Danica Urges Shipping Industry to Manage Crew Turnover, Not Just Retention
items.original_title: Danica Urges Shipping Industry to Manage Crew Turnover, Not Just Retention
items.summary: Shipping companies need to pay as much attention to managing crew turnover as they do to retaining seafarers if they are to maintain safe and efficient vessel operations, according to Henrik Jensen, founder and CEO of Danica Crewing Specialists. Speaking ahead of this week’s Crew Connect Global 2026 in Manila (20-22 October), Mr Jensen warned that while retaining experienced seafarers remains a priority, changing attitudes towards employment mean shipowners and managers must accept that some crew turnover is inevitable and be better prepared to manage it. “Having a stable crew pool makes a significant difference to the safe and efficient operation of a vessel. We also need to think about how we manage these changes when they happen.” Mr Jensen explained that traditional retention strategies, including competitive salaries, bonuses, insurance, pensions and promotion opportunities, have largely been built around the expectations of older generations, who tend to value stability and long-term employment. Mr Jensen believes shipping companies should focus on making it easier for new crew members to familiarise themselves with onboard equipment, procedures and working practices.

He also highlighted the importance of strong tripartism to enable PSA’s management team, the unions and the workers to work together in a “relationship of trust” to build a “disciplined and skilled workforce”. Mr Lee was speaking at a dinner celebration for the 80th anniversary of the Singapore Port Workers Union (SPWU), which represents PSA employees. But other ports in the region are making progress digitalising and automating too,” said Mr Lee, citing Shanghai’s Yangshan port as an example. “Each required close coordination between port management and the unions – to help workers accept radical changes in their work processes, to upgrade themselves as their roles changed, and then safely and successfully adopt new ways of working, sometimes in new places.” There were also many port moves – including to Keppel, Brani, Pasir Panjang and Tuas Port – that needed workers to adjust to different work environments and commuting arrangements.

items.title: Canadian wheat outlook improves as harvest advances, quality fears ease
items.original_title: Canadian wheat outlook improves as harvest advances, quality fears ease
items.summary: The outlook for Canada’s spring wheat crop has become more optimistic as improving harvest conditions and better-than-feared quality results ease concerns over widespread crop deterioration, while strong grain movements through Vancouver provide further confidence in the export market. After weeks of heavy rainfall across the Canadian Prairies raised concerns over sprouting, lower falling numbers and potential downgrades, market participants said recent harvest progress suggested that overall wheat quality could be better than initially expected. “Sounds like harvest is making progress in Canada with drier weather and not as much feed wheat as previously concerned,” a trader said. “Very hard in some areas to find 13.5% pro,” the trader said, explaining that exporters holding larger volumes of lower-protein wheat could offer wider protein spreads to manage their inventories. Market participants said the spread had expanded considerably beyond typical levels, reflecting regional differences in crop quality and the difficulty of sourcing wheat that meets specific milling requirements. The improving crop outlook has therefore not translated into uniformly weaker basis levels, as limited farmer selling, regional protein shortages and varying export capacity continue to support physical wheat values. Still, the combination of better-than-feared crop quality, advancing harvest activity and strong grain transportation has contributed to a more constructive outlook than earlier in the season.

items.title: InterManager Warns Enclosed Space Deaths Demand Urgent Industry Action
items.original_title: InterManager Warns Enclosed Space Deaths Demand Urgent Industry Action
items.summary: InterManager has called for urgent industry action on enclosed space safety after its latest research highlighted persistent failures in procedures, training, leadership and accident prevention. The organisation has recorded 354 enclosed space accidents over the past 30 years, between 1996 and 2026, across tankers, bulkers, general cargo ships, passenger vessels, containerships and other vessel types. Its latest seafarer survey identifies a recurring gap between safety procedures and operational reality onboard. InterManager says this must now be enhanced to deliver competence, rather than just training, particularly as enclosed space entry training is being considered as part of the current review of STW requirements, with the International Chamber of Shipping leading industry input. InterManager will explore the survey findings and wider enclosed space safety concerns during a webinar, run in conjunction with The Nautical Institute, on 27 October 2026 at 10am GMT. The webinar will bring together industry experts, Captain Pradeep Chawla, CEO of Marie Pals, Captain Garry Hallett from InterManager and Richard Cowburn, human factors specialist, to discuss where the industry stands now on enclosed space safety, how seafarers and shore-based stakeholders feel about current practice, and what practical action is needed next.

The report reflects AD Ports Group’s gains in mitigating the environmental impact of its integrated global trade, transport, logistics, and economic development activities, through measures such as increased operating efficiencies and the use of solar electricity, lower-impact maritime fuels, and electric-powered vessels. The Group’s total emissions intensity, which calculates tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e) per AED 1 million in revenue across emissions Scopes 1, 2 and 3, fell by 6% to 190.68 tCO₂e in 2025 from 203.06 tCO₂e in 2024. In 2025, the Group adopted a decarbonisation pathway covering its operations and value chain, with 139 initiatives planned between 2025 and 2050. The Group continued to advance its decarbonisation journey as the business grew robustly in 2025, reducing the total emissions intensity of our business per AED 1 million of revenue by 6% from 2024 levels through greater efficiencies and the use of solar and alternative energy.

items.original_title: Ethanol debut for WinGD as Maersk vessel makes landmark US bunkering and voyage
items.summary: WinGD has recorded the first in-service operation of its X-DF-M/E alcohol fuel engine platform on ethanol fuel, following a successful bunkering and voyage in the US. The 9,000 TEU container ship Tangier Maersk, owned by the Maersk shipping line, successfully sailed from Houston to New York on ethanol fuel. The vessel took on the bunker at the Port of Houston in late September, with the world’s largest bioethanol producer POET supplying fuel for the WinGD X82DF-Mengine powering the vessel. The occasion marked the first marine bunkering of a 100% bioethanol blend in the US, and the first ever in-service bunkering of ethanol to a WinGD engine. The first X-DF-M/E engine capable of using methanol entered service in 2025, with multi-alcohol fuel capability added this year – enabling both methanol and ethanol fuel to be used on six mid-sized sister vessels ordered by Maersk. (Image credit: Alabama Port Authority) WinGD Vice President Research & Development Sebastian Hensel said: “The use of bioethanol as a marine fuel is a natural progression for WinGD after successful operating experience with methanol using the same engine platform. This debut, a result of the strong momentum of Maersk in validating the use of this cost-effective low-carbon fuel, enabled us to confirm important operational and safety functions.

items.title: Shipping: The El Niño Effect
items.original_title: Shipping: The El Niño Effect
items.summary: According to Mr. Vasilis Fousekis, Research Analyst with Intermodal, “for dry bulk, the canal is the most direct link. The Panama Canal Authority, after cutting daily transits to 32 in September – only the second such reduction in history, eased restrictions following late-September rain. “In coal, El Niño brings drought to Southeast Asia, reducing hydropower output, and increasing coal burn, notably in India and Vietnam, contributing to the shift to coal as a source of energy, in a period of high natural gas prices. Similarly, “in grains, El Niño is expected to affect Brazil’s 2026/27 crop mainly through irregular rainfall in central and northern Brazil, while the south faces excess rain. Any delay to the soybean cycle would also push second-crop corn planting beyond its ideal window, threatening yields and Brazil’s corn exports in the second half of 2027. The United States stands to benefit, as a record soybean crop and the second-largest corn crop on record leave it well placed to fill the gap, with a longer export window into Asia in early 2027 and stronger demand for its corn later in the year. Overall, El Niño effects on shipping spread through reshuffling of logistics and trade flows rather than through large swings in volumes, as also past events showed.

items.title: Who owns shipping’s carbon decisions?
items.original_title: Who owns shipping’s carbon decisions?
items.summary: In an industry where a position list is a competitive weapon, the question is no longer just how to comply—but where carbon decisions are made and who controls the data behind them, said Argyris Zafeiropoulos, principal advisor at Resilience & Compliance Advisory. With the EU Emissions Trading System fully phased into shipping and FuelEU Maritime tightening year by year, carbon is now a line item in every fixture. On a single laden Aframax voyage from the Gulf to Rotterdam, the FuelEU penalty alone climbs to about €246,000 ($276,000) by 2040 — same ship, same route, same fuel. Far less attention goes to a quieter question: where are these carbon decisions actually made, and who can see the data behind them? On that voyage, ETS and FuelEU together come to about €104,000 ($116,600) at an €81 ($91) allowance price — roughly one euro ($1.12) on every tonne of a 100,000-tonne cargo, rising to about €1.36 ($1.53) by 2030. In commodity trades, the choice between CIF and FOB helps decide who absorbs it. Carbon has moved beyond the charter party and into the commodity contract. Shipping has always rewarded those who control their critical assets — ships, cargo relationships, market intelligence and commercial judgement.

items.title: Oil tanker on fire after hitting mine in Hormuz: Iran’s Guards
items.original_title: Oil tanker on fire after hitting mine in Hormuz: Iran’s Guards
items.summary: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said Monday an oil tanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine, the latest such incident since Tehran tightened its grip of the waterway. Iran seized control of the strait after war broke out against the United States and Israel late February, choking off the vital shipping route which normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil. The Islamic republic has demanded that all ships seek its authorisation before transiting. “An oil tanker, which was in violation, struck a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in an explosion and a fire in its engine room,” Iranian state media quoted the Guards as saying. The tanker was travelling in the strait’s “unauthorized southern route” and had disabled its positioning and navigation systems, the statement said. It came a day after the Guards said two oil tankers caught fire in the strait, both after hitting mines. The Guards’ naval commander Admiral Ali Ozmaei warned this week that any vessel that deactivated its navigation systems would be considered “hostile.” The United States has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian oil exports in response to Tehran’s blockade on the waterway. Source: AFP

items.title: Gemini signals full Suez return by Q1 as it launches new Asia-Med service
items.original_title: Gemini signals full Suez return by Q1 as it launches new Asia-Med service
items.summary: Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have revealed a further redesign to the Gemini Cooperation’s Asia-Mediterranean network which will see a reorganisation of the regional hub-and-spoke model. Slated for introduction over the course of the second half of November, the move comes as the two carriers eye a full resumption of Suez transits by early next year, according to Hapag-Lloyd chief executive Rolf Habben Jansen. “We have announced a fair number of services that already have returned, and some more are returning in the weeks to come,” he said in a press beefing last week. The chief development in the revamped network is that Gemini will launch a new “transhipment hub-only” service between China and the west Mediterranean via the Suez Canal, dubbed AE18 by Maersk and SE5 by Hapag-Lloyd, featuring the following port rotation: Shanghai-Xiamen-Tanjung Pelepas-Algeciras-Tangier-Algeciras-Xiamen. Maersk said the new service was designed to complement its other Asia-Europe strings as well as flows from Asia to West Africa and South America with its west Mediterranean hubs taking on more relay transhipment responsibilities. As a result, Gemini’s Asia-North Europe Loop 1 (Maersk AE2/Hapag NE1) will replace its current first European port of call of Tangier with Rotterdam, “providing an alternative and improved service from Ningbo and Shanghai to Rotterdam”.

items.title: Solar power a shining example of export progress across sub-Saharan Africa
items.original_title: Solar power a shining example of export progress across sub-Saharan Africa
items.summary: Solar energy is becoming increasingly important for bolstering sub-Saharan Africa’s trading potential, with supply chain executives telling The Loadstar that Kenya and Nigeria are two of the fastest-growing markets for the technology. By the end of the first quarter, Nigeria had climbed into the top 10 of solar panel suppliers to the US, with some 40% of the country’s total exports of the technology, totalling $64bn, ending up in the US. That growth has been felt by forwarders and logistics partners. DHL Express’s chief executive for Sub-Saharan Africa, Hennie Heymans, told The Loadstar the company was seeing “incredible growth” in solar-panel exports out of Nigeria – and nor is that country alone. “We actually see an incredible growth in solar panel exports towards the United States from Nigeria and Kenya,” he said, pointing out that for Africa in general the “new energy” vertical was proving something of a winner, experiencing 20% growth year on year. Interestingly, local forwarders told The Loadstar solar panels were also proffering volumes in the reverse direction for Kenya, although there was debate around whether the volumes were part of a local redevelopment of energy infrastructure or the result of chaos in the supply chains.

items.original_title: New EU parcel charges add pressure for rethink on cross-border fulfilment
items.summary: Higher EU parcel charges could further strengthen the case for retailers to hold stock in Europe, as reduced China–Europe freighter capacity and elevated airfreight rates add to the cost pressures facing cross-border supply chains. An additional €2 EU handling fee per product category is expected from 1 November, on top of the €3 customs duty introduced in July on qualifying consignments worth €150 or less. For a parcel containing three product categories, the combined charges would reach €15 before transport, clearance, and VAT costs. The €3 duty started on 1 July, and the €2 fee is expected from 1 November. Rotate data shows capacity on the trade down 20% year on year between 18 September and 18 October. Holdwise provided an illustrative comparison, involving a €90 consumer order containing a Chinese-made T-shirt and watch, bought by the brand for €30. Shipping the order directly from outside the EU would incur €6 in customs duty and an expected €4 handling fee. Adding assumed postage and clearance costs of €7, plus €2.50 for storage, picking and packing, produces a total of €19.50. Holdwise calculated €2 in normal customs duty, 50 cents per order for allocated freight and clearance, €2.50 for warehouse fulfilment and €5 for delivery within the EU: a total of €10.

items.title: Analysis: The ETS question – did carriers redesign Asia-Europe services to avoid carbon tax?
items.original_title: Analysis: The ETS question – did carriers redesign Asia-Europe services to avoid carbon tax?
items.summary: Would a carrier really design its Asia-Europe network around shaving marginal ETS dollars, which it can recoup through surcharges anyway? In short, carriers did redesign for the ETS – though not around the ETS alone. Carriers have redesigned Asia–Europe loops to cut their exposure, and they were right to. A few months ago, the EU ETS Observatory published a report stating that UK volume growth was a direct result of shippers seeking to minimise the EU-ETS charges – bullocks, if you ask me. The first is above – carriers optimised their networks within the rules, as they were entitled to, and importers were spared hundreds of millions of euros a year: the Observatory puts the allowances not collected at the three UK ports alone at about €316m. It removes the carbon price from the Asia leg, the longest of the voyage, and with it any ETS reason to slow down or burn a bio-blend there. The commission’s carbon market report found about 5% of national ETS revenue went to industrial decarbonisation, and only France and Estonia ringfence a share for shipping. Its July proposal would create a reserve of up to 110m allowances from 2028 to 2040, covering 55%–90% of the price gap for sustainable fuels and zero-emission propulsion.

items.title: Northern Sea Route Transits Surpass 2025 Total as Arctic Shipping Gains Momentum
items.original_title: Northern Sea Route Transits Surpass 2025 Total as Arctic Shipping Gains Momentum
items.summary: Nuclear icebreaker Yamal escorting four cargo ships along the Northern Sea Route in November 2024. (Source: Atomflot) Cargo volumes rise as tanker, bulk carrier and container traffic expand, with 2026 transits potentially reaching 150. The number of commercial transit voyages through Russia’s Northern Sea Route (NSR) surpassed the full-year 2025 total by the end of September, putting Arctic shipping on course for another record season. The center estimates that the final 2026 total could approach 150 transits and exceed 4.5 million tons of cargo. 30, another 45 potential voyages were either underway or within the NSR area and could still qualify as completed transits. The pattern underscores how the NSR serves not only as a cargo corridor but also as a seasonal route for moving commercial tonnage between operating regions. CHNL recorded 13 container ship transits by the end of September, including voyages between Asian and European ports that did not originate or terminate in Russia. Four international Asia-Europe transits had been completed, compared with just one during the entire 2025 season. Although still a small share of total NSR traffic, these voyages demonstrate growing interest in using the Arctic as an alternative Asia-Europe corridor.

items.summary: MSC-controlled Global Car Carriers (GCC) has added another two large LNG dual-fuel car carriers in China, taking its rapidly expanding newbuilding programme to 22 ships. The former Gram Car Carriers has booked two 8,600 ceu pure car and truck carriers at Zhoushan Changhong International Shipyard, with both vessels scheduled for delivery in 2030. The latest additions, listed as Viking NB 21 and Viking NB 22 on the Oslo-based owner’s fleet register, bring its orderbook to eighteen 8,600 ceu ships and four of 7,000 ceu, representing a combined carrying capacity of 182,800 vehicles. Zhoushan Changhong is already a major shipbuilding partner of parent MSC, with a string of LNG dual-fuel containership contracts, including a series of 21,700 teu vessels. The latest move comes just weeks after GCC added eight 8,600 ceu car carriers at China Merchants’ Weihai yard, Guangzhou Shipyard International and Fujian Mawei Shipbuilding, lifting its programme at the time to 20 ships worth more than $2bn. As recently as July, GCC had 12 newbuildings lined up. Its entire orderbook is now concentrated at Chinese yards, with deliveries scheduled between 2028 and 2030. The expansion has gathered pace since MSC took over Oslo-listed Gram Car Carriers in 2024 in a deal worth around $700m.

items.title: AEMA offers specialized training to steer ammonia-fueled ships
items.original_title: AEMA offers specialized training to steer ammonia-fueled ships
items.summary: World’s leading shipping conglomerate based in Hong Kong and one of the largest employers of Indian seafarers, Anglo-Eastern features specialized facilities like the LNG and ammonia bunkering station skid and alternative fuel training simulators at the Anglo-Eastern Maritime Academy and training centres located in India state to train seafarers for steering next-generation and specialized green fuel cargo ships. Anglo-Eastern has supported the technical development, crew management, and operational preparation of ‘Mineral Europa – the world’s first ammonia-powered dry bulk cargo ship which began its maiden voyage recently. At Anglo Eastern Maritime Academy (AEMA), India’s premier maritime training college located near India’s Mumbai city and owned by Anglo-Eastern, seafarer training for ammonia-fuelled cargo ships covers various safety protocols, chemical hazard controls, bunkering simulations, and regulatory standards as the maritime industry transitions to green propulsion. Daily average port pick-up volume edged down 50,000 mt to 3.185 million mt. As of October 16, SMM’s latest statistics show that total iron ore inventory across 35 main ports nationwide stood at 148.3 million mt, up 2.85 million mt MoM, with overall inventory on an upward trend. Daily average port pick-up volume edged down 50,000 mt to 3.185 million mt. Hot metal production of steel mill blast furnaces declined notably, further weakening support for iron ore concentrates demand and dragging port pick-up volume lower in tandem. With arrivals declining while port pick-up fell more sharply, port inventory continued to accumulate overall. However, steel mill profits are currently in significant losses, and procurement strategies remain largely need-based, with limited restocking willingness, so the boost to port pick-up volume is expected to be limited. Therefore, even if demand shows marginal improvement, the supply-demand pace remains loose, and port inventory is highly likely to continue accumulating. Overall, iron ore fundamentals remain weak in the short term, and port inventory pressure is unlikely to ease soon.

items.title: Global Energy Scenarios 2026: Pathways to resilience
items.original_title: Global Energy Scenarios 2026: Pathways to resilience
items.summary: Rystad Energy’s fifth edition of its flagship annual report, Global Energy Scenarios (GES) 2026, finds that global reliance on imported energy is projected to peak by 2034 as energy security concerns accelerate the shift towards electrification. Against the backdrop of two major energy crises in five years, the report highlights how a broader range of rapidly deployable technologies is helping the energy system withstand major disruptions to energy flows. It explores how energy import dependency could evolve under three possible future scenarios, each reflecting a different pace of change. The longer the conflict lasts, the harder it will affect interlinked systems like food, logistics and manufacturing, Jarand Rystad, Founder & Executive Chairman, Rystad Energy The report introduces Pragmatism as a new reference scenario to 2050. Under Pragmatism, primary energy demand reaches 702 exajoules (EJ) by 2050, equivalent to adding another India to global energy demand in less than 25 years. Electricity overtook oil in 2025 as the largest carrier of useful energy for direct fuel use, and its share is projected to rise from around 28% today to 41% by 2050 under Pragmatism. Primary energy demand among importers peaks in 2038 at 421 EJ, yet the energy they put to work grows 22% through 2050 because electric end uses lose less energy than combustion.

As Splash reported last week, Rheinmetall secured the Black Sea yard at auction, but today’s announcement confirms that the Aponte-controlled shipping giant will participate in the acquisition, with the two companies jointly funding the purchase. The transaction is expected to close within weeks. Rheinmetall already has a €920m Romanian naval programme involving four vessels, comprising two 96 m offshore patrol vessels and two 43 m diver support ships. Splash first reported the Swiss group’s interest in Mangalia in June 2025, with cruise ships, ropax vessels and tugboats among the potential construction opportunities. Rheinmetall subsequently confirmed in May this year that the two companies were exploring a joint takeover. The latest deal comes as MSC is also pursuing a potential investment in Germany’s Meyer Werft, the cruise shipbuilder in which federal and regional governments hold an 80% stake. Mangalia, which boasts three drydocks, entered insolvency in June 2024 following a protracted dispute between Dutch shipbuilder Damen and the Romanian government over management rights. The acquisition offers the yard a route back to large-scale construction while potentially giving MSC a significant new foothold in European shipbuilding.
