items.title: India rolls out credit risk backstop for shipbuilders
items.original_title: India rolls out credit risk backstop for shipbuilders
items.summary: India has introduced two government-backed credit-risk insurance products for shipbuilders, aiming to protect domestic yards against missed payments and buyer defaults on vessel construction contracts. The measures, unveiled by shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal, form part of New Delhi’s wider shipbuilding development programme, which has earmarked INR14.43bn ($152m) for credit-risk coverage. The first product, Shipbuilding Project Credit Risk Insurance Policy, has been developed by state-owned export credit insurer ECGC and will cover shipbuilding contracts for overseas owners. The second, Business Credit Shield Policy–Shipbuilders, has been developed by New India Assurance and targets domestic shipbuilding projects. The initiative addresses one of the financial risks facing shipbuilders, particularly on large contracts where construction can take several years and payments are tied to milestones. Delayed instalments or buyer defaults can leave yards exposed to substantial working capital requirements while vessels remain under construction. The two products were introduced under India’s $2.1bn shipbuilding development scheme, part of a wider maritime investment package approved by the government in September 2025. The roughly $152m allocation is part of that existing programme. India has been stepping up financial support for its shipbuilding industry as it seeks to expand domestic construction capacity and attract more international orders.

items.title: China Merchants and COSCO move to exit Qingdao ore terminal
items.original_title: China Merchants and COSCO move to exit Qingdao ore terminal
items.summary: China Merchants Port and COSCO Shipping Ports are joining forces with IMC to sell a controlling stake in an iron ore terminal at China’s Qingdao port, setting a minimum price of CNY1.92bn ($287m). The three shareholders have launched a public tender for their combined 70% holding in Qingdao Port Dongjiakou Ore Terminal, according to Hong Kong stock exchange disclosures. China Merchants Port and COSCO Shipping Ports each hold 25% of the terminal company, while Singapore-based IMC owns another 20%. The minimum consideration has been set at $287m, including $102m apiece for the holdings of China Merchants and COSCO. The terminal company is responsible for the construction, operation and management of iron ore handling facilities at Dongjiakou, one of Qingdao’s main bulk cargo areas. Its 400,000 dwt iron ore terminal entered service in 2013, giving the port the ability to receive very large ore carriers employed in trades between Brazil and China. China Merchants Port said the proposed sale would allow it to realise the value of its investment and improve its financial flexibility. COSCO Shipping Ports separately described the disposal as part of its wider strategy to optimise resource allocation and support future business development.

items.title: European shipowners demand bigger share of EU carbon revenues
items.original_title: European shipowners demand bigger share of EU carbon revenues
items.summary: European shipowners are calling for a threefold increase in the carbon allowances earmarked to support shipping’s energy transition, arguing that the sector contributes almost twice its share of emissions to the EU Emissions Trading System’s auction revenues. A study published by European Community Shipowners’ Associations (ECSA) estimates that the proposed Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion (SMAP) mechanism needs at least 330m allowances, compared with the 110m currently envisaged by the European Commission. The association puts the required support at around €30bn ($33.6bn), aimed at narrowing the cost gap between conventional marine fuels and cleaner alternatives. The proposal forms part of the ongoing revision of the EU ETS and remains subject to approval by the European Parliament and Council. With the phase-in period completed, shipping companies must surrender allowances covering 100% of their emissions falling within the ETS framework from the 2026 emissions year. The association estimates that shipowners purchase roughly 90m allowances annually. At an illustrative carbon price of €100 per allowance, that would represent an annual outlay of approximately €9bn ($10.1bn). ECSA argues that the proposed reserve, covering 2028 to 2040, would meet only about one-third of the industry’s estimated requirements. The intervention comes as shipowners weigh increasing carbon compliance costs against the substantial premiums associated with alternative fuels, fleet upgrades and new propulsion systems.

Union Maritime’s fleet register identifies the vessels as MW656-1 and MW656-2, each with a deadweight capacity of 4,334 tonnes. The vessels, set to be built by Fujian Mawei Shipbuilding, are set to be delivered in 2028 and 2029. The deal adds another vessel type to an established relationship between the London-based owner and the Chinese shipbuilding group, which previously placed a series of tanker orders with Union Maritime. The company’s latest fleet listing shows eight 113,600 dwt LR2 tankers on order at Fujian, with deliveries scheduled between 2027 and 2029. For Fujian, the PSV deal was part of a wider order batch announced at the anniversary event. Exports of disk media products more than quadrupled year on year, while PC shipments more than doubled; and IC shipments jumped by about 75%, the agency said.

items.title: Tankers: Is a Clean Slate Coming for 15% of the Tanker Fleet?
items.original_title: Tankers: Is a Clean Slate Coming for 15% of the Tanker Fleet?
items.summary: According to Gibson, “some 878 tankers, 15% of the trading fleet, are under sanctions, rising to 25% for Aframax/LR2s. The US can only waive its own designations, however, and EU and UK cooperation looks unlikely. That leaves 325 tankers listed by OFAC alone as the possible pool, and 153 of them are VLCCs, covering almost all of the 164 sanctioned VLCCs. Only 28 of the 116 sanctioned Suezmaxes and 42 of the 322 Aframax/LR2s are OFAC-only, and clean tonnage is limited, as around 40 CPP MRs, mostly in the East, potentially available for mainstream trade. The length of any waiver matters too, as a short-term reprieve may not be enough for charterers to commit to longer voyages, and the risk of renewed tensions after next month’s midterm elections may further limit appetite”, the shipbroker said. Most of the tonnage it could add is old, mostly VLCCs, sitting East of Suez. Since any delisting would follow OFAC’s usual full review, it may take time for a significant number of ships to be freed for mainstream trade. The TD3C VLCC FFA market has corrected downwards over the past couple of days, in part due to this news. In the end, the number of waivers given out will decide whether any impact is felt at all”, Gibson concluded.

items.title: Japan to provide P&I, compensate cargo, hull cover for crude, oil products, LNG transport
items.original_title: Japan to provide P&I, compensate cargo, hull cover for crude, oil products, LNG transport
items.summary: Japan is set to provide protection and indemnity cover and partially compensate cargo and hull insurance payments for the transportation of crude oil, oil products and LNG, as part of a bill approved by the Cabinet on Oct. 13, a senior official at the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry said. In response to the Middle East situation and to ensure a stable supply of energy to Japan, METI said the government will establish a program under which it will partially compensate non-life insurance companies for the funds required to pay insurance claims under marine property insurance, such as cargo and hull insurance, covering the transportation of crude oil, oil products and LNG, even in cases where the provision of reinsurance is prohibited. “To address such circumstances, the government will establish a mechanism to fill the gap left by the unavailable foreign reinsurance coverage.” Japan introduced a law in 2012 to compensate P&I cover as a sovereign guarantee for each tanker carrying Iranian crude amid EU sanctions against Iran — an initiative that remains in effect to date. The Japan P&I Club, formally known as the Japan Ship Owners’ Mutual Protection & Indemnity Association, provides insurance cover of up to about $9.8 billion per tanker.

The incident followed a claim by Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree that the group had shot down a Saudi Apache helicopter near Najran on Saturday. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi pledged to defend Saudi Arabia if necessary, seeking parliamentary authorisation for potential military assistance. However, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth warned Iran of further military devastation unless it abandoned its nuclear ambitions.

items.title: nOn Cyber Extortion Incident Involving 38 Maritime Companies Likely traces Back to a Single Vendor
items.original_title: nOn Cyber Extortion Incident Involving 38 Maritime Companies Likely traces Back to a Single Vendor
items.summary: On 12 October 2026, the cyber extortion group n0n listed a batch of 38 maritime organizations on its dark web leak site. The targets include shipping companies, port terminal operators, container operation companies, logistics companies, ship managers and agents, and other maritime-related companies in 18 countries. The listings carry ransom demands ranging from USD 400 thousand to 400 million per company, almost all with the same deadline: 19 October 2026, 13:27 UTC. Cydome’s research team analyzed the available information on this incident and assessed that it is likely linked to data from CyberLogitec, a Korean company that provides software and IT services to maritime companies. At least 21 of the 38 companies are publicly documented CyberLogitec customers, and other details in the 85 sample files published by n0n also point to CyberLogitec as the source. Key Findings • On 12 October 2026, n0n listed 38 maritime organizations in 18 countries, with demands totaling about USD 1.22 billion and a common deadline of 19 October 2026, 13:27 UTC. • Our interim assessment is that the data likely comes from a single support and project archive linked to CyberLogitec, split into separate listings per customer. The October 12 Maritime Listings The maritime listings appeared in a single batch on 12 October, according to ransomware.live.

Trade data is a record of what parties declared. items.title: News in Brief Podcast | Week 41 2026 | Congestion, cyberthreat and capacity constraint
items.original_title: News in Brief Podcast | Week 41 2026 | Congestion, cyberthreat and capacity constraint
items.summary: Port congestion is putting pressure on global supply chains, from West Africa and Europe to the Middle East, while escalating conflict is creating fresh challenges for air cargo. In this episode, Drewry’s head of Ports and Terminals, Eirik Hooper, joins us to discuss the causes of congestion, whether major investments in African ports will deliver meaningful improvements, and how automation could help terminals boost efficiency. We also examine the growing cyber threat facing shipping and port operators. Plus, Loadstar publisher Alex Lennane joins us to unpack the impact of the US/Iran war on air cargo capacity in Saudi Arabia, the squeeze on airfreight capacity as peak season approaches, and Samsung SDS’s move to strengthen its airfreight business through the acquisition of Woojung Air. And what’s making headlines on The Loadstar Premium? We take a look at Kuehne+Nagel’s growth ambitions, the world’s leading freight forwarders and ransomware threats targeting the logistics sector. items.title: Weathernews and HD Hyundai Marine Solution Sign First Commercial Contract for OSR-OW, with H-Line Shipping
items.original_title: Weathernews and HD Hyundai Marine Solution Sign First Commercial Contract for OSR-OW, with H-Line Shipping
items.summary: Weathernews Inc. and HD Hyundai Marine Solution Co., Ltd. have signed a three-year contract with H-Line Shipping, a major South Korean shipping company, to deploy their jointly developed route optimization solution, OSR-OW, across eight large bulk carriers. The agreement, finalized on October 1, 2026, marks the first commercial contract secured since the two companies signed their Framework Agreement in July. From Framework to Fleet When Weathernews and HD Hyundai Marine Solution signed their Framework Agreement in July, the companies outlined a plan to pursue initial commercial contracts with Korean shipping operators as a first step toward wider global deployment. OSR-OW, short for Optimum Ship Routeing × OceanWise, combines Weathernews’ weather forecasting technology with HD Hyundai Marine Solution’s AI-based vessel performance modeling to recommend more fuel-efficient routes. What’s Next With the H-Line Shipping contract as an early proof point, Weathernews and HD Hyundai Marine Solution plan to continue expanding OSR-OW toward the roughly 8,000 vessels identified in July as the solution’s addressable market. HD Hyundai Marine Solution said, “This agreement shows that shipping companies see real value in combining our AI-based performance modeling with Weathernews’ weather data. We’ll build on this work with H-Line Shipping as we expand OSR-OW to more operators around the world.” Source: Weathernews Inc.

items.title: AVS+ targets fragmented vessel procurement with centralised fleet management platform
items.original_title: AVS+ targets fragmented vessel procurement with centralised fleet management platform
items.summary: AVS Global Ship Supply has developed AVS +, a digital platform designed to give ship managers greater visibility and control over vessel procurement by bringing ordering, expenditure, inventory and operational records into a single system. The platform addresses a common challenge in maritime procurement, where orders, quotations, invoices and operational information can be spread across emails, telephone conversations and separate files, making it difficult for managers to establish the status of an order or obtain an up-to-date view of vessel expenditure. Through AVS+, customers can manage supply activities covering provisions, technical stores and port services through one web-based application. Fleet information is presented through both interactive map and list views, giving users access to vessel-specific operational records and invoices from a central repository. The system also allows companies to define procurement and catering parameters at fleet level, including target victualling rates, portion weights and supply lead times, while retaining the flexibility to adjust those requirements for individual vessels. Reporting tools provide access to information covering consumption, budget performance, price history and catering analysis, with reports available for export in PDF or Excel formats.

items.title: What lessons can we learn from declining carrier schedule adherence and rising port congestion?
items.original_title: What lessons can we learn from declining carrier schedule adherence and rising port congestion?
items.summary: Look at it from the viewpoint of a shipper moving goods by containership on the Asia-Europe route. The proportion of ships on this route which arrived on the scheduled day of arrival declined from 51% in May to just 31% in September (average of all ports and all carriers), according to the Drewry Container Capacity Insight. Even the Gemini alliance, which has a higher-than-average track record for on-time arrivals, managed just 34% in September. The Asia-Europe trade’s schedule reliability scores by carrier in September ranged between 19% and 38% and the proportion of sailings not cancelled ranged between 0% and 23%, according to Drewry’s analysis for this route. Looking at this from a carrier viewpoint, the logic is that cargo volumes were strong in the peak season, port congestion got worse in Asia, but the carriers could make higher profits by throwing more ship capacity at the market and cancelling fewer sailings… which must have made port congestion worse. At Drewry, we are looking more closely at how carrier performance, port congestion and network exposure can be brought together to give shippers a clearer picture of where they may be vulnerable. Ultimately, the aim should be to move away from simply reacting to delays and towards building those risks into carrier selection, procurement strategies and contingency planning.

items.original_title: A complete guide to port calls
items.summary: A port call is a stop a vessel makes along its route to load or unload cargo, take on supplies or let passengers go ashore. For a port authority it is a berth booking. For a ship agent it is a service opportunity. This guide covers what a port call is, who relies on port call data, and how to read port call activity as a trend rather than a list of events. Port calls serve different audiences, each asking a different question of the same underlying activity. • Commodity and trade-flow analysts use port calls as an early signal that a route is emerging, declining or recovering. Volume is not the story: composition is Port traffic is often reduced to a count of arrivals and departures. Cruising from the port was suspended for roughly fifteen months and resumed in July 2021, so any chart starting in 2021 shows a steep rise that reflects recovery as much as growth. items.title: Wind-Assisted Shipping Gains Ground as Airbus RoRo Adds Rotor Sails
items.original_title: Wind-Assisted Shipping Gains Ground as Airbus RoRo Adds Rotor Sails
items.summary: Caption: LD Armateurs’ Spirit of Toulouse, built for Airbus transatlantic transport operations, fitted with six 35-meter-tall Norsepower rotor sails at an outfitting site in Shanghai, China. Photo: LD Armateurs/Norsepower French shipowner LD Armateurs has completed the installation of six towering rotor sails aboard Spirit of Toulouse , a new roll-on/roll-off vessel being built to transport aircraft components for Airbus across the Atlantic. The installation, completed at a shipyard outfitting site in Shanghai, makes the 168-meter vessel the largest RoRo ship equipped with wind-assisted propulsion and gives it more mechanical sails than any other ship, according to LD Armateurs and Finnish wind propulsion specialist Norsepower. Airbus expects the new fleet to cut annual emissions from its transatlantic shipping operations by more than half, from approximately 68,000 metric tons of CO2 in 2023 to 33,000 metric tons by 2030. “Completing installation of six Norsepower Rotor Sails on Spirit of Toulouse is a significant milestone for wind propulsion in the RoRo segment,” said Heikki Pöntynen, CEO of Norsepower. items.original_title: Fog of War Deepens in Hormuz as UKMTO Says Most Ship Attacks Go Unreported
items.summary: Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, September 28, 2026. Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/via WANA (West Asia News Agency) via REUTERS Conflicting traffic figures and competing claims of control are making it increasingly difficult to establish what’s happening in the Strait of Hormuz, even as attacks on merchant shipping intensify. The true extent of attacks on merchant ships in the Strait of Hormuz remains unclear, with a new report from UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) acknowledging that most vessels struck in the region are not reporting incidents directly to the maritime security organization. In its weekly overview published Friday , UKMTO said it is struggling to establish the true number of attacks because the majority of vessels targeted are refusing to submit reports. UKMTO recorded 12 attacks during its latest reporting period, including 10 in the Strait of Hormuz, one in the Arabian Gulf and one in the Gulf of Oman. UKMTO’s latest report adds that most vessels broadcasting AIS continue to use the Iranian route, even as U.S.-facilitated traffic accounts for the majority of reported transits. And with UKMTO now acknowledging that most attacked vessels are not reporting incidents directly, even the growing number of documented strikes may offer only a partial picture of the dangers facing seafarers.

items.title: Southern California Ports Shatter Cargo Records as Imports Surge
items.original_title: Southern California Ports Shatter Cargo Records as Imports Surge
items.summary: The ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach both set all-time monthly cargo records in September, handling a combined 2.04 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) as strong imports and shifting global trade patterns continued to drive cargo through the nation’s busiest port complex. The Port of Long Beach reported Thursday that it handled 997,177 TEUs in September, up 25% from a year earlier and surpassing its previous record of 987,191 TEUs set in October 2024. It was the busiest month in the port’s 115-year history. Together, the neighboring ports moved 2,039,829 TEUs in September, including more than 1.05 million TEUs of loaded imports, as retailers continued replenishing inventories and shippers adjusted their routing strategies amid high fuel costs, trade uncertainty and disruptions along other major shipping routes. Imports led the surge at Long Beach, climbing 31.3% from a year earlier to 509,390 TEUs. container ports would ease from 2.3 million TEUs in August to 2.28 million TEUs in September, followed by 2.25 million TEUs in October and 2 million TEUs in November. Notably, both Southern California ports have reported handling the increased volumes without the congestion that disrupted operations during the pandemic. Georgia Ports has secured federal approval for a $2.3 billion container terminal that will add 3.5 million TEUs of capacity at the Port of Savannah.

items.summary: DP World has deployed 55 electric yard tractors (E-YTs) at its Busan terminal in South Korea, marking a significant step up in its efforts to reduce emissions from terminal operations. The new E-YTs replace Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG)-powered vehicles and account for approximately 36% of the terminal’s 154-strong yard tractor fleet. Used to move containers across the terminal, the electric tractors are expected to reduce CO₂ emissions by approximately 70% per unit compared with the LNG-powered tractors they replace. As a participant in South Korea’s Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS), DP World Busan is taking steps to reduce emissions from its operations. Anders Dømmestrup, Chief Operating Officer, Ports & Terminals, Asia Pacific, DP World APAC, said: “Deploying these electric yard tractors marks an important milestone in DP World’s efforts to reduce emissions from terminal operations. It shows how we can make progress on that goal while continuing to deliver the safe, efficient and reliable services our customers depend on.” In addition to the environmental benefits, the electric tractors offer quieter operation, smoother acceleration and more consistent performance during frequent stop-and-go movements. DP World Busan plans to continue expanding the use of electric equipment as part of its longer-term efforts to reduce terminal emissions.

items.title: IEA Moves to Accelerate Oil Reserve Releases as Hormuz Crisis Drags On
items.original_title: IEA Moves to Accelerate Oil Reserve Releases as Hormuz Crisis Drags On
items.summary: The International Energy Agency (IEA) has agreed to accelerate the release of approximately 100 million barrels of emergency oil stocks, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel, as the prolonged Strait of Hormuz crisis continues to strain global energy supplies. The decision, announced Thursday following a meeting of the agency’s Governing Board, comes amid mounting concerns over diesel shortages, high fuel prices and renewed attacks on commercial shipping in the Middle East. According to the IEA’s statement , member countries have already released approximately 330 million barrels under the emergency stock release agreed in March in response to the Iran war. The agency said it would take steps to accelerate the remaining releases, with more than 20 million barrels of diesel to be made available as soon as possible. In its October Oil Market Report , published Wednesday, the IEA said disruptions to production and exports from the Middle East and Russia removed approximately 1.3 million barrels per day of diesel and gasoil exports from the market in September compared with a year earlier. It forecasts global oil demand will decline by 2.6 million barrels per day in 2026 as higher prices and weaker economic activity take their toll.

items.original_title: DHL Express puts its faith – and its cash – in Africa’s trade potential
items.summary: DHL Express has committed €300m in investment across Africa through to 2030, as the logistics group urges UK businesses to diversify supply chains and pursue opportunities in an area expected to become a major global growth engine by 2035. Hennie Heymans, CEO of DHL Express Sub-Saharan Africa, said the investment “reflected the company’s confidence in the continent’s long-term prospects”, amid shifting global trade relationships, geopolitical tensions, and changes to supply chains. “We would not commit to €300m if we didn’t believe in the future of this continent,” he said today. He said only 12% of African cities were connected by at least one commercial flight a week, underscoring the challenges facing companies seeking to expand manufacturing and distribution. DHL is looking to address some of these constraints through its existing network, which Mr Heymans said spanned every African country and territory. In sub-Saharan Africa, the company operates 12 dedicated aircraft, alongside road transport, facilities and other air connections. The executives stressed that businesses should not approach Africa as a single market, given the differences in languages, legal systems, currencies, and trade regulations. “Be specific to which countries in Africa you want to offer trade to,” Mr Heymans said, and advised companies to identify markets and sectors best suited to their products before expanding.

Emma Crumpton, enterprise solutions director at freight intelligence platform Portcast, highlighted detention and demurrage as a particularly complex source of margin erosion. But both guests stressed that automation depended on reliable data and understanding the task. Mr Crook said Neolink’s staff were handling 80% to 90% more shipment volume than three years earlier, without an increase in staff numbers. Mr Crook said receiving orders two or more weeks in advance helped the forwarder make earlier bookings and choose services suited to customers’ actual inventory requirements, avoiding unnecessary premiums for speed they did not need. Meanwhile, The Loadstar’s State of AI in Supply Chain 2026 report found 48.7% of respondents cited integration with existing systems as a major barrier to scaling AI; while 53.8% identified insufficient in-house AI expertise and change-management capability.

items.title: We’re ‘shouldering cost burden of green transition’, say carriers
items.original_title: We’re ‘shouldering cost burden of green transition’, say carriers
items.summary: Shipping lines claim they are bearing the cost of investments in alternative fuels and lower-emission vessels, as shippers and their freight forwarders remain reluctant to pay more for greener shipping. That is according to speakers at the Singapore International Bunkering Conference and Exhibition yesterday. Pacific International Lines (PIL) head of operations and procurement (China) Chia Yujin said shippers in price-sensitive markets were not yet ready to pay for the industry’s transition to alternative fuels by 2050, leaving carriers to finance much of the investment. “We don’t have any shippers we could share the cost with. Because we believe that when it comes to 2030, we will need to operate more ships with the same fuel, and I can’t go and find a trained crew at that time. There are now 650 containerships capable of using alternative fuels including methanol and liquefied natural gas (LNG) on order, compared with around 330 in September 2023. Maersk Line has 56 dual-fuelled ships on order and is already operating 24. Its head of fleet operations (East), Dinesh Kumar Balraj, said alternative fuels must be available at commercially viable prices, while ports need suitable bunkering facilities and ship operators must ensure their crews are trained to handle them.

items.title: Ex-India spot rates and surcharges ease as peak comes to an end
items.original_title: Ex-India spot rates and surcharges ease as peak comes to an end
items.summary: Container lines, sensing a gradual slowdown in Indian westbound volumes, are revisiting their surcharges and penalties, indicating a hot market may be turning decidedly cooler. The liners had been increasingly rolling booking cancellation and container no-show fees into their freight bills in recent months to maximise profitability from booming demand. Now, according to industry sources, Hapag-Lloyd, for one, has revised its cancellation fee drastically for Indian customers to $100 per container, from the $300 in force since late July. There is now no room for carriers to recover all kinds of surcharges, as they want.” The disruption in the Middle East had prompted a wave of hefty emergency surcharges by all carriers, sparking pushback and questions from various maritime regulatory authorities across their markets, including in India. As a result, ocean rates, ex-India to Europe and the US, are trending down, with expectations that the recent elevated levels will halve over the next few weeks. Indeed, Hapag-Lloyd yesterday advised forwarders it had revised spot rates for bookings on the 8,000 teu Tucapel , one of the vessels deployed on its TPI service between India (leaving JNPA on 24 October) and the US east coast, to $8,000 per 40ft – a reduction of around $1,500.

items.summary: Low levels of gas in storage leave the EU with less of a buffer against liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargoes being diverted to Asia, further disruption in the Middle East or the loss of Russian LNG from January 2027. The EU is heading into winter with gas storage about 72.4% full as of 3 October, the lowest level for this time of year since records began in 2011. Together with the EU’s full ban on imports of Russian LNG from January 2027, this shortfall could require the bloc to cut winter gas demand by 7%, or 14bcm, compared with last winter. Gas demand creeps up as imports stay flat Before 2022, EU gas storage was a seasonal buffer: fill in summer, withdraw in winter, with flexible (mainly Russian) pipeline imports absorbing demand swings. Storage’s share of EU winter gas consumption rose from 25% in 2021–22 to 30% in 2025–26, with a five-year high of 33% in 2024–25, according to Eurostat. Winter gas consumption fell sharply from roughly 222bcm in 2021–22 to around 185bcm in 2022–23, as high prices and emergency gas-saving measures cut demand. In late September, the German government instructed state-owned gas importer SEFE to procure and store 8 terawatt-hours of gas, about 3% of the country’s storage capacity, by 15 December.

The delays come as Indonesia prepares to transition to a new export framework from Jan. 1, 2027, giving a bigger role to PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia, or DSI, in supervising strategic commodity exports, including coal. “We might sign an umbrella contract for 2027 with a pre-condition of subject to RKAB approval. “Not hearing any 2027 contract till now, but if any, contracts now will be subject to various conditions,” another miner told Platts. The uncertainty comes as miners are also waiting to know how much coal they will be allowed to produce in 2027. If the production approved remains at 2026 levels, the market could remain tight in 2027 as well,” a large Asian buyer of Indonesian coal said. Price implications The tighter supply situation has already pushed Indonesian coal prices higher in 2026. Market participants said progress on 2027 contracts would depend in part on greater clarity over miners’ approved production volumes, DMO commitments and how the new export system will operate from January.

items.title: Korea’s Integrated Ship Survivability Design Framework
items.original_title: Korea’s Integrated Ship Survivability Design Framework
items.summary: A Korean-developed integrated design framework has been developed to comprehensively analyze “ship survivability”—a naval vessel’s ability to avoid enemy attack, withstand damage when hit, restore key functions after damage, and continue its mission. The key achievement is the integration of survivability analyses that had previously been performed using separate software tools into a single software environment. The AX Convergence Research Center of the Virtual Engineering Platform Research Division at the Korea Institute of Machinery and Materials (KIMM, President Seog-Hyeon Ryu) developed ‘isSAFE,’ an integrated ship survivability design framework. isSAFE provides an integrated design environment in which a ship model can be built, various weapon hit scenarios can be generated, and vulnerability, recoverability, and results analyses can be performed in a continuous workflow. Ship survivability consists of three elements: susceptibility, the ability to avoid enemy detection and attack; vulnerability, the ability to withstand damage when hit; and recoverability, the ability to restore key functions after damage. This enables users to compare survivability under different ship configurations and conditions and is expected to support the Republic of Korea Navy (ROK Navy), shipyards, and other end users in ship design and survivability assessments.

items.title: China: Coal use reaching peak plateau amid green goals
items.original_title: China: Coal use reaching peak plateau amid green goals
items.summary: China’s coal consumption is expected to enter a peak plateau transition during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30), following a steady deceleration in growth as the country’s green energy transformation reshapes its economic fundamentals, said a think tank. During the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-25), the country’s coal usage was characterized by rising total volume but a markedly slowing growth rate, according to the Report on China Energy Development 2026, released by the China Electric Power Planning and Engineering Institute in Beijing. In 2025, total coal consumption reached 4.76 billion metric tons, edging up a mere 0.1 percent year-on-year. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period, as China accelerates the construction of a new energy system, promotes the clean and efficient utilization of coal, upgrades traditional industries and replaces scattered coal — referring to coal of poor quality which is used throughout the civil sector for household cooking, heating and various commercial applications — national coal consumption will enter a peak plateau period, the report said. The steel and building materials sectors — which account for about 15 percent and 6 percent of coal consumption, respectively — also registered declines.

items.title: Reinforcing the ETS SMAP to guarantee long-term shipping decarbonisation
items.original_title: Reinforcing the ETS SMAP to guarantee long-term shipping decarbonisation
items.summary: The SMAP mechanism introduced under the ETS represents an opportunity to help the maritime sector to transition towards clean fuels and propulsion technologies, and strengthen Europe’s industrial leadership. With an estimated support of €15 billion between 2028 and 2040, such a mechanism could encourage shipping companies to use green e-fuels, which will need to be scaled up in this period to meet long-term decarbonisation targets. The European Commission’s Sustainable Transport Investment Plan (STIP) mentions that in less than a decade, 4.6 million tonnes of e-fuels could be needed to reach FuelEU targets. A high price difference coverage in favour of e-fuels compared to other alternative fuels under SMAP is a welcome step, but is unlikely to be sufficient in itself to ensure a genuine move towards e-fuels. Because of the capital-intensive nature of e-fuels production, these projects will require producers to enter long-term offtake agreements with companies in order to secure investment. The current SMAP proposal is unlikely to provide sufficient support to this process. While some alternative fuels and zero-emissions propulsion technologies have a role to play in reducing maritime GHG emissions, SMAP should be used primarily to reward long-term e-fuel use, rather than short-term fuel and propulsion technological options which may already be incentivised under existing legislation.

items.title: Dry bulk safety: scrap metal fires, fumigation and enclosed spaces
items.original_title: Dry bulk safety: scrap metal fires, fumigation and enclosed spaces
items.summary: BIMCO’s Dry Bulk Cargo Network discussed three persistent safety challenges at its latest meeting: fire risks from contaminated scrap metal cargoes, the shift of fumigation duties from specialists to ships’ crews, and continuing fatalities in enclosed spaces. Members highlighted the need for clearer cargo information, stronger charter party provisions, and practical measures to protect crews. The eighth meeting of the BIMCO Dry Bulk Cargo Network was held on Thursday 8 October 2026 and covered the following agenda items: Scrap metals had previously been discussed at the sixth meeting in early 2025, when views differed over whether the IMSBC Code schedule for scrap adequately covers the different types of scrap and the effects of contamination by materials such as plastics, tyres, and oils. These include questions about the meaning of “as dry as possible;” surveyors finding more plastics, tyres, oils and flammable material than the declared impurity percentage suggests; and the implications of lithium batteries being present, including whether this introduces dangerous goods considerations under Class 9 of the IMDG Code. These include confusion about the distinction between different scrap metal cargoes and how they should be described and classified, and a general lack of understanding of the hazards.

The freight rate for a Very Large Crude Carrier on a route from the Middle East Gulf to Asia had climbed to around $36 per barrel by early October, more than five times the cost before the Iran war, the agency added. Refiners can partially offset this by purchasing US crude, but those freight rates have also increased, with costs for the US Gulf Coast to China route exceeding $37 per barrel, the IEA said. items.summary: British ports have challenged European Union claims that shipping lines are diverting container traffic to the UK to escape carbon charges, warning that proposed anti-evasion measures risk penalising billions of pounds of investment in British terminals. The British Ports Association (BPA) has rejected findings from Spain’s EU ETS Observatory linking rising UK container activity to the bloc’s Emissions Trading System, arguing that new capacity, changing liner networks and commercial competition offer more convincing explanations. In a new report, the association said around 85% of the UK’s container traffic growth in 2025 was concentrated in London, following the opening of DP World’s £350m ($465m) fourth berth at London Gateway in late 2024. Government figures show UK ports handled 11% more containers last year, equivalent to an additional 600,000 units. The association also disputes treating the widely cited 76% figure as evidence of carbon-driven diversion specifically to Britain, arguing that the available analysis does not isolate the effects of ETS from alliance restructuring, congestion and new terminal capacity. The disagreement comes after the European Commission proposed tightening rules designed to prevent containerships from using neighbouring non-EU ports to reduce their ETS exposure.

items.title: Liquimar lines up suezmax trio at New Hantong
items.original_title: Liquimar lines up suezmax trio at New Hantong
items.summary: Greek tanker owner Liquimar Tankers has been linked to an order for three suezmax newbuildings in China, adding fresh crude carrier capacity after cashing in on the strong secondhand tanker market. The Dimitris Papadimitriou-controlled company has contracted three 157,000 dwt vessels at Jiangsu New Hantong Ship Heavy Industry, according to shipbuilding sources. The conventionally fuelled tankers are scheduled for delivery in the second half of 2030, with pricing estimated at just under $86m apiece, putting the potential investment at close to $258m. The pair changed hands for a reported $68m each, generating approximately $136m in gross sale proceeds. Liquimar has already emerged behind another Chinese tanker project this year. In August, shipbuilding intelligence identified the company as the owner of the 113,500 dwt aframax/LR2 Priamos under construction at Hengli Heavy Industries. Liquimar was set up in 1990, as a way for its parent company, Dioryx Maritime Corp, to expand from dry cargo and containerships into the oil tanker sector, before becoming a standalone entity in 1995. The latest reported deal would add another name to New Hantong’s suezmax orderbook. Earlier this year, Eyal Ofer’s Zodiac Maritime contracted four suezmaxes at the Chinese yard for 2029 delivery, taking its programme in the segment to nine vessels.

items.title: HMM commits $1.6bn to 12 more containerships
items.original_title: HMM commits $1.6bn to 12 more containerships
items.summary: South Korea’s HMM is pressing ahead with its fleet expansion programme, approving a $1.62bn investment in 12 containerships comprising eight 13,000 teu newbuildings and four smaller vessels. The Seoul-listed carrier’s board approved spending KRW2.168trn ($1.617bn) yesterday, according to a stock exchange filing. The investment includes fresh orders for eight 13,000 teu ships, alongside the acquisition of three 2,800 teu vessels and one 1,700 teu ship through resale transactions involving newbuildings already under construction. The 12 vessels will add a combined 114,100 teu of capacity, with deliveries scheduled to be completed by December 2029. HMM has yet to identify the shipyards responsible for the eight larger vessels or the sellers of the four smaller ships. Propulsion specifications have also not been disclosed. The latest investment follows last year’s KRW4trn ($2.8bn) commitment covering 12 LNG dual-fuel 13,000 teu containerships and two VLCCs, with HD Hyundai and Hanwha Ocean securing the boxship contracts. Under HMM’s business plan through to 2030, the carrier aims to expand its containership fleet to 166 vessels totalling 1.47m teu by the end of the decade, alongside 110 bulk carriers with a combined capacity of 13.52m dwt.

items.title: West Africa’s ore boom meets China’s growing VLOC armada
items.original_title: West Africa’s ore boom meets China’s growing VLOC armada
items.summary: West Africa is fast becoming dry bulk shipping’s biggest growth engine, with its mineral export boom poised to absorb the equivalent of another 120 capesizes by 2030. UK consultancy Tradeviews forecasts in a new report that shipments from the region will surge 50% from 2025 levels to 303m tonnes by the end of the decade, with Guinea’s giant Simandou iron ore project leading the charge. Crucially for shipowners, the long voyages to China will magnify the impact on vessel demand. Liberian iron ore exports nearly doubled to 10.1m tonnes. Tradeviews expects regional exports to reach 267m tonnes next year, with Guinean iron ore shipments climbing to 45m tonnes in 2027 and approximately 112m tonnes by 2030. Tradeviews calculates that moving a tonne from West Africa consequently absorbs around 2.6 times as much vessel time. On this basis, the consultancy estimates West African trades will require the equivalent of 330 capesizes by 2030, compared with 210 last year. The broker described the situation as a “test of elasticity” rather than the start of another cargo boom, pointing out that Shandong alumina refineries processing imported ore lost RMB261.8 per tonne in September.

items.title: Chemnav steps up suezmax bet with Jinglu pair
items.original_title: Chemnav steps up suezmax bet with Jinglu pair
items.summary: Greek tanker owner Chemnav Shipmanagement has expanded its suezmax newbuilding programme with two more vessels in China, taking its orderbook in the segment to four ships. The Paul Coronis-backed company has been linked by shipbroking sources to a contract for two 158,000 dwt crude carriers at Penglai Zhongbai Jinglu Ship Industry, with deliveries expected in 2029. No price has been disclosed. The latest deal follows a low-profile order for two suezmaxes at New Times Shipbuilding in September last year, with delivery scheduled for the first quarter of 2029. Chemnav has since updated its website to confirm four suezmax newbuildings scheduled for early 2029 and early 2030, although it has not named the yards involved. The company has been rebuilding its newbuilding exposure since returning to South Korean yards in 2023 after a lengthy absence. The owner previously ordered three MR tankers at K Shipbuilding, a programme expanded in 2024, and had operated a secondhand suezmax several years ago after buying a 2003-built vessel from Teekay Tankers. The Chinese builder has also secured an order for four 157,000 dwt suezmaxes from Eastaway, the tanker arm of Singapore-based X-Press Feeders, with deliveries stretching into 2030. Those vessels were reported at around $80m apiece, although no price guidance has emerged for Chemnav’s latest pair.

items.title: GSI taps bridge builder to ease ship block bottleneck
items.original_title: GSI taps bridge builder to ease ship block bottleneck
items.summary: Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) has turned to one of China’s oldest bridge builders for outsourced hull block construction, joining a growing number of shipyards tapping manufacturers outside the traditional maritime supply chain to keep pace with swelling orderbooks. The CSSC-controlled yard has signed a framework agreement with China Railway Shanhaiguan Bridge Group, bringing the heavy-steel fabricator into its shipbuilding operations. GSI said its expanding orderbook and increasingly complex vessel mix would drive up demand for hull blocks over the coming years, prompting the move to bring in additional manufacturing capacity. A separate project launched in September will see a new facility built at Longxue North, with GSI lined up to operate the yard once completed in 2029. The China Railway Construction Corporation subsidiary is fabricating 10 cargo-hold bottom sections weighing up to 96 tonnes each, which are to be transported to Shanghai for final assembly. The company has established three outdoor block assembly lines and is targeting annual ship block production of up to 100,000 tonnes, with longer-term ambitions to move into complete vessel construction. Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding also proposed a new block fabrication and assembly facility last year to address capacity constraints and reduce its reliance on external subcontractors.

items.title: Battery Storage Can Help Britain’s Ports Power the Next Phase of Clean Shipping
items.original_title: Battery Storage Can Help Britain’s Ports Power the Next Phase of Clean Shipping
items.summary: Britain’s ports are no longer simply gateways for trade. They are becoming part of the country’s future energy system. Across the UK, a structural shift is underway as ports evolve into hubs for electrification, battery storage, clean transport and industrial energy resilience. The ports that will hold the greatest strategic value over the next decade will not simply be those that can move goods efficiently. Shore power, battery storage and electric vessel charging can help ships reduce emissions while berthed and increasingly support electrified short-sea routes operating on fixed commercial schedules. NatPower Marine is developing privately financed clean power infrastructure designed around the needs of ports, vessels and shipping corridors, combining shore power, cold ironing, e-ship charging and battery-backed energy systems. Making better use of Britain’s clean power The opportunity extends well beyond shipping. If Britain can store more of the clean electricity it already produces and use it where demand is concentrated, including at ports, it can reduce wasted renewable generation, improve resilience and support cleaner trade. On one evening in March 2026, batteries supplied more than 12GW to the grid, demonstrating how storage has become an increasingly important component of system flexibility and reliability.

items.title: LR launches new guidance to help shipowners navigate the growing complexity of retrofit projects
items.original_title: LR launches new guidance to help shipowners navigate the growing complexity of retrofit projects
items.summary: New guidance highlights the practical challenges shipowners face as they retrofit existing vessels for alternative fuels and energy-saving technologies to meet evolving environmental regulations. Lloyd’s Register (LR) has published new Guidance Notes for Retrofit of Alternative Fuels and Energy Saving Devices highlighting the growing complexity of ship retrofit projects. As regulatory and commercial pressures increase through measures such as FuelEU Maritime, the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) and the IMO’s greenhouse gas reduction ambitions, retrofitting existing vessels is becoming an increasingly important pathway for owners seeking to improve efficiency, reduce emissions and extend asset life. To help the industry navigate these challenges, LR’s new publication brings together alternative fuels and energy-saving devices within a single retrofit framework. The guidance emphasises the importance of early collaboration between owners, shipyards, equipment manufacturers, flag administrations and classification societies to avoid delays and reduce project risk. Wind-assisted propulsion systems, for example, can benefit from incentives under FuelEU Maritime through a reward factor designed to recognise their contribution to lowering greenhouse gas intensity At the same time, the guidance notes reflect growing industry recognition that retrofit projects must address both technical and human factors.

items.title: A complete guide to container tracking
items.original_title: A complete guide to container tracking
items.summary: The operational question around container tracking has shifted from “where is it now?” to “when will it arrive, and what will it cost if it doesn’t?” For beneficial cargo owners (BCOs), freight forwarders, and terminal operators, schedule reliability is volatile – chokepoints can close in days and congestion at a single terminal can ripple across an entire trade lane. This guide covers: 1. How container tracking works 2. Container tracking is the monitoring of a container’s status and location as it moves across ships, terminals and inland transport, from booking at origin to gate-out at destination. • Vessel name and voyage number link the container to a specific sailing. The B2B challenges in container tracking For a handful of shipments, a carrier portal is usually adequate. A team managing five carriers is effectively running five parallel tracking workflows that do not talk to each other. Teams know a container is on the water but not whether the voyage is going to plan. Delayed carrier updates A vessel can sit at anchor outside a congested port for 36 hours before the tracking system reflects any change.

items.title: MR Freight Divergence: A Market Poised for Rebalancing
items.original_title: MR Freight Divergence: A Market Poised for Rebalancing
items.summary: M R demand shifts back towards regional trading Pacific origin MR earnings have maintained a substantial premium over Atlantic routes throughout 2026, while regional tonne mile demand has shifted considerably since April as trade patterns adjusted to disruptions in the Middle East Gulf. Following the disruption, MR vessels ballasted from the Pacific into the Atlantic in search of alternative employment, subsequently undertaking longer Atlantic to Pacific voyages. This temporarily lifted Atlantic origin tonne mile demand to an April peak, while Pacific demand declined sharply. China’s diesel exports subsequently reached a four year high in September, generating 29 MR voyages predominantly towards Southeast Asia and Oceania. Although this has supported US Gulf MR employment, the additional voyages have not fully compensated for lost Baltic tonne miles. Russian diesel recovery and Asian refinery activity shape the demand outlook US government’s recent announcement of a deal with Russia to supply the global diesel market raises the prospect of recovering Russian exports, but an immediate rebound remains unlikely given uncertainty over refinery capacity. A return of Russian diesel to Brazil could also displace US Gulf cargoes, limiting the net increase in Atlantic MR tonne mile demand. In the Pacific, Chinese clean product exports face a weaker outlook following September’s 36 month high of 3.9mt.

items.title: US oil production starts to respond to higher prices
items.original_title: US oil production starts to respond to higher prices
items.summary: “No plan survives first contact with the enemy.” That military maxim, adapted from the writings of the Prussian general Helmuth von Moltke the Elder, could be usefully applied to a lot of the thinking around US energy security. When the US tight oil industry emerged in the 2010s, setting the country on course to become the world’s largest producer, there was a lot of speculation about how calculations around American energy security had changed forever. The US no longer needed to care about what happened in the Middle East, said some. A surge in US production that helps ease tightness in world oil markets and brings down prices would be one clear way for American consumers to benefit. On the other hand, expecting the US tight oil industry not to respond to higher prices would also be a mistake. Wood Mackenzie’s rule of thumb is that production typically takes about nine to 12 months to respond after prices have moved. That increased activity has led him to raise his forecasts for US Lower 48 oil production. By December 2027, Wood Mackenzie projects that US Lower 48 production will be about 11.8 million b/d, a full 1 million b/d higher than we were forecasting before the war began.

items.original_title: Oil Shipping Costs Spike, Lifting Prices from Pump to Grocery
items.summary: FILE PHOTO: Tankers sail in the Gulf, near the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from northern Ras al-Khaimah, near the border with Oman’s Musandam governance, amid the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran, in United Arab Emirates, March 11, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer/File Photo HOUSTON/LOS ANGELES, Oct 15 (Reuters) – When the oil supertanker Esteem Explorer sails from the United States to Japan in late November, loaded with about 2 million barrels of crude, the journey will cost $81 million. The same journey would have cost $9.1 million last year, on average. Refiners process oil into fuel to move food, retail goods and construction materials, and rising costs are stoking inflation in countries that depend on imports. Every $10-per-barrel increase in shipping costs adds about 23 cents per gallon to gasoline, said Kenneth Medlock, a fellow in energy and resource economics at the Houston-based Baker Institute for Public Policy. On that basis, the Esteem Explorer’s shipping cost works out to at least 80 cents more per gallon of gasoline than last year, according to Reuters calculations. “Everything gets more expensive because that’s how we move stuff around.” Freight rates account for more than 40% of the price of US oil, based on Wednesday’s price around $95 per barrel, compared with 7% on average in 2025, according to LSEG shipping and oil price data.

items.title: Ship Fuel Market Fragments as Middle East Conflict Hits Trade
items.original_title: Ship Fuel Market Fragments as Middle East Conflict Hits Trade
items.summary: A general view shows the Novorossiysk Fuel Oil Terminal (NMT) in the Black Sea port of Novorossiisk, Russia May 30, 2018. Picture taken May 30, 2018. REUTERS/Natalya Chumakova Oct 15, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Shipowners are facing an increasingly fragmented fuel market as disruptions triggered by the Middle East conflict raise concerns about the availability and quality of supply. “No one can treat bunkering as a routine, last-minute decision anymore,” said Frederik Guttormsen, Asia Pacific president at Stolt-Nielsen Ltd., an operator of 167 tankers that transport chemicals worldwide. “We’re securing fuel earlier and tracking availability and lead times at key ports because the risk is now as much about prompt supply as about price.” Middle East oil flows are coming under renewed strain from recent attacks in the region, including on vessels transiting Hormuz. Disruptions are also becoming more frequent, leading to vessel diversions that are shifting fuel demand to other locations, said Peter Grünwaldt , head of bunkering at tanker owner Hafnia Ltd. “We’re making sure we have fuel available at these ports,” he said. Saudi Arabia is looking at ways to expand its oil pipeline capacity to destinations outside the Persian Gulf to 10 million barrels a day within two to three years, said Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman.

items.title: UK port volume growth not due to EU shippers avoiding ETS, says BPA
items.original_title: UK port volume growth not due to EU shippers avoiding ETS, says BPA
items.summary: UK lobbyists today pushed back at attempts to have the EU designate the ports of Felixstowe, London, and Southampton as “neighbouring container transhipment ports”, in the ongoing question of whether shippers are rerouting cargo to avoid ETS scheme charges. In July, the EU ETS Observatory – developed by Spain’s state-owned ports administrator Puertos del Estado as a way of monitoring “carbon leakage” from its transhipment hub of Algeciras to Morocco’s Tanger Med after the introduction of EU-ETS at the beginning of 2024 – published a report which appeared to suggest that the container volume growth seen in UK ports during 2025 was the direct result of shippers seeking to minimise EU-ETS charges. It had led to a “reduction in the connectivity of container traffic for long-distance services operated at EU ports, compared with neighbouring countries not subject to European environmental regulations, measured in terms of the teu-mile parameter”. However, the British Ports Association (BPA) today argued that 2025’s volume growth seen at the UK’s three main ports was caused by a combination of new capacity coming onstream at London Gateway and the reorganisation of the deepsea shipping alliances that took place at the start of the year.

items.title: Low Rhine water level driving barge cargo to capacity-strained road and rail
items.original_title: Low Rhine water level driving barge cargo to capacity-strained road and rail
items.summary: Terminals at Antwerp and Rotterdam are coming under growing pressure as unseasonably low water along the Rhine continues to restrict container barge movements on the river, with cargo being pushed towards already-constrained rail and road networks. SeasC4U’s Gunther Ginckels told The Loadstar barges around Duisburg-Ruhrort were operating at roughly two-thirds of normal capacity, while vessels further upstream were carrying substantially smaller loads. “Some services are suspended further upstream on the Kaub gauge, where low water has severely restricted navigation, while large volumes are being shifted to rail and truck, but alternative capacity is limited,” said Mr Ginckels. “Cargo is still moving, but carrying capacity is sharply reduced, transport costs have risen, transit times are longer and less predictable, while inland terminals, rail networks, and trucking markets are absorbing displaced cargo at higher cost and delays.” Some 35% of box movements along the Dutch hinterland tend to travel by inland waterway, meaning that even seeing a part of that traffic transferred to alternative modes piles massive pressure onto already constrained transport networks. Back in August, Metro Global stated that more than 200 trucks would be required to replace lost barge capacity, and while low water levels have become part and parcel of the Rhine’s summer months in recent years, the persisting into October presented additional problems.

items.title: Big forwarders are failing shippers on service, says Ascent’s new COO
items.original_title: Big forwarders are failing shippers on service, says Ascent’s new COO
items.summary: Former Apple and UPS executive Gal Dayan has just joined Ascent as COO, and talks big forwarders, tech – and aircraft ownership Large freight forwarders are struggling to deliver the customer service their marketing promises, according to Mr Dayan, who argues that specialist operators have more room to invest in shipper relationships. Mr Dayan, who became chief operating officer of Ascent Global Logistics on 1 October, told The Loadstar consolidation and the pursuit of efficiency had come at a cost to customers. Drawing on his experience as head of logistics at Apple, he questioned whether large forwarders’ claims to put customers ‘at the centre of their operations’ were reflected in the service they actually delivered. USA Jet has one MD-83F, and five MD-88Fs, while a further two are parked, according to planespotters. The fleet has an average age of more than 35 years, and while cheap to own, they are not fuel efficient – 2013 data shows that on a trip between Miami and Memphis, an MD-88F would burn 13% more fuel than a 737-400F. The airline remained central to Ascent’s proposition because it gave time-critical customers confidence that capacity would be available. items.title: Germany puts $448m behind 47-point green shipping plan
items.original_title: Germany puts $448m behind 47-point green shipping plan
items.summary: Germany has approved a national shipping decarbonisation programme backed by €400m ($448.8m) in funding, including proposals for greener shipping corridors, alternative fuel infrastructure and financial incentives for vessel renewal. The federal cabinet adopted the National Action Plan for Climate-Friendly Shipping yesterday, establishing 47 measures aimed at accelerating the transition of both seagoing and inland fleets. The funding, drawn from Germany’s Climate and Transformation Fund, will support new assistance programmes over the coming years. Other priorities include accelerating the availability of low-carbon marine fuels, developing alternative propulsion systems, modernising existing vessels and expanding green shipping corridors. German transport minister Bilger said the programme would help the maritime industry manage its transition while positioning Germany as a leading centre for the development of cleaner shipping technologies. Reducing administrative obstacles is another priority, with the government seeking to accelerate the commercial deployment of technologies already demonstrated in pilot projects. The programme forms part of Germany’s wider 2026 climate protection strategy and was developed in consultation with shipping companies, industry associations, researchers and regional governments. Implementation begins this autumn, with further measures scheduled for discussion at a government maritime conference on November 5. The plan represents a substantial new financial commitment, although the government has yet to establish detailed funding allocations or implementation deadlines for every measure.

Transition to Net-Zero by 2050 Singapore’s harbour craft sector comprises more than 1,600 predominantly diesel-powered vessels providing essential marine services, from passenger transport and towage to bunkering and maintenance operations. In line with Singapore’s national climate targets, the harbour craft sector is expected to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. As harbour craft typically remain in service for more than 20 years, fleet renewal decisions over the coming years will be critical to achieving the sector’s net-zero transition. From 2030, all new harbour craft operating in Singapore must be fully electric, capable of using B100 biofuel, or compatible with net-zero fuels. items.summary: The Suez Canal Authority (SCA) has introduced mandatory inspections and trials for vessels aged 25 years and older, adding further costs and potential delays for operators of ageing tonnage. The new regulations, already effective, require vessels to undergo a comprehensive inspection and trials before securing permission to transit the canal, with all applicable fees payable in advance. According to instructions issued by the authority’s Movement Department and circulated to shipping agents this week, vessels returning within six months of their last inspection will be exempt from repeating the procedure, provided no defects, breakdowns or adverse technical observations have been recorded. The requirements come as the global merchant fleet reaches unprecedented levels of ageing tonnage. Clarksons Research reported last Friday that more than 150m gt of shipping is now aged 25 years or older, up 75% in five years, while a record 68m gt has passed 30 years. The new Suez requirements apply across vessel types. Shipowners and agents will need to factor the additional checks into voyage planning, particularly for vessels operating irregular schedules. The authority has not specified inspection fees or how long the process will take.

items.summary: Nasdaq-listed Greek dry bulk owner Icon Energy is expanding its containership investments, agreeing to take a minority stake in a second feeder vessel employed under a long-term charter. The Ismini Panagiotidi-led company said it would acquire approximately 2.8% of the entity being established to own a 2023-built, 1,800 teu eco-design containership. The vessel is chartered to an unnamed major liner operator at $24,750 per day until at least February 2028, generating approximately $12m in minimum contracted revenue for the vessel over the remaining employment period. The investment will be funded from existing cash, with completion expected by the end of October, subject to final documentation. The vessel is being acquired by a consortium led by an established containership owner and operator, which will also handle commercial and technical management. Icon will be entitled to appoint a representative to the vessel-owning company’s board. The transaction marks Icon’s second move into container shipping this year. In June, the Athens-based owner agreed to acquire approximately 5% of a company formed to purchase a 2008-built, 2,000 teu geared feeder. Icon’s core business remains dry bulk shipping, where the company operates a small fleet comprising panamax, kamsarmax and ultramax tonnage.

items.title: US shadow fleet proposal sparks tanker stock rout
items.original_title: US shadow fleet proposal sparks tanker stock rout
items.summary: Asian shipping stocks took a beating on Thursday as reports that Washington is considering easing sanctions on shadow fleet tankers sent investors scrambling to reassess the extraordinary freight boom that has sent some spot segments into million-dollar territory for the first time in history. COSCO Shipping Energy plunged more than 13% in Hong Kong, while China Merchants Energy Shipping, COSCO Shipping Energy’s Shanghai-listed shares and China Merchants Nanjing Tanker hit their 10% daily downward limits in mainland trading.The sell-off also spread to other shipping sectors. The sharp reversal followed reports that the Trump administration is discussing exemptions allowing blacklisted tankers linked to Russia, Iran and Venezuela to carry oil and petroleum products not themselves subject to American sanctions. A US official told Reuters that companies would need Treasury approval to employ the vessels, with the initiative designed to release additional tanker capacity and bring down record freight rates. The proposal follows Washington’s decision last Friday to temporarily authorise Russian diesel trade until April 7, 2027, drawing criticism from Kyiv and US lawmakers. Clarksons Research estimates that 1,010 oil tankers totalling 121m dwt are individually sanctioned, representing 17% of global tanker capacity. Analysts are sceptical that the proposed sanctions relaxation would significantly alter tanker supply.

items.original_title: Podcast: How AI will transform freight forwarding beyond the hype
items.summary: AI is everywhere in logistics right now, but what does it actually mean for freight forwarding? In this episode of The Loadstar Podcast , host Charlotte Goldstone speaks to Erik Muttersbach, founder of Zauber and former Forto technology executive, about where AI and agentic AI really stand today, what is already happening in forwarding, and what could change over the next three to five years. Erik shares what he is learning from real-world deployments with customers, tackles some of the biggest misconceptions around AI, and explains why adoption and change management may be just as important as the technology itself. They also discuss the buy-versus-build question, the patterns Erik has seen across a decade of technology adoption in forwarding, and how companies can separate genuine AI capability from the hype. Looking ahead, what will AI actually change across the forwarding value chain – and which parts of the industry will prove hardest to transform? items.title: Hormuz claims two more ships in fresh wave of strikes
items.original_title: Hormuz claims two more ships in fresh wave of strikes
items.summary: Two ships have sunk near the Strait of Hormuz as fresh attacks on commercial shipping have hit three containerships linked to Abu Dhabi’s AD Ports Group. The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride , a 2008-built, 2,824 teu feeder operated by Dubai-based Global Feeder Shipping (GFS), was struck by an unidentified projectile on Tuesday, caught fire and subsequently sank. Singapore’s Maritime and Port Authority (MPA) confirmed that all 21 crew members were evacuated without injury. A second GFS boxship, the Singapore-flagged 4,400 teu GFS Giselle , sustained hull damage in a separate strike on Wednesday, Singapore time. The Abu Dhabi company increased its stake in GFS to 81% in June, while another of its feeder operators, Safeen Feeders, also had a vessel targeted in the latest wave. The 2002-built, Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulker was hit on September 23 in an attack that sparked an engine room fire, killed an Indian seafarer and forced the evacuation of the remaining 27 crew members. Separately, US Central Command disclosed on Wednesday that American forces had destroyed an Iranian-affiliated dhow in the Gulf of Oman on October 6. The latest incidents bring the IMO’s tally to 113 confirmed maritime incidents across the region since the conflict began in late February, with 24 seafarers killed.

items.title: NATO’s Black Sea flank on alert after series of attacks
items.original_title: NATO’s Black Sea flank on alert after series of attacks
items.summary: A chemical tanker has reported a suspected drone strike inside Romanian territorial waters. The Comoros-flagged Yara J was anchored approximately 10 nautical miles southeast of Sulina on Wednesday evening when its crew reported an explosion and fire onboard. The vessel, which was in ballast and reportedly preparing to enter the Danube, extinguished the fire without outside assistance. Unlike the previous attacks in the exclusive economic zones of Romania and Bulgaria, both NATO members, Wednesday’s incident occurred inside Romanian territorial waters. The latest incident follows five reported drone attacks on merchant shipping off the two countries since October 5, with three vessels sinking. It followed this morning with claims of attacks on two more dry cargo vessels bound for the Ukrainian port, alongside strikes against infrastructure at the Danube port of Izmail. Another drone was detected over Romanian territorial waters southeast of Sulina at 01.34 this morning, prompting further deployments of Spanish F-18s and Romanian F-16s. Bulgaria is working with Türkiye and Romania on an initiative to protect commercial shipping in the Black Sea, foreign minister Velislava Petrova-Chamova announced in Berlin yesterday. Petrova-Chamova also highlighted plans to establish a Black Sea Maritime Security Centre, with operations in Varna and Constanța, to improve surveillance and protect critical infrastructure.

items.title: Capital Axis behind capesize deal of the year
items.original_title: Capital Axis behind capesize deal of the year
items.summary: Broking sources are reporting the highest-priced capesize vessel transaction of 2026, with Greek owner Capital Axis Maritime reportedly in the process of selling a newbuilding for $90m. Brokers report the Arriktos, a 181,250 dwt capesize under construction at China’s Hengli Shipbuilding, also known as Hengli Dalian Hl-B181k-25, is reportedly attracting Chinese buyers at $90m. The vessel, scheduled for delivery in October 2027, is valued at $82.95m by VesselsValue, which also records its sale from Hengli Petrochemical to Capital Axis Maritime for $74m in January. If concluded at the reported price, the latest transaction would represent a $16m increase, or nearly 22%, over the January acquisition price, highlighting the sharp appreciation in modern capesize asset values. Capital Axis Maritime is the Greek dry bulk venture established earlier this year through a partnership between Evangelos Marinakis-backed Capital Executive Ship Management and Nicholas E. In January, Greek owner Seanergy Maritime contracted a sister vessel for $75.2m, with delivery scheduled for the third quarter of 2027. The Arriktos resale, if concluded at $90m, would represent a premium of almost $15m over Seanergy’s January contract price,. The latest deal comes amid strengthening dry bulk asset values. Secondhand bulkcarrier prices have continued to gain ground, with Clarksons reporting a 5% increase in its overall index over the past two months.

items.title: LD Armateurs unveils world’s first six-sail cargo ship
items.original_title: LD Armateurs unveils world’s first six-sail cargo ship
items.summary: French shipowner LD Armateurs has completed the installation of six Norsepower rotor sails on Spirit of Toulouse, creating what it says is the world’s first cargo vessel fitted with six mechanical sails. The ship, being built in China for Airbus logistics work, is the lead vessel in a three-ship series designed to transport large aircraft sub-assemblies between Europe and North America. LD Armateurs said the six 35 m by 5 m rotor sails had now been installed at a coastal outfitting site in Shanghai by Wuchang Shipbuilding Industry Group, ahead of upcoming sea trials. The installation gives Spirit of Toulouse the highest number of mechanical sails yet fitted to a commercial cargo ship, and makes it the largest roro vessel equipped with wind propulsion, according to the company and rotor sail supplier Norsepower. The wind-assist system will work alongside two dual-fuel main engines and two dual-fuel generator sets capable of running on e-methanol, bio-methanol or marine diesel oil. LD Armateurs said the combination of methanol capability and wind propulsion was designed to cut fuel consumption and emissions on the vessel’s transatlantic route rather than rely on a single decarbonisation technology. “Spirit of Toulouse is much more than a new vessel,” said Samira Draoua, chief executive of LD Armateurs.

items.title: An Ageing Fleet Needs Greater Care
items.original_title: An Ageing Fleet Needs Greater Care
items.summary: Shipping is investing heavily in the next generation of vessels, fuels and propulsion technologies, but a large part of the existing fleet will still be trading well into the next decade. This will mean the steel structure must be protected for much longer. For instance, Clarksons data from July 2025 showed that 38% of global fleet capacity was more than 15 years old, including 30% of bulk carrier capacity and 33% of containership capacity. PATCH TESTS A three-year comparative trial aboard a 15,300TEU containership provides one example. Steelpaint’s single component zinc-rich polyurethane system was applied to a lashing bridge during drydocking in March 2023. At inspection in July 2026, the coated area showed only minor corrosion and required no crew maintenance. In the year up to June 2026, Stelpant has been trialled on some 16 bulk carriers with many going on to order full coats. An older ship is not necessarily a corroded ship, just as corrosion does not automatically make a vessel structurally unsafe. But with substantial proportions of the bulker and containership fleets already beyond 15 years, corrosion protection should increasingly be viewed as part of through-life asset management.

items.title: Cyprus ports need joint energy and investment strategy, shipping agents chief says
items.original_title: Cyprus ports need joint energy and investment strategy, shipping agents chief says
items.summary: Cyprus needs a coordinated strategy for shipping, energy and environmental protection to support port investment and modernisation, Cyprus shipping agents association president Reginos Tsanos said, warning that separate planning and regulatory priorities risk undermining commercially viable projects. Speaking at the Italy-Cyprus Maritime Business Forum, held at the DP World Limassol passenger terminal, Tsanos called for closer cooperation between government authorities, energy providers, municipalities and the maritime industry. According to a statement issued by the association on Wednesday, he said the three sectors were closely connected but often operated with different priorities, decision-making processes and timelines. Tsanos identified five areas for closer cooperation, including transforming ports into smart energy hubs, aligning regulatory frameworks, integrating investment planning across the blue economy, developing a shared maritime digital platform and coordinating marine spatial planning. However, he warned that “the capacity of Cyprus’ electricity networks remained a major challenge”, requiring coordinated planning between the state, local authorities, shipping companies and energy providers. At the same time, Tsanos argued that “assessing maritime, energy and environmental projects together could improve investment viability and risk management, rather than treating each development separately.” He also proposed a shared maritime digital platform to improve infrastructure planning, accelerate decisions and strengthen environmental monitoring.

Dombrovskis addressed a range of topics, including spiking sovereign bond yields in Europe, concerns around inflation due to rising energy prices and a recently concluded trade deal with China under which Beijing agreed to cap hybrid car exports to the 27-nation bloc.
