items.title: Slash emissions with shipping: New report shows coastal shipping can help reduce freight emissions and bolster Australia’s supply chain resilience
items.original_title: Slash emissions with shipping: New report shows coastal shipping can help reduce freight emissions and bolster Australia’s supply chain resilience
items.summary: Up to 90 per cent of freight emissions can be cut simply by moving more cargo to coastal shipping, a new independent report reveals. Comparing the emissions performance of road, rail and shipping across four essential Australian freight routes, The Emission Reduction Potential of Mode Shift to Maritime Transport report found greenhouse gas emissions reductions of between 60 to 90 per cent by rebalancing freight between road and coastal shipping. Launched at Parliament House today by the Hon. Catherine King, the report was developed by Transport Emissions/Energy Research and commissioned by the Maritime Union of Australia in collaboration with Maritime Industry Australia Limited (MIAL) and supported by the Energy Futures Foundation. Clare Grandison, Principal Advisor – Decarbonisation and Industry Transformation, said the report shows significant diesel fuel use and emissions reductions are possible using today’s technology and maritime footprint. “The Australian transport sector is a significant contributor to greenhouse gas emissions, making up more than 21 per cent of total emissions each year. The report shows emissions reductions are feasible now, using today’s vessels, infrastructure and capability.” Angela Gillham, CEO of MIAL, said the said greater use of coastal shipping could improve productivity for the freight sector and strengthen supply chain resilience.

items.summary: Shipping containers are seen at the port of Barcelona, Spain, October 3, 2024. REUTERS/Nacho Doce The U.S. Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) is proposing $200,000 fees on Spanish-flagged vessels entering American ports, along with restrictions on billions of dollars in Spanish imports, after concluding that Spain’s refusal to admit certain U.S.-flagged ships has created unfavorable conditions for American shipping. The proposed measures include a $200,000 fee each time a Spanish-flagged vessel enters a U.S. port from abroad, as well as potential restrictions on imports of Spanish cosmetics, oils and fats, ceramics, stone products, and sugar and confectionery. The dispute began in November 2024, when Spanish authorities refused port access to the U.S.-flagged Maersk Denver and Maersk Seletar , both operated by Maersk Line, Limited, over cargo connected to Israel. The regulator said the restrictions undermine the ability of U.S.-flagged ships to compete for cargo moving to and from Spain, while also affecting vessels that could be called upon to support U.S. The Commission has now narrowed its proposed vessel fee to $200,000 per voyage while identifying specific categories of Spanish goods that could face import restrictions. The FMC said the proposed penalties are intended to address shipping conditions created by Spain’s port restrictions, rather than the broader political dispute over the transportation of military cargo to Israel.

EuroDry currently operates 11 bulkers totalling 766,420 dwt, including two kamsarmaxes, six supra/ultramaxes and three older panamaxes. items.summary: Missiles struck two container ships in Global Feeder Shipping’s (GFS) fleet in the Strait of Hormuz in the last 24 hours, with one vessel subsequently sinking after catching fire. Singapore’s Maritime and Port Authority (MPA) said that the 2008-built 2,824 teu GFS Pride was damaged and caught fire before sinking. All of its 21 crewmen were evacuated, with no injuries reported. The other ship, 2015-built 4,350 teu GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage but remained operational and proceeded under its own power to a safe anchorage. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said an unnamed container ship carrying more than 2,500 containers had struck a mine while transiting what it described as an “unauthorised and dangerous” route through the strait. The sinking of GFS Pride is the second vessel loss since the US-Israel-Iran war began on 28 February, according to data from the International Maritime Organization, the United Nations’ shipping agency. The earlier incident involved a bulk carrier, Cape Dao, which sank in the Gulf of Oman yesterday, after being hit by two torpedoes on 23 September. Both GFS Pride and GFS Giselle were originally owned by Dubai-based Simatech Shipping, before the latter’s liner operations were acquired by GFS in October 2018.

items.title: Cyber-crime group hits 38 shipping and port groups with data leak threat
items.original_title: Cyber-crime group hits 38 shipping and port groups with data leak threat
items.summary: Cyber extortion group ‘n0n’ has named 38 organisations across the global shipping and ports sector on its dark-web leak site, raising concerns that data may have been stolen. Cybersecurity firm SOCRadar reported yesterday n0n published the listings in a single batch on 12 October, that included container terminals, shipping lines, port IT providers, and logistics businesses across 18 countries. The group emerged last month, listing 21 organisations across sectors including telecoms, retail, pharmaceuticals, and education. SOCRadar said the pattern of data described in the listings suggested a possible common point of entry, rather than 38 separate network intrusions. The amounts did not appear to correspond with the volume of data allegedly stolen: EUSU Logistics faced a $14m demand for 60mb, with ILCS Pelindo at $2.4m for 2.4gb. Of its 21 earlier victims, SOCRadar said 19 remained at the claimed stage, one was listed as negotiating, and one, Chibitek, had experienced a data leak. SOCRadar warned that maritime businesses that exchange EDI with companies named in the attack should plan for the possibility that their operational data could appear in the 19 October release. It advised them to identify the port community systems, EDI hubs, and file-transfer services handling their data; to check with providers for potential breaches, patch exposed systems, and investigate unusual access or bulk downloads.

items.summary: As the International Maritime Organization (IMO) tightens its carbon-reduction rules, more ships are adopting wind-assisted propulsion systems (WAPS) that use wind as thrust. The method installs wind devices on ships to supplement propulsion with wind power, reducing main engine fuel consumption and associated carbon emissions, and is drawing attention as a decarbonization technology. According to the shipbuilding and shipping industries on the 13th, domestic shippers HMM and Wooyang Shipping recently signed long-term charter contracts with Brazilian miner Vale and ordered eight and four 210,000-ton (t) bulk carriers, respectively, equipped with rotor sails. Global shipper Maersk worked with U.K.-based wind propulsion specialist Anemoi Marine Technologies in early last month to apply 35-meter-long, 5-meter-diameter rotor sails to an 8,700-TEU container ship (1 TEU equals one 20-foot container). Container ships must carry containers on deck, making it difficult to install wind-assisted propulsion systems. The International Windship Association (IWSA), in a report released early this year, said container ships lack deck space and retrofitting existing vessels with wind propulsion systems is difficult, slowing adoption of wind propulsion technology relative to other ship types. Last month, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries launched a project with the Korean Register and U.K.-based BAR Technologies to develop a 174,000-cubic-meter LNG carrier outfitted with Windwings.

items.title: EIA raises oil price forecasts for 2027
items.original_title: EIA raises oil price forecasts for 2027
items.summary: The US Energy Information Administration (EIA) expects the Brent crude spot price to average $105/bbl in the fourth quarter of 2026 before declining to around $84/bbl in 2027. The EIA forecasts Brent crude’s price to stay elevated this year, amid escalating Middle East hostilities that have rattled global energy markets and choked maritime transit through the Strait of Hormuz. Declining oil flows through critical chokepoints including the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb Strait, coupled with mounting crude production shut-ins, have accelerated over the past months, the EIA noted. Moreover, the attacks on the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia has highlighted the “potential for continued volatility in physical oil flows and oil prices,” the EIA said. Declining global crude oil inventories, which the EIA estimates have decreased by an average of 1.9 million b/d in the third quarter of this year, have put further upward pressure on oil prices, the EIA said. Crude oil production shut-ins averaged 4.8 million b/d in September, down from 5.8 million b/d in August, the EIA assessed. The US agency expects most production shut-ins to be restored by the end of the second quarter of 2027 and oil inventories to restart building.

The ship then transferred its full ammonia cargo to the 25,000 mt Searambler in Oman over Oct. 11-12. items.title: CMA CGM and ENGIE join forces to invest in biomethane production in Le Havre
items.original_title: CMA CGM and ENGIE join forces to invest in biomethane production in Le Havre
items.summary: The CMA CGM Group, a global player in sea, land, air and logistics solutions, and ENGIE Group, a major player in the energy transition, are joining forces to develop a major biomethane production facility at the heart of the Le Havre industrial-port zone. This major logistics hub in Europe, is a strategic location for the development of new low-carbon energy solutions, particularly renewable gases, serving the maritime and industrial sectors. ENGIE will lead the development of the project, including its technical design and permitting process. Starting in 2029/2030, the facility will convert livestock waste, household biowaste and agricultural residues into biomethane, which will be supplied to the CMA CGM fleet through the European gas grid under a certified mass-balance system. As a minority shareholder alongside ENGIE, CMA CGM will invest in the project through PULSE, its energy fund dedicated to innovative technologies and infrastructure that support the decarbonization of the Group’s transport and logistics activities. The Group aims to reach 10 TWh of annual biomethane production capacity in Europe by 2035, up from 1.2 TWh today. As we invest together in biomethane production in France’s largest container port, Le Havre, we are pursuing our long-term vision in securing access to renewable fuels, while contributing to the energy sovereignty of France and Europe.

items.title: Shipping firms and ports caught in mass cyber extortion claim
items.original_title: Shipping firms and ports caught in mass cyber extortion claim
items.summary: A cyber extortion group has threatened to publish data it claims it stole from 38 shipping, port, and logistics companies unless they pay multimillion-dollar ransoms by October 19. Cybersecurity firm SOCRadar said the group, known as n0n, added the 38 organisations to its dark web leak site in a single batch on October 12, marking a sharp shift towards maritime targets. The list includes 12 port and container terminal operators, 10 shipping lines and ship operators, port IT providers, logistics companies, and other maritime businesses across 18 countries. n0n is described as a financially motivated data-theft extortion operation rather than a conventional ransomware group. The group is threatening to release the alleged stolen material at 13:27 UTC on October 19. SOCRadar said ransom demands it reviewed ranged from $2.4m to $14m, payable in Bitcoin. In one example SOCRadar cited, Eurogate Tanger was allegedly asked to pay 10% of a $6m demand before being given access to a private negotiation room. The data n0n claims to possess varies between companies and includes EDI archives, container manifests, vessel schedules, gate movement records, commercial documents, internal system configurations, employee accounts, and financial records. SOCRadar said the relatively small, application-specific datasets claimed for several victims could indicate a common application or shared vulnerability rather than 38 separate compromises, although this too remains unconfirmed.

items.title: New project: Shipping must be a key part of Denmark’s electric future
items.original_title: New project: Shipping must be a key part of Denmark’s electric future
items.summary: The electrification of Danish shipping is advancing rapidly. Access to electricity and sufficient grid capacity remains the biggest barrier. A new project will provide practical recom­men­da­tions for policymakers and other key stakeholders, paving the way to unlock its full potential. Danish Shipping, Danish Maritime, Danish Ports and Green Power Denmark have joined forces on a project to support the electri­fi­ca­tion of shipping and help policymakers and investors make the right decisions to realise its considerable potential. Denmark’s maritime sector should play a central role in the green transition and in the ambitions to accelerate electri­fi­ca­tion across Denmark, as set out in the government’s new budget proposal,” says Nina Porst, Director of Sustainable Ships and Skills at Danish Shipping. The electrification of shipping is rapidly becoming a viable and energy-efficient solution for decarbonisation. The planning and development of Denmark’s future electricity infrastructure must take this into account. Specifically, the project will provide an evidence base for future investments and policy decisions by analysing developments in battery-electric shipping and their implications for electricity supply, charging infrastructure and the wider energy system. Its findings will highlight shipping’s future needs in electricity grid planning and support Denmark’s position as a leading maritime nation in the green transition.

items.summary: An industry coalition has been formally launched to develop a green shipping corridor between India’s VO Chidambaranar (VOC) Port and Europe, with a focus on green methanol and green ammonia. Indian and European officials signed a letter of intent to formally launch the industry coalition, according to India’s Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. The coalition, which includes the VOC Port Authority, will explore the potential use of green ammonia and green methanol as bunker fuels along the corridor. It will also identify suitable European ports for the corridor, building on a pre-feasibility study launched in 2025. The Indian government has not disclosed a timeline for developing the proposed India–EU green shipping corridor. The latest agreement follows earlier efforts to establish green shipping links between India and Europe. In April 2025, the Indian government and the Port of Rotterdam Authority announced plans to explore a green shipping corridor between the two countries. Freight costs for exporting Urals crude to Asia currently total around $30 per barrel or more, based on traders and calculations. items.original_title: Zhonggu steps up boxship investments with larger newbuilds
items.summary: China’s Zhonggu Shipping Group has signed up for two 14,000 teu containerships at Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding, moving into significantly larger tonnage as investment across the group gathers pace. The Shanghai-based company has contracted the conventionally fuelled pair, without disclosing the value or delivery dates. Last month, fellow Chinese carrier China United Lines contracted two conventionally fuelled 14,000 teu ships at the yard, following earlier business from German tonnage provider Peter Döhle. Zhonggu Shipping Group is also the controlling shareholder of Shanghai-listed Zhonggu Logistics, holding 57.46% of its shares. The listed carrier has been building up its own newbuilding programme throughout 2026. In June, it confirmed plans to increase the capacity of eight previously ordered containerships from 6,000 teu to 6,300 teu, following a revision of their design. Together with 10 smaller 1,800 teu vessels ordered earlier in the year, that programme involves investment of RMB6.86bn ($1bn). The company has earmarked RMB3bn from a planned convertible bond issue to help finance the vessels. Its earlier contracts were spread between Hengli Heavy Industries, China Merchants Jinling Shipyard and Wuhan Qingshan Shipyard.

items.title: India’s Aegis takes over Dubai tanker and logistics group Tristar
items.original_title: India’s Aegis takes over Dubai tanker and logistics group Tristar
items.summary: India’s Aegis Logistics has struck a deal to acquire 89.8% of Dubai-based Tristar for $809m, taking control of a global energy logistics group with a sizeable tanker and dry bulk shipping operation. The Mumbai-listed group is buying the stake through Singapore-based Aegis Logistics International from shareholders including Agility, Gulf Investment Corporation and Diamond Holdings. The transaction remains subject to competition and other regulatory approvals and is targeted to close by the end of March 2027. Tristar has been valued at $1.5bn on an enterprise basis and $882m on an equity basis, equivalent to around six times its 2025 EBITDA. The group generated about $1.4bn in revenue and $257m of EBITDA last year and operates across more than 30 countries. By early 2017, after consolidating the Tristar and Eships shipping teams in Dubai, the company described shipowning as a core part of the business and counted 22 ships in its fleet. Agility said Tristar had 26 ocean-going and coastal vessels at the end of 2025, alongside more than 1,000 trucks, 14 fuel farms and over 60 remote fuel sites. Tristar disclosed last year that it had agreed to build and operate four MR product tankers under Project Griffin, with the first scheduled to enter service in 2028.

items.title: SmartSea links crew travel and gangway access in dual launch
items.original_title: SmartSea links crew travel and gangway access in dual launch
items.summary: Maritime technology provider SmartSea has launched two connected platforms aimed at simplifying crew changes, linking journey planning with digital identity checks at ports and vessel gangways. SmartJourney brings together flight information, ground transport, accommodation, vessel schedules and crew rosters in one interface. It tracks travel status in real time, allowing crewing teams to respond to missed connections and schedule changes before they disrupt crew handovers. Companion product SmartAccess handles entry permissions at terminal gates, gangways and offshore installations. The platform checks personnel credentials, required certifications and authorisations against access requirements, including those associated with the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code. It can also be paired with SmartSea’s FacePod biometric units to match arriving seafarers and contractors with authorised personnel records, reducing reliance on manual documentation checks. “Crew movements involve ongoing coordination between travel coordinators, port agents, technical managers, and vessels,” said SmartSea CEO Kris Vedat. “When systems operate independently, small itinerary changes can create scheduling difficulties and extra administrative work.” SmartSea said the platforms provide operators with a connected view of who is expected to arrive, their current transit status and whether they have the necessary clearance to board. Both products are being offered to commercial shipping fleets, offshore support vessels, marine terminals and offshore energy facilities.

items.summary: Nasdaq-listed Greek shipowner Pyxis Tankers has agreed to acquire the remaining 40% stake in one of its ultramax bulkers from a company linked to its chairman and chief executive, Eddie Valentis. The deal, valued at approximately $6.83m before a separate working capital adjustment, will give Pyxis full ownership of the company holding the 2016-built Japanese ultramax Konkar Ormi . The 63,250 dwt, scrubber-fitted vessel was acquired for $28.5m in October 2023 through a joint venture in which Pyxis took a 60% controlling interest and a Valentis-affiliated company acquired the balance. The latest transaction values the bulker at approximately $32.08m, based on three independent shipbroker appraisals. After deducting $15m of vessel-related debt, the ship’s net appraised equity value stands at approximately $17.08m, putting the minority stake at $6.83m. Pyxis entered the dry bulk market in 2023 through the original joint venture with Valentis, subsequently expanding its exposure with two kamsarmax acquisitions. The company currently operates three bulk carriers alongside three MR product tankers.

items.title: The floating container platform turning heads
items.original_title: The floating container platform turning heads
items.summary: Every so often a ship comes along that makes even seasoned shipping watchers look twice. Meet the Fan Zhou 8, an extraordinary floating container platform that has just carried more than 3,000 teu out of China. According to Alphaliner, German independent carrier Carrier53′ Shipping chartered the 2024-built, 58,405 dwt heavy-load deckship from China’s Jiangsu Fanzhou Shipping for a September loading at Taicang, near Shanghai. The boxes were arranged in 17 bays and 20 rows, stacked five tiers high, with just two tiers on the outer rows. The voyage was arranged in cooperation with container trader Lotus Containers. Carrier53′ specialises in unconventional cargo movements, including oversized 53 ft containers manufactured in China for the North American market. The Fan Zhou 8 headed towards the Red Sea after loading, although its final destination has not been disclosed. Sea Legend’s 1,480 teu Tiger Maanshan recently reached Felixstowe and Rotterdam after sailing from China via the Northern Sea Route. Unlike the Fan Zhou 8, however, that vessel was specifically designed to carry LNG tank containers.

items.title: Tsakos returns to containership contracting in China
items.original_title: Tsakos returns to containership contracting in China
items.summary: Greek shipping group Tsakos has returned to the containership newbuilding market, emerging behind an order for two 3,200 teu vessels at China’s Hengli Heavy Industries. The pair appear in the Athens-based owner’s latest fleet register, with both scheduled for delivery in the fourth quarter of 2028. Both will be scrubber-fitted and equipped with alternative maritime power systems, allowing them to connect to shore-side electricity while alongside. The deal marks Tsakos’ first return to boxship contracting since 2022, when the group booked a series of approximately 2,800 teu vessels at HD Hyundai Mipo in South Korea. The ships are scheduled for delivery in 2028 and were reported at about $78m apiece. Tsakos’ fleet now stands at 112 vessels including newbuildings, with a 23-ship orderbook spanning tankers, LNG carriers, dry bulk vessels and the latest containership pair. The Greek owner is not alone in targeting Hengli’s 3,200 teu design. German non-operating owner Elbdeich Reederei has now also been linked by shipbuilding sources to two 3,200 teu ships at Hengli, again for 2028 delivery. The pair are reported at about $48m each, matching the market indications around the Tsakos vessels.

items.title: Hormuz shock briefly makes biofuel the cheapest bunker option
items.original_title: Hormuz shock briefly makes biofuel the cheapest bunker option
items.summary: The upheaval in global energy markets caused by the war in the Middle East has produced an unexpected winner in the marine fuels market, with biodiesel briefly emerging as the cheapest bunkering option in Rotterdam once European carbon costs are factored in. A new white paper from energy pricing specialist General Index and the London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) reveals that B30, a blend of 30% used cooking oil methyl ester (UCOME) and 70% very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO), became $74.61 per tonne cheaper than conventional VLSFO in April. The calculation incorporates EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) allowances and potential FuelEU Maritime penalties. In the preceding three months, B30 had been between $11 and $27 per tonne more expensive than conventional VLSFO on the same basis. The researchers also found that B100 UCOME, after incorporating carbon costs, traded at a discount to marine gasoil for eight weeks between March and May. The reversal came as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz sent fossil fuel prices soaring. SAF prices jumped $636 per tonne between February and March despite having supply chains largely independent of Hormuz. The findings highlight a widening difference between shipping and aviation.

items.title: Elisabeth Braw: The Undersea War
items.original_title: Elisabeth Braw: The Undersea War
items.summary: A ship’s anchor can wreak havoc on the world’s undersea infrastructure, something that has provided plenty of rich material for Splash reporting in recent years. For Elisabeth Braw, the Cook Islands-flagged tanker Eagle S provides one of the most brazen examples. On Christmas Day 2024, the vessel was accused of dragging its anchor 90 km across the Gulf of Finland seabed, severing the Estlink 2 power link and four telecommunications cables before Finnish authorities intervened. That collision between maritime law and an emerging security threat runs through Braw’s new book, The Undersea War: The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World , published by John Murray this month. Braw, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who leads research into threats to the global maritime order, started writing in October 2024, having followed the subject for considerably longer. The 2022 Nord Stream pipeline explosions remain in the headlines. The Eagle S affair followed the Yi Peng 3 cable investigation and has been succeeded by further suspected anchor-dragging incidents in the Baltic. The book ranges from the Baltic to the Pacific, drawing on interviews with naval officers, undersea engineers and cable operators to show just how dependent modern economies have become on infrastructure that is difficult to monitor and harder still to defend.

items.title: Lloyd’s Register, Shell and GTT to explore hybrid-electric 200,000m³ LNG carrier concept
items.original_title: Lloyd’s Register, Shell and GTT to explore hybrid-electric 200,000m³ LNG carrier concept
items.summary: The project will explore how hybrid-electric propulsion and GTT NEXT1®cargo containment system technology could support potential improvements in LNG transport efficiency. Lloyd’s Register (LR), Shell and GTT have launched a Joint Development Project (JDP) to develop a conceptual 200,000m³ LNG carrier combining hybrid-electric propulsion with GTT NEXT1® cargo containment technology. By bringing together a larger-capacity vessel concept with hybrid-electric propulsion and GTT NEXT1® cargo containment technology, the partners aim to explore how future LNG carrier designs could transport more cargo, operate more efficiently and provide greater flexibility as industry requirements continue to evolve. Under the JDP, the partners will work on the development and safety verification of the vessel’s hybrid-electric propulsion system, focusing on system architecture, redundancy philosophy and battery integration, while also exploring the commercial evaluation from a total cost of ownership (TCO) model. In parallel, the integration of GTT NEXT1® cargo containment technology will be assessed as part of the overall vessel concept. The project will also establish technical requirements and guidance for hybrid-electric propulsion in LNG carrier applications, helping to support further technical understanding of the technology.

The mass-balancing approach allows Shell to use existing LNG infrastructure to bring certified LBM into Singapore, without having to build dedicated facilities. The operation shows the “practical feasibility of bringing certified renewable gas into Singapore through existing LNG infrastructure, covering sourcing, certification, transportation, discharge and storage,” Shell added. items.title: The Confidence To Act: Why R&D And Lifecycle Support Are The Real Enablers Of Fleet Decarbonisation
items.original_title: The Confidence To Act: Why R&D And Lifecycle Support Are The Real Enablers Of Fleet Decarbonisation
items.summary: Industry analysis suggests that roughly two-thirds of the existing global fleet will not undergo major retrofits for next-generation fuels, primarily because of vessel age and the economics involved. For this majority, the industry needs solutions that deliver measurable emissions reductions today, without introducing operational risk or requiring capital commitments that cannot be justified. One approach to this challenge is in adopting a layered strategy, one that matches the right solution to the right vessel, at the right point in its lifecycle. Fuel supply systems are an enabler of that strategy, and the confidence to invest in them depends, more than anything else, on the quality of the engineering, R&D and lifecycle support that underpins them. Documented, applied research into how alternative fuels behave in practice, and how fuel supply systems must be designed to handle them, is the foundation on which ship owner confidence is built. This is why lifecycle services are integral to the value of any decarbonisation investment, not an optional extra. In a sector defined by long asset cycles and the need to make durable capital decisions under uncertainty, that matters. R&D provides the foundation, and lifecycle support sustains it. Together, they give ship owners the confidence that their decarbonisation strategy remains resilient as the transition unfolds.

items.title: Freight surge traps Americas heavy crude as Asia chases supply
items.original_title: Freight surge traps Americas heavy crude as Asia chases supply
items.summary: While Brent, the global benchmark for crude oil, is topping $100 a barrel, an unusual glut of heavy crude (high-density oil used to produce diesel, gasoline, and more) is building in North and South America. Competition to secure crude continues in Asia and Europe, but freight rates for tankers have surged in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war, making it harder to ship excess heavy crude from the Americas. In the Americas, crude supply has increased, but additional processing capacity at refineries is limited, causing inventories to pile up. But lately, even as heavy crude prices fall, refiners in Asia and Europe are finding it difficult to buy. Shipping to Asia costs $40 a barrel; even cheap crude is hard to export The biggest reason is the spike in tanker freight rates. Last week, the cost to ship crude from the Americas to Asia on a very large crude carrier topped $80 million (about 107.5 billion won). Scott Shelton, an energy specialist at energy broker TP ICAP, told Reuters, “The key is the shipping cost,” adding, “There is demand for tankers, but rates are rising and the number of available vessels is shrinking.” As shipping costs rise, prices for heavy crude from the Americas have fallen.

Through our collaborations with the DOE and industry leaders, ABS is pioneering the future of nuclear energy in maritime. We’re well-positioned to help turn this technology into a safe, real and practical option for commercial maritime applications.” DOE is leading U.S. Under the MOU, ABS will co-manage the Maritime Nuclear Applications Group (MNAG) and provide technical, regulatory, economic and policy support on concept and feasibility studies. (L to R): Ted Garrish, United States Assistant Secretary for Nuclear Energy, and John McDonald, ABS Chairman and CEO “Advanced nuclear technology has the potential to transform the commercial maritime industry and open new markets for American innovation,” said Assistant Secretary for Nuclear Energy Ted Garrish.

items.title: Fuel Switch Snapshot: Pooling slump erodes LBM’s compliance edge
items.original_title: Fuel Switch Snapshot: Pooling slump erodes LBM’s compliance edge
items.summary: All bunker prices described in the text below have been adjusted for calorific content to make them VLSFO-equivalent. They have estimated EU-EU voyage compliance costs included for Rotterdam, and nonEU-EU compliance costs included for Singapore. These account for EU ETS costs and FuelEU Maritime penalties, and the average price of compliance surpluses we have picked up from the FuelEU pooling market over the past week. LBM’s potential pooling values for EU-EU voyages have dropped by $74-87/mt depending on engine type. For nonEU-EU voyages, a smaller $36/mt drop in B100’s potential pooling value has pushed Singapore’s B100 prices up by $30/mt over the past week. Some deals even closed below the cost of generating a surplus, which OceanScore saw as a sign of “market overshooting.” Rotterdam LBM’s premiums over VLSFO have widened by $167-176/mt to $400-516/mt and its discounts to LSMGO have narrowed by $103-112/mt to $120-236/mt depending on engine type over the past week. LBM’s premiums over B100 have widened by $250-259/mt to $484-600/mt depending on engine type. Singapore’s conventional fuel prices have gained $1-54/mt, with HSFO up the most. Its potential pooling values have dropped by $74-87/mt, far more than the $13/mt drop in LNG’s potential pooling value for vessels with diesel slow speed (diesel SS) engines.

items.summary: Luxembourg has no coastline. But it is increasingly attracting some of the biggest names in Greek shipping. The latest is Metis Ship Management, the Athens-based venture associated with Nicos V. Vardinoyannis, whose 60,447-dwt Ultramax bulk carrier METIS MARU transferred from the Marshall Islands to the Luxembourg flag on 8 October 2026. Extensive delegation to leading classification societies allows owners to continue using familiar technical partners, while the Luxembourg Maritime Administration (CAM) offers direct access to decision-makers and a 24/7 duty service for urgent operational matters. Major maritime groups including Jan De Nul and DEME have long entrusted technically demanding vessels to the Luxembourg flag, while established operators such as Cobelfret have contributed to its maritime presence. 8419 aims to modernise the maritime register, bringing ship mortgage registration directly under CAM and reducing its dependence on other administrative bodies. The reform would also lay the groundwork for 24/7 maritime mortgage registration, a capability Stanley Maritime Luxembourg expects could become a first among EU registries. With METIS MARU joining the growing ranks of Greek-managed vessels under its flag, Luxembourg is showing that size is not everything.

items.title: Record-breaking tanker rates pile pressure on already high fuel prices
items.original_title: Record-breaking tanker rates pile pressure on already high fuel prices
items.summary: At the same time, demand for tanker capacity has surged as traders seek alternative routes and sources of supply, including increased shipments from the US. The opening of a protected corridor through Omani waters has enabled additional crude exports and vessel movements, but has also placed further strain on an already stretched market. Shuttle services now operate around the Strait of Hormuz, with under the radar activity and ship-to-ship transfers taking place outside the chokepoint. Crude tanker earnings rose tenfold on rush for capacity The capacity squeeze, combined with operating in risky war zones and facing highly elevated insurance premiums, has sent tanker rates soaring. Over the pandemic years of 2020-21, tanker earnings hit lows due to lower oil consumption and shipments. This resulted in an order book of just 4% of global crude carrier capacity, the lowest on record since the 1990s. With the recovery of oil demand and tanker rates in 2022 and 2023, order intake began to rebound. Although the average age of the crude fleet has also reached a multi-decade high of over 13 years and more scrapping can be expected, we can also expect more supply pressure. It’s all about geopolitics and how the Middle East conflict evolves, but tanker markets could still see a solid 2027.

items.title: Port of Los Angeles Sets All-Time Cargo Record as Imports Surge
items.original_title: Port of Los Angeles Sets All-Time Cargo Record as Imports Surge
items.summary: The Pier 300 channel at the Port of Los Angeles. Photo courtesy Port of Los Angeles The Port of Los Angeles handled a record 1,042,652 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in September, marking the busiest month in its 118-year history as strong consumer demand and shifting global trade routes continued to drive cargo volumes through the nation’s busiest container port. September’s total surpassed the previous monthly record, set in July 2025, by more than 20,000 TEUs. “September was a month for the record books, and it was part of an extraordinary run for the Port of Los Angeles,” said Executive Director Gene Seroka. “Consumer demand remains resilient, importers are replenishing inventories and more cargo is being allocated to Los Angeles as shippers navigate continued challenges along other global trade routes.” Loaded imports reached 545,696 TEUs in September, up 19% from a year earlier, while loaded exports climbed 10% to 125,751 TEUs. “With so much uncertainty in global trade, businesses are looking for greater flexibility in where they source, manufacture and move their goods.” For the first nine months of 2026, the Port of Los Angeles handled nearly 8.1 million TEUs, more than 3% ahead of the same period last year.

items.title: Look beyond AI productivity gains, forwarders told
items.original_title: Look beyond AI productivity gains, forwarders told
items.summary: Freight forwarders should focus on using artificial intelligence to capture lost gross profit and deliver more tailored customer service, rather than treating the technology primarily as a productivity tool, according to Erik Muttersbach, founder of AI software company Zauber. Speaking on The Loadstar Podcast , Mr Muttersbach said AI could transform freight forwarding into a higher-value, higher-margin business over the next three to five years, with a growing divide between companies that adopt the technology quickly and those that struggle to keep pace. Mr Muttersbach said 2025 saw a wave of AI start-ups and funding announcements, while 2026 has been characterised by companies running pilots and proofs of concept, alongside industry leaders committing to larger-scale deployments. He highlighted that rather than using AI to increase productivity, forwarders should instead target opportunities to improve profitability. AI could also help forwarders deliver on complex customer-specific requirements that have traditionally been difficult to manage consistently across global operations. “There’s an opportunity to do incredibly individual customer service every single time,” he stressed, and underscored that forwarders that continue offering only standardised services risk losing their competitive edge as customers increasingly expect individualised service to become the norm.

(Source: EMA) PARIS/MOSCOW, Oct 13 (Reuters) – France’s military was taking a tanker suspected to be part of Russia’s “shadow fleet” skirting Western sanctions to Reunion island on Tuesday in what Moscow called another act of “piracy.” Sanctions on Russia for invading Ukraine and aimed at cutting its oil revenue have spawned a fleet of often aging and unregulated vessels helping Moscow keep its crude exports flowing. The DF Peak, previously named the Kaliningrad and flagged from Benin, is at least the fifth Russian-linked tanker to be seized by France since 2024. France had also not notified Russia about the tanker’s seizure, it said. In a post on X on Monday evening, President Emmanuel Macron showed French military personnel intercepting and boarding the tanker from helicopters in what he said was some 450 nautical miles south of Reunion, a French territory in the Indian Ocean. The vessel has been hit by US, UK and EU sanctions in 2024. It was partially loaded and last seen off the coast of Madagascar on October 12 at 0429 GMT with its previous port listed as Guanta in Venezuela, LSEG ship tracking data showed.

items.summary: Bangladesh has signed a $336m loan agreement with China to expand and modernise Mongla port, as workers at the country’s main container gateway of Chittagong threaten an indefinite hunger strike over a deal handing a major terminal to DP World. Signed in Dhaka on Sunday, the loan will fund the construction of two container jetties, as well as a cargo and delivery yard, at Mongla, alongside the purchase of modern port equipment, with expectations of an increase in annual capacity of 394,000 teu. Dhaka-based garment exporter Rafayet Ullah said construction of the Padma Bridge would make Mongla a genuine alternative to Chittagong, telling The Loadstar: “The increased number of jetties and modern equipment means the port will be able to facilitate significant volumes.” The China-backed expansion comes as authorities in Bangladesh face opposition from port workers over a decision to award DP World a 15-year concession to operate Chittagong’s largest container terminal, the New-mooring Container Terminal (NCT). Signed on 8 October, extending the concession, the agreement has seen workers and members of left-wing political parties stage mass “symbolic” hunger strikes outside the port as they demanded the deal’s cancellation. The company’s own fleet register now lists six LR1 newbuildings, with the first two scheduled for delivery in 2029 and the remaining four in 2030. Splash reported in June that Emarat signed for three firm 930 teu feeder vessels plus three options at Hubei Guangji Xinneng Shipbuilding. The company’s current fleet page now lists six feeder newbuildings, four for 2028 delivery and two for 2029. That leaves Emarat with a newbuilding pipeline spanning 12 product tankers, four large gas carriers and six feeder containerships — a major expansion for a company whose current operating fleet numbers 19 ships.

items.title: Strong US import demand will support transpacific rates till new year
items.original_title: Strong US import demand will support transpacific rates till new year
items.summary: Transpacific container freight rates are likely to remain higher than on Asia-Europe for some time, as stronger economic conditions in the US support import demand and weaker European growth weighs on cargo volumes and freight rates. Evergreen general manager Wu Kuang Hui said the rate divergence had become increasingly pronounced: “strong on US routes, weak on Europe routes”. And he said on Friday he expected the stronger US market to continue supporting transpacific rates at a premium to Asia-Europe rates, and there was “no reason to be pessimistic” about the US routes before the lunar new year 2027 as “there are record-high import volumes at several major US ports, low inventory levels, and optimistic consumer demand”. US imports from the Far East have grown about 5.1%, but volumes to Europe have increased more rapidly, by 12.2%. On Friday, the Shanghai Containerised Freight Index showed Shanghai-US east and west coast rates relatively stable, at $10,524 and $7,584 per 40ft, respectively. Shanghai-Europe rates continued to decline, losing 3%, to $2,274 per teu. By contrast, transpacific capacity remains supported by robust US import demand. Mr Wu noted that US spot rates were significantly higher than negotiated rates in Q4 last year, and expects long-term contract prices next year to exceed this year’s.

items.summary: Malaysia’s Lianson Fleet Group (LFG) has added a third ultramax bulker, paying $23m (RM93.9m) for a 2013-built Japanese vessel as it continues to expand beyond its traditional offshore support vessel business. The purchase is being funded entirely from internal cash and will have no effect on group gearing. The latest purchase takes LFG’s disclosed spending on ultramaxes to around $75.3m in little more than three months. The pair came in at about $26.16m apiece. In June it agreed to pay $15.5m for the 2012-built, 56,735 dwt supramax Sea Affluence , taking disclosed spending on bulker acquisitions since June to about $90.8m. Managing director Lim Chern Wooi said the ultramax sector offered long-term opportunities as LFG develops into a more diversified maritime group. The company currently says it owns and operates 12 OSVs and 41 marine transportation assets spanning bulk carriers, tugs and barges.

items.title: Fujian Guohang maps out Hong Kong fleet expansion
items.original_title: Fujian Guohang maps out Hong Kong fleet expansion
items.summary: Chinese bulker owner Fujian Guohang Ocean Shipping is preparing to establish 12 wholly owned shipping companies in Hong Kong as it lays the groundwork for a newbuilding investment programme valued at approximately CNY2.49bn ($372m). The Beijing Stock Exchange-listed company disclosed on October 12 that its board had approved the creation of the subsidiaries through Guohang Ocean Shipping (Hong Kong) Holdings. Each company will have registered capital of $100,000, giving the proposed structure combined subscribed capital of $1.2m. Guohang has estimated the six-vessel investment at CNY2.49bn ($372m) and intends to raise up to CNY700m ($105m) through a private share placement. Of the proposed proceeds, CNY680m ($102m) has been earmarked for the vessels, with the remaining CNY20m ($3m) allocated to working capital. The Hong Kong restructuring comes just weeks after Guohang abandoned plans for a secondary listing on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. In September, the company said it would instead pursue a domestic equity placement to support fleet investment and strengthen its capital structure. Guohang has traditionally concentrated on dry bulk shipping, with its latest investment plans signalling an expansion into product tankers and specialised multipurpose tonnage. The new Hong Kong companies will also provide additional capacity for future shipowning arrangements beyond the initial six-vessel programme.

items.title: Bluecore takes nuclear barge plan beyond the drawing board
items.original_title: Bluecore takes nuclear barge plan beyond the drawing board
items.summary: US maritime nuclear startup Bluecore Energy has secured low-enriched uranium for its first floating power system as it moves ahead simultaneously with fuel, regulatory and class work. The Long Beach-based company has purchased uranium hexafluoride, or UF₆, enriched to 4.95% uranium-235 through nuclear fuel intermediary WMC. The material is being held at an undisclosed US nuclear fuel facility outside California while Bluecore works towards fuel fabrication, testing and validation. The move takes Bluecore another step beyond engineering and non-fuelled prototype work as it develops a compact water-cooled reactor designed from the outset for deployment on a floating platform. WMC buys, sells, stores, finances and transports materials across the nuclear fuel cycle, including enriched uranium products typically containing up to 5% uranium-235. Bluecore held its first pre-application meeting with the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission in August, presenting the reactor concept and discussing a potential licensing route. California planning records show the startup has leased warehouse, landside and submerged space at the port for its research operation and barge testing. The work sits within a wider US effort to bring nuclear technology into commercial maritime applications. Bluecore founder and chief executive Kofi Asante said the latest step is part of building the fuel, testing, engineering, safety, regulatory and class pathways together rather than sequentially.

The International Energy Agency also projected in September that global coal demand would reach a record high this year, despite ongoing efforts to transition to cleaner energy sources and the closure of numerous coal-fired power plants across Europe and North America. items.title: IMOS Fuel Types Expand from Six to Ten to Support Growing Operational Complexity
items.original_title: IMOS Fuel Types Expand from Six to Ten to Support Growing Operational Complexity
items.summary: A changing fuel landscape The fuels powering vessels have shifted sharply in recent years, and the first shift was regulatory. Heavy fuel oil made up about 79% of international shipping fuel consumption in 20181 until the International Maritime Organization (IMO) cut the sulfur limit from 3.50% to 0.50% in 2020.2 Singapore, the world’s largest bunkering port and an indicator of the global market, shows how fast the market moved: low-sulfur fuel oil rose from under 1% of bunker sales in 2018 to 63% in 2020.3 Then the market shifted again. Scrubbers brought high-sulfur fuel back,3 and HSFO reached 29.5% of fuels tested by Veritas Petroleum Services (VPS) in 2023,4 alongside 54.3% VLSFO and 14.2% MGO. Biofuel blends, LNG, LPG, and methanol add further fuel types, and biofuel volumes tested by VPS rose 50% in 2025, to 1.2 million MT.5 Regulation, which triggered the previous shifts, is now driving the next one. Expanded fuel types in IMOS To keep pace with these shifts, IMOS now supports up to ten fuel types per vessel, up from six. The same limit applies to time charter contracts, so a long-term charter can reflect the vessel’s full fuel configuration.

items.title: 1 in 12 Ocean Shipments Has a Blank Carrier ETA
items.original_title: 1 in 12 Ocean Shipments Has a Blank Carrier ETA
items.summary: Tradlinx, a supply chain data platform based in South Korea, today released findings from an analysis of more than 500,000 ocean container shipments a year, showing that carrier ETAs are not only inaccurate but frequently missing. Carriers left the ETA blank in 42,832 cases, or 8.43% of shipments, most often while cargo was waiting at a transshipment port. Across more than 500,000 shipments a year, carriers left the ETA blank in 42,832 cases. The ETA for the intermediate transshipment port was missing in 30,929 cases (6.09%), the final-destination ETA of transshipment cargo in 6,168 cases (1.21%), and the destination ETA of direct shipments in 5,735 cases (1.13%). In this group of 25,341 shipments (4.99%), the average carrier ETA error was 90.0 hours. Our data points to a more basic gap: for roughly one in twelve shipments, the ETA simply goes missing somewhere along the way,” Tradlinx said. The model produced an estimate wherever the carrier ETA was missing, and its average error came in 31.4% lower than that of carrier ETAs, at 10.6 hours versus 15.4 hours. The difference was largest where carrier ETAs went furthest off course: on shipments missed by 48 hours or more, average error fell from 90.0 hours to 9.2 hours.

items.title: Dutch bio-methanol plant targeting bunker market eyes 2027 investment decision
items.original_title: Dutch bio-methanol plant targeting bunker market eyes 2027 investment decision
items.summary: Renewable fuels producer Perpetual Next’s planned 220,000 mt/year bio-methanol plant in Delfzijl could start production by the end of the decade, with bunkering as a key target sector. Perpetual Next expects to take a final investment decision on its DeltaNor bio-methanol plant by the end of 2027, a company spokesperson told ENGINE. Permits are among the factors the decision depends on, the spokesperson added. On Monday, Perpetual Next and renewable hydrogen producer Lhyfe announced a memorandum of understanding to study supplying up to around 12,000 mt/year of renewable hydrogen to the plant. The hydrogen would come from a 120 MW project Lhyfe is developing in the same Delfzijl industrial area. Adding hydrogen to the gas DeltaNor makes from biomass could let the plant turn more of its carbon into methanol and raise output. Last month, Perpetual Next hired engineering firm Bilfinger to help bring the project to an investment decision. DeltaNor is one of five bio-methanol plants Perpetual Next is developing, alongside three in the US and one in Estonia. Source: By Nachiket Tekawade, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news/

items.title: Soybean Futures Hit 6-Week Low
items.original_title: Soybean Futures Hit 6-Week Low
items.summary: Soybean futures fell below $12.8 per bushel, hitting a six-week low as expectations for a record-large US crop and active harvesting weighed on prices. The USDA raised its 2026 soybean production forecast to 4.562 billion bushels from 4.535 billion in September, above expectations of 4.534 billion, while lifting its average yield estimate to 53.1 bushels per acre from 52.8. Mostly dry weather across the Midwest is allowing farmers to accelerate harvesting, with the USDA’s weekly crop progress report due Tuesday. Meanwhile, Brazil’s soybean planting is advancing at a record pace, with favorable rainfall supporting fieldwork. Traders are now monitoring potential Chinese demand following recent talks between Trump and Xi Jinping, although punitive Chinese tariffs continue to discourage private buyers. China also lowered its 2026/27 soybean production forecast to 20.36 million tonnes but kept its import outlook at 95.5 million tonnes, well below the USDA’s 115 million-tonne estimate. items.title: Iran threatens ships going dark in Hormuz
items.original_title: Iran threatens ships going dark in Hormuz
items.summary: Iran has warned that merchant ships switching off their identification and tracking equipment during what it deems unauthorised passages through the Strait of Hormuz will be treated as hostile, raising the stakes for vessels navigating one of the world’s most dangerous stretches of water. The warning comes as fresh details emerge of a wave of attacks on Sunday that extended beyond tankers to containerships. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) issued four retrospective alerts on Monday covering three tankers and a containership struck on October 11, bringing the day’s reported total to six. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), meanwhile, claimed to have attacked a VLCC attempting to transit without permission, releasing footage purportedly showing the fire-damaged, 298,800 dwt Al Maqam , owned by ADNOC Logistics & Services. It remains unclear whether the purported strike was among those reported by UKMTO or represents another incident. Two Indian seafarers remain missing after Sunday’s drone strike on the Nicaragua-flagged Petro Dolphin off Sohar, Oman. Nine crewmembers were rescued. The latest violence follows Saturday’s American airstrike against the Panama-flagged Ocean Molica in the Gulf of Oman, with Washington accusing the vessel of attempting to breach its naval blockade of Iranian ports.

items.title: Panagiotidis reveals stake in Trafigura-backed VLCC owner
items.original_title: Panagiotidis reveals stake in Trafigura-backed VLCC owner
items.summary: Petros Panagiotidis-controlled Robin Energy has taken a minority stake in Trafigura-backed Volare Shipping, adding indirect exposure to the VLCC market through the newly listed Oslo tanker owner. The Nasdaq-listed LPG carrier owner disclosed in a US Securities and Exchange Commission filing that it had participated in Volare’s private placement. Robin acquired 90,000 shares at NOK154 each, putting the investment at NOK13.86m ($1.45m). The investment follows Volare’s $500m capital raise and its move onto Euronext Growth Oslo earlier this month. Trafigura launched the shipping company in September to hold its expanding VLCC portfolio. Volare raised approximately $500m through an oversubscribed equity placement priced at NOK154 per share, valuing the company at around NOK11.5bn ($1.2bn) after the fundraising. The proceeds are intended to support outstanding newbuilding commitments, debt reduction and other corporate requirements. The company previously held a tanker alongside its gas carriers before selling that vessel earlier this year. In September, affiliated owner Toro outlined another fleet reshuffle involving the proposed separation of its remaining LPG vessels into a standalone Nasdaq-listed company.

items.title: French marines swoop on former Sovcomflot tanker in the Indian Ocean
items.original_title: French marines swoop on former Sovcomflot tanker in the Indian Ocean
items.summary: France has taken its crackdown on Russia’s shadow fleet into the Indian Ocean, boarding a former Sovcomflot aframax more than 450 nautical miles south of Réunion. French marines descended by helicopter onto the 110,119 dwt DF Peak on Monday after authorities questioned the validity of its claimed Benin registration. President Emmanuel Macron said the vessel was suspected of sailing under a false flag and involvement in illicit fuel transportation. “France is determined to combat the shadow fleet, wherever it may be in the world,” Macron declared. The French military said the boarding was conducted under Article 110 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which permits inspections of vessels suspected of lacking valid nationality. Built in 2006, the tanker previously traded as NS Captain for Russian state-controlled Sovcomflot before becoming Kaliningrad in 2024 and subsequently DF Peak. The vessel has been under EU sanctions since June 2024 and is also blacklisted by Washington and London. Ukrainian intelligence links the ship to Russian crude exports. The operation follows several French interventions against Russia-linked tankers in European waters, including the interception of the Deliver off Sicily in June.

items.title: Washington teams up with ABS to accelerate nuclear shipping
items.original_title: Washington teams up with ABS to accelerate nuclear shipping
items.summary: The US Department of Energy (DOE) has joined forces with classification society ABS to accelerate the development of commercial nuclear-powered shipping and floating power plants. The agreement with DOE’s Office of Nuclear Energy covers feasibility studies for floating reactors, dedicated nuclear shipping corridors and the ports, shipyards and industrial infrastructure required to build and support nuclear-powered vessels. ABS will co-manage the Maritime Nuclear Applications Group, providing technical, regulatory and economic expertise, while coordinating related work through the US Maritime Administration’s Center for Maritime Innovation. “Advanced nuclear technology is moving from concept to application, and the maritime industry needs to be ready for it,” said ABS chairman and CEO John McDonald. In 2022, DOE contracted ABS to examine barriers to commercial nuclear propulsion, while the class society subsequently published the industry’s first comprehensive rules for floating nuclear power plants. As Splash reported in July, ABS approved in principle a South Korean 15,000 teu containership concept incorporating a molten salt reactor, following earlier approvals for floating nuclear power modules developed by HD Hyundai. Last month, ABS backed a study examining the economics of a 174,000 cu m nuclear-powered LNG carrier. The vessel would cost approximately 2.5 times as much to build as a conventional LNG carrier, although researchers projected lower lifetime costs under certain carbon-pricing scenarios.

items.title: TGS expands frontier basin data coverage offshore Brazil
items.original_title: TGS expands frontier basin data coverage offshore Brazil
items.summary: Oslo-listed seismic specialist TGS, in joint venture with SLB, has announced the Pelotas Sul Phase 2 multi-client 3D survey offshore southern Brazil. The survey will cover about 11,200 sq km, and a Ramform Titan-class vessel is scheduled to begin data acquisition in October 2026, with completion in the second or third quarter of 2027. Building on Pelotas Sul Phase 1, acquired earlier this year, the new survey will further expand TGS’ high-quality 3D seismic coverage in a frontier basin that continues to attract industry interest. Geological analogues along the conjugate margin support the Pelotas Basin, and discoveries in Namibia de-risk it. The basin offers a broad range of underexplored play concepts, including turbidite systems, deep-water channels, and stratigraphic and structural traps. Pelotas Sul Phase 2 includes a balanced mix of held and open acreage. This provides data coverage relevant to companies evaluating existing acreage, while also creating opportunities linked to future licensing rounds and potential farm-in activity. “The project will provide additional high-quality subsurface insight across both held and open acreage, supporting our customers as they evaluate existing positions and future exploration opportunities in the southern Pelotas Basin,” said Kristian Johansen, CEO of TGS.

The warning extends well beyond electronic charts. The guidance urges operators to identify precisely which systems depend on satellite-derived data, establish procedures for detecting interference and regularly drill crews in alternative navigation methods. Maritime intelligence firm Windward’s latest figures show an average of 5,131 GPS jamming incidents a day during the third quarter, with more than 124,000 individual vessels affected. More recently, SplashTech reported how four tankers in the Black Sea had apparently broadcast positions placing them in Lima, Peru, more than 12,000 km away. items.summary: HOUSTON, Oct 12 (Reuters) – Dense heavy crude, which oil refiners around the world favor for its typically low cost, is piling up in the Americas as soaring freight rates have stifled exports and US refiners have been running close to their limits. The glut in North and South America has opened an unusual split in the global oil market, as buyers in Asia and Europe struggle with supply shortages and benchmark prices hold above $100 a barrel. Heavy crude is a denser type of oil that Asian, many US, and some European refineries are typically configured to process. Flagship Canadian, Colombian and Ecuadorian heavy crude grades have all eased more than $10a barrel to trade at their lowest level in six weeks, according to price reporting agency Argus Media. The cost of a tanker from the Americas to Asia rose to more than $80 million, or about $40 a barrel, last week compared with around $10-15 million near the start of the year. Cokers convert residual crude oil into feedstocks for diesel and gasoline production, and a heavier crude slate requires them to run at a higher capacity. Many US refineries are also configured for offshore Gulf of Mexico crude such as Mars Sour, rather than Canadian or Venezuelan oil that must be mixed with lighter feedstock.

items.title: Yangzijiang Maritime adds kamsarmax bulkers to newbuild spree
items.original_title: Yangzijiang Maritime adds kamsarmax bulkers to newbuild spree
items.summary: Singapore-listed Yangzijiang Maritime Development has struck a bulk carrier newbuilding deal in China, for up to six kamsarmaxes at Jiangsu Watts Energy & Engineering. The Ren Yuanlin-led maritime investment group has signed for four firm 82,000 dwt vessels, with options for another two, according to Chinese shipbuilding sources. The deal would mark Yangzijiang Maritime’s first reported order at Watts, which has only recently entered conventional merchant ship construction. In August, the Qidong-based yard secured its first kamsarmax contract from Xiamen-based Amoysailing Maritime, covering four 82,000 dwt vessels for delivery in 2028. That contract was estimated at around $35m to $38m per vessel for standard specifications, although no pricing has surfaced for the latest reported Yangzijiang Maritime series. The order adds another chapter to Yangzijiang Maritime’s aggressive expansion across several shipping segments. That programme lifted its disclosed newbuilding portfolio to 98 vessels, comprising 75 firm ships under construction, 16 options and seven vessels already delivered. Yangzijiang Maritime has increasingly turned to smaller Chinese yards to secure competitively priced newbuildings, combining its shipbuilding investments with chartering, leasing and pre-delivery vessel sales. The company has also been expanding its tanker exposure, with its reported programme at Jiangsu Haifeng Shipbuilding now covering six firm and two optional 114,000 dwt LR2s.

items.summary: Malaysian shipping group MISC is preparing another five LNG carrier newbuildings in China after securing a fresh long-term charter award from compatriot Petronas. The Bursa Malaysia-listed owner has accepted a letter of award from Petronas LNG, covering five new LNG carriers on firm 20-year charters. MISC said it would enter into shipbuilding contracts with Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding, part of China State Shipbuilding Corporation, to construct the vessels. The latest award comes on top of a separate five-vessel programme agreed earlier this year . MISC initially contracted three 174,000 cu m LNG carriers at Hudong-Zhonghua, adding another two in February. Petronas subsequently confirmed a 20-year charter agreement for all five, with employment scheduled to begin between 2029 and 2030. MISC has steadily expanded its gas carrier orderbook through long-term employment agreements with the Malaysian energy group. items.title: Shippers warned: spot rates no pointer to wider box shipping market
items.original_title: Shippers warned: spot rates no pointer to wider box shipping market
items.summary: Spot rates have become more volatile, relative to the wider box shipping market, since the pandemic, with overall prices increasingly diverging from signals provided by the spot market. In its latest analysis, Sea-Intelligence, compared spot rate movements on the Asia-Europe and transpacific trades with broader market developments, using World Container Index (WCI) and Container Trade Statistics (CTS) data. The consultant compared monthly average WCI rates for Shanghai-Rotterdam and Shanghai-Genoa with CTS data for Asia-Europe. Sea-Intelligence used this relationship to forecast the overall market rate index from spot rate movements, and then compared its predictions with the actual CTS figures. Before the pandemic disruptions, Sea-Intelligence found, the difference between forecast and actual market rates fluctuated relatively little, suggesting spot rates provided a reasonably reliable indication of wider market developments. However, deviations became substantially larger from 2020, which the analyst said reflected a greater disconnect between spot rate movements and the market as a whole – also evident when fluctuations were measured relative to overall rate levels, meaning it could not simply be attributed to higher freight rates. Sea-Intelligence also identified a gradual upward trend in the difference between forecast and actual rates on Asia-Europe, indicating that the overall market increasingly recorded higher rates than would have been predicted from spot prices alone.

items.title: UK Natural Gas Prices Rise to 2022 High
items.original_title: UK Natural Gas Prices Rise to 2022 High
items.summary: UK natural gas prices rose to 205.3 pence per therm, the highest since December 2022, as increased tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and escalating regional tensions heightened concerns over the security of LNG supplies. Despite a steady rise in European gas inventories in recent weeks, storage facilities are around 73% full, still below year-ago levels. However, this recovery could be threatened by forecasts of cooler autumn temperatures, which may lead to an earlier start to the heating season and increase gas consumption. Last week, European gas network operators said the system was flexible enough to meet winter demand but warned that limited supplies could push storage below 30% by winter’s end, increasing vulnerability to late-season cold snaps. Meanwhile, growing renewable output in the UK has reduced dependence on gas-fired electricity, but the country remains exposed to fuel price swings. Source: Trading Economics

items.title: LNG Shipping Market Softer, But LPGs On the Rise Again
items.original_title: LNG Shipping Market Softer, But LPGs On the Rise Again
items.summary: The LNG market softened this week, despite an increase in spot, multi-month and longer-term requirements entering the market. While activity picked up compared to recent weeks, vessel availability continues to outweigh cargo demand, keeping pressure on freight rates across both basins. On the BLNG1 Australia–Japan route, rates declined by $2,300 week-on-week to settle at $34,600/day. The six-month rate fell by $1,600 to $46,300/day, while the one-year term declined by $334 to $52,033/day. Further out the curve, the three-year period eased by $350 to $69,950/day. The LPG market strengthened this week, with a relatively tight tonnage list and several outstanding cargoes supporting freight rates. On the BLPG1 Ras Tanura–Chiba route, rates settled at $265.00/tonne, with the corresponding TCE at $258,182/day. The BLPG2 Houston–Flushing route increased by $18.00 over the course of the week to close at $190.83/tonne, while TCE rose by $25,114 to $227,905/day. Similarly, the BLPG3 Houston–Chiba route gained $22.00 to settle at $344.71/tonne, with TCE increasing by $15,331 to $214,030/day.

items.title: The Commodities Feed: Oil lower despite Middle East escalation
items.original_title: The Commodities Feed: Oil lower despite Middle East escalation
items.summary: Energy – Middle distillate cracks trade lower on Trump diesel deal After a weekend of escalation in the Middle East and the risk of the conflict broadening, one would think oil prices would be trading firmer this morning. However, this is not the case. ICE Brent has been down more than 2% at one stage this morning, despite the Houthis launching a deadly attack on an airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Still, events show that risks to supply from the region remain, despite oil flows from the Persian Gulf being at their highest levels since the start of the US-Iran war. It would appear that the move in oil today is probably less to do with developments in the Middle East and more to do with Russia. Clearly, in the run-up to the midterm elections, pressure is growing on Trump to address high oil and diesel prices – but in order to see a more meaningful move lower in refined product prices, we will need to see normalisation in the Middle East. Inefficient trade flows of oil from the Middle East have led to a significant surge in tanker freight rates, which will likely keep product prices elevated.

items.title: Why are EU gas prices not higher already?
items.original_title: Why are EU gas prices not higher already?
items.summary: European natural gas prices have remained relatively contained despite major disruptions to Middle Eastern liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports, as additional supply and weaker demand have cushioned the impact, according to UBS analysts. In an October 5 report, UBS said higher LNG production outside the Middle East and reduced consumption across Europe and Asia had helped offset supply losses caused by the Iran war. Middle Eastern LNG supply declined by approximately 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) between March and September, while additional production elsewhere contributed nearly 40 bcm, including 17 bcm from the United States. European gas storage remains roughly 15% below seasonal averages, with inventories expected to enter winter at 74% capacity and decline to approximately 25% by spring. UBS consequently raised its fourth-quarter Dutch TTF gas price forecast to €75 per megawatt-hour from €62 previously. Its 2027 forecast increased to €45 from €40, reflecting expectations of a slower recovery in Qatari LNG exports and continued European efforts to phase out Russian gas. Under a prolonged disruption scenario accompanied by colder weather, UBS sees fourth-quarter TTF prices averaging €90/MWh, with potential peaks near €120/MWh. A faster recovery in Qatari shipments and milder temperatures could instead bring fourth-quarter prices towards €50/MWh.

items.summary: As Klaveness entered its eighth decade, the direction set during the previous period began to take shape. The combination carrier business prepared to enter new markets, digital initiatives moved closer to customers, and the foundations of the Klaveness business we know today was beginning to emerge. Over the next ten years, many of these initiatives would evolve into focused businesses in their own right. A new generation of combination carriers In 2018, Klaveness Combination Carriers was established as a separate company and began trading on the Norwegian stock exchange, creating a dedicated platform for the combination carrier business and its continued development. New partnerships and investments In its dry bulk business, Klaveness increasingly focused on the areas where it believed it could create the greatest value for customers: building long-term partnerships, developing innovative pool solutions, and using data and technology to support better commercial decisions. That direction was reinforced in 2020 through the partnership with Marubeni Corporation to operate the Baumarine Panamax pool, which entered a new phase in 2023 when Marubeni acquired a 25% stake in Klaveness Dry Bulk. items.title: Chinese buyers snap up capesizes
items.original_title: Chinese buyers snap up capesizes
items.summary: While tankers have dominated headlines in October, Chinese buyers are quietly putting money on the table for more capesize tonnage, emerging behind some of the dry bulk market’s most eye-catching deals. Estonian outfit Klip Marine is reportedly exiting the segment by selling the Ekaterini V (173,555 dwt, built 2012 at Bohai Shipbuilding) to Chinese buyers for $35m, with its special survey and drydocking due in January. The vessel has changed hands at a discount of more than $5m to another Chinese-built capesize sale. The comparable transaction is the Golden Myrtalia (177,979 dwt, built in 2011 at Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding), which reportedly fetched more than $40m, also from Chinese buyers. Brokers suggest the price gap may partly reflect the Ekaterini V’s slightly smaller size and differences in market reputation between the two Chinese shipyards. These are the first two reported capesize sales since September, a month that was closed with a sale in the same age bracket, sealed by Shanghai-listed HNA Technology, who agreed to 175,900 dwt Bulk Joyance (built 2012 at Jinhai Heavy Industry) for $31.1m, with relatively prompt delivery.

items.title: Hapag-Lloyd suspends bookings to three Philippine ports as container crisis deepens
items.original_title: Hapag-Lloyd suspends bookings to three Philippine ports as container crisis deepens
items.summary: Hapag-Lloyd has suspended new bookings to Manila, Batangas and Subic Bay until the end of December, as worsening congestion and a chronic shortage of empty-container storage capacity disrupt Philippine supply chains. The German carrier stopped accepting bookings to the three gateways from all origins and across every trade lane on September 29, citing severe constraints on container returns. Existing bookings may also face cancellation or revised arrangements. The crisis centres on the Philippines’ longstanding trade imbalance, with significantly more laden containers arriving than departing, leaving carriers struggling to find space for empty boxes. Philippine Ports Authority general manager Jay Santiago has urged foreign shipping lines to establish additional empty-container depots, describing this as the quickest solution to the worsening logistics bottleneck. Mary Zapata, president of the Confederation of Truckers Associations of the Philippines, told local newspaper Daily Tribune that some operators have waited as long as 40 days to return empty boxes. The problems triggered industrial action earlier this month, prompting the Philippine Bureau of Customs to acknowledge the severe pressure on truckers, customs brokers, importers and exporters. Subic Bay waiting times, however, remain below 12 hours, while Batangas operations are described as normal.

items.title: Pollution Risk from Overboard Pipes Routed Through Fuel Oil Tanks
items.original_title: Pollution Risk from Overboard Pipes Routed Through Fuel Oil Tanks
items.summary: There have been two more pollution incidents arising from a similar arrangement. In both cases, an Oil Discharge Monitoring Equipment (ODME) overboard discharge pipe was routed through a bunker fuel tank before terminating at the ship’s side. Why These Arrangements Warrant Attention An overboard pipe routed through a bunker or cargo oil tank can create a single-point failure with potentially significant pollution consequences. If a defect develops in a section of pipe located between the isolation overboard valve and the vessel’s shell, fuel oil may enter the pipe downstream of the closed valve and continue flowing directly overboard. Recommended Actions The West of England strongly recommends that Members and ship managers review the overboard piping arrangements across their fleets, giving particular attention to any overboard pipe that passes through a bunker or cargo oil tank and is capable of creating a direct route between a tank containing oil and the sea following loss of pipe integrity. Members may wish to consider the following: Identify Vulnerable Arrangements Review piping diagrams, tank plans, construction drawings and onboard arrangements to identify any overboard pipe routed through a bunker or cargo oil tank. Review Maintenance and Inspection Programmes Planned maintenance systems should identify and specifically address concealed or difficult-to-access overboard pipework routed through oil tanks.

According to Clarkson Research, a British shipbuilding and shipping market analysis agency, on Oct. Among these, South Korean shipyards won orders for 44 vessels, recording a 53.7% market share. The gap between the two countries, which was 29 vessels last year when South Korea accounted for 32 vessels and China for 3 vessels out of the global order volume of 37 vessels, has narrowed to within 10 vessels this year. Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding, which is leading the construction of Chinese LNG carriers, began building a 271,000 cubic meter-class LNG carrier starting in June. Compared to the 174,000 cubic meter-class LNG carriers that South Korean shipbuilders focus on, the cargo loading capacity increases by about 56%.
