items.title: Appetite for US crude oil exports climbs despite high freight
items.original_title: Appetite for US crude oil exports climbs despite high freight
items.summary: US crude exports remained elevated at 3.5 million b/d in September, edging up from 3.4 million b/d in August, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) data, but well below the May peak of 4.4 million b/d. South Korea was the largest single destination at 568,600 b/d, followed by the Netherlands at 459,000 b/d, with Japan, France, Canada and the UK also among the top receivers. Volumes into Asia climbed across the region, including Northeast Asia, where US exports rose from 793,000 b/d in August to 1.1 million b/d. Surging tanker rates have effectively closed the spot eastbound arbitrage for US crude exports to Asia. The arbitrage for WTI MEH into Rotterdam was $19.99/b as of Oct. South Korean and Japanese refiners, in particular, may continue to lift WTI cargoes under term supply arrangements or for crude diversification, regardless of whether the prompt spot arbitrage is open. The Netherlands’ 459,000 b/d intake is consistent with the strongly positive Rotterdam arbitrage and reflects the country’s dual role as both a refining center and a transshipment hub for the broader Northwest European market. With the WTI MEH-versus-Forties incentive at $14.72/b, Europe is the economic clearing destination for incremental US barrels, and transatlantic flows are likely to remain supported even after the climb in freight costs.

Danaos cautioned that there is no certainty a transaction will proceed and gave no timetable. The business sits under Danaos Bulk Inc and currently comprises 11 capesize bulkers on the water and four 211,000 dwt newcastlemaxes under construction for delivery in 2028. Splash tracked the expansion earlier this year when the owner moved into bulker newbuildings for the first time and subsequently doubled the programme to four ships. The latest addition to the operating fleet was the 2009-built, 182,425 dwt John Junior , formerly Hebei No.1 , which joined Danaos in March. A successful carve-out would leave Danaos with two more clearly defined shipping platforms, separating a bulker business that has grown to almost 2.8m dwt on a fully delivered basis from its much larger containership operation. items.title: Shipping’s extraordinary boom refuses to peak
items.original_title: Shipping’s extraordinary boom refuses to peak
items.summary: Global shipping earnings have reached another extraordinary milestone, with Clarksons Research’s cross-sector ClarkSea Index surging 12% in a week to an unprecedented $84,951 a day, its fifth consecutive all-time high. The index, a widely followed overall earnings barometer, measures average daily earnings across tankers, bulk carriers, containerships and gas carriers, weighted by vessel numbers in each sector. It covers approximately 80% of global shipping capacity, providing a broad measure of the industry’s fortunes. The latest reading dwarfs the previous shipping supercycle’s 2007 peak of $50,714 a day. Average VLCC earnings jumped another 21% last week to $804,601 a day, while suezmaxes climbed 17% to $724,398 and aframaxes surged 46% to $393,951. Elsewhere, dry bulk has softened, with capesize earnings retreating 16% to $31,130 and overall bulker earnings slipping 3% to $22,319. VLGCs are enjoying record earnings, reaching $209,000 a day on the US Gulf-Japan route, although LNG carriers remain the conspicuous laggard, with modern spot earnings down 19% to $34,250. The present boom is universal, transcending shipping sectors, as demand remains robust and ton-miles have been added as ships detour around war zones by taking longer routes home.

The proposal remains subject to shareholder approval, with a vote scheduled for October 26. The LNG dual-fuel vessel, built at CIMC Raffles in China and backed by Greek owner Atlas Maritime and Danish investment firm European Maritime Finance, began carrying Chinese-made vehicles to Europe in August, with calls including Gioia Tauro and Barcelona. Ningbo Ocean, controlled by Ningbo-Zhoushan Port Group, has traditionally concentrated on container and dry bulk shipping, building up its fleet through successive newbuilding programmes at Chinese yards.

The takeover remains conditional on Xin Yuan resuming share trading, which has been suspended since February 2025 following allegations concerning the company and certain directors. The current deadline for satisfying that precondition is October 30, although the buyer can extend it. Singapore-based Pioneer Logistics Holdings is looking to exit its indirect investment in Xin Yuan as part of the proposed transaction.

items.title: Tanker war spreads across Gulf
items.original_title: Tanker war spreads across Gulf
items.summary: Attacks on commercial shipping are spreading deeper into the Gulf as Iran widens its campaign beyond Hormuz, with a fully laden VLCC struck off the UAE and another tanker hit in the strait over the weekend. The Panama-flagged, 302,000 dwt Gem No.2 was struck by an unidentified projectile on Friday around 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera, UAE, sparking a fire that was subsequently extinguished. Maritime security firm Vanguard identified the vessel, which is managed in Taiwan and linked to U-Ming Marine Transport. India’s minister for ports, shipping and waterways, Sarbananda Sonowal, subsequently said the tanker had come under drone attack at Sharjah Anchorage and confirmed that all 22 Indian seafarers were safe. The attack followed another tanker strike off Qatar and came as Iran’s Revolutionary Guards warned they would pursue ships taking what Tehran considers unauthorised routes anywhere in the region, rather than just inside Hormuz. UK Maritime Trade Operations reported that an unidentified outbound tanker was struck on its port side by a projectile within Hormuz, triggering another fire. The vessel was not named and the account remains unverified. Meanwhile, in the Gulf of Oman, US forces struck the stern of the Panama-flagged bulker Ocean Molica, also known as Arika Sun, disabling its propulsion after it allegedly ignored warnings under Washington’s blockade of Iranian ports.

items.original_title: Saudi Aramco reportedly restores full crude oil supply to Europe for November
items.summary: Saudi Aramco has reportedly informed European oil refiners that it will supply them with all the crude oil they requested for November after the kingdom’s main cross-country pipeline returned to operation following attacks. At least three European refiners confirmed they will receive full allocations of crude oil from Saudi Arabia’s state oil company next month, Bloomberg news reporting citing people familiar with the matter. The return of supplies will help address a tight market in Europe after the disruption forced refiners to search for alternative sources. Last month, Aramco notified European refiners that they would receive no crude in October after an attack on the East-West pipeline. The situation prompted a rush to secure replacement cargoes. Orlen SA, the largest buyer of Saudi crude, issued more than ten tenders to purchase alternative barrels. Saudi Arabia typically exports an average of 700,000 to 800,000 barrels per day of crude to Europe, according to ship tracking data compiled by Bloomberg. Source: Investing.com

items.summary: A fire-damaged HMM containership is seeking a port of refuge in South Africa after salvors were appointed under Lloyd’s Open Form (LOF), with cargo interests facing the prospect of general average. The 5,593 teu HMM Platinum suffered a fire while sailing from Kattupalli, India, towards Santos, Brazil. The blaze reportedly originated in a container off southern Madagascar. Claims specialist W.E. Cox said the Liberian-flagged ship, built in 2013, was carrying around 2,300 containers and warned that damage could be substantial. Salvage specialist SMIT has been engaged under LOF terms, while a declaration of general average is considered likely. The vessel was initially expected to divert to Durban, with an anticipated arrival on October 8. However, the latest casualty advisory says alternative arrangements are being explored, with Gqeberha, formerly Port Elizabeth, identified as a possible port of refuge. items.title: Brazil unveils $4.1bn port concession programme and $858m infrastructure financing
items.original_title: Brazil unveils $4.1bn port concession programme and $858m infrastructure financing
items.summary: Brazil is preparing a major expansion of private investment in its ports, outlining a $4.1bn concession programme alongside new infrastructure financing opportunities and proposed regulatory changes designed to accelerate terminal development. The Ministry of Ports and Airports plans to auction 34 port concessions between 2027 and 2030, representing an estimated R$20.6bn ($4.1bn) in private investment. Among the largest projects is the Santos 10 container terminal, with estimated investment of $1.29bn. The government also plans to issue 70 authorisations for privately developed port facilities, representing a further potential $6.6bn in investment. Separately, Brazil’s Merchant Marine Fund has granted financing priority to three port infrastructure projects worth a combined R$4.28bn ($858m). The largest is the Terminal Mar Azul project at São Francisco do Sul, in Santa Catarina, with planned investment of approximately $381m in facilities for steel products and fertilisers. Another $252m has been earmarked for the concession covering the access channel to the Port of Paranaguá, while Hanseatic Global Terminals’ proposed container and general cargo terminal at Aracruz accounts for approximately $224m. A public consultation has been opened on proposed amendments to regulations governing port terminal leases, including changes that could make it easier for operators to expand facilities, replace equipment and undertake new investments.

items.summary: Two container terminals at Vietnam’s Cai Mep-Thi Vai port complex have begun joint commercial operations, creating a continuous 1,200-metre berth with the potential to add nearly 900,000 teu of annual capacity. Cai Mep International Terminal (CMIT) and Tan Cang-Cai Mep Thi Vai Terminal (TCTT) have connected their adjacent facilities to allow vessels, cargo-handling equipment and operational resources to be managed across both terminals. The arrangement enables three large containerships to be handled simultaneously, compared with a maximum of two previously. The operators estimate that the combined infrastructure could increase operating capacity at each terminal by 30% to 40%, equivalent to an additional 400,000 to 500,000 teu annually per facility. The joint berth follows more than two years of planning and operational trials. CMIT is a joint venture involving Vietnam Maritime Corporation, Saigon Port and APM Terminals, while TCTT is part of Saigon Newport Corporation.

items.summary: FuelEU Maritime has created a new market for compliance surplus. The price of that surplus now shapes how shipowners, charterers and fuel suppliers weigh their options, yet much of the industry still has to estimate what pooling really costs. Rystad Energy and OceanScore are working together to close that gap. Under a new data agreement, Rystad Energy will integrate two sets of OceanScore data. The first is offer data from the OceanScore FuelEU Marketplace, where surplus providers post offers to companies holding compliance deficits. The second is the OceanScore Pool Price Index (OPX), a volume-weighted benchmark for FuelEU pooling prices. The data will feed into Rystad Energy’s Clean Shipping Solution, which tracks the maritime energy transition across fleet development, ports and bunkering, fuel costs, and fuel supply and demand. items.title: Back to Suez – Why the rush?
items.original_title: Back to Suez – Why the rush?
items.summary: This is an extract from the Container Forecaster Issue 3 2026, released 30 September. The apparent eagerness of container lines to return to the Suez Canal is difficult to explain if the calculation is reduced to a simple voyage-cost comparison between Suez and the Cape. Drewry’s slot cost comparison shows only a marginal economic benefit to using Suez (see Table 1) with a saving of approximately $1 million per round-voyage, or $43 per slot, when comparing two services deploying ships of 24,000 teu that use either Suez or the Cape in both directions. If we assume a valuation of $225 million for the same example 24,000 teu containership going through Suez from Asia to Europe, a one-way war-risk premium of 0.3% of the hull value would heap an extra $1.35m for a round-voyage with two trips through the Joint War Committee listed area. The more convincing explanation for why carriers are so keen to return to Suez is that they are not really making a binary Suez versus Cape voyage decision based on economics alone. As such, we have adjusted our base case assumptions to a phase back of Suez transits starting July/August of 2026, reaching 80% of pre-diversion level by February 2027.

items.title: High stake fuel decisions
items.original_title: High stake fuel decisions
items.summary: That is the challenge at the heart of DNV’s latest white paper on methanol in shipping, which finds that many of the ship-related barriers surrounding methanol have fallen substantially since 2020. The bigger uncertainties now lie in fuel price and availability, regulation and, ultimately, whether owners can formulate strategies robust enough to withstand a changing decarbonisation landscape. Methanol has moved rapidly towards the mainstream. “The analysis should assess a ship or a fleet under a range of varying fuel and CO2 prices, covering all GHG regulations and associated GHG trajectories, to provide a clearer picture of the robustness of each fuel strategy,” DNV says. The strongest candidates then progress to a technical assessment examining what those fuel strategies mean for the actual ship. That covers storage capacity, bunkering frequency and operations, tank designs and possible locations, fuel preparation and supply, energy converters and changes to the vessel’s general arrangement. For owners unwilling to commit immediately to a single alternative fuel, the report also highlights Fuel Ready approaches, under which newbuildings can incorporate preparations for later conversion, including consideration of trim, stability and structural modifications. The fuel remains liquid at ambient temperature and pressure, bunkering infrastructure is comparatively close to conventional bunker arrangements and the technology is relatively mature.

items.title: Russian tanker operators lift crude exports to highest level since G7 price cap
items.original_title: Russian tanker operators lift crude exports to highest level since G7 price cap
items.summary: Russia increased crude exports in September by relying more heavily on non-G7 tankers, particularly those operated by domestic companies, whose shipments reached their highest level since Western nations imposed a price cap. Tankers flagged, owned and operated by companies not based in G7 countries and their allies, and not insured by Western protection and indemnity clubs, lifted nearly 2.89 million barrels/day in September, compared with 2.7 million b/d in August, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) and Maritime Intelligence Risk Suite data. The increase came as overall Russian seaborne exports rose to 4.09 million b/d from 3.82 million b/d in the same period. While the overall share of Russian crude exports on non-G7 tankers, mainly from the shadow flee established to bypass Western sanctions, showed little change month on month, Russian tanker operators were shouldering more responsibilities for their home country’s overseas sales. Continuing the upward trajectory seen in recent months, shipments rose from 18.6 million barrels in August to 20.6 million barrels in September — the highest since the G7 and EU began banning maritime service firms from participating in Russian crude exports unless the barrels were sold below a certain threshold in December 2022.

REUTERS/Hamad I Mohammed For a sign of just how extraordinary oil shipping costs have become, consider this: It’s now more expensive to hire a tanker from the US to China than to launch a rocket into space. That journey costs about $80 million, compared with $74 million for a standard SpaceX Falcon 9 launch, shipbroker Gibson said this week. The eye-watering prices are the result of a global tanker shortage that is getting worse with every additional barrel of oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz. “We’ve had pretty parabolic pricing.” The surge is a fresh complication for an oil market that has spent months adapting to the historic disruption caused by the Iran war. The value of a new oil tanker on the second-hand market has climbed to $240 million, the highest on record, according to Clarkson Research Services Ltd., a unit of the world’s largest shipbroker, and more than 60% above its level at the end of last year. While European refiner Repsol reported margins of $36 a barrel in the third quarter, analysts at RBC say those numbers contracted in October to about $15, partly as a result of high tanker costs.

The report, Ethanol as a Marine Fuel: Exploring Its Usability, published Thursday, examines whether ethanol can be used in existing marine engines and what modifications would be needed to make it commercially viable. Maersk has been testing ethanol aboard its methanol-fueled container vessel Laura Maersk since 2025, initially using a 10% ethanol blend before moving to higher concentrations. Despite those limitations, the study found that converting some existing vessels to operate on ethanol blends could make economic sense. For example, researchers found that a large container ship consuming approximately 25,000 tonnes of fuel annually could economically operate on a 30% ethanol blend across a wider range of fuel carbon intensities. The report also stops short of determining how much ethanol could realistically contribute to shipping’s overall decarbonization.

items.title: Is FOMO driving sentiment in the containership charter market?
items.original_title: Is FOMO driving sentiment in the containership charter market?
items.summary: The containership timecharter (T/C) market has taken another lurch upwards in recent months, with numerous participants describing a renewed scramble by liner operators – especially the largest European players – to secure any available tonnage. Most market benchmarks have participated in the recent strengthening, with the assessed one-year T/C rate for MSI’s 1,700 teu Grd (geared) Non-Eco benchmark rising from $28,800 a day in June to $34,100/day in September, and our 6,500 teu Gls [gearless] Non-Eco benchmark increasing from $68,400/day to $78,300/day over the same period. As noted in MSI’s Containerships Q3 26 report, the market cooled a little in the second half of September, compared with the height of the northern hemisphere’s summer, but this remains a market in which non-operating owners (NOOs) are firmly in the driving seat, and charterers are still willing to fix vessels in the liquid market segments for two-to-three years at healthy rates, and often for forward delivery dates. The lack of charter market-sized vessels available to hire, in both the near- and medium-term, means an upward movement in rates is the unsurprising outcome of a renewed fixing drive by the major liners.

items.title: BIMCO moves to break ship retrofit cost deadlock
items.original_title: BIMCO moves to break ship retrofit cost deadlock
items.summary: Shipping association BIMCO has adopted a new contractual framework designed to settle one of the industry’s longstanding commercial disputes: who pays for energy-saving upgrades when the charterer receives much of the financial benefit. The Copenhagen-based organisation announced that its Documentary Committee had approved the Energy Saving Device Retrofit Addendum 2026, giving shipowners and charterers a standard framework for negotiating retrofit projects during existing time charters. The addendum covers how the two parties share installation costs, time implications and the financial gains generated by lower fuel consumption. Rather than setting fixed percentages, it allows the parties to negotiate arrangements for individual projects. BIMCO said the addendum is technology-neutral and can accommodate different energy-saving systems, as well as the financial implications of existing and future environmental regulations. In June, BIMCO said development had reached its final stages, following consultation with industry participants and its Documentary Committee. The drafting process included representatives from Stena Rederi and Cargill Ocean Transportation. The new agreement is intended to provide a common contractual basis for retrofit projects that have previously required individually negotiated commercial arrangements. BIMCO said the addendum would be made available through its SmartCon contract platform, together with explanatory guidance.

He said natural gas prices are expected to increase further in the US, which is already among the most expensive locations globally for LNG production. “Henry Hub is going to get to the point where it becomes too expensive or you are not going to be too competitive,” Bronchalo said, referring to the US gas price benchmark. Joshua Lubarsky, president of maritime firm Seapath Group, noted at the same conference that while the US ranks among the world’s highest-cost LNG producers, its gas price dynamics provide stability that appeals to buyers. The financing structure for US LNG projects is shifting, with growing reliance on private equity supported by government-backed sovereign wealth funds, said Julie Mayo, general counsel at Sempra Infrastructure. Mayo pointed to Sempra’s use of private equity funds for expansion as an example of the new financing approach for US LNG projects, moving away from traditional external loans. Sempra operates as one of the largest US LNG exporters through its Cameron LNG facility and Port Arthur development. Source: Investing.com

items.title: US-Iran gunboat diplomacy and the challenge of reopening the Hormuz corridor
items.original_title: US-Iran gunboat diplomacy and the challenge of reopening the Hormuz corridor
items.summary: The US used its naval superiority, blockades, and economic sanctions to exert pressure; Iran responded by restricting traffic in the world’s most important shipping lane – the Strait of Hormuz. Therefore, the challenge of reopening the Hormuz Strait is not simply about getting oil tankers back on the shipping lane, but about finding a mechanism for the US and Iran to simultaneously step back from confrontation without either side being seen as unilaterally de-escalating. After more than seven months of the US-Iran conflict, the Strait of Hormuz holds a crucial position in all military , diplomatic, and economic calculations. Hormuz is also the shipping route for about 19% of global LNG trade, primarily from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that the 2026 Middle East conflict created “the biggest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market,” with the 15 million barrels of crude oil and 5 million barrels of refined products that normally pass through Hormuz daily at times being reduced to a fraction of that amount. Iran has employed another tactic, restricting and threatening the operations of numerous vessels deemed to be violating transit regulations, and expanding its list of banned ships from passing through Hormuz to at least 56 by early September.

items.title: BIMCO adopts addendum to support investments in retrofit projects
items.original_title: BIMCO adopts addendum to support investments in retrofit projects
items.summary: The shipping industry is working to improve fuel efficiency and ship performance to address decarbonisation requirements, new regulations and rising operational costs. To support these developments, BIMCO has adopted the Energy Saving Device Retrofit Addendum 2026. The new contractual framework is designed to facilitate the installation of energy-saving devices during the period of a time charter. Energy-saving technologies have become increasingly sophisticated, but investments in retrofit projects have been complicated by a misalignment of commercial interests between owners and charterers,” says Stinne Taiger Ivø, Deputy Secretary General & Director of Contractual Affairs at BIMCO. As a result, the incentive for parties to implement retrofit projects has been reduced, even when such projects could generate significant fuel savings and environmental benefits. The new addendum addresses this gap by allowing parties to customise how costs and benefits are shared for each project, rather than prescribing a single commercial model. Our objective has been to create a practical tool that can help unlock investments in retrofit solutions and support the industry’s decarbonisation efforts,” says Nicholas Fell, Chairperson of BIMCO’s Documentary Committee. The addendum has been drafted as a technology-neutral framework to accommodate a broad range of current and future energy-saving technologies.

items.summary: Lloyd’s List Intelligence (LLI) has launched Satellite Confirmed Spoofing, a new capability within its proprietary maritime intelligence platform, Seasearcher. This new functionality combines AIS spoofing detection with automatic satellite imagery validation, helping compliance, risk and intelligence teams identify deceptive vessel behaviour with greater confidence. The launch reflects growing demand for defensible intelligence, helping maritime organisations prioritise investigations, strengthen compliance processes, and make decisions based on independently validated evidence. Vessels seeking to evade scrutiny are broadcasting false positions that look entirely legitimate,” said Arne Staal, Chief Research Officer at Lloyd’s List Intelligence. “We’ve detected this behaviour for some time, but detection models are by nature probabilistic. We can now take our users from flagging probable spoofing events, to corroborating the event with satellite imagery. For compliance teams, insurers, and regulators, this marks a shift from inference to independent evidence, so they can decisively act on what the imagery shows rather than what a vessel chose to report.” Satellite Confirmed Spoofing is designed to support that mission by helping customers move from an inferred risk signal to a validated event. By combining maritime expertise, advanced analytics and satellite technology, we are making it easier for organisations to identify deceptive shipping practices and understand the evidence behind them. items.summary: Members of the UK P&I Club and TT Club have approved a merger to create United Transport Mutual Limited (UTM), a transport mutual covering shipping, logistics, ports, and terminals. Members voted at separate special general meetings on October 7 and 8, following member consultations that began in September. The merger is scheduled to take effect on February 20, 2027, subject to regulatory approval. The UK P&I Club insures more than 250m tonnes of owned and chartered tonnage, while TT Club covers about 80% of the world’s container fleet and has interests in more than 70 of the world’s 100 largest ports. The combined group expects annual premium income of about $750m and free reserves of around $888m. The clubs said the merger should improve the combined ratio by about 5%, while providing greater financial capacity, technical resources and access to specialist expertise. Both organisations will retain their names, brands, underwriting teams, claims operations and separate club committees. “For more than 50 years the TT Club and the UK P&I Club have worked side by side, so this merger is a natural evolution of a relationship built on shared values,” said TT Club chairman Morten Engelstoft. William Beveridge will succeed him as UK P&I Club chief executive, while Kevin King remains TT Club chief executive.

items.title: Tokyo Gas moves into Indonesian inter-island LNG shipping
items.original_title: Tokyo Gas moves into Indonesian inter-island LNG shipping
items.summary: Japan’s Tokyo Gas has acquired an Indonesian LNG infrastructure developer, paving the way for a new domestic shipping network supplying power stations across the country’s vast eastern archipelago. The Japanese utility, together with its wholly owned subsidiary Tokyo Gas Asia, has acquired 100% of PT AGP Indonesia Utama, which is developing a project to distribute domestically produced LNG using small-scale carriers and floating infrastructure. The venture will involve Indonesian state electricity company PLN’s fuel procurement arm, PLN Energi Primer Indonesia, and local shipping company PT Suasa Benua Sukses. The initial development envisages one floating LNG facility, six onshore installations and a small-scale LNG carrier serving six locations across Sulawesi and the Maluku Islands. The shipping network will operate around a central hub, with the LNG carrier supplying five other destinations. The acquisition gives Tokyo Gas a foothold in a market where geography presents both a challenge and an opportunity for small-scale gas shipping. Indonesia comprises more than 17,000 islands, many of which depend on relatively expensive diesel-fired power generation because of limited access to pipeline infrastructure. The proposed LNG distribution network is intended to reduce generation costs, cut emissions and lessen reliance on imported petroleum products.

items.title: German ports demand national funding pact
items.original_title: German ports demand national funding pact
items.summary: German port operators are pressing Berlin for a national funding partnership, arguing that infrastructure essential to trade, energy security and industrial supply chains cannot remain a purely regional responsibility. The Allianz Deutsche Häfen renewed its call at a Berlin gathering this week, bringing together port executives, industrial groups, retailers and federal transport representatives. Participants included parliamentary transport state secretary Christian Hirte and Lidl Germany boss Friedrich Fuchs. Salzgitter chief executive Gunnar Groebler argued that ports deserve the same national recognition as energy networks. “We should also treat our ports as what they are: strategic infrastructure of national interest,” he said. Participants stressed that spending must extend beyond terminals to the roads, railways and waterways connecting them with industry and consumers. The alliance’s wider demands include substantially higher federal contributions to port funding and money from Germany’s special infrastructure fund to tackle the modernisation backlog. Its members include bremenports, Brunsbüttel Ports, Duisburger Hafen, Hamburg Port Authority, Seehafen Kiel, Lübeck Port Authority, Niedersachsen Ports and Rostock Port. The group wants faster delivery and closer coordination between government, industry and port operators, presenting reliable gateways as a prerequisite for German competitiveness rather than a concern confined to coastal states.

items.title: Old LNG carriers keep changing hands
items.original_title: Old LNG carriers keep changing hands
items.summary: Sales of vintage large LNG carriers remain brisk as the secondhand market keeps ageing LNG tonnage afloat after the Strait of Hormuz conflict escalated in late February, with disruptions to regional LNG exports adding uncertainty to global supply. The latest sale has been completed by South Korean shipowner and manager Kmarin Group, selling the 18-year-old, 152,000 cu m Kmarin Diamond to Indonesian buyers for around $65m. Indonesian players have been among the most active buyers of ageing gas carriers this year. The first is the 18-year-old, steam-powered LNG carrier Tangguh Batur (145,700 cu m), reportedly sold for $30m. NYK has also sold the 2013-built, 177,427 cbm Grace Dahlia to Golar LNG for conversion. In August, Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha (K Line) sold its 20-year-old Arctic Voyager (142,759 cu m) for $28.5m to Karpowership interests, with the steam-powered vessel earmarked for conversion into a floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU). This week on the recycling side, BW has let go of the 2007-built LNG carrier Kano, a vessel reported to have cracked cargo tanks. The ship has been sold for recycling in India at $530 per ldt. LNG Kano is the seventh LNG carrier to be sent for recycling this year.

items.title: Hapag-Lloyd exits MSC and ONE Asia–South America pact
items.original_title: Hapag-Lloyd exits MSC and ONE Asia–South America pact
items.summary: Mediterranean Shipping Co (MSC) and Ocean Network Express are restructuring their vessel-sharing partnership between Asia and South America’s east coast, with Hapag-Lloyd dropping out of the existing three-carrier arrangement. MSC said that the current agreement covering the Ipanema service would end in its present form, leaving the Swiss carrier and Singapore-based ONE to operate the weekly service jointly. The first sailing under the revised agreement is scheduled to depart Shanghai on April 3, 2027. MSC will contribute additional ships to replace capacity associated with Hapag-Lloyd’s departure. ONE confirmed that it would continue operating the trade under its East Coast South America Express 1, or SX1, brand, maintaining weekly sailings between major Asian export centres and South America’s principal container gateways. The revised service will connect Shanghai, Ningbo, Shekou, Hong Kong and Singapore with Brazilian ports including Santos, Paranaguá, Navegantes and Rio Grande, as well as Montevideo and Buenos Aires.ONE said the final rotation remains subject to further operational review. The move ends a longstanding three-way cooperation on the route. MSC, ONE and Hapag-Lloyd expanded their Asia–South America east coast partnership in late 2018, with ONE adding weekly services to broaden coverage between the two regions. The latest restructuring leaves MSC and ONE continuing their cooperation while Hapag-Lloyd withdraws from the vessel-sharing arrangement.

items.title: Baltic Exchange joins industry leaders at SGX Commodities Forum in London to discuss the future of freight markets
items.original_title: Baltic Exchange joins industry leaders at SGX Commodities Forum in London to discuss the future of freight markets
items.summary: Baltic Exchange CEO Mark Jackson joined industry leaders at the SGX Commodities Forum on 29 September at the Royal Automobile Club in London, taking part in the FFA Freight Panel alongside John Banaszkiewicz of Freight Investor Services, Bilal Muftuoglu of Howe Robinson Partners and Alexis Ellender of Kpler. The session was moderated by Holly Birkett of TradeWinds. The panel examined the challenges facing freight markets amid geopolitical disruption, changing trade routes and increasingly complex supply chains. Mark Jackson and fellow panellists discussed the importance of protecting landed cargo margins in a volatile market and the growing role of freight derivatives in managing risk. The discussion also considered how freight is increasingly being viewed not simply as a cost of moving cargo, but as a strategic trading and risk management tool. The wider forum was well attended, with a near-full house reflecting strong market interest in the challenges and opportunities facing commodity markets. It brought together traders, producers, consumers, brokers, analysts, investors and risk managers to discuss the forces reshaping global commodity markets. The event concluded with a networking reception, giving the Baltic an opportunity to connect with market participants and industry partners in London and continue conversations around the outlook for global commodities and freight. Source: Baltic Exchange

items.summary: The maritime industry’s decarbonization transition has reached another historic milestone, with the global fleet of battery-powered commercial vessels officially surpassing the 2,000-ship mark. Data collected on the Maritime Battery Forum (MBF) Ship Registry confirms that 2,000+ commercial ships have been delivered with battery installations or are currently on order. Overall, this fleet represents a massive 2.4 GWh of installed maritime battery capacity, the same electricity to power 240k European homes for the entire day in. “Reaching 2,000+ ships marks a significant moment for marine electrification,” says Syb ten Cate Hoedemaker, Managing Director of the Maritime Battery Forum. This milestone proves the technology is ready to scale.” The data show that 68% of these vessels operate as hybrids, utilizing a battery in combination with another energy source such as a diesel engine or hydrogen fuel cell. While passenger vessels account for the largest segment at 570 ships, the register demonstrates that every type of commercial vessel is now available in a battery-powered configuration. The milestone fleet encompasses a highly diverse profile, including 313 offshore vessels, 265 cargo vessels, 219 fishing vessels, and 149 workboats, alongside hundreds of specialized vessels (145), yachts (116), tugs (83), and cruise ships (83), proving that scalable energy storage can adapt to varied operational requirements across the sector.

items.title: LR2 demand grows despite 28% fall in clean product volumes
items.original_title: LR2 demand grows despite 28% fall in clean product volumes
items.summary: LR2 product tankers loaded on average 2.1 million barrels per day (mbpd) of clean products during the first three quarters of 2026, 0.8 mbpd less than in the same period of 2025. In 2025, more than 40% of clean product volumes carried by LR2s were loaded in the Persian Gulf, equivalent to 1.2 mbpd. Following the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, this fell to 0.4 mbpd in 2026, accounting for just 18% of all clean product volumes loaded on LR2s. However, the decline in clean products has been more than offset by increased crude oil and heavy product volumes carried by LR2s. Despite the increase in volumes, total tonne-mile demand rose by only 2% year-on-year in the same period. Higher volumes from the Mediterranean and the Americas accounted for 80% of the increase in crude oil and heavy product volumes, although LR2s gained volumes in almost all loading regions. In the US and Canada, the increase in crude oil and heavy product volumes loaded on LR2s exceeded the overall increase in exports from both countries. LR2s also captured nearly 30% of the increase in Venezuela’s crude oil and heavy product exports.

items.title: Dry Bulk Shipping Fleet Growing, But Ageing as Well
items.original_title: Dry Bulk Shipping Fleet Growing, But Ageing as Well
items.summary: According to Xclusiv, “annual fleet growth remained close to 3% in both 2024 and 2025 before accelerating modestly so far in 2026. The main feature of this expansion is not simply its pace, but its uneven distribution. Handysize capacity has grown much faster than the rest of the fleet since end-2023, while Capesize/Newcastlemax supply has expanded considerably more slowly. The dry bulk orderbook has increased from around 8.0% of the fleet in DWT terms at the end of 2023 to approximately 15.0% currently. Around 12.8% of the existing dry bulk fleet by vessel count is already more than 20 years old, with the proportion even higher in several smaller and mid-sized segments. Total seaborne dry bulk trade is expected to increase by around 1.7% in 2027, with iron ore growing at a similar pace, while coal and grains remain comparatively subdued. Bauxite continues to stand out as the strongest growth area, with volumes expected to rise by around 7.3%, while minor bulks are also projected to post moderate gains. At the same time, the ageing fleet and the possibility of stronger demolition mean that the headline orderbook may overstate the true increase in effective capacity.

items.title: The Decarbonisation of European Ports
items.original_title: The Decarbonisation of European Ports
items.summary: European ports are being remade. Long established as cargo-handling facilities, they are becoming multi-functional nodes at the intersection of the energy transition, digitalisation and infrastructure resilience: gateways for conventional trade, industrial platforms for renewable energy and sustainable fuels, receiving terminals for hydrogen, ammonia and captured CO2, and marshalling hubs for offshore wind. The transformation is not voluntary. Whether a global fuel intensity standard and carbon pricing mechanism is adopted, and in what form, determines whether the EU’s regional measures remain the operative constraint on shipping calling at European ports or become one layer of a two-tier system. Brent moved from below $60 at the start of 2026 to above $100, European gas prices rose by between 40% and 67%, and the Commission’s spring 2026 forecast revised its Brent assumption upwards by 46%. They also explain why the EU Ports Strategy of March 2026 gives as much weight to security, dual-use capability and foreign ownership as to decarbonisation. 3.1The FuelEU Maritime Regulation The FuelEU Maritime Regulation (“FuelEU”) imposes progressively stringent limits on the greenhouse gas intensity of energy used by ships calling at EU ports, measured well-to-wake.

The slowdown comes after months of stronger-than-expected cargo volumes at major U.S. container ports to reach 25.8 million TEUs, up 1.4% from 25.4 million TEUs in 2025. Looking ahead, January 2027 imports are forecast at 2.07 million TEUs, down 1.9% year over year, followed by 1.92 million TEUs in February, up 1%. The Port of Savannah handled a record 504,015 twenty-foot equivalent units in September, up 3.7% from a year earlier as strong imports and a later-than-usual peak season boosted volumes. The Port of Los Angeles capped its strongest three-month cargo stretch on record in August, adding to evidence that Southern California’s container gateway is carrying stronger-than-expected momentum into the fall.... container imports remained stronger than expected through the late summer peak season.

items.title: Supertankers Racing to Middle East Worsen Global Ship Crunch
items.original_title: Supertankers Racing to Middle East Worsen Global Ship Crunch
items.summary: Supertankers are racing to the Middle East to cash in on soaring fees for carrying oil through the Strait of Hormuz , exacerbating a global shortage of vessels that has spiked freight rates. Crude flows through the waterway, which connects the Persian Gulf to international markets, have recovered to near pre-war levels in recent weeks despite continued attacks on ships. But the perils of the trade have prompted tanker fees to skyrocket: Moving oil from the gulf to East Asia costs more than six times as much as it did prior to the conflict. Meanwhile, crude producers outside of the Middle East — particularly in the Americas – are still maintaining high levels of output, even as flows from the Persian Gulf rebound. At least one VLCC was offered this week to sail from the US Gulf to Japan at a potential record fee of $82 million, or more than $40 a barrel. For the Persian Gulf to East Asia journey, which takes about three weeks, assessed supertanker rates reached an all-time high of nearly $1.4 million per day on Wednesday. The scarcity and sky-high fees for supertankers have prompted a switch to smaller Suezmax and Aframax vessels for non-Middle Eastern routes.

items.summary: Philippine rice import prospects for 2027 remain mixed, with front-loaded purchases and strategic stockpiling providing a supply cushion, while intensifying El Niño risks and elevated fertilizer costs could weigh on domestic production, market participants told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, Oct. 7. The resulting stock cushion could temper Philippine rice import demand in early 2027, but a sharper-than-expected hit to domestic production from El Niño and high fertilizer costs could quickly revive buying interest. The stock build could limit the Philippines’ immediate import requirement in 2027, although the extent of El Niño-related production losses remains a key uncertainty for the market. A local rice buyer expects imports to increase by around 30% under controlled importation as El Niño approaches, while a second local importer expects imports to remain at similar levels to 2026. High fertilizer costs and El Niño have further strained farmers and weighed on domestic food production, particularly rice, the Department of Agriculture said Oct. “While distributors generally view current retail fertilizer prices as reasonable, smallholders and local farmers continue to regard them as high, as elevated diesel costs and interest charges have been passed down the supply chain to end users,” a second Manila-based fertilizer buyer said.

REUTERS/Stringer A chemical tanker was struck by multiple projectiles off the coast of Qatar on Wednesday, with casualties reported among its crew, in the latest attack on commercial shipping as violence spreads beyond the Strait of Hormuz. The incident occurred at approximately 1900 UTC on October 7, about 51 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, Qatar, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) . At least 12 oil and gas tankers were attacked between September 28 and October 5, according to Reuters, making it the most intense week of tanker attacks since the war with Iran began in February. Several recent incidents have involved vessels struck by unidentified projectiles while transiting Hormuz, including an October 5 attack that caused a fire in a tanker’s engine room. Wednesday’s strike is especially troubling because it demonstrates that the threat to commercial shipping is not confined to vessels attempting to enter or leave the Gulf through Hormuz. UKMTO has not attributed the attack on the Acers to any party. Attacks on tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz hit their highest last week of any week since the Iran war began, according to maritime security sources tracking incidents, amid a bigger export push by Gulf producers.

items.title: The battle against supply chain chaos keeps SMBs ‘in overdrive’
items.original_title: The battle against supply chain chaos keeps SMBs ‘in overdrive’
items.summary: Small and mid-sized shippers (SMBs) are in a state of permanent overdrive, according to a report by Netstock. Inventory moves have accelerated, dead stock is threatening to pile up on them, and traditional, linear supply chain planning is failing. The 2026 Supply Chain Planning Benchmark Report , based on data from over 2,500 Netstock customers and a survey of more than 150 users at businesses with less than $250m in annual revenue, shows shippers under unceasing strain managing their supply chains. For one thing, the percentage of SMBs sourcing from two or more regions grew, from 45% in 2024 to 55% in 2026. This points to a fundamental shift in the challenges with which supply chain planners are struggling. The report said that, last year, supply chain planning was largely dictated by trade policies – tariffs – which brought about an emphasis on front-loading and building buffer stock. The landscape shifted from a year of singular shocks to one defined by supply chain chaos, where trade policy changes, shipping route disruptions, raw-material costs, demand shifts, and uneven supplier performance converged at once. “This report uses the term ‘supply chain chaos’ to describe a different kind of disruption: volatility shifts one variable at a time, while chaos moves several at once; leaving planners without a stable baseline for decision-making.

Its latest move is the 84,000 cu m Hellas Hercules, a 2015 Hyundai-built ship, sold for about $95.5m by Greek owner Latsco Shipping, marking its first VLGC sale in years. The company has previously tapped Dorian LPG for two vessels in the same bracket. In September, it moved twice, adding a 50,000 dwt oil and chemical tanker, a 17-year-old vessel from Oman Shipping, the Korean built unit is freshly renamed SPM Invictus (ex-Al Amera). A $17.5 m price tag is attached to this deal. SPM Shipping is a rapidly growing shipowner headquartered in the UAE. The company is affiliated with Priya Blue, one of India’s largest ship recyclers, and is the shipowning arm of Best Oasis, a major global cash buyer of ships.

items.original_title: High yields spark new container services on ‘bumpy’ India-Middle East trade
items.summary: Historically high freight yields are driving a wave of dedicated container services between India and the Middle East, a tradelane that has been through a number of upheavals since the outbreak of Iran-US military tension. The latest example: Maersk has just rolled out a new container shuttle loop from India’s Nhava Sheva port (JNPA) to Khor Fakkan in the UAE, “to support customers seeking better service reliability”. The service, which began with the 2,600 teu Maersk Namibia departing JNPA on 24 September, is to initially offer a fortnightly frequency, according to industry sources. Ocean rates have also continued to spike sharply for bookings out of JNPA to other Gulf ports – as high as $9,500 per 40ft for Dammam in Saudi Arabia, and around $10,000per 40ft hi-cube to Umm Qasr in Iraq. Emerging Chinese carrier CULines is said to have firm plans for an Asia-Middle East service, beginning in late 2026 or early 2027. Hapag-Lloyd last week told customers it would not accept new Upper Gulf bookings to be transhipped via Salalah until further notice. Much of the pressure plaguing Middle East gateways is linked to a shortage of assets needed to move imports across the border overland, especially using truck fleets, industry updates suggest.

items.summary: Customer expectations are forcing SME forwarders to adopt new technologies, even as the most valuable applications may never be seen by those customers, threatening the qualities the operators offer over their larger rivals. Sophia Huluta, president of GLC, said changing everyday relationships with technologies, including AI and real-time visibility, was leaving forwarders with no choice but to provide the same digital speed and visibility as much larger logistics companies. She told The Loadstar : “Customers absolutely expect technology. Their expectations are based on how tech works everywhere else in their lives. I don’t think a customer is going to be impressed much longer because you have a portal. They are just going to wonder what is wrong if you don’t.” All this, she added, was putting pressure on SMEs to ensure they have the services to remain competitive, but noting that “forwarders have an unbelievable amount of information inside their organisations”, Ms Huluta questioned whether the tech could be better used. Forwarders would be more likely to benefit from systems affording greater visibility of their own business, she suggested, including the profitability of individual customers and tradelanes, as well as where opportunities and resources are being wasted.

Decades ago, Hong Kong competed with Singapore and Rotterdam as the world’s busiest port. By 2025, Hong Kong was ranked the 12 th busiest port, as volumes dropped 6%, to 12.91m teu. Among the services already linking Hong Kong to China’s western land-sea corridor are a Hong Kong-Guizhou daily service and a Chongqing-Qinzhou-Hong Kong sea-rail intermodal service. And Ms Chan said Hong Kong port retained significant operational strengths. items.title: Why supply and demand no longer tell the whole story in container shipping
items.original_title: Why supply and demand no longer tell the whole story in container shipping
items.summary: For much of container shipping’s history, market conditions could be understood through a relatively straightforward equation. When cargo demand grew faster than available vessel capacity, utilisation and freight rates generally rose. Supply and demand remain at the heart of container shipping, but the equation now contains more variables than it once did. The decline in inventory levels coincided with a period in which North American container imports also softened following the introduction of tariffs in April 2025 and broader uncertainty around consumer demand. Capacity therefore needs to be considered across the full cargo journey, not only in terms of ships and container slots. Geopolitical developments increasingly connect the demand and supply sides of container shipping. Electrification, growing energy demand and investment in digital infrastructure are contributing to growing demand for equipment, components and materials that may move through corridors already carrying substantial volumes of consumer goods. This is another reason supply and demand need to be considered at trade-lane and network level, rather than solely through global totals. Freight rates ultimately reflect the balance between supply and demand.

items.title: Strengthening flag State oversight in Asia
items.original_title: Strengthening flag State oversight in Asia
items.summary: Maritime officials from across Asia enhanced their capacity to implement flag State obligations and strengthen oversight of recognized organizations under the RO Code during an IMO regional workshop in Bandar Seri Begawan, Brunei Darussalam (21-25 September). Jointly organized by IMO and the Maritime and Port Authority of Brunei Darussalam (MPABD), the workshop brought together 22 participants from Bangladesh, Brunei Darussalam, Malaysia, Mongolia, Pakistan, the Philippines, Thailand and Viet Nam. Reinforcing national maritime oversight During the five-day workshop, participants examined flag State obligations related to surveys and certification, as well as the authorization and oversight of recognized organizations under the Code for Recognized Organizations (RO Code). The RO Code establishes the framework through which flag States assess, authorize and monitor third-party entities that carry out statutory surveys and certification on their behalf. Attention was given to recurrent findings identified through the IMO Member State Audit Scheme (IMSAS), the mandatory mechanism that assesses how effectively Member States implement and enforce IMO instruments. Key findings related to the implementation and enforcement of IMO instruments, oversight programmes, delegation of authority to recognized organizations (ROs), and the evaluation of maritime administration processes. The workshop highlighted the value of regional cooperation and information sharing in supporting consistent implementation.

items.original_title: Rosatom folds Delo into expanding logistics platform

Rosatom, which previously held 49% of Delo, has acquired Shishkarev’s remaining 51% and will now begin consolidating the company with its other transport holdings, including shipping and logistics group FESCO. Neither side disclosed the final consideration. Rosatom is pitching the consolidation as the creation of Russia’s largest national logistics company. Delo brings a sizeable container platform to the state corporation. Rosatom controls 92.5% of the Vladivostok-based group, whose assets include more than 30 ships, container and rail operations and the Commercial Port of Vladivostok. Rosatom triggered the mutual buyout process in February after disagreements with Shishkarev. The Delo founder initially elected to acquire Rosatom’s stake but subsequently abandoned that route, handing the purchase right back to the state corporation. Rosatom said the combined logistics assets now account for around 50% of Russia’s container handling market and 44% of rail container transportation.

Before the war, exports averaged about 18 million bpd. Gulf countries, she suggested, may be paying Iran to allow their oil through – potentially handing Tehran a significant portion of the value of the cargo. “I also suspect that these countries know that this is unsustainable from a perspective of [the] US escorting [ships], and also unsustainable from them paying Iran 10 percent of their cargo, or 20 percent of their cargo,” she added. But as early as March, the shipping journal Lloyd’s List reported that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had already imposed a “toll booth” system to control vessel traffic through the strait. items.title: Bearish signs on oil markets emerge
items.original_title: Bearish signs on oil markets emerge
items.summary: Oil markets have been in constant flux since the start of the US-Iran conflict, with market participants closely monitoring the situation in the Middle East Gulf (MEG). The conflict has expanded towards the Red Sea since August, disrupting oil flows at Bab-el-Mandeb as the Houthis resumed attacks on Saudi-linked vessels and on the East-West pipeline in early September, crippling crude loadings from Saudi Arabia’s Yanbu port. That said, operating rates at the East-West pipeline have recovered to ~80% capacity (Bloomberg), while recent satellite imagery at the Yanbu reflects continued VLCC loadings, refuting claims that the pipeline has been severely damaged. Crude stock draws concentrated in China One key reason oil prices have not surged toward $150/bbl is China restraining its crude purchases. One key reason is the inability to access Iranian crude/condensate supplies under the current US blockade, prompting private refiners to draw on onshore crude stocks to levels below their 3-year seasonal range. Recent announcements of the strategic stock release pledge could further dampen oil import demand, with a combined 100mb of crude and diesel set to be distributed among G7 countries over four months under IEA coordination. In addition, the latest round of 40mb of sour crude bidding from the US SPR adds another source of oil supply.

items.title: Berlin blocks COSCO takeover of German freight forwarder
items.original_title: Berlin blocks COSCO takeover of German freight forwarder
items.summary: Germany has blocked COSCO Shipping’s planned acquisition of an 80% stake in Hamburg freight forwarder Konrad Zippel, overriding an earlier competition clearance on national security grounds. The federal cabinet approved the prohibition on Wednesday, with the economy ministry saying the transaction would have deepened strategic dependencies and threatened the resilience of German and EU supply chains. Zippel specialises in container hinterland transport, moving cargo arriving at Hamburg and Bremerhaven onwards by rail, road and inland waterway to industrial centres in eastern Germany and neighbouring markets. German intelligence officials subsequently raised concerns about the deal. Zippel handles between 35% and 90% of container volumes at inland terminals in Berlin, Schkopau and Elsterwerda and also plays a role in logistics supporting Germany’s armed forces. Government officials warned that control of such infrastructure could create dependencies capable of being used as leverage during a political crisis. The decision marks a harder line from Berlin following the long-running controversy over COSCO’s investment in Hamburg’s Container Terminal Tollerort. COSCO originally sought 35% of the terminal operator but was ultimately permitted to take just 24.99% after the German government intervened in 2022 over security concerns. The latest prohibition comes as Germany prepares tougher investment-screening legislation aimed at giving Berlin greater powers to scrutinise acquisitions involving strategic infrastructure and technology.

items.title: Intergr8 Fuels: Global fuel quality remains broadly stable, but localised risks are becoming more important than headline averages
items.original_title: Intergr8 Fuels: Global fuel quality remains broadly stable, but localised risks are becoming more important than headline averages
items.summary: The biannual report, covering fuel quality performance from February to July 2026, finds that global quality averages increasingly mask significant differences between ports, supply chains and fuel characteristics. Changes in crude flows, refinery slates and regional supply pools are contributing to more localised quality exposure. • Localised quality risk: Quality performance varies significantly by port, grade and supply chain, with global averages often masking higher-risk locations and specific quality characteristics. • Biofuel quality: Headline notification rates for biofuel blends remain elevated against conventional ISO reference grades, but much of the apparent exposure is linked to parameters that may not reflect contractual or operational risk. Chris Turner, Technical Manager at Integr8 Fuels: “The headline quality rates tell only part of the story. Risk is increasingly determined by the port, the supply chain and the characteristics of the available fuel pool, rather than by the global average for a grade. Buyers therefore need to look beyond specification and headline price to understand the value and operational implications of the fuel they are actually purchasing.” The report also examines loss control in bunker procurement, showing how energy variance, density differences, additional heating and handling requirements can create costs that remain invisible when fuel is assessed solely against specification limits.

items.original_title: Coal in Focus — China’s 2027–28 US Coal Commitment
items.summary: Recorded sailings have already recovered from a very low base. Signal loading data show 918,364 tonnes of coal shipped from the US Gulf to China in January–September 2026, against 51,726 tonnes a year earlier. August and September alone accounted for 695,375 tonnes, close to 76% of the 2026 total, placing the improvement firmly in the late-summer loading programme. The recovery nonetheless remains below the 2024 level: China took 4.6% of US Gulf coal exports to all destinations this year against 9.8% in 2024, and the China-bound tonnage is some 47% below 2024. For Panamax, the Baltic Exchange reports improving demand from the US Gulf and a tightening October position list in East Coast South America, and Signal’s forward balance for the P1/P2/P7 group shows total supply running below expected demand across the entire twenty-day window. For the geared sizes the Gulf moved the other way: S1C (US Gulf to China–South Japan) fell $937 to $31,794/day, S4A (US Gulf to Skaw-Passero) $606 to $32,038/day and HS4_38 (US Gulf trip) $807 to $24,107/day — matching the Baltic Exchange’s account of a North American Supramax market softening for fronthauls and a Handysize US Gulf easing through the week.

items.title: Port call optimisation pilot projects reveal significant emissions savings potential, new report shows
items.original_title: Port call optimisation pilot projects reveal significant emissions savings potential, new report shows
items.summary: Commercial ships spend between 4% and 6% of their operating year waiting outside ports. That idle time is one of the clearest inefficiencies in shipping, and a combination of slower sailing speeds and port call optimisation can reduce the emissions and fuel currently wasted as ships await an available berth. Instead of sailing fast only to then wait at anchor, port call optimisation allows a ship to arrive when its berth is ready. Cargill Ocean Transportation set out to test the fuel and emissions savings of combining slower sailing speeds with port call optimisation in live commercial operations. With pilot projects at two Australian ports and one in Brazil, the company tested three different mechanisms across 16 voyages and found that the combination can deliver meaningful emissions savings across a range of operational and commercial settings. The findings of the pilots are the subject of a new Global Maritime Forum report, ‘Turning waiting time into savings: Lessons from Cargill’s port call optimisation pilot’. Detailing the pilot projects at the Port of Albany and the Port of Newcastle in Australia, and at Cargill’s grain export terminal in Santarém, Brazil, the report explores the interdependent relationship between port call optimisation and speed reduction.

items.title: IMarEST: From MASS Code to Maritime Practice
items.original_title: IMarEST: From MASS Code to Maritime Practice
items.summary: As shipping becomes increasingly automated, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has introduced legislation to ensure future technology is safe and secure. But there are significant challenges with taking the new Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) Code from policy to practice. The adoption of the International Maritime Organization’s MASS Code marks an important step in the development of maritime autonomy. Adopted at Marine Safety Committee (MSC) 111, it applied as a non-mandatory code from July 2026, with a mandatory code targeted for 2032. This is a sensible approach as maritime autonomy covers everything from small uncrewed survey vessels to large remotely operated ships, and technology is developing too quickly for a regulation built around particular technical solutions. For each relevant requirement, we should be able to trace a path from the intent of the Code through the functions required to satisfy it, the evidence needed to support the claim, and the organisations or individuals responsible for providing and accepting that evidence. Through the MASS SIG, the Institute has an opportunity to convene the maritime autonomy communities around the practical implementation of the Code and capture lessons as autonomous operations move from controlled trials towards routine use. Timing is also important because the current non-mandatory code provides an opportunity to accumulate operational experience before development of the mandatory code progresses.

items.title: Rebounding oil exports through Strait of Hormuz are vulnerable to stepped-up Iranian tanker attacks
items.original_title: Rebounding oil exports through Strait of Hormuz are vulnerable to stepped-up Iranian tanker attacks
items.summary: Iran has stepped up its attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, threatening a fragile rebound of crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf. Nearly 20 commercial ships, mostly tankers, have come under attack over the past month while sailing through Hormuz, the Persian Gulf or off the coast of Oman, according to the Joint Maritime Information Center, a group of U.S.-allied militaries that provide security updates to merchant vessels. Iran attacked roughly two ships for every 100 vessels that crossed the strait in the third quarter, said Michelle Wiese Bockmann, senior maritime intelligence analyst at Windward, which tracks ships for defense departments and governments. Shuttle system In many cases, tankers are bringing crude through Hormuz and then transferring the oil onto ships in the Gulf of Oman that haul it to Asia. Crude oil shipments through Hormuz fluctuate daily, sometimes matching or even exceeding levels before the Iran war, according to data from Kpler, a firm that tracks tankers and global trade flows. Windward estimates crude through Hormuz is averaging 9-10 million bpd compared with a prewar baseline of 14.5 million bpd. High costs But shippers are ferrying crude through Hormuz at high cost to the lives of their crews and in freight and insurance rates, Bockmann said.

items.title: What a 25-Day AIS Blackout Off Libya Tells Us About Mediterranean Narcotics Routes
items.original_title: What a 25-Day AIS Blackout Off Libya Tells Us About Mediterranean Narcotics Routes
items.summary: The 25-Day Gap Between Albania and Libya In late August 2026, a Mali-flagged general cargo vessel left an Albanian port, declared Egypt as its destination, and switched off its AIS transponder in open water off eastern Libya. For 25 days and 8 hours, nothing was transmitted. When it reappeared on September 23, it was at nearly the same position where it had gone dark. What happened off Libya in late August was consistent with a pattern the vessel had been establishing for months. What One Voyage Says About Mediterranean Narcotics Routes What makes this case worth attention is not the single dark activity, but the repeatability built into it. A vessel that returns consistently to the same Albanian base, under a flag with no oversight behind it, with a documented history of going dark off the same coasts, is a vessel whose operational pattern can be run again. The March 2026 Sinai gaps and the August–September Libya gap are consistent with a methodology, not an improvisation. For interdiction and compliance stakeholders tracking Mediterranean narcotics routes, the question is not whether this specific voyage carried something. The vessel that vanished for 25 days off Libya may be one example of a wider operational practice.

items.title: Sanctioned 22-Year-Old Tanker Makes Rare Late-Season Arctic Voyage
items.original_title: Sanctioned 22-Year-Old Tanker Makes Rare Late-Season Arctic Voyage
items.summary: A 22-year-old product tanker sanctioned by the European Union is making an unusual late-season voyage along Russia’s Northern Sea Route, highlighting the growing use of older, lower-specification vessels to move petroleum products through the Arctic. The Dakar , a 21,300-dwt oil and chemical products tanker built in 2004, is carrying methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), a gasoline additive, and appears to be heading west along Russia’s Arctic coast, according vessel tracking data. The cargo was loaded onto another vessel in China in August before being transferred to Dakar off Yeosu, South Korea, in September. That distinguishes it from non-ice-class tankers, while placing it well below the Arc4 and higher ice-class vessels purpose-built for regular Arctic operations. A similar voyage last year demonstrated the risk: the non-ice-class Suezmax Lynx was forced to wait for several day s after encountering sea ice near 72 degrees north while carrying Russian crude toward China. Dakar ’s voyage also follows a sharp increase in Russian oil exports to Asia through the Arctic this year. Reuters reported in August that seven tankers had already moved roughly 6 million barrels of crude through the NSR, nearly half the total shipped by tankers through the route during all of 2025.

At closing, Chevron expects to recognize a one-time after-tax loss estimated at approximately $3 to $4 billion,1 given that the company is unable to recognize future Bakken midstream cost savings as an asset. “This transaction resets the commercial framework between our upstream and midstream assets in the Bakken and DJ Basins,” said Andy Walz, Chevron’s President of Downstream, Midstream and Chemicals.

items.title: New cover protects forwarders from late or temperature-hit cargo
items.original_title: New cover protects forwarders from late or temperature-hit cargo
items.summary: Forwarders shipping flowers, pharmaceuticals and other sensitive cargo are being offered a tracking and insurance package combining fixed payouts for qualifying delays with cover for temperature-related losses. Airfreight wholesaler Solent Freight Services, technology provider Tag-N-Trac and insurance specialist Otonomi have launched TRACinSURED, bringing shipment monitoring and insurance into a single subscription product. For a flower shipment from Ecuador, a forwarder would enrol the consignment by assigning its airway bill to the system, receiving confirmation once insurance was bound. Final commercial pricing and the trigger schedule are still being approved but customers will be offered monthly and annual subscriptions, with tracking available from airport to door or door to door. “It is therefore less about simply offering a cheaper version of conventional cargo insurance and more about providing a new type of bundled risk-management product,” she said. “Solent has spent more than 30 years handling fresh-cut flowers, fruits, pharmaceuticals and other highly perishable cargo where temperature, timing and visibility can determine whether a shipment succeeds or fails,” said chief executive Simon Milne. “Operational decisions remain with the freight forwarder or logistics operator handling the shipment.” Solent is targeting global distribution, with active countries, lanes and underwriting arrangements subject to confirmation during the rollout.

items.title: Trafigura Buys Seven Oil Tankers From SFL as Shipping Costs Rise
items.original_title: Trafigura Buys Seven Oil Tankers From SFL as Shipping Costs Rise
items.summary: Trafigura Group bought seven oil tankers from New York-listed SFL Corp., in the latest example of how trading houses and state energy companies are acquiring vessels to ship crude and products. Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have drawn in scores of tankers to shuttle key oil flows out to the global market, while growing risks in the Red Sea are leading to longer voyage routes and times. That’s prompted a rush to snap up tankers as rates to charter vessels soar. Trafigura bought four oil product tankers known as LR2s — built in 2014 and 2015 — and three suezmax tankers built in 2019, SFL said in a statement on Wednesday. SFL said it had made an “aggregate book gain” of $175 million from the deal, without disclosing the sale price of the vessels. Strong demand for prompt availability of oil carriers have pushed the resale values of tankers higher. A 10-year-old Aframax, which is the same size as an LR2 tanker, was assessed to be worth $72.5 million last week, while a Suezmax of the same age could sell for $110 million, Clarkson data show. Trafigura recently made its first foray into launching a public company, listing a supertanker vehicle Volare Shipping Ltd.

items.title: German port strikes averted, but low Rhine still delaying barge cargo
items.original_title: German port strikes averted, but low Rhine still delaying barge cargo
items.summary: The prospect of widespread industrial action at Germany’s ports retreated yesterday after dockworker members of the ver.di union agreed to accept new contract terms offered by the Central Association of German Seaport Operators (ZDS). “Strikes at the ports of Hamburg, Bremen, Bremerhaven, Emden, Brake, and Wilhelmshaven have thus been averted for the time being,” said ver.di. Workers have won: a 3.4% wage increase for the next year, backdated to 1 August; a €200 increase in holiday pay; and dockers involved in “high-turnover container operations” will receive an additional annual lump sum, increased by €416 from 1 January. “It was a difficult round, but the bottom line was acceptable,” added ver.di, while union officials said a 24-hour ‘warning strike’ by members in mid-August had been the catalyst for this week’s agreement. The agreement staves off the potential for further cargo backlogs building in Germany’s three main container gateways of Hamburg, Bremerhaven, and Wilhelmshaven – although shippers and freight forwarders are still encountering some congestion. However, German shippers in the central Rhine industrial belt continue to face hinterland congestion caused by low water levels on the Rhine, and the subsequent restrictions on barge movements to the key gateways of Rotterdam and Antwerp.

In addition to two 7,100 ceu units listed as hulls 641 and 642 for delivery in 2030, the databases show another two ships, hulls 651 and 652, against NOCC for delivery in 2030 and 2031. Schulte Marine Concept, which is supervising construction, said last month that hull 612 was the fourth ship in the four-vessel series and is scheduled for delivery in June 2027. Splash tracked NOCC’s expansion at CIMC Raffles last December when chief executive Olav Sollie revealed that the company had signed for its fourth vessel shortly before the end of 2025. That ship followed an initial pair contracted in 2024 and a subsequent third unit. NOCC operates as a tonnage provider, chartering its vessels to global and regional car carrier operators.

items.title: Bad weather creates headwinds for trade between the Americas
items.original_title: Bad weather creates headwinds for trade between the Americas
items.summary: The easing of restrictions on Panama Canal transits has brought some relief to exporters in South America, but other headwinds remain, which could accelerate the widening gap between imports and exports. This month, Seaboard Marine is expanding its West Coast South America service to the US East Coast with a call at Gloucester City. The first arrival at the New Jersey port is scheduled for 25 October. The gap widened 20%, to 1.7m teu. Likewise, CTS data show South America’s maritime exports to North America shrank 1.1% year on year in July, whereas volume in the opposite direction expanded 7.2%. On a positive note, the Global Liner Performance Report for September, by Sea-Intelligence, shows schedule reliability between South and North America improved in both directions in the July/August period. Southbound it rose 1.2%, to 81.2%, year on year, while northbound it recovered from a drop the previous month, climbing 5.2 percentage points from June/July, to 80.6%, up 0.8%, year on year. The average delay for late vessels extended slightly, (up 0.09 percentage points from June/July) to 5.32 days, 1.55 days longer than a year ago. However, the average delay for all vessels shrank 0.20 days from June/July, to 1.10 days.

items.title: Another Ceva reboot, another 10,000 staff. Can it deliver?
items.original_title: Another Ceva reboot, another 10,000 staff. Can it deliver?
items.summary: Ceva Logistics has had a long history of re-writes. From its birth under Apollo – an era tarnished by a restructuring that left employee shareholders’ investments worthless – to life as a public company, and now as a mere arm of the opaque CMA CGM group, the 3PL has seen many new beginnings, some more successful than others. Yesterday, it announced another new version of itself – offering a simpler structure, stronger accountability, and a renewed focus on customers. Then-CEO Mathieu Friedberg said the vision for Ceva was “taking its final form” – but perhaps it was not so final after all. Ceva will now organise its activities around two global business units, Freight Management and Contract Logistics, headed by Henri Le Gouis and Chris Walton, respectively, as it continues to integrate acquisitions. “We all know huge cuts are coming, so it’s very uneasy times and it’s impacting our staff and customers.” CMA CGM completed its $1.4bn acquisition of FedEx Supply Chain on 1 October, adding nearly 10,000 employees and approximately 350,000 sq metres of warehouse space. That is another substantial business to incorporate, while Ceva says it will also focus on completing the integration of its previous acquisitions. On 13 August, it still could not give sellers a reopening date; sales began restarting in stages on 20 August.
