items.title: Gallagher Bassett buys second London shipping law firm in five months
items.original_title: Gallagher Bassett buys second London shipping law firm in five months
items.summary: Arthur J. Gallagher’s claims and risk management arm, Gallagher Bassett, has acquired London-based maritime law firm Winter & Co Solicitors, continuing a run of deals aimed at expanding its marine business. Winter & Co advises P&I clubs, marine insurers, shipowners and charterers on shipping-related legal matters, with Glenn Winter and his team remaining in London under Manan Sagar, head of Gallagher Bassett’s Europe, Middle East and Asia operations. The transaction is Gallagher Bassett’s second acquisition of a London shipping law firm in five months. In May, the company bought Mays Brown Solicitors, another specialist maritime practice whose client base includes owners, operators, charterers, P&I clubs, insurers and shipyards. In February it acquired Bremen-based Reck & Co, which provides surveying, claims handling, recovery and loss-prevention services to the global transport and marine markets. Those deals follow Gallagher Bassett’s takeover of London-headquartered W K Webster in February 2025. W K Webster specialises in marine and transit claims management and operates offices in Singapore, the US and the Netherlands. items.title: Exports stranded as Adani Russia-embargo creates Indian air cargo chaos
items.original_title: Exports stranded as Adani Russia-embargo creates Indian air cargo chaos
items.summary: India-Russia trade, which has been active despite the US sanctions on Moscow, now faces new supply chain hurdles, according to industry sources. The biggest barrier is that the eight Indian airports, including Mumbai’s two, managed by Adani Group have temporarily suspended handling Russia-related shipments. The stoppage has already left some 150 tonnes of Indian exports for Russia – primarily pharmaceuticals, machinery, and spare parts – stranded over the past week. While there is no official word from Adani, industry watchers are viewing the abrupt cargo ban as an extended fallout of the sanctions, as it occurred a few weeks after US-based asset management group BlackRock agreed to funnel some $1bn in equity to Adani Airport Holdings. And India-Russia trade disruption is not limited to air freight: container carriers have also stopped accepting bookings from India to Russia’s Novorossiysk port, a major hub in the Black Sea, over fears of escalating drone attacks on vessels, as well as other growing security risks in the region, sources told The Loadstar . The disruption and export congestion is an added blow for Mumbai air freight stakeholders as the hub switch from the old Mumbai airport to Navi Mumbai (NMI) continues to generate controversy.

items.title: China Completes First Season of Regular Arctic Container Service
items.original_title: China Completes First Season of Regular Arctic Container Service
items.summary: Eight planned sailings carried high-value exports through the Northern Sea Route, with service to resume next summer. China has completed the first season of regular weekly container shipping between China and Europe via the Northern Sea Route, with the operator completing all eight sailings planned for 2026 before ending departures slightly earlier than scheduled because of Arctic ice forecasts. Sea Legend Shipping launched its China-Europe Arctic Express in Augus t, deploying seven ice-strengthened container ships for eight weekly westbound voyages from Ningbo-Zhoushan and other Chinese ports. The season carried more than 14,000 twenty-foot equivalent units of export cargo across the eight voyages, according to preliminary figures reported by Zhejiang authorities. The first voyage of the season by Dubai Tower carried 1,370 TEUs from Ningbo, Shanghai, Taicang and Qingdao to Europe. The Arctic route takes about 18 to 20 days between China and Northern Europe, roughly half the transit time of traditional routes via the Suez Canal, according to Chinese transport authorities. The end of Sea Legend’s departures does not mark the end of Chinese container activity on the Northern Sea Route for 2026. The completion of all eight planned voyages marks a step beyond last year’s experimental voyages, when the Sea Legend service was still testing the commercial and operational feasibility of Arctic container shipping.

items.title: Seven north European ports back cross-border automated freight push
items.original_title: Seven north European ports back cross-border automated freight push
items.summary: Seven major ports across Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany have secured government backing for a wider cross-border programme aimed at cutting regulatory barriers and accelerating automated freight and energy infrastructure across the Antwerp-Rotterdam-Rhine-Ruhr corridor. The agreement was reached at a Port Summit in Meise this week between the governments of Flanders, the Netherlands and North Rhine-Westphalia and the port authorities of Duisport, North Sea Port, Antwerp-Bruges, Cologne/HGK, Moerdijk, Oostende and Rotterdam. One of the more concrete logistics measures is a plan to use cross-border corridors such as Antwerp-Rotterdam for automated freight transport by road and inland waterway. The three governments also want closer cooperation on drones, with rules and procedures to be aligned across borders. The wider programme covers a common market for secondary raw materials, coordinated development of hydrogen and CO2 transport infrastructure and joint work on inland navigation and strategic water management. Ports in the region have also been pushing for so-called acceleration areas to shorten planning and permitting times for major infrastructure and industrial projects. That call has now been incorporated into the summit declaration, alongside moves to reduce regulatory differences between the three jurisdictions. The three governments will take the programme to Brussels, asking the European Commission to recognise the Antwerp-Rotterdam-Rhine-Ruhr Area, or ARRRA, as a strategic European port-industrial cluster.

items.title: Busan shipmanager launches Arctic LNG fleet push
items.original_title: Busan shipmanager launches Arctic LNG fleet push
items.summary: New South Korean shipmanager IOB has started operations with four ice-class LNG carriers and is already targeting a move into full icebreaking Arc7 tonnage. The Busan-based company says it currently has four Arc4 LNG carriers under management, with plans to add three to six Arc7 vessels in 2027, followed by additional Arc7 newbuilding management from 2028. The four 174,000 cu m ships have been identified as the North Moon, North Light, North Ocean and North Valley . All were built at Hanwha Ocean in 2024 and 2025 for Mitsui OSK Lines. The quartet traces back to a 2021 project in which MOL, through a subsidiary, signed time-charter contracts for four LNG newbuildings with NOVATEK Gas & Power Asia, a wholly owned unit of Russia’s Novatek. Three of the ships — North Moon, North Light and North Ocean — were placed on the European Union sanctions list in May 2025 before being removed two months later. The vessels subsequently spent extended periods idle amid uncertainty around Russian LNG trades. IOB describes itself as an Arctic LNG shipmanagement specialist covering technical, marine and QHSE, crewing and shore-based operational support. Despite only beginning operations this year, the company says its team brings 13 years of accumulated LNG fleet-management experience.

items.title: Aframax Rio blaze underscores widening Black Sea threat
items.original_title: Aframax Rio blaze underscores widening Black Sea threat
items.summary: The Aframax Rio was ablaze off Sochi on Tuesday after being struck by unmanned surface vessels, adding another tanker casualty to a rapidly worsening Black Sea security picture. Russia’s transport ministry said the Liberia-flagged aframax was attacked off the Russian resort city, triggering a major fire and an oil spill. All 23 crew, all Indian nationals, were rescued and no injuries were reported. The Aframax Rio is a tanker linked to Russian oil exports and listed under Ukrainian sanctions. The attack comes as maritime security specialist Ambrey warns that the threat to merchant shipping is broadening sharply across the western Black Sea. Odesa-cluster volumes fell from 7.9m tonnes in April to just 430,000 tonnes in August, while Danube cargo nearly doubled in a month to 1.24m tonnes. Port calls rose from 363 to 737, and grain loadings increased 3.5-fold. Ambrey said as many as 125 vessels were queued there on October 5 after weather disruption, while waits have stretched to 14–17 days. Ambrey said many underwriters no longer offer cover for Ukrainian port calls, even as war-risk premiums have moved into double digits, while the Joint War Committee expanded the Black Sea Listed Area in September.

items.title: Twelve injured in latest Hormuz attack
items.original_title: Twelve injured in latest Hormuz attack
items.summary: Twelve seafarers have been injured after the Panama-flagged tanker On Peace was struck by a projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz yesterday, the latest casualty in what has become the most intense spell of attacks on commercial shipping since the US-Iran war began in February. The vessel, owned by Dubai-based Onex, was carrying 19 crew, 17 of them Indian nationals. Eleven Indians were among those injured. Onex ordered the 2021-built 114,600 dwt ship at Hyundai Samho for $57m in 2019 as part of a three-ship package. The attack follows a remarkable cluster of incidents around the strait in recent days. On October 5, another tanker north of Khasab was ordered by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to turn around or face being targeted; the master complied. Since late February, 93 ships have been hit and 24 seafarers killed. Tanker captains are reportedly being offered as much as $100,000 a month plus $50,000 per Hormuz transit, with some crew earning multiples of normal wages. War-risk insurance for individual tanker voyages has climbed to as much as $20m, while extreme voyage economics have pushed some tanker earnings towards $1.3m a day.

items.title: Clarksons’ ClarkSea Index At All-Time High, Surpassing 2008 Record
items.original_title: Clarksons’ ClarkSea Index At All-Time High, Surpassing 2008 Record
items.summary: See below for more details, and visit Shipping Intelligence Network for the full report and underlying data. Driven by exceptionally elevated, disruption-driven rate environments in crude and LPG and supported by strong market conditions across container, car carrier and bulkers, our cross-segment shipping market “barometer”, the ClarkSea Index, has hit an all-time high (Q3: $46,384/day). Strong newbuild flow continued to build orderbook backlog and asset prices in crude tankers “surged”. The ClarkSea Index reached its highest ever quarterly level ($46,384/day vs $44,222/day of Q2-2008 and 2x the 10 year trend) and highest individual week ($66,000/day). This combination of improved volumes plus additional “inefficiencies” and distances has pushed VLCC earnings to exceptional levels (>$600,000/day, Q3 avg $277,995/day, some routes now over $1.6m/day) whilst demand for ships for the “shuttle” operations also helped S&P prices “surge” to all-time highs (15 yr old VLCC price > newbuild, resale VLCC index at record $240m). In LPG carriers, cargo volume loss has been more than offset by higher tonne-mile demand from long-haul US-Asia trade (notably via the Cape with Panama congested), with VLGC earnings averaging a record $154,853/day. Bulkcarrier markets have firmed, basis more “traditional” supply-demand factors, led by Capesize (peaking at >$50,000/day, avg $33,100/day) with Guinea volumes growing and Chinese import demand firm.

items.title: Shipping rewinds the future
items.original_title: Shipping rewinds the future
items.summary: Rather than forecasting from today, backcasting starts with possible futures and works backwards — an approach gaining traction as shipping’s long-term bets become harder to call. Splash’s Europe Editor Bojan Lepic explains. Shipping has never been short on forecasts. Japanese liner Ocean Network Express (ONE) has brought the concept into sharper focus through its View of the World project, which examines several possible versions of the global economy and container shipping in 2050 and considers what those futures mean for decisions made today. We set out multiple plausible scenarios for how the global economy and container shipping could look in 2050, drawing on a wide range of external and internal perspectives. For an industry that commits capital to ships trading well into the 2050s, that discipline is valuable.” Rex says the Poseidon Principles trajectories effectively work backwards from the IMO’s 2050 ambition into annual carbon-intensity pathways. It says nothing about when to buy, at what price or with how much leverage, and in shipping, that is where most capital is made or lost.” As is noticeable, backcasting has many positives, and some believe it is a potent tool in the shipping toolbox for building a clearer picture of the future. “I’m afraid the 1990s just called and would like its scenario planning tool back.

items.title: ShipGod AI: Why every vessel needs its own digital memory
items.original_title: ShipGod AI: Why every vessel needs its own digital memory
items.summary: After four decades at sea and ashore, Bing Hou has reached a simple conclusion about shipmanagement: too much of what keeps vessels safe still depends on paper, spreadsheets and what individual seafarers happen to remember. The 56-year-old master mariner, founder of ShipGod AI, spends 25 years with China Yangtze Shipping, rising from deck cadet to Class-1 ocean-going master and serving on everything from containerships and tankers to LNG carriers, passenger ships and offshore vessels. Since 2016, Hou has worked ashore in marine management, ship surveying, DPA roles and teaching. “ISM got the principle right decades ago: every ship must operate its own Safety Management System, fitted to that specific ship. That frustration became the basis for ShipGod AI, which he describes as an offline-first workspace giving each vessel its own digital environment and AI assistant. Every ship, its own system. ShipGod AI instead allows companies to mirror their existing safety management structures while giving each vessel its own documents, checklists, records, inspections and equipment history. The AI runs locally onboard and answers from the ship’s own information rather than the wider internet. As a young seafarer in the 1980s, Hou listened to shortwave radio during long voyages and dreamt of creating a station for seafarers.

items.title: Bunker prices jump by three-quarters since Iran war began
items.original_title: Bunker prices jump by three-quarters since Iran war began
items.summary: The cost of fuelling ships has risen by roughly three-quarters since the US-Iran war erupted on February 28. In Singapore, the world’s largest bunkering hub, VLSFO was assessed by ENGINE at $509 per tonne on February 27, the final trading day before the war began, while high-sulphur fuel oil stood at $432 per tonne. By Monday this week, VLSFO had climbed to $886 per tonne and HSFO to $764, increases of 74% and 77% respectively. Prices initially went vertical after US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28 and the subsequent disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. Ship & Bunker data shows Singapore VLSFO rising from $521.50 per tonne immediately before the conflict to a peak of $1,120.50 by March 13. The market subsequently retreated as supply chains adjusted and hopes periodically surfaced of a diplomatic breakthrough, but bunker prices have never returned close to their pre-war levels, and have been increasing again in recent weeks. In Singapore, the absolute discount enjoyed by scrubber-fitted ships burning HSFO has widened from around $77 per tonne immediately before the war to roughly $122 today, even though the price of HSFO itself has surged.

items.title: Iran’s Offshore Oil Stockpile Nears Exhaustion as Blockade Chokes New Supply
items.original_title: Iran’s Offshore Oil Stockpile Nears Exhaustion as Blockade Chokes New Supply
items.summary: Iran’s offshore crude stockpile in Southeast Asia is being rapidly depleted as the U.S. maritime blockade prevents fresh barrels from leaving the Persian Gulf, according to new tracking data from United Against Nuclear Iran. UANI said an estimated 9 million barrels of Iranian crude were transferred through ship-to-ship operations in waters off Malaysia during September, drawing down inventories accumulated before the blockade took effect. “Given that no Iranian crude has made it past the blockade line, Iran’s offshore floating storage in the South China Sea is rapidly dwindling,” the group said. The crude transfers totaled an estimated 9 million barrels and were ultimately destined for Chinese independent refiners, commonly known as “teapots.” The activity has continued despite growing scrutiny of the large network of sanctioned and Iran-linked vessels operating in the region. The depletion of offshore storage comes even as oil exports from other Persian Gulf producers have recovered. If UANI’s estimate of roughly 10 million barrels remaining in Malaysian floating storage is accurate, the pool of crude available outside the blockade has fallen sharply. With no new crude reaching those offshore inventories, continued deliveries to China would increasingly depend on drawing down a finite stockpile rather than replacing exported barrels.

Volare follows Capital Tankers Corp., which listed in Oslo in March, and OMC Tankers Ltd., which joined Euronext Growth in August. According to Euronext, Oslo is now Europe’s largest stock market for shipping companies by number of listings, due to an active strategy to attract more shipping companies. Chief Executive Officer Alexandre Duff said Oslo’s concentration of shipping investors, banks, lawyers and industry expertise made the city “the only option for this particular transaction,” speaking in an interview in the Norwegian capital. The listing also allows Volare to tap an exceptionally strong tanker market as disruption around the Strait of Hormuz has pushed up freight rates and vessel values. items.title: Gulf Oil Flows Rise to Average 81% of Pre-war Rate in September
items.original_title: Gulf Oil Flows Rise to Average 81% of Pre-war Rate in September
items.summary: File Photo: Oil tanker Al Shaffiah sails at the sea near the Omani coast, as seen from Musandam, Oman, June 26, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer LONDON, Oct 6 – Gulf oil flows excluding Iran surged to over 81% of pre- war levels in September, data showed, led by a recovery in Saudi exports despite attacks on the kingdom’s oil infrastructure and escalating Iranian attacks on regional shipping, while Iranian exports fell to zero due to a US blockade. The blockade has all but choked off Iranian exports, while other Gulf producers have adapted to attacks on energy infrastructure and shipping by relying on so-called dark transits — switching off tankers’ tracking systems to evade detection — to protect the oil flows that underpin their economies. Flows of crude, condensate and refined fuels including LPG averaged 19.2 million barrels per day (bpd) from Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain, Iraq and the UAE, Vortexa data showed, compared with an average of about 23.6 million bpd in the year that preceded the outbreak of the Iran war on February 28. Crude and condensate flows recovered to 91% of their pre-war levels of 16.3 million bpd, Vortexa data showed.

items.title: Aramco CEO calls for greater global alignment to strengthen energy resilience
items.original_title: Aramco CEO calls for greater global alignment to strengthen energy resilience
items.summary: Amin Nasser, Aramco President and CEO, has called for closer coordination among governments, energy suppliers and customers to strengthen global energy resilience and better withstand geopolitical disruptions. Speaking at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London, Nasser highlighted the continuing importance of oil and gas to global energy security, economic stability and geopolitical resilience. He warned that disruptions to regional energy flows could create prolonged pressure on markets and take significant time to resolve. Even then, replenishing inventories while meeting demand could take up to two years.” Nasser also stressed that oil and gas remain deeply embedded in the global economy and that the energy transition faces resource and supply-chain challenges. “Oil and gas are not just tradable commodities – they are the lifeblood of modern civilization… With shortages of aluminum, sulfur, helium, and petrochemicals, solar, wind, and EVs are not immune either… Half the world’s proven oil reserves are in the Middle East, along with most of its spare production capacity… Our region’s strategic importance is set to grow, as the other resource bases mature, and new ones are potentially harder to find and less economically competitive.” He pointed to Aramco’s diversified resilience measures, including strategic storage, spare production capacity, multiple crude grades, domestic gas storage and its tanker fleet through Bahri.

items.original_title: Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline oil flow reaches 5.8 million bpd
items.summary: Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline is operating with oil flows reaching 5.8 million barrels per day as of Tuesday morning, Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said. The pipeline, which transports crude to the Red Sea export terminal at Yanbu, has not experienced any interruptions, a source said Monday. The statement came after media reports suggested a recent disruption amid ongoing tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis. Saudi Arabia restarted the pipeline operations following drone attacks on September 11 that forced the kingdom to shut down the pipeline and halt crude loadings at Yanbu, three sources briefed on the matter said. The kingdom has attributed the attacks to Iraqi militias. The pipeline has become increasingly important after the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted oil flows from Saudi Arabia and neighboring Gulf states through the Strait of Hormuz. Riyadh has been using the East-West Pipeline to reroute approximately 4 million barrels per day to Yanbu, representing about 4% of global oil supply. Source: Investing.com

items.title: Search for missing crew after drones sink cargo ship off Bulgaria
items.original_title: Search for missing crew after drones sink cargo ship off Bulgaria
items.summary: A passing ferry found an overturned lifeboat and life jackets at the scene of the missing boat. A second ship was also attacked and both are Turkish-owned. A search is under way in the Black Sea for the crew of a cargo ship that sank after drones struck two commercial vessels off Bulgaria early on Tuesday. Sea and aerial drones hit the ships at about 3am local time (2am CET), around 70 nautical miles east of the town of Byala in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. The crew of the Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria, which was in the area, saw an explosion on the first ship and sailed to the scene, Radev confirmed. The second ship caught fire and all 18 of its crew were rescued by the Dioscuria. Ship tracking website vesselfinder.com shows the Alfa Watan was sailing under the flag of Togo and was headed for the Romanian port of Sulina. Radev, who called the attack “absolutely unacceptable”, did not say who launched the drones while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the developments “concerning”. The incident occurred a day after a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying grain in the Black Sea was attacked by at least one drone and sank after catching fire.

items.original_title: War in Ukraine Escalates With Drone Strikes on Cargo Ships
items.summary: Cargo ships are seen from a patrol boat of Ukraine’s coast guard as they sail in the Black Sea, amid Russia’s attack on Ukraine, February 7, 2024. REUTERS/Thomas Peter (Bloomberg) — Attacks on commercial vessels off the Black Sea’s western coast are on the rise, threatening already-choked trade flows in the region while testing NATO’s readiness to react. Two general cargo ships were hit by air and naval drones overnight in the exclusive economic zone of Bulgaria, a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, Prime Minister Rumen Radev told reporters on Tuesday. “What is happening severely hampers shipping in the Black Sea, drives up insurance costs even further, and makes maritime operations extremely difficult.” The strikes in NATO countries’ exclusive economic zones add to previous cases of drone incursions in countries such as Poland and Romania, helping Russia to test the alliance’s readiness to protect its borders while remaining short of full-fledged attacks on its territory. Radev said the strikes can’t trigger NATO’s protective clauses — including formal consultations and the principle that an attack against one member state is an attack against the alliance — on the ground that more serious incidents have happened in the past without such a forceful response.

items.title: Panama Canal Expands Advance Transit Reservations for 2027 Dry Season
items.original_title: Panama Canal Expands Advance Transit Reservations for 2027 Dry Season
items.summary: The Panama Canal is expanding its long-term transit reservation program to the Panamax locks for the first time, giving more shipping customers the ability to secure passage months in advance during the 2027 dry season. The Panama Canal Authority said Monday that the next phase of its Long-term Slot Allocation, or LoTSA, program will cover transits from January 3 through April 3, 2027. The program will continue at the Neopanamax locks while a new pilot program introduces long-term slot allocations for vessels using the Panamax locks. The expansion comes as the Panama Canal continues adjusting its operating model following the severe drought that sharply restricted daily transits in 2023 and 2024 and exposed the vulnerability of the freshwater-dependent waterway to changing rainfall conditions. For carriers and vessel operators, the attraction of LoTSA is straightforward: guaranteed access to scarce transit capacity can make voyage planning more reliable, particularly during the dry season when water availability has historically placed the greatest pressure on Canal operations. By extending the program to the Panamax locks, the Canal is making that option available to a broader portion of the commercial fleet for the first time. The Panama Canal is easing restrictions on vessel draft and daily transits after improved rainfall and water-saving measures helped stabilize conditions in the waterway’s drought-sensitive watershed.

State oil firm Orlen's wholesale petrol prices have risen this week after falling in the leadup to Sunday’s elections Some had accused Orlen of artificially lowering prices to help the ruling party’s election campaign and warned they would rise afterwards https://t.co/FLUs1n8EA9 Figures from the then-opposition accused Orlen of lowering prices to win popularity for the government ahead of the elections. “The charges concern abuse of power and failure to fulfil managerial duties, causing damage to Orlen in the amount of over 4.1 billion złoty in connection with the implemented pricing policy,” wrote prosecutors. items.original_title: Capacity conundrum for shippers as carriers unveil post-Golden Week blanks
items.summary: With China’s Golden Week holiday under way and factories closed, supply chain planners’ attention has shifted to calculating shipping capacity out of Asia once Chinese workers return and container flows gear up again. According to Drewry’s Cancelled Sailings tracker, 39 blanked sailings have been announced in the period from Week 41 (5–11 October) to Week 45 (2–8 November) across three deepsea east-west trades – the transpacific, transatlantic and Asia-Europe – 5% of the 710 scheduled voyages. Half of the blanks will be on the transpacific, a third on Asia-Europe, and the remainder on the transatlantic. However, while carrier capacity management has been blamed for the persistently strong transpacific container spot freight rates over he past two months, the scale of the blanks customers currently face – both in terms of voyages and overall slot capacity – is actually on the low side, in comparison with post-Covid norms.

items.summary: Strong volume growth along the West African coast growth is proving the double-edged sword some had warned of, with many of the ports that had been reaping rewards now subject to heavy and intensifying congestion. Ghana, Guinea, and Sierra Leone are among the countries most affected by delays sprouting up along the coast, all three rapidly approaching similar volumes to those handled in the entirety of 2025. Forwarders active on West African trades told The Loadstar they too had observed the congestion hobbling many of the ports’ ability to function effectively, one expressing concern over looming temperature-controlled cargo due for delivery. The carrier has warned customers to expect delays of 10 days for discharging and loading goods, although Portcast claims that the situation at the Ghanian port may be improving, average waits having fallen below the four-day average, an improvement on last week. Instead, it singles Conakry and Freetown as the ports to be concerned about, congestion delays at both exceeding 10 days – a rapid deterioration at the Sierra Leone capital’s gateway saw delays increase by four days, week on week, and by more than a day at Conakry.

items.title: ‘More liberal’ India ends licence requirement for box ship reflagging
items.original_title: ‘More liberal’ India ends licence requirement for box ship reflagging
items.summary: As its emerging economy pursues maritime-driven growth, India appears willing to simplify the regulatory system for foreign-flag containerships operating out of the country. Reflecting a more liberalised approach, the Indian authorities have scrapped a licensing requirement for vessels chartered by foreign lines through local entities registered in the new business district in Gujarat State better known as “GIFT City”. Business units operating on the financial centre have multiple regulatory advantages – more particularly, significant tax exemptions – and several mainline and shortsea container lines reportedly already have presence at GIFT City, including CMA CGM, Maersk, and Unifeeder. And, acting on that strength, several container line heavyweights have implemented vessel reflagging in India – six changes by CMA CGM and twoby Maersk. While reflagging one vessel the Marseille-based carrier said: “With India playing an increasingly important role in the global trade, CMA CGM remains dedicated to supporting the country’s maritime ecosystem and contributing to its economic development through strategic initiatives and enhanced service offerings. The move to abolish a licensing requirement that involved considerable documentation for each call seeking to enter Indian waters is a significant policy relaxation, aimed at pushing the “ease-of-doing-business environment” for investors. And industry sources claimed it would allow “greater operational flexibility” for carriers.

items.summary: London-listed Taylor Maritime has moved its wind-down to the final vessel, completing the sale of three handysize bulkers while chief executive Ed Buttery builds up a private dry bulk position through his T3 Holding vehicle. The company said on Tuesday that the three previously announced handysize disposals have closed, generating gross proceeds of about $48.6m. Taylor Maritime is now “in the process of disposing of the last vessel in the fleet”, with another update to follow. The wording indicates the disposal programme has moved beyond the two-vessel position left after the September transactions, when Taylor Maritime still had one handysize and one ultramax on its books. Hermes World Maritime took the remaining 49%. Taylor Maritime will provide commercial management and corporate administration services to T3 and the two-ship vehicle during a transitional period. Taylor Maritime formally opted for a managed realisation in March, bringing an end to an expansion story that at its peak saw the company control more than 50 bulkers following the takeover of Grindrod Shipping. By the end of March, Taylor Maritime had sold 51 ships since the start of 2023 for $839.2m. Following a $45m capital return in July, the board intends to distribute a further $45m in November through a fourth compulsory partial redemption of shares.

items.summary: Teu-mile demand growth has regressed for the first time since January, reflecting a combination of blanked sailings by major carriers during China’s Golden Week, increased newbuild vessel deliveries, and more ships returning to the Suez Canal on Asia-Europe routes. The blanked sailings are concentrated on Asia-US East Coast and Asia-Europe trades. Linerlytica said: “The return to the Suez route poses the biggest threat to carrier efforts to reverse the rate slide on the Asia-Europe route that have persisted for the past three months. “All carriers are making a concerted rate push from the end of October, with MSC among the latest to announce new Asia-North Europe FAK (freight all kinds) rates from 19 October of $3,150 per teu and $4,500 per 40ft.” Rates on that trade have fallen around 60% since July as the early peak-season momentum faded. Nearly 200,000 teu of new capacity arrived last month, against no vessels demolished, adding further pressure to market capacity. The faster-than-expected resumption of Suez Canal transits, however, remains the biggest obstacle to carrier efforts to support and increase freight rates.

items.title: Europe’s diesel tightness persists into Q4
items.original_title: Europe’s diesel tightness persists into Q4
items.summary: Europe’s diesel/gasoil imports from outside the region hit the lowest September on record. Diesel/gasoil exports pointed to Europe from outside regions averaged only 1mbd in September, down 600kbd y-o-y. Russia and the Middle East account for most of the drop, together down 580kbd compared to last year. Diesel on the water pointed to Europe is more than 25% below last year’s levels, all points indicating that October will be another month of weak arrivals. Europe’s implied refinery runs fell by around 600kbd in September (according to our estimates), after reaching a year-to-date high in August. Strong margins have delayed maintenance at key refineries into 2027, including Tarragona (180kbd), Thessaloniki (66kbd) and Gonfreville (247kbd) (Argus), so maintenance season is likely to already have peaked in September this year, as opposed to the usual October. The US is still the key external supplier The US supplied 41% of Europe’s external diesel in September, at 400kbd, above year-ago levels but down from a dataset high of 445kbd in August. A growing portion of China’s diesel cargoes are moving on LR2s. Unless Asia’s diesel arb to Europe widens, China’s Q4 barrels will likely keep prioritising shorter-haul destinations amid high freight costs.

items.title: Copper Gains on Risk-On Mood
items.original_title: Copper Gains on Risk-On Mood
items.summary: Copper futures rose to around $6.6 per pound on Tuesday, advancing for a third consecutive session amid a rally in risk assets, highlighted by gains in technology and artificial intelligence stocks. Demand for copper is benefiting from the rapid expansion of data centers and power infrastructure required to support AI development. Still, the near-term demand outlook remains constrained by signs of weakening industrial activity in China, the world’s largest consumer of the metal. On the supply side, Chilean copper output dropped in August to its lowest level since February 2011, while workers at Antofagasta’s Centinela mine voted in favor of strike action after wage negotiations failed to reach an agreement. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has yet to decide on potential tariffs targeting refined copper. Earlier threats of US duties on refined metals encouraged traders to divert shipments toward American warehouses, contributing to the recent surge in copper prices. Source: Trading Economics

items.title: Goldman sees upside risks to European gas on supply, weather
items.original_title: Goldman sees upside risks to European gas on supply, weather
items.summary: Goldman Sachs reiterates its view that European natural gas and liquefied natural gas prices depend primarily on Middle East LNG exports and weather conditions, with risks skewed to the upside. The firm estimates that Title Transfer Facility prices could rally to 150 EUR/MWh by year-end under specific conditions. The scenario assumes winter Persian Gulf LNG exports do not improve beyond 25% of normal levels. The price projection also requires winter temperatures to realize one standard deviation colder than average. Both factors would need to occur simultaneously to reach the 150 EUR/MWh level. Goldman Sachs maintains that the path for European natural gas prices from current levels remains primarily dependent on these two variables. Middle East LNG export volumes and weather patterns continue to drive the market outlook. The firm’s analysis focuses on the combination of supply constraints from the Persian Gulf region and potential demand increases from colder-than-normal winter conditions. The upside risk assessment reflects the possibility of both factors materializing together.

items.title: Korea pushes SMR ship lead as outdated rules spur global standards race
items.original_title: Korea pushes SMR ship lead as outdated rules spur global standards race
items.summary: As Korea’s shipbuilding industry accelerates development of vessels equipped with small modular reactors (SMRs), calls are growing for the creation of international rules. Existing nuclear safety regulations focus on land-based nuclear power plants, and maritime regulations focus on conventional ships, leaving a gap for “ships carrying reactors,” where standards to apply are not fully established. With the offshore SMR market preparing for commercial use, leading the formation of international standards and rules—no less than technology development—is seen as a factor that will determine future market competitiveness. For ships carrying next-generation SMRs to call at ports around the world, standards are needed that cover not only reactor safety but also maritime accidents such as collisions and groundings, port entry, and emergency response. International liability rules for damages in the event of an accident involving a nuclear-powered ship are also not functioning properly. IMO and International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) standards on port entry conditions were last revised in 1968. The Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute (KAERI) and Samsung Heavy Industries are developing a 174,000-cubic-meter LNG carrier based on a marine MSR, and HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering has designed a nuclear-powered container ship equipped with an SMR, winning approval in principle from DNV in Oct.

items.title: The Commodities Feed: Oil supported by geopolitical risks despite supply gains
items.original_title: The Commodities Feed: Oil supported by geopolitical risks despite supply gains
items.summary: Energy — Persian Gulf supply increases While there are growing signs of a recovery in oil flows from the Persian Gulf, the market remains nervous about potential supply disruptions from the region. This is keeping prices well-supported for now. This nervousness is likely to persist until there are signs of progress in a deal between the US and Iran. Kuwait said that it is producing at 75% of pre-war levels, while the Saudis also cut the official selling price of their Arab Light into Asia for November loadings, a sign of an improving supply picture. This is down from 83% at the same stage last year, and below the 5-year average of 88%. However, gains may remain capped by elevated Treasury yields, persistent inflation concerns and a firmer US dollar. The rally is being driven by mounting concerns over tightening global supplies as adverse weather conditions threaten production across key producing regions. In India, below-normal monsoon rainfall has lowered production forecasts, while European sugar beet yields are expected to be 11% below the five-year average. Data from Ukraine’s Agriculture Ministry shows that grain and legume exports so far in the 2026/27 harvest season fell 26% year-on-year to 5.4mt as of 5 October.

items.title: Exmar confirms lucrative suezmax resale
items.original_title: Exmar confirms lucrative suezmax resale
items.summary: Belgium’s Exmar has confirmed the sale of the first suezmax in its four-ship newbuilding programme at South Korea’s DH Shipbuilding, crystallising a profit of around $22m on the transaction. The Antwerp-listed company said it has signed an agreement to sell the first tanker under construction, with the vessel to pass to its buyer simultaneously with delivery from the yard in the third quarter of 2027. Exmar did not disclose either the buyer or sale price. Greek shipping and financial sources previously identified Evangelos Marinakis-led Capital Group as the buyer of the 157,000 dwt hull HN5112, with the resale priced at more than $106m. The $22m gain disclosed by Exmar is broadly consistent with those market numbers. Exmar ordered four scrubber-fitted, 157,200 dwt suezmaxes at DH Shipbuilding in September 2025 in the Belgian gas shipping specialist’s first move into crude tanker ownership. Exmar’s 2025 accounts subsequently showed $309.4m of remaining capital commitments attached to the suezmax programme at year-end. Deliveries were scheduled to start in the third quarter of 2027 and run through October 2028. The resale comes against a sharp run-up in suezmax values and earnings, with prompt tonnage commanding significant premiums to later-delivery newbuildings.

items.title: China’s tariff cut plans skip soybeans, spurring hopes for higher buys of other US farm goods
items.original_title: China’s tariff cut plans skip soybeans, spurring hopes for higher buys of other US farm goods
items.summary: China’s exclusion of soybeans from its planned tariff-reduction framework has left exporters optimistic that Beijing will increase purchases of other US farm and food products in the coming months to fulfill a commitment made earlier this year. China’s Ministry of Commerce said Sept. 28 that Beijing would consider reducing tariffs on a range of US agricultural and animal-protein products, including beef, pork, corn and wheat, but excluded soybeans. China purchased more than $10 billion in US farm and food products from January through July 2026, including $4.9 billion of soybeans and $5.2 billion of other agricultural commodities, according to US Census Bureau trade data. “Removal of the remaining 10% tariff that China has on US agricultural commodities could be key to boosting US competitiveness in the Chinese market,” S&P Global Energy CERA analysts said in a Sept. US beef and pork exports have historically accounted for a significant share of China’s purchases of US agricultural and food products, US traders said. During the tariff dispute in early 2025, China reduced its purchases of US pork and suspended US beef imports after Beijing stopped renewing export licenses for US meat-processing facilities in March 2025. China imposes a 13% duty on US soybeans, comprising a 3% most-favored-nation tariff and an additional 10% levy.

items.title: Existing Methanol-Capable Shipping Fleet Could Consume 2 Bil Gal/Year Of Ethanol
items.original_title: Existing Methanol-Capable Shipping Fleet Could Consume 2 Bil Gal/Year Of Ethanol
items.summary: The existing fleet of methanol-capable ships could consume nearly 2 billion gallons/year of ethanol if operated primarily on the fuel, offering ethanol producers a potentially significant new outlet for demand as the shipping industry seeks lower-carbon alternatives, according to a US laboratory study released last week. The 112 to 120 methanol dual-fuel vessels currently operating could consume about 6 million mt/year of ethanol, assuming an average fuel use of 100 mt/day of conventional marine fuel and operation for 330 days/year, the National Laboratory of the Rockies said in Evaluation of Ethanol Use in Marine Shipping. The study was produced under the direction of the ethanol industry group Growth Energy. 28 that it completed the first ship-to-ship commercial ethanol bunkering of a deep-sea container vessel in the US, fueling the Tangier Maersk with 100% domestically produced corn ethanol in an operation that could open new trade flow pathways for US agricultural commodities into the marine fuel supply chain. Methanol fleet offers entry route Ethanol could use much of the engine technology, handling infrastructure and operating experience already developed for methanol because the two alcohol fuels have similar characteristics, the study said. A vessel requires about 1.8 times the storage volume when using ethanol instead of marine gas oil, compared with 2.4 times for methanol, the study said.

items.title: Three tanker incidents reported in Hormuz Strait in 24 hours: UKMTO
items.original_title: Three tanker incidents reported in Hormuz Strait in 24 hours: UKMTO
items.summary: At least two tankers have been struck in the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said on Monday, adding that a third vessel avoided being hit after complying with instructions from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The British navy monitor said it received “a time-late report of an incident within the Strait of Hormuz” in which a “verified source” reported that “a crude oil tanker has been struck by unknown projectiles,” adding that “authorities are investigating.” In a second statement published minutes later, UKMTO said it had received another delayed report, citing a “verified source” as saying that a liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) tanker “transiting inbound has been struck by an unknown projectile.” “Vessels are advised to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity to UKMTO,” the agency said. A third incident was also recorded 11 nautical miles north of Khasab, in Oman’s northern Musandam governorate, UKMTO relayed, detailing that “a tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz inbound was hailed by the IRGC and instructed to turn back or the vessel would be targeted.” “The Master of the tanker has confirmed that they have complied with the instruction,” the monitor said.

items.title: India’s VOC port runs drills for methanol bunker pilot
items.original_title: India’s VOC port runs drills for methanol bunker pilot
items.summary: The port authority of VO Chidambaranar (VOC) in India has carried out training and mock drills to prepare for a methanol bunkering pilot at the port. VOC Port is located on India’s south-eastern coast along the East-West international shipping route. The port authority held a methanol bunkering training session for personnel from its traffic, marine, mechanical and fire and safety departments, along with representatives from project contractor SOPAN. The session included a live demonstration and mock drills at the planned bunkering site, focusing on safe methanol handling and preparations for future bunkering operations. The authority has not disclosed when the methanol bunkering pilot will take place, or how the fuel will be supplied to vessels. Earlier this year, another Indian port hosted the country’s first shore-to-ship methanol bunkering pilot. A Stolt Tankers-owned vessel received an undisclosed quantity of grey methanol during the trial at the Port of Kandla. The port authority also adopted a methanol bunkering manual and standard operating guidelines to support bunkering operations. Source: By Konica Bhatt, ENGINE, https://www.engine.online/news

items.title: Markets ablaze as Middle East conflict continues
items.original_title: Markets ablaze as Middle East conflict continues
items.summary: Renewed fighting in the Middle East has pushed gas markets back into crisis. US strikes on Iranian targets, Houthi advances on the Bab el-Mandeb strait and a shutdown of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline have combined to send Brent above $100 per barrel and LNG prices racing toward $30 per MMBtu, erasing the price gap that once separated European and Asian buyers. The impact on supply is significant and growing. Rystad Energy now estimates conflict-related LNG production losses from Qatar at 64.8 Mtpa in 2026 and 22.9 Mtpa in 2027, a sharp increase from last month’s figures. In response, we have raised our 2026 price forecasts for TTF and Northeast Asian spot LNG by $1.0 per MMBtu, to $16.0 and $17.0 respectively, as low storage levels in Europe and uncertainty over winter arbitrage keep buyers on edge. The longer-term picture tells a different story. Supply and demand are expected to rebalance by 2028, and from 2029 the market is set to tip into oversupply, peaking at 81 Mtpa in 2032. For buyers and producers alike, the challenge is navigating a market that is tight today but loosening fast. Source: Rystad Energy

items.summary: Petroleum markets in the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26) were characterized by increasing prices for crude oil and petroleum products amid persistent conflict in the Middle East. items.title: d’Amico brings last leased tanker back in-house
items.original_title: d’Amico brings last leased tanker back in-house
items.summary: Italian product tanker owner d’Amico International Shipping has exercised a $14m purchase option on the 2014-built MR tanker High Fidelity , paving the way for its entire operating fleet to return to full ownership. Operating arm d’Amico Tankers is expected to take ownership of the 50,000 dwt Hyundai Vinashin-built vessel around mid-January 2027, with the final price subject to a small adjustment depending on the actual transfer date. The ship is one of the last two vessels in d’Amico’s fleet still operating under bareboat arrangements. The company currently controls 28 product tankers on the water — 16 MRs, six handysizes and six LR1s — comprising 26 owned ships and two bareboat-chartered units. The move follows d’Amico’s decision in August to exercise a $15.3m option on sister-era MR High Discovery, which is due to return to full ownership in November. Once both transfers are completed, d’Amico will have no remaining bareboat-chartered ships. Both vessels were refinanced through sale-and-leaseback structures in 2022. At the time, d’Amico exercised previous options on High Discovery and High Fidelity for $20.3m and $19.2m respectively before refinancing them under new 10-year bareboat leases containing fresh purchase options. D’Amico meanwhile has 10 newbuildings on order, comprising four LR1s due in 2027 and six smaller product tankers — two handysizes and four MRs — lined up for 2029.

In June, it sold the 2008-built Lila Kochi after owning it for about a year. Lila Global acquired the ship in May 2025 for $46.75m and sold it for $79m. The tanker segment has become an increasingly important part of Lila Global’s activity this year. Having added six tankers in 2026, its latest purchase is the 2010-built suezmax Cape Benat, the former Front Loki, which it recently acquired for $62.5m. The ship has since been renamed Renat and is listed with a market value of $74.4m, according to the VesselsValue sales register.

It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack by air and sea drones about 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, but there are growing concerns about hybrid attacks by Russia as it wages war in Ukraine. items.title: HD Hyundai delivers world’s first lashing-free containership
items.original_title: HD Hyundai delivers world’s first lashing-free containership
items.summary: HD Hyundai has delivered what it says is the world’s first containership designed to eliminate manual lashing, removing one of the most labour-intensive jobs in container shipping. The 13,000 teu vessel, which is methanol dual-fuelled, has been handed over toFrance’s CMA CGM after being built using HD Hyundai’s proprietary hybrid lashing-free system. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries developed and verified the core technology, while HD Hyundai Samho carried out detailed design and construction. HD Hyundai’s new arrangement does away with that work by extending cell guides above deck, allowing containers to be held in place without traditional lashing. The breakthrough centres on what HD Hyundai calls a portable bench, a standardised structure fitted between cell guides. The unit is the same size as a 40 ft container, meaning terminal cranes can handle it as part of normal cargo operations. HD Hyundai says the design boosts deck cargo capacity by more than 10% compared with similar existing ships while improving operational stability in heavy weather. The technology was presented to the IMO’s Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers in 2024 and has since secured multiple patents. The Korean yard plans to expand the lashing-free technology to small and mid-sized vessels soon.

items.title: Tanker attacks around Hormuz hit wartime high
items.original_title: Tanker attacks around Hormuz hit wartime high
items.summary: Commercial shipping around the Strait of Hormuz is enduring its most intense spell of attacks since the US-Iran war began on February 28, with four tankers struck and another directly threatened in incidents disclosed by UK Maritime Trade Operations on Monday. The latest attack came at 1637 UTC yesterday when a tanker transiting Hormuz was hit by an unknown projectile, starting a fire in the engine room. The crew was fighting the blaze when UKMTO issued its warning, with no casualties or pollution initially reported. Separately, an inbound tanker around 11 nautical miles north of Khasab was hailed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and ordered to turn around or face attack. Oil exports through Hormuz have returned close to, and on several days exceeded, pre-war levels, leaving an increasingly uncomfortable combination of more barrels moving through the strait and more ships being attacked. That is feeding directly into extraordinary tanker economics. Owners willing to undertake Gulf shuttle voyages are commanding huge premiums, with some round trips reportedly costing charterers as much as $40m. BRS Shipbrokers said in its latest tanker report the pool of tonnage prepared to trade the region remains central to freight pricing.

items.title: Black Sea merchant shipping comes under fresh drone attack
items.original_title: Black Sea merchant shipping comes under fresh drone attack
items.summary: Commercial shipping in the western Black Sea has come under a fresh wave of attacks, with another general cargoship sinking and a second catching fire off Bulgaria barely a day after the loss of the Royad Mammadov off Romania. According to UK maritime security specialist Vanguard Tech, the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan and Palau-flagged Able issued distress signals around 70–80 nautical miles east of Byala and Cape St Atanas, inside Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. Bulgarian sources state that both vessels had been struck by drones. The Turkish-owned, St Kitts and Nevis-flagged vessel was carrying corn from Izmail to Italy when it caught fire and sank around 30 nautical miles south of Sfantu Gheorghe. Two seafarers were killed and 11 rescued. If the Bulgarian reports are confirmed, the latest incidents would mark a significant westward expansion of the threat facing merchant shipping in the Black Sea, taking the danger well beyond waters immediately off Ukraine. The attacks also come just as Turkey and the United Nations are trying to revive talks aimed at securing a limited Black Sea maritime truce. Ankara has been pushing a framework focused on protecting commercial navigation, ports and energy infrastructure, drawing in part on the architecture of the former Black Sea Grain Initiative.

items.title: Panama Canal extends long-term slot system to panamax locks
items.original_title: Panama Canal extends long-term slot system to panamax locks
items.summary: The Panama Canal is extending its long-term slot allocation programme to the Panamax locks for the first time as it looks to give more customers greater certainty through the coming dry season. The new Long-term Slot Allocation, or LoTSA, phase will cover January 3 to April 3, 2027, with the established neopanamax system running alongside a new panamax pilot. For neopanamax vessels, 36 packages covering 270 slots will be offered, split between 165 northbound and 105 southbound passages. The panamax pilot will offer 51 packages and 288 slots, evenly spread at roughly three transits per day. The move builds on a system first introduced for the larger locks in 2024, when the Panama Canal Authority began offering blocks of future reservations to customers seeking greater scheduling certainty after the severe 2023-24 drought. Splash reported in May that neopanamax auction prices had surged to as much as $4m as Middle East disruption redirected more US energy cargoes through Panama. By August, one LPG carrier had paid a record $5.3m for priority passage as deteriorating water conditions and strong demand squeezed capacity. The canal subsequently cut daily booking capacity to 32 ships and tightened draft limits as rainfall disappointed, before recent rains allowed some restrictions to be eased again.

items.title: From Cost To Choice: Supply Chain Chiefs Redesign Networks To Navigate Uncertainty
items.original_title: From Cost To Choice: Supply Chain Chiefs Redesign Networks To Navigate Uncertainty
items.summary: Supply chain leaders are redesigning their networks around greater choice and flexibility, as resilience increasingly becomes a source of competitive advantage and growth, according to new research from DP World’s Global Trade Observatory. The Chief Supply Chain Officer (CSCO) Pulse Report, based on a survey in August of 103 CSCOs across 14 markets and nine industries, finds that 84% say resilience and optionality have overtaken cost reduction as the primary drivers of supply-chain strategy. The shift is already changing how businesses design their networks. The report describes this shift as a move from optimisation to optionality: away from designing supply chains primarily around cost and efficiency, towards creating viable alternatives that businesses can call upon as trade rules, tariffs, demand and geopolitical conditions change. Businesses are responding to uncertainty not by retreating from growth, but by creating more choices about where they source, how they move goods and how they reach customers. The opportunity is to build networks that combine efficiency with flexibility – giving businesses the options, visibility and connectivity they need to keep growing through uncertainty.” SUPPLY CHAIN MOVES TO THE HEART OF GROWTH The report finds that this changing operating model is being accompanied by a broader transformation in the role of supply-chain leadership.

But internationally uncompetitive, non-domestic electricity prices are one of the main barriers to shore power uptake across the UK port sector, according to a white paper published by the port authority, with input from British Ports Association (BPA), in September. items.title: Aramco CEO says global oil stocks are ’scarily thin’ amid Hormuz risks
items.original_title: Aramco CEO says global oil stocks are ’scarily thin’ amid Hormuz risks
items.summary: Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said global oil inventories have fallen to “scarily thin” levels and markets will remain under pressure until the Strait of Hormuz fully reopens. Speaking at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London, Nasser said supply constraints were affecting both crude and refined fuels, with fuel prices rising even more sharply. He said planned releases of up to 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel stocks by major economies would provide temporary relief but would not resolve supply-demand imbalances. Even after Hormuz fully reopens, it could take up to two years for oil-consuming countries to rebuild their inventories, Nasser said. Crude flows have recovered to near pre-war levels, but Brent has remained around $100 a barrel over the past month as markets continue to price in risks to supplies through the Persian Gulf and Red Sea. Aramco has increased crude shipments from its Ras Tanura export terminal and restored flows on its East-West pipeline to about 80% of capacity after a temporary shutdown caused by an attack last month. Nasser said Aramco had maintained supplies during the conflict by using international storage and quickly repairing damaged infrastructure. The company is also seeking alternative export routes and additional overseas storage to reduce its reliance on any single supply route. Source: Investing.com

items.title: The diversification of MEG trading patterns is already underway
items.original_title: The diversification of MEG trading patterns is already underway
items.summary: MEG exporters are diversifying trade patterns. Skipping local shuttle hubs lengthens turnaround times, elevating structural freight rates across the region. Key Takeaways: • The scaling of MEG trades has already forced Middle East Gulf (MEG) exporters to bypass local Ship-to-Ship (STS) transfers in favour of direct voyages and alternative hubs. However, as MEG loadings continue to scale, recently boosted by the redirection of Saudi exports to the East, challenging STS capacity in the GoO, a diversification of the region’s trading patterns becomes increasingly inevitable. To truly assess the trajectory of volumes, it is important to exclude volumes loaded during the MoU (for this piece spanning from June 17 to July 11) as this period was characterised by higher navigational flexibility. Approximately 0.7 Mbd of the region’s post-MoU loaded cargoes (30%) did not include a GoO STS in July, a figure that rose above the 1.0 Mbd (27%) in August and is assessed at 0.5 Mbd (43%) thus far in September. As a significant share (82%) of the running month’s barrels are still in transit, this latter figure is subject to significant revisions. A distinct pattern is also evident in the case of Saudi Arabia, where the country’s national fleet appears to have captured a significant share of these direct voyages.

The share of Qatar, once the country’s dominant supplier, plunged to 4.3 percent, as India continues to diversify its energy sourcing in the wake of West Asia conflict. The country imported 585,000 tonnes of LNG from Oman in September, up 11.6 percent from August, data from commodity analytics firm Kpler shows. Qatar used to account for around 45 percent of India’s LNG imports. However, supplies have been disrupted after Iran struck its Ras Laffan Industrial City in March, its LNG hub and single largest supply of natural gas to India. ICRA’s senior vice president and co-group head Prashant Vasisht said that Qatar accounts for 19 percent of the global LNG supply and it could take months to bring the full capacity back online after the Iran attack. India imports about half of its total LNG consumption, with roughly 60 percent transiting through the Strait of Hormuz from West Asian suppliers such as Qatar and the UAE. The country’s cumulative LNG imports fell by 14 percent to 2.17 million tonnes in September against 2.5 million tonnes in August.

items.title: How close is shipping to the top?
items.original_title: How close is shipping to the top?
items.summary: Shipping markets rarely announce the top with any clarity. More often, the argument about whether the peak has arrived only really starts when freight rates are still climbing, asset values are making less and less conventional sense and owners are sufficiently confident to keep buying ships at prices that would have looked ridiculous a few months earlier. Chief correspondent Adis Adjin assesses where we are in today’s record high shipping cycle. But there are enough signs beneath the surface to start asking a more awkward question: how much of this cycle is left, and which sectors are closest to finding out? The comparison with the last supercycle has its limits — today’s orderbook is equivalent to around 23% of the fleet, against more than 50% at the 2008 peak — but the direction of travel is clear. The bigger issue is what happens to the amount of large tonnage still scheduled to emerge from Asian yards, much of it above 12,000 teu, while a large share of the chartered fleet that can be returned sits below 8,000 teu. Around 14% of current capacity is due to arrive before the end of the decade, while recycling potential amounts to roughly 8% of today’s fleet.

items.title: HIP Crosses One Million TEU Milestone
items.original_title: HIP Crosses One Million TEU Milestone
items.summary: Hambantota International Port (HIP) has surpassed one million TEUs in cumulative container throughput since the commissioning of new quay cranes in 2025, marking a significant milestone in the rapid growth of its container operations. The port handled 428,036 TEUs in 2025, while throughput reached 574,196 TEUs in 2026 year-to-date, bringing the combined volume to 1,002,232 TEUs. The achievement reflects the continued expansion of HIP’s container business and growing customer confidence in its operational capabilities. “Crossing one million TEUs is an important achievement for HIP and a strong indication of the confidence our customers are placing in the port. In April, HIP established a new single-vessel handling record when the MSC Marie Leslie recorded 7,968 container moves, equivalent to 13,260 TEUs, during its call at the port. HIP subsequently achieved its highest-ever monthly container throughput in June, handling 80,325 TEUs. Central to the programme are six new quay cranes and 16 rubber-tyred gantry cranes, forming part of the port’s wider USD 108 million investment in container-handling machinery and supporting assets. “The one-million-TEU milestone shows that HIP’s container business is moving into a new stage of growth. The latest milestone reinforces HIP’s progression from an emerging container operation into a growing regional gateway, supported by expanding infrastructure, established shipping-line partnerships and a clear path towards higher capacity.

items.title: Iraq’s state tanker firm moves crude through Hormuz strait
items.original_title: Iraq’s state tanker firm moves crude through Hormuz strait
items.summary: Iraq’s state-owned Oil Tanker Company has transported 2 million barrels of Iraqi crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz using a very large crude carrier, marking the company’s first operation of this kind in decades, according to its director general on Saturday. The shipment represents a shift in operations for the company, which now transports crude through the strait instead of delivering it at the port of Basra. This change provides state oil marketer SOMO with more flexibility in selecting where and how to sell Iraqi crude. Ali Qais Abdul Jabbar, the company’s director general, said in a statement that the new arrangement could enable SOMO to access better sales and pricing opportunities. The Oil Tanker Company is working to purchase and operate specialized crude oil tankers to grow its fleet and improve its competitive position against regional shipping companies, Abdul Jabbar added. Source: Investing.com

items.title: OBT expands into Mauritania as demand for shipping and project logistics continues to grow
items.original_title: OBT expands into Mauritania as demand for shipping and project logistics continues to grow
items.summary: Growing activity across Mauritania’s mining, energy, offshore, infrastructure, oil and gas, renewable energy and development sectors has prompted African shipping and logistics specialist OBT to establish a local presence in the country. The new operation will be connected to OBT’s wider African network. Youssef Bouricha, OBT’s Mauritania Country Manager, said: “Mauritania is a natural next step for OBT. OBT Mauritania will offer shipping agency, freight forwarding, customs clearance, husbandry, project logistics, heavy-lift operations, warehousing, inland transportation and last-mile delivery. One recent logistics operation involved 33 containers, including offloading, temporary storage and distribution to more than 20 destinations. In addition, OBT has successfully handled several heavy-lift and project cargo operations in the country, including oversized and heavy equipment requiring specialized lifting, port coordination and inland transportation. These projects have given OBT valuable experience in managing complex logistics operations in Mauritania, particularly where coordination between the port, customs, transporters, stevedores, suppliers and final receivers is critical. OBT Mauritania will connect local execution with the group’s Dubai headquarters, African offices and international partner network, giving customers one point of coordination across markets. Combining local expertise with the strength of OBT’s wider African network, the new office will deliver reliable shipping and logistics solutions with effective coordination across the supply chain.

items.original_title: Vessels Loiter Over Subsea Cables and Pipelines Across Five Theaters

A Chinese-flagged fishery patrol vessel operated by a state fishery research institute has run research-pattern grids on both sides of the Guam subsea cable hub for seven weeks. Both grids sit on cable routes landing at Guam, the landing point for 11 subsea cables and a principal link between the U.S. Over 18 days, it made 27 low-speed research stops across an area crossed by the JUNO, Jupiter, FASTER, Topaz, Unity, PLCN, Pacific Crossing-1 and TGN-Pacific cables, which link Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines to the U.S. The loitering box sits over the cables that run through the Luzon Strait: SEA-ME-WE 3, the China-US Cable Network, SJC, EAC-C2C, APCN-2 and the FLAG North Asia Loop, all of which also land in mainland China or Hong Kong.

items.title: Opinion: Oil’s New Problem Isn’t Supply. It’s Logistics
items.original_title: Opinion: Oil’s New Problem Isn’t Supply. It’s Logistics
items.summary: A ship off the port of Aden, where traffic remained steady after the Iran-aligned Houthis said their forces had carried out missile and drone strikes on Saudi oil tankers, in Aden, Yemen, July 23, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer LONDON, Oct 5 (Reuters) – Middle East crude exports recently climbed to their highest levels since the start of the Iran war as more Gulf producers resume transit through the Strait of Hormuz – despite the continued threat of Iranian attacks. Yet oil prices remain stubbornly elevated, suggesting logistical problems are proving as disruptive as outright supply losses. Instead, Brent remains above $100 a barrel, more than 40% above pre-war levels. At the same time, buyers are increasingly sourcing crude from the Atlantic Basin and shipping it to Asia over longer routes, further tightening tanker supply. Rates to transport crude from the Middle East to Asia aboard a VLCC recently exceeded $1.2 million per day, up from roughly $30,000 a day in January, according to shipping broker Poten & Partners. As a result, freight costs that once accounted for around 3% of the delivered price of a barrel now represent roughly 27%.

items.title: Strong Freight Markets Keep Aging Ships Out of Recycling Yards
items.original_title: Strong Freight Markets Keep Aging Ships Out of Recycling Yards
items.summary: Strong freight markets kept aging vessels trading through the third quarter despite rising scrap prices and strong demand from ship recyclers, according to a new market review from GMS, the world’s largest cash buyer of ships for recycling. The ship recycling market entered the quarter looking ripe for an increase in demolition activity. GMS said it was tracking roughly 550 merchant vessels preparing to exit the Gulf at the start of July, including around 200 bulk carriers, while recycling yards in the major South Asian markets had available capacity and appetite for tonnage. The report argues that owners were weighing recycling offers against a much broader set of alternatives, including freight earnings, secondhand sale opportunities, remaining vessel life, route risks and compliance costs. GMS expects recycling supply to remain tight into the fourth quarter as long as vessel earnings remain strong, particularly where ships continue to find lucrative employment linked to the Strait of Hormuz. But those delayed recycling decisions may be creating a larger pool of aging tonnage that will eventually need to leave the fleet. If freight earnings normalize, secondhand liquidity weakens or employment opportunities narrow, GMS said some of that deferred supply could reach recycling markets over a much shorter period.

items.title: From Residue to Resource – the Rise and Risks of Marine Biofuels
items.original_title: From Residue to Resource – the Rise and Risks of Marine Biofuels
items.summary: While corn, sugarcane, wheat, or vegetable oils can be converted into fuel, their use for foodis driving demand to develop waste or bi-products from agricultural, forestry, food-processing and other biological industries as more prudent alternatives. Already, Fuel EU Maritime regulations financially incentivise the use of bio-residue, where areduced emissions ‘surplus’ can be sold to ship operators in deficit to avoid compliance penalties. “For vessels currently on order, 60.6% of the tonnage and 79.5% of the ships by number face similar limitations.” Against this backdrop, it is likely that suppliers seeking to satisfy maritime demand will increasingly look beyond conventional feedstocks towards more complex bio-residuesources. As RED III applies to all industries, there will also be competition from the airline and heavy transport industries in the use of bio-residues, and we suspect this will create additional risksin the maritime sector. Buyers in the sector may be exposed to lower-quality residues, for example, chemically variable feedstocks and/or blends from multiple residue streams. Pressure may mount on traceability systems, fraud risks may increase (due to misclassification of sustainabilityvalues in Proof of Compliance documents) and disputes over the chain of custodyaccumulate. Given the rising uptake of biofuels and the consequent risks, NorthStandard is recommending particular care in this area of marine fuel management.

items.title: LNG Trade Through Hormuz Extends Rebound Despite Shipping Risks
items.original_title: LNG Trade Through Hormuz Extends Rebound Despite Shipping Risks
items.summary: LNG carriers at the Qatari LNG export facility at Ras Laffan. Photo: RasGas Oct 5, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Shipments of liquefied natural gas through the Strait of Hormuz extended a rebound that began in September, as the region’s producers seek to restore supplies to energy-starved customers. At least three LNG shipments have exited the key waterway since late last week, according to ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg and Kpler. The market is closely watching LNG shipments through Hormuz for signs of relief from a supply crunch that last month pushed prices in Europe and Asia to the highest since late 2022. The increase in traffic comes as risks to shipping remain acute following a flurry of incidents in recent days. UK Maritime Trade Operations said it received a report of a tanker being hit by an unknown projectile within Hormuz on Oct 4. US President Donald Trump's push to steer $54 billion of South Korean investment into Alaska LNG is putting a fresh focus on a 20 million-ton-a-year export project that would cost more than twice as much as a comparable US Gulf Coast plant. Crude oil flows from the Middle East are returning toward pre-war levels despite continued risks to shipping, according to separate estimates from JPMorgan Chase & Co.

items.original_title: Seatrium bags ninth Karpowership FSRU conversion
items.summary: Singapore shipyard group Seatrium has secured a contract from Karpowership to convert an LNG carrier into the FSRU LNGT Akdeniz , extending a partnership that has produced seven delivered units since 2018. The work is scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027. LNGT Akdeniz will be the ninth FSRU conversion awarded by Karpowership to the Singapore yard group and the second to materialise under a 2025 letter of intent covering three LNG-carrier conversions and potential powership integration work. The FSRU will join Kinetics, Karpowership’s LNG infrastructure and energy-transition business, expanding its fleet to 12 LNG vessels. The award follows the September delivery and sailaway of LNGT Türkiye , the final vessel in a seven-unit FSRU conversion programme that began in 2018. Seatrium is also converting LNGT Karadeniz , the partnership’s eighth project and the first under the later LOI. Conversion work on that vessel began at Seatrium’s Tuas Boulevard yard in the third quarter of 2026. “The successful delivery of LNGT Türkiye and the award of LNGT Akdeniz are important milestones in the continued growth of Karpowership’s LNG-to-power business,” said Gokhan Kocak, Karpowership CTO. Seatrium has completed 22 FSRU and FSU conversion projects since 2007.

items.title: U-Ming doubles down in China with six-ship bulker spend
items.original_title: U-Ming doubles down in China with six-ship bulker spend
items.summary: Taiwan’s U-Ming Marine Transport has committed up to $312m on six more bulkers in China, adding four ultramaxes and firming another pair of Newcastlemaxes as it presses ahead with plans to build a 100-ship fleet. Two separate Taiwan exchange disclosures from U-Ming’s Singapore subsidiary put the combined investment at between $296m and $312m. The larger ships are two 211,000 dwt newcastlemaxes at Jiangsu Hantong Ship Heavy Industry, priced at between $77m and $80m each for a total of $154m to $160m. U-Ming is also paying between $142m and $152m for four 64,000 dwt ultramaxes at Sumec Marine-controlled New Dayang Shipbuilding, equating to $35.5m to $38m per ship. The first of the ultramaxes is scheduled for delivery in the fourth quarter of 2029, with the remaining three following during 2030. The latest contracting advances an expansion plan approved by U-Ming earlier this year covering four 210,000 dwt bulkers and four ultramaxes. U-Ming has been steadily renewing and expanding its core dry bulk fleet while moving into new sectors. At its May investor presentation, the company was targeting a fleet of more than 100 vessels, with dry bulk remaining at the centre of the expansion. U-Ming said at the end of September that its owned, joint venture and newbuilding fleet had reached around 90 ships and passed the 10m dwt mark.
