items.title: South Korea-Russia ocean volumes boosted by rail congestion in China
items.original_title: South Korea-Russia ocean volumes boosted by rail congestion in China
items.summary: Growing congestion along the Trans-China and Trans-Siberian railways, linking China and Russia, has boosted South Korea-Russia container volumes, encouraging shipping lines to consider deploying larger vessels this month. In August, more than 33,000 teu was transported from Busan to ports in Russia’s far east, such as Vladivostok, a slight increase on July. Of this, exports, excluding transhipment cargo, were 8,000 teu. Volumes are said to have remained at the same level in September, as South Korean shippers rushed to get cargo out before the country’s Thanksgiving Day holiday on 25-26 September and China’s week-long National Day on 1 October. Consequently, cargo “rollovers”, where shipments are delayed due to a lack of space, are becoming increasingly frequent and Busan-Vladivostok freight rates now average $1,700 per teu, up from $1,500 per teu in August, which had seen a $300 jump from July. A representative at Dong Young Shipping, which offers South Korea-Russia services, said: “We’re considering deploying larger vessels than those currently in use, so we can offer more slots.” Congestion around major Chinese hub ports following the East Asia typhoon season in August resulted in more Chinese shippers opting for rail freight to Europe. And as rail capacity has failed to keep pace with the surge in cargo volume, waiting times for train departures now exceed one week.

items.title: Empty box pile-up at port of Manila sparks truckers’ strike
items.original_title: Empty box pile-up at port of Manila sparks truckers’ strike
items.summary: Customs brokers and hauliers are expected to voluntarily stop work today in advance of a three-day trucking strike in Manila, as a year-long standoff on carriers failing to remove their empties reaches its limit – Hapag-Lloyd having suspended bookings amid the chaos. Warning the protest could “last a week”, Reynaldo Soliman, chair of the Practicing Customs Brokers and Port Truckers Alliance, urged brokers not to secure gate passes, book trucks, or release shipments, until carriers reduced the number of empties at Manila. “Even though we want to ship, we cannot move,” Mr Soliman told local reporters, with the number of empties scattered around terminals, hauliers yards, and waiting on flatbeds to be removed, measured in the thousands with just 10% of volumes moving out of Manila’s ports. In a letter seen by The Loadstar , Bureau of Customs commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno told Port of Manila it needed to take measures to address the worsening empties backlog, suggesting boxes that had been waiting for more than 10 days be moved offsite. “Increasing yard utilisation levels at the Manila International Container Port and the port of Manila continue to adversely affect the efficient movement of cargo and the overall flow of port operations,” he wrote.

items.summary: Dubai-based Grace Energy Shipping-linked interests are cashing in on the surge in tanker asset values, with brokers reporting the sale of the 2011-built suezmax Vendavel for $94.5m, close to double its acquisition price a little over two years ago. S&P sources list the 149,999 dwt New Times Shipbuilding-built tanker with the buyer undisclosed. Brokers note that the ship was acquired for $50m in May 2024. Vessel records show it subsequently became Vendavel, with Vendavel Shipping as registered owner and Grace Energy Shipping as manager. Against the $50m acquisition figure, the reported resale would represent a gross uplift of about $44.5m, or 89%, before ownership and transaction costs. Grace Energy has been steadily building its presence in the suezmax sector. Splash noted last year that the UAE-based outfit acquired Frontline’s Front Thor for about $48m, while in March it was linked to the $40.5m purchase of Tsakos Energy Navigation’s 2009-built Pentathlon. The deal lands in an exceptionally strong suezmax market. Brokers’ latest assessments put five-year-old secondhand values at $130m, up 19% over three months.

items.summary: Greek dry bulk owner Almi Marine Management has added another three ultramax newbuildings in China, expanding a fleet renewal drive that began earlier this year. Greek shipping sources report that the Athens-based owner has booked three 64,000 dwt bulkers at COSCO Shipping Heavy Industry’s Zhoushan yard, with delivery scheduled for 2030. The fresh deal follows Almi’s return to the newbuilding market in February after a four-year absence. Managing director Christos Hadjigeorgiou confirmed at the time that the company had signed for two 64,000 dwt next-generation ultramaxes at Nantong COSCO KHI Ship Engineering, or NACKS, for delivery in the second quarter of 2029. The latest Zhoushan trio takes Almi’s known forward programme to five 64,000 dwt newbuilds across two COSCO-linked yards. The owner already has close ties with the Chinese-Japanese NACKS and DACKS yards, taking three ultramaxes from DACKS in 2024. Almi currently controls six bulkers. Its fleet renewal has also included the disposal of older supramax tonnage, including the 2008-built Anasa. For a price marker, Splash noted in August that Xclusiv was assessing a standard Chinese-built ultramax at around $36m, which would put three ships at roughly $108m if Almi contracted near prevailing levels.

items.title: South Africa’s port reform takes an important step forward
items.original_title: South Africa’s port reform takes an important step forward
items.summary: One battle doesn’t win a war, but just getting to a stage where South Africa’s port system can now be reformed is an achievement by itself. The decision of South Africa’s government to formally endorse the separation of Transnet National Port Authority (TNPA), the country’s de facto port landlord, from the Transnet rail operations is a step in the right direction – one that its shippers, forwarders, and other supply chain stakeholders have been demanding for years. Operations at South Africa’s key container gateways of Durban, Cape Town, Coega and Port Elizabeth have been plagued by congestion and delays for years. And while it’s great the government has finally kicked off the reform process of Transnet, it also means some of the really hard work begins now, as the South African Association of Freight Forwarders argues when it says the real imperative is “getting corporatisation right”. The central point of the reform is that TNPA will be moved out of the Transnet group – which will continue to manage Transnet Port Terminals, but with much reduced investment power – and become a standalone state organisation with the ability to take its own investment decisions on both infrastructure and superstructure, and independently manage landlord revenues.

items.title: Europe’s scrap demand set to surge as new EAFs loom: Eurofer
items.original_title: Europe’s scrap demand set to surge as new EAFs loom: Eurofer
items.summary: Europe’s transition toward more electric steelmaking, with up to 20 electric arc furnaces expected to be commissioned in 2026-2030, adding 34 million-44 million metric tons of steel capacity, will increase the need for ferrous scrap, especially for high-quality material, the European Steel Association told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. In 2025, the EU steel industry consumed 74.4 million mt of ferrous scrap. Its H1 2026 intake of 38.1 million mt has kept EU steel production and ferrous scrap utilization broadly in line with the first half of 2025, but Europe’s accelerating transition toward more electric steelmaking will trigger a surge in the EU’s steel scrap demand, according to Eurofer. This means Europe’s future steelmaking system will use a combination of scrap and primary iron units, rather than simply replacing today’s production with 100% scrap-based EAF output. But there won’t be a uniform European scrap-to-DRI ratio: mixes will be plant-specific with EAFs operating on a spectrum ranging from near-100% scrap to 50:50, or even DRI/hot briquetted iron-dominant blends, French said.

Meanwhile, the latest EIA report showed a 64 bcf storage build for the week ended September 25, below the five-year average increase of 80 bcf, indicating that the inventory surplus is gradually narrowing. items.title: Shadow Fleet Traffic on Northern Sea Route Surges as Arctic Safety Concerns Grow
items.original_title: Shadow Fleet Traffic on Northern Sea Route Surges as Arctic Safety Concerns Grow
items.summary: Nuclear icebreaker Vaygach escorting a convoy of crude oil and oil product tankers along the Northern Sea Route in July 2024. (Source: Atomflot) The number of shadow-fleet vessels carrying Russian oil and LNG through the Northern Sea Route has surged this summer, according to a new analysis by Bellona’s Environmental Transparency Center, raising concerns about the ability to respond to accidents in one of the world’s most remote shipping environments. Bellona has identified more sanctioned oil tankers and LNG carriers on Russia’s Northern Sea Route in the first two months of the 2026 navigation season than during the whole of 2025, with many vessels lacking meaningful ice capability and information about accidents increasingly difficult to obtain. Sanctioned vessels accounted for about three-quarters of all oil tankers and almost 40% of LNG carriers observed on the route during the period, according to Bellona’s monitoring. Bellona notes that Russia’s Northern Sea Route administration has stopped publishing information about incidents and accidents along the route since 2025. Russian insurer AlfaStrakhovanie recently disclosed that it had paid compensation for damage to a tanker hull following an accident while the vessel was sailing along the Northern Sea Route under icebreaker escort.

items.title: DP World in talks to extend Callao concession to 2066
items.original_title: DP World in talks to extend Callao concession to 2066
items.summary: DP World is in talks with the Peruvian government over a 30-year extension of its concession at Callao in return for a further $1.47bn investment programme. Peru’s Ministry of Transport and Communications (MTC) has held fresh discussions with DP World Callao over proposed Addendum No. 4 to the concession for the South Pier container terminal. The amendment would extend DP World’s tenure from 2036 to 2066. The investment package would expand terminal infrastructure and equipment, improve road access and create the long-planned Callao antepuerto, or truck staging facility, designed to tackle congestion around Peru’s principal container gateway. The proposal is now being evaluated by the government and will require coordination between the MTC, National Port Authority, Provías and Callao municipality. DP World has already invested heavily at the port. Its $400m Bicentennial Pier expansion, completed in 2024, increased annual capacity to 2.7m teu and gave the terminal a 1,050 m quay capable of handling three ultra-large containerships simultaneously. The South Pier handled a record 2.079m teu last year, accounting for around 62.5% of Callao’s container throughput.

items.title: Japan targets 35 shadow fleet ships in first vessel sanctions
items.original_title: Japan targets 35 shadow fleet ships in first vessel sanctions
items.summary: Japan has imposed sanctions directly on individual vessels for the first time, targeting 35 ships linked to Russia’s shadow fleet as Tokyo steps up efforts to restrict Moscow’s oil-export network. The measures took effect on October 2 under Japan’s Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act. Japanese companies will now need government permission to provide specified services to the 35 vessels and for capital transactions, including loans and debt guarantees, connected with their sale, purchase, lease or charter. Japan’s foreign ministry has identified all 35 ships by IMO number. It is the first time Tokyo has placed vessels themselves under sanctions, bringing Japan closer to the approach already adopted by the UK and European Union against ageing tankers moving Russian oil outside mainstream Western shipping, finance and insurance channels. The shipping measures formed part of a wider package that also froze the assets of 33 Russian organisations and nine individuals and introduced export restrictions against four entities in Turkey and the UAE. Tokyo said the vessel measures were aimed at ships being used to transport Russian crude and petroleum products while circumventing existing sanctions. Seventy-two of those ships subsequently transported an estimated €7.5bn ($8.8bn) of Russian fossil fuels. Clarksons data showed the Russian registry up 38.2% this year through September 1.

items.title: Oil exports surge back through Hormuz despite mounting attacks
items.original_title: Oil exports surge back through Hormuz despite mounting attacks
items.summary: Oil flows from the Middle East have climbed back above pre-war levels even as attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz accelerate to their fastest pace since the conflict with Iran erupted on February 28. Provisional Kpler data shows regional crude exports exceeded pre-war volumes on four days during the final week of September, reaching between 19.5m and 22.5m barrels per day. The seven-day moving average stood at 18.5m barrels per day on October 1, compared with an average of around 18m barrels per day in the year before the war. The numbers cover Hormuz and Red Sea movements as well as terminal exports and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Iraqi Oil Tankers Company has transported a 2m-barrel cargo through Hormuz on a chartered VLCC, taking responsibility for the crude beyond the strait rather than selling it on the traditional free-on-board basis at Basra. The surge in cargoes transiting Hormuz is being matched, however, by an equally sharp escalation in attacks. The 115,100 dwt Lipsi, operated by Greece’s Dynacom Tankers Management, was hit by an unknown projectile in Hormuz on Sunday, suffering engine-room damage. Off Yemen, the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Chrystal Sky reported several explosions around 60 nautical miles south of Al Mukha on Sunday.

items.title: Where freight forwarders actually lose money
items.original_title: Where freight forwarders actually lose money
items.summary: More often than not, a forwarder closes a clean month and still watches the margins come in light. Most forwarders already know where it went: into the charges that were never recovered and the costs that were never meant to happen. A demurrage charge that was never passed on to the customer. Forwarders already have more data than they can read. Everything after is just a record of money already gone. So, the job is narrower than what most tech pitches: flag the handful of shipments where an unexpected charge is about to be incurred, whether that is demurrage building, a customs delay, port congestion that holds up haulage, or a misinterpreted contract, and put them in front of the operator early enough for them to act. Command Center surfaces the risks, the AI agents take routine tracking and reconciling off the operator’s plate, and Freight Audit checks carrier invoices against the contract and the actual shipment, so overcharges and miscalculated D&D are caught before they are paid rather than written off after. BCOs are already benchmarking their forwarders on exactly that, and it is often the difference between an account that renews and one that goes out to tender. For most forwarders, the honest answer is uncomfortable, and it is also the easiest money they will find all year.

items.title: Gunvor rebrands as Centalion and heads for Singapore
items.original_title: Gunvor rebrands as Centalion and heads for Singapore
items.summary: Commodity trading giant Gunvor is changing its name to Centalion and moving its corporate base to Singapore less than a year after completing a management buyout. The employee partnership that owns the business has voted to rename Gunvor Group as Centalion Group and intends to redomicile its parent holding company from Cyprus to Singapore, subject to approvals. Singapore, Geneva and Houston will remain its main trading centres, with chairman and chief executive Gary Pedersen based in Houston. The December transaction left the company fully owned by senior employees and brought Pedersen into the chief executive role. Centalion said the legal entity will continue through the redomiciliation process, while existing contracts and commercial obligations will remain unaffected. The new brand took effect on October 2 and will be rolled out across the group over the coming months. The group has had a Singapore presence since 2006 and is one of the world’s largest privately held commodity traders. It moved 253m tonnes of commodities last year, including around 3.3m barrels per day of liquids, generating $144bn in revenue and ending 2025 with $6.1bn of equity. The founder’s departure followed renewed scrutiny of the trader’s historical Russia links and a US-blocked attempt to acquire international assets from sanctioned Russian oil major Lukoil.

items.title: Russia could partially open diesel exports in case of surplus output: Novak
items.original_title: Russia could partially open diesel exports in case of surplus output: Novak
items.summary: Russia could consider partially opening diesel exports once it returns to a production surplus, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told its Federation Council Oct. 2, describing the market as balanced and sufficiently supplied, local media reported. Traditionally the world’s number-two diesel exporter, Russia started shutting in its diesel production in July following persistent Ukrainian drone attacks on its refining sector, now extended until the end of October. For non-producers, which include traders and refineries with capacities of less than 1 million metric tons/year, the ban will remain in place until the end of January. The deputy prime minister added that given Russia produces more diesel than it consumes, it is necessary to avoid accumulating more stocks than the country has the capacity to store, which would force refineries to reduce throughput and affect the output of other products. Novak’s comments come a day after Russia’s President Vladimir Putin said at the Valday Forum in Moscow that Russia had sufficient diesel but warned the fuel wouldn’t make it to international markets because of foreign sanctions. Gasoline was the first type of fuel export banned by the Kremlin back in April, and the restriction has since been extended through to the end of January 2027.

items.title: EU steel exports fall 20% as demand outlook remains flat
items.original_title: EU steel exports fall 20% as demand outlook remains flat
items.summary: Europe’s steel market remains under significant pressure, with exports falling sharply, production at historic lows and demand expected to remain almost flat in 2026, according to the European Steel Association’s (EUROFER) latest Economic and Steel Market Outlook 2026-2027. EU steel exports to third countries fell by 20% in the first half of 2026, with declines across all major export destinations covered by the report. At the same time, crude steel production continued to falter, after reaching a historic low of 125.8 million tonnes in 2025, while apparent steel consumption is forecast to grow by just 0.1% in 2026, before increasing by 2.3% in 2027. Axel Eggert, EUROFER’S Director-General remarked, “The 20% fall in exports is an alarming signal of the pressure facing European steel. Now we need to build on that progress with an industrial recovery that works across regions and across the value chain, bringing back production, investment and quality jobs in Europe.” EU crude steel production fell by 2.9% to a record low of 125.8 million tonnes in 2025 and declined by a further 1% in the first five months of 2026 (+1.1% in May 2026). EU steel exports to third countries fell by 20% in the first six months of 2026.

items.summary: One Nominee, Forty-Five Companies, Forty-Five Tankers Windward’s visual link analysis has identified 45 Russia-trading shadow fleet tankers connected through 45 single-ship Hong Kong companies to one beneficial owner. All but three share 19 different ISM managers with addresses in the same industrial cluster in the Azerbaijani city of Sumqayit. 42 of the fleet are sanctioned, and the three that are not have ISM managers in the UAE rather than Azerbaijan. Shadow Fleet Ownership Is Consolidating in China and Hong Kong The cluster underscores the accelerating shift in shadow fleet ownership and management structures to China, Hong Kong and Russia across 2026. The Cluster Only Became Visible This Year Consolidated into the cluster are tankers that have changed names, flags, and companies as many as eight times since 2023 and only became linked as they shifted ownership to Hong Kong between January and August. The beneficial owner of all 45 is a nominee director who cannot be traced, a common tactic used by shadow fleet operators to obscure the identity of the real owner. Twenty Virtual Offices Across Hong Kong Registered ownership addresses were tracked to 20 locations across Hong Kong, with 13 addresses hosting between two and five vessels.

items.title: Neptune Bunker Information Update: Off-Spec Trends Highlight Risk Areas
items.original_title: Neptune Bunker Information Update: Off-Spec Trends Highlight Risk Areas
items.summary: The Neptune Bunker Information tab has been updated with bunker quality data covering April to September 2026, providing Members with further insight into regional fuel quality trends and areas of elevated risk. Several ports record high levels of technical off-specification results across the residual and low-sulphur fuel sectors. Among HFO samples, the highest technical off-specs were recorded in Antwerp (46.2%), Norfolk (41.4%), Panama Canal (38.0%), and Rotterdam (35.5%). Rotterdam samples recorded a sulphur off-spec rate of 68.6%, while samples in Antwerp reached 58.9%, the highest levels seen in the current dataset. Although the number of samples involved is substantially smaller than in other major bunkering ports, the results underline the importance of maintaining robust bunker procurement, testing and fuel management procedures, particularly in respect of emission control regulatory requirements. Within the ULSFO category, the highest technical off-spec percentages were reported in Barcelona (70.3%) and Genoa (51.0%). In both ports, the results were primarily associated with pour point non-compliances, highlighting the need for careful consideration of storage and handling requirements, particularly where low ambient temperatures may become operationally significant. Members are encouraged to continue following established bunker testing and fuel management practices and to make use of Neptune’s fuel quality intelligence when evaluating supply risks and preparing bunkering plans. Source: West of England

items.title: From Regulation to Implementation: Why the Flag State Matters
items.original_title: From Regulation to Implementation: Why the Flag State Matters
items.summary: This year’s IMO theme for World Maritime Day is “From Policy to Practice: Powering Maritime Excellence”. Can you tell us what this actually means from a shipowners’ and managers’ perspective? For owners and managers, it comes down to what happens once new requirements or standards are introduced following the adoption of international regulations. This is where The Bahamas Maritime Authority, as a Flag State, has an important role to play. Equally important is the feedback we receive from owners, managers and seafarers, who are often the first to identify what works well in practice and where challenges may arise. As regulation becomes more complex, how can Flag States help owners in understanding the changes? One of the key responsibilities of a Flag State is to provide clarity, ensuring that stakeholders understand their obligations and can achieve compliance without unnecessary disruption to operations. Today, the Greek-owned fleet under the Bahamian flag comprises more than 275 vessels, representing approximately 13 million gross tonnes. For The Bahamas, our role as a Flag State is to remain actively engaged within the IMO, ILO and other international bodies while working closely with owners, managers and industry partners.

items.title: Singapore puts ship registration on AI fast track
items.original_title: Singapore puts ship registration on AI fast track
items.summary: Singapore is preparing an AI-powered overhaul of its ship registry that will cut standard registration processing times from as much as three working days to a matter of minutes. The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said that a new end-to-end registration platform will be launched in the first half of 2027, covering everything from submission of an application through to issuance of the vessel’s certificate of registry. AI will be used to support vetting and processing. The move comes after a sharp expansion of the Singapore flag. The Singapore Registry of Ships ended 2025 at a record 137m gt, up 27% year on year, with more than 4,400 vessels on its books. That put Singapore fourth among the world’s largest registries, while its approximately 11-year average fleet age was the youngest among the top 10 flags. Singapore has also been tightening registry oversight. Last month MPA warned owners and agents that false or unverifiable vessel identity, ownership, registration and trading information submitted in connection with port calls could trigger enforcement action, against the backdrop of growing concern internationally over fraudulent registries and flag-hopping. Eight methanol-fuelled ships have joined the Singapore flag since 2020, and MPA said the country expects to register its first ammonia dual-fuel vessel in November.

items.title: Namura absorbs Imari steel arm ahead of shipbuilding expansion
items.original_title: Namura absorbs Imari steel arm ahead of shipbuilding expansion
items.summary: Japan’s Namura Shipbuilding is absorbing its wholly owned Imari Steel Center as the shipbuilder moves to tighten control of production ahead of a major expansion of its newbuilding business. The Osaka-listed builder has approved the merger, with the transaction scheduled to take effect on April 1, 2027. Namura will remain the surviving company and Imari Steel Center will be dissolved. Imari Steel Center sits next to Namura’s main Imari yard in Saga prefecture and handles the upstream steel functions supporting vessel construction, including unloading, sorting, storage, processing and quality assurance of shipbuilding plate. Namura said combining the operations should speed up decision-making, allow better deployment of personnel and other resources, improve manufacturing efficiency and help with recruitment and training as the group increases newbuilding output. The internal reshuffle comes as Namura embarks on one of its biggest capacity pushes in years. Japan’s transport ministry last month approved up to ¥49.9bn ($319m) of government backing for an investment programme involving Namura and subsidiary Hakodate Dock, part of Tokyo’s wider drive to rebuild domestic shipbuilding capacity. Namura is also moving ahead with a new large construction dock, the first major shipbuilding dock to be developed in Japan since Imabari Shipbuilding completed its Marugame facility in 2017.

items.title: GMS Week 40 – Scarcity Puts Chattogram On Top
items.original_title: GMS Week 40 – Scarcity Puts Chattogram On Top
items.summary: The Gulf supplied another reminder this week that improved cargo flows do not equal normal shipping conditions. Several tankers were reportedly struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, followed by another tanker incident on October 1 in which a vessel caught fire, with the crew reported safe. Gulf crude movements have recovered significantly from earlier disruption, but passage risk, security and insurance remain firmly embedded in the voyage calculation. The Baltic Dry Index recovered modestly to 3,140 on Thursday after four consecutive declines, with Capesizes at 5,010, Panamaxes at 2,379 and Supramaxes at 1,794. The Turkish Lira slipped beyond 49 to the Dollar. Pakistan delivered the week’s fresh regional inflation number, with September CPI easing to 10.26% from August’s 11.1%, providing some macro relief without materially altering Gadani’s buying equation. Chattogram has processed a substantial run of previously secured tonnage, including large gas and tanker units, while Gadani has also received and delivered vessels secured during its earlier buying run. Bangladesh moved ahead of Pakistan to reclaim the top position across the conventional board, with Chattogram recyclers bidding more aggressively for the very limited selection of available candidates. items.title: The Week in Alt Fuels: Back to the future
items.original_title: The Week in Alt Fuels: Back to the future
items.summary: Shipping is turning back to one of the oldest tricks in the book as modern sails find their way onto tankers, container ships and LNG carriers. The past couple of months have seen a streak of developments around wind-assisted propulsion, spanning installations, orders, vessel launches, technology approvals and new trials. These are not just small-scale demonstrations, with major shipping companies across multiple ship types now entering the field. Just 99 vessels are currently equipped with the technology, according to DNV data. Be it the 1863 iron windjammer Star of India, the 1765 warship HMS Victory or the Spanish galleons of the 16th century, ships have harnessed wind to cross oceans for centuries. In September, Lloyd’s Register assessed SunRui’s technology, ClassNK granted approval in principle to OceanWings’ rigid wingsail systems and Bureau Veritas assessed a new suction sail design from Bound4blue. Moller-Maersk was bunkered with an unspecified quantity of 100% bio-ethanol at the Port of Houston in the US. Barge operator Kirby delivered the stem, sourced from biofuel producer POET, to the Tangier Maersk in a ship-to-ship bunker operation. The production cost of e-methanol at the planned plant at Deendayal Port in Kandla, Gujarat, is estimated at $750/mt.

items.title: Clean tanker markets size up impact of potential US diesel export curbs
items.original_title: Clean tanker markets size up impact of potential US diesel export curbs
items.summary: US restrictions on diesel exports would upend Atlantic Basin clean tanker demand at a moment when the global middle-distillate market is reeling from simultaneous supply shocks in Russia and the Middle East, BRS Shipbrokers said in a report. The impact on medium-range tanker earnings in particular could be swift and severe, BRS said Sept. 28. US President Donald Trump had floated a diesel export ban in response to record domestic fuel prices ahead of midterm elections. Tanker implications A full ban could strand around 1.35 million b/d of US Gulf diesel exports — the equivalent of four MR2-sized cargoes per day — with Europe and Latin America most exposed given the absence of readily available alternative supply, BRS said. Pressure would fall most heavily on MR2s, which carry more than 90% of US diesel exports, BRS said. There could also be bleed-in to MR1 markets as MR2s compete for smaller stems, while clean tankers would likely ballast away from the US Gulf, putting pressure on tonnage lists elsewhere, BRS said. The offsetting factor for the broader clean tanker complex is a potential redirection of Asian barrels westward. “With the potential diesel ban coming, the appetite for US diesel exports is declining because these products are needed at home, whether there’s a ban or not,” Simpson said.

items.title: What Is the Shadow Fleet, and Why Is It So Hard to Count?
items.original_title: What Is the Shadow Fleet, and Why Is It So Hard to Count?
items.summary: There Is No Official Shadow Fleet List The shadow fleet, also called the dark fleet, refers to tankers and support vessels that rely on deceptive shipping practices to move sanctioned or high-risk commodities while concealing their true origin, ownership, or destination. It has no standing in law, and that is where the difficulty starts. Why Every Published Estimate Is Different Ask five organizations how large the shadow fleet is, and you will get five answers, sometimes differing by a factor of three. The useful question is narrower: Does this vessel exhibit the behavior, and what is my exposure if it does? A vessel flying a legitimate flag has the right of innocent passage through the territorial sea, and on the high seas it is subject to the jurisdiction of its flag state. There is a lag between a vessel starting to operate as part of the shadow fleet and that vessel appearing on a sanctions list. During that gap, the vessel is detectable through its behavior and invisible to a list check. Vessels without a valid flag are stateless, and under Article 110 of UNCLOS, a warship may board a ship on the high seas where there are reasonable grounds to suspect it is.

items.title: Strait of Hormuz security, decarbonisation among key issues discussed by BIMCO committees
items.original_title: Strait of Hormuz security, decarbonisation among key issues discussed by BIMCO committees
items.summary: The security situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black and Red Seas, as well as environmental topics, were among the key issues discussed when BIMCO’s Maritime Safety & Security Committee (MSSC) and Marine Environment Committee (MEC) met on 30 September and 1 October. Members considered the implications of regional conflicts, attacks on shipping, drones, mines and navigational disruption. The committees also discussed a broad range of other regulatory, safety and environmental issues affecting the day-to-day operation of ships. Our committees bring together industry expertise to identify practical challenges and help shape BIMCO’s positions in discussions with the IMO, governments and regulators. Digitalisation was another major theme, including the opportunities it offers for efficiency, compliance and safety, as well as the growing importance of cyber security and supporting seafarers as technology develops. Members also discussed the safe adoption of alternative fuels, including ammonia, hydrogen and methanol, and future safety frameworks for advanced modular nuclear reactors. The proposed legally-binding international convention on biofouling was also discussed, with an emphasis on ensuring that future requirements are practical, science-based and capable of consistent implementation across the global fleet. Other topics included search and rescue and mixed migration, underwater radiated noise, marine plastics and plastic pellet transportation, and implementation of the Hong Kong Convention on ship recycling. Source: BIMCO, https://www.bimco.org/news-insights/bimco-news/2026/10/01-mec-mssc/

items.title: Six Vessels Hit in Strait of Hormuz Since Sunday
items.original_title: Six Vessels Hit in Strait of Hormuz Since Sunday
items.summary: Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, July 31, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer Another tanker has been struck in the Strait of Hormuz, bringing the number of vessels reported hit in the strategic waterway since Sunday to at least six. UK Maritime Trade Operations said Friday that the master of a tanker reported being struck by an unknown projectile while conducting an outbound transit of the strait at 1122 UTC. The latest strike adds to a growing tally of attacks around the Strait of Hormuz over the past several days. gCaptain reported Wednesday that the delayed disclosures were adding to uncertainty over how quickly incidents in the strait were reaching the public record. Combined with the attacks reported Thursday and Friday, the notices bring the tally to at least six vessels struck since Sunday, September 28. The tanker captain summoned his years of experience when he saw the blast in front of him. He veered his 300-meter-long ship around the vessel ahead and could see a fire had started. He called the US Navy to tell them of the attack.

items.original_title: Saudis Plan Assault on Houthis to Break Red Sea Chokehold
items.summary: Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, August 3, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer RIYADH, Oct 2 (Reuters) – Saudi Arabia is planning an offensive against Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, with options being considered including a coastal push to secure the Red Sea shipping route or an assault on multiple fronts, regional and Western officials told Reuters. The operation, expected to be launched in the coming weeks, will by led by Yemeni forces on the ground, which are overseen by Riyadh, and supported by Saudi air strikes, according to six people with knowledge of the preparations. A truce agreed between the warring parties in 2022 largely held until this year when the Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi shipping and oil infrastructure in a spillover from the Iran war. France, meanwhile, has announced it will send defensive systems and troops to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port ?city of Yanbu. Any ground operation inside Yemen will rely on the disparate coalition of Yemeni fighting factions that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates armed and trained at earlier stages of the civil war when the conflict ground to a bloody stalemate.

items.title: DP World Expands Contract Logistics Network In Thailand With New Bang Na Distribution Centre
items.original_title: DP World Expands Contract Logistics Network In Thailand With New Bang Na Distribution Centre
items.summary: DP World today announced the opening of a new contract logistics distribution centre in Bang Na, expanding its logistics capacity in Thailand and strengthening its ability to support customers across key manufacturing and consumer sectors. The approximately 10,000-square-metre facility is located in a modern industrial park in Bang Na, an established distribution hub within the Greater Bangkok metropolitan area, with connectivity to Laem Chabang Port and major manufacturing centres along Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC). The distribution centre provides storage and distribution services for high-value and time-sensitive products, including consumer electronics, semiconductors and automotive cargo. Jeanie Tan, Chief Commercial Officer, Logistics, Asia Pacific, DP World, said: “Thailand sits at the heart of some of Asia Pacific’s most important manufacturing and distribution networks. Our investment in Bang Na gives customers additional capacity in this important market while connecting them with DP World’s wider freight and logistics capabilities. By bringing these services together, we help customers reduce complexity, respond more quickly to changing demand and keep goods moving reliably within Thailand and across the Asia Pacific region.” The opening of the Bang Na distribution centre is part of DP World’s continued investment in contract logistics capabilities across Asia Pacific, following recent investments in Singapore and Johor, Malaysia.

items.title: G7 to Release Up to 100 Million Barrels of Diesel, Crude
items.original_title: G7 to Release Up to 100 Million Barrels of Diesel, Crude
items.summary: (Bloomberg) — The Group of Seven nations and its partners are to release as much as 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel stocks amid pressure from the Trump administration to quell rising fuel prices. The release, being coordinated by the International Energy Agency, will take place over the next four months, Emmanuel Macron, France’s president and the current chair of the G7, told journalists in a briefing on Friday. The G7 would like to trigger a drop in fuel prices, he added. The IEA already coordinated a plan to release 400 million barrels in March soon after the Iran war broke out, but US President Donald Trump has criticized Europe for not making those barrels available fast enough. A subsequent G7 statement suggested that the 100 million barrels may include barrels that have not yet been made available under the March release. “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil,” Trump said. “The process will begin immediately.” Diesel’s premium over crude oil, a closely watched measure of market strength, slumped as low as $69 a barrel, down from $76.77 on Thursday, fair-value data compiled by Bloomberg show.

items.title: Pressure on India-US trades as Colombo becomes a transhipment hot-spot
items.original_title: Pressure on India-US trades as Colombo becomes a transhipment hot-spot
items.summary: Colombo’s increasing popularity as a transhipment hub is heaping cost pressure onto forwarders and shippers on the India-US tradelane, the Sri Lankan gateway’s newfound revenue stream having provoked a worsening tide of congestion. Recognising India is facing its own congestion issues, particularly at Mundra and Nhava Sheva, CH Robinson said Colombo’s status as a transhipment hot-spot was elevating the risks of rolled cargo. “When mainline services omit Colombo to recover schedules, South India cargo can miss planned connections even when space is available on the onward vessel. Feeder timing, container availability, dwell time during transhipping, and whether the mainline vessel makes its planned Colombo port call determine whether the container can use space,” it said. Consequently, the forwarder warned, the issue cargo owners were being left to grapple with was not just whether they could secure allocations, but whether the feeder and mainline connections on these routings would hold together. Much of the congestion Colombo is contending with is a consequence of vessels and services routing away from their traditional transhipment hubs in the Middle East, amid the war between the US and Iran – a situation that seems to have affected US consumers most.

items.title: No Lights, No Radio: Getting Oil Through Hormuz Is a Risky Job
items.original_title: No Lights, No Radio: Getting Oil Through Hormuz Is a Risky Job
items.summary: A sailor observes the oil tanker HELGA, which is moored at one of Iraq's southern offshore oil terminals near Basra, as it prepares to load crude oil, April 24, 2026. Picture taken with a mobile phone. REUTERS/Mohammed Aty Oct 2, 2026 (Bloomberg) –The tanker captain summoned his years of experience when he saw the blast in front of him. The maneuver in the Strait of Hormuz with drones and missiles overhead is the sort of quick thinking that’s proving vital to getting oil supplies to the global market as Washington and Tehran fail to reach agreement on reopening the waterway to regular traffic. His vessel is among the ships engaged in shuttle runs through the strait, ferrying barrels often at night and with strict instructions about what equipment can be used — no lights, no phones and with only one radar. They were often just a mile from the coast of Oman, though the depth of the sea there is about 100 meters, more than enough for even the biggest supertankers to sail through. American forces “have assisted thousands of ships through the Strait of Hormuz in recent months by providing coordinated protection,” US Central Command said in a statement. Much of the time crossing Hormuz is spent talking to the US Navy.

items.title: Aviation Connect: air cargo’s favourite event, but with an unfortunate early dip…
items.original_title: Aviation Connect: air cargo’s favourite event, but with an unfortunate early dip…
items.summary: Athens provided the backdrop for Aviation Connect 2026 this week, with sunshine, warm temperatures, and the occasional rain shower – a fittingly changeable setting for an event that had plenty going on. The Tuesday-to-Thursday event spread delegates across a collection of rooms and tracks covering pharma, GSSAs, air cargo handling, cargo airport development, road feeder services, airline ground services, GSE, and ramp operations. It is one of the things that makes Aviation Connect different from the traditional air cargo conference: rather than sitting through a 45-minute panel because it happens to be on the agenda, delegates could pick and choose sessions relevant to them. There was also an exhibition hall, with companies showing off their latest products and services, as well as plenty of networking. The rooftop event featured synchronised swimmers – six women dressed as cabin crew, who removed their outfits to reveal swimwear before performing a 10-minute routine in the pool. The performance was impressive, but its positioning immediately before the Women in Air Cargo Awards, however, felt rather awkward. Celebrating women’s professional achievements directly following a performance of women dressed as air staff stripping off, seemed an unfortunate juxtaposition.

items.title: MOL lands Vale charter for two tri-fuel ore carriers
items.original_title: MOL lands Vale charter for two tri-fuel ore carriers
items.summary: Japanese shipping giant Mitsui OSK Lines (MOL) will operate two 210,000-dwt ore carriers for Vale under a 25-year contract, introducing tri-fuel propulsion to the long-haul iron ore trade. MOL Ocean Bulk, the group’s Singapore-based capesize bulker operator, signed the agreement with Vale International for vessels scheduled to enter service in 2030. The ships will primarily transport Brazilian iron ore to China and other global destinations. MOL described the project as the first involving 210,000-dwt ore carriers with this three-fuel configuration. The 210,000-dwt size places the ships in the newcastlemax segment, widely used on the Brazil–Asia iron ore route. MOL said ethanol could reduce lifecycle carbon emissions by up to 90% against heavy fuel oil, depending on the fuel’s production pathway. The deal forms part of Vale’s shipping decarbonisation strategy and is intended to lower the miner’s Scope 3 emissions from seaborne transport. It also adds to a wider wave of Vale-backed tri-fuel ore carrier commitments, including eight similar 210,000-dwt ships chartered from HMM under 25-year agreements beginning in 2030. MOL said it would work with Vale and other partners across ethanol and methanol procurement, supply, and bunkering to develop the required fuel chain.

items.title: Soybeans Near 5-Week Low
items.original_title: Soybeans Near 5-Week Low
items.summary: Soybean futures fell to around $12.7 per bushel, nearing a five-week low as harvest pressure from an expected record-large US crop weighed on prices. A wet late summer and early autumn slowed the harvest pace, but the arrival of new supplies continued to pressure the market. The harvest was 17% complete as of September 27, matching the five-year average, with the crop rated 58% good or excellent. Expectations of a weaker August soybean crush added pressure, with processors crushing 209.6 million bushels, below the average trade estimate. Weak Chinese demand also weighed on prices as soybeans were excluded from China’s latest US agricultural tariff cuts and remain subject to an additional 10% tariff. Chinese crushers have covered much of their needs through early 2027 with South American supplies, while high inventories and weak margins limit fresh purchases. Still, US export demand remains firm, with weekly sales at 1.03 million tonnes for 2026/27, including 589,400 tonnes to China. Source: Trading Economics

items.title: Electric and hybrid ferries could cut emissions by 63% in Sea of Marmara, IMO study finds
items.original_title: Electric and hybrid ferries could cut emissions by 63% in Sea of Marmara, IMO study finds
items.summary: Türkiye’s Sea of Marmara ferry network could cut greenhouse gas emissions by 63% by switching to a mix of hybrid and fully electric vessels, while avoiding nearly half a billion euros in health and environmental damage costs and supporting around 1,100 jobs a year, according to a new IMO study. Commissioned by IMO’s GreenVoyage2050 programme in partnership with Türkiye’s Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure, the study assessed 67 Ro-Ro and Ro-Pax ferries carrying vehicles and passengers across 26 ports. The network transports around 25 million passengers and seven million vehicles each year. Significant potential to cut emissions The study found that battery-electric and hybrid propulsion are technically feasible options across all Ro-Pax and Ro-Ro ferry operations assessed in the Sea of Marmara. It identified an optimum scenario combining hybrid and fully electric vessels to balance emissions reductions and costs. Under this scenario, annual GHG emissions could fall by around 63% by 2050 compared with business-as-usual operations using diesel fuel. The transition would also reduce local air pollution and could avoid an estimated €492 million in cumulative health and environmental damage costs. Going further, converting the entire fleet to fully electric operations could cut GHG emissions by 84% by 2050.

items.title: New successful pilot at the Valenciaport Sandbox: a new material “cools” containers without consuming energy
items.original_title: New successful pilot at the Valenciaport Sandbox: a new material “cools” containers without consuming energy
items.summary: The Valenciaport Sandbox adds a new pilot to its track record as a testing ground for innovation in the port and logistics environment. This time, the spotlight was on a new passive radiative cooling film developed by the startup Cooling Photonics, which was tested with very positive results at the Transbase Soler depot last summer, and whose results are now being presented. The trial was made possible thanks to the collaboration of the port community, the Fundación Valenciaport and the support of Opentop, Valenciaport’s open innovation hub, which acted as facilitator, connecting the innovative company with the real-world environment in which its technology could prove its value. A test in real summer conditions This summer, over fifteen consecutive days, four identical 20-foot containers with the same solar exposure were monitored: one untreated as a reference, one with a conventional internal thermal blanket, a third with the material on the roof only, and the fourth with the material on the roof and side walls. A material like this opens up applications of great interest for ports, terminals, logistics operators and depots: Juan Manuel Díez, Head of Innovation at the Port Authority of Valencia, stated that the Valenciaport Sandbox was created so that innovative ideas can prove their value in a real port operations environment, with data gathered on the ground.

items.title: Fresh attacks hit Hormuz tanker and Saudi oil gateway
items.original_title: Fresh attacks hit Hormuz tanker and Saudi oil gateway
items.summary: Kuwait Oil Tanker Company has suffered its second VLCC strike in four days, while a separate projectile attack at Saudi Arabia’s Yanbu port briefly disrupted loading operations, piling fresh security pressure on two of the Middle East’s key oil export routes. Maritime security firm Vanguard Tech identified the latest Hormuz casualty as the Kuwait-flagged Kazimah III , which was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday. UK Maritime Trade Operations, which did not name the vessel, said it received a third-party report that a tanker had been hit, triggering a fire onboard. Maritime security sources identified them as ADNOC-operated VLCC Mersin Prosperity , the 115,949 dwt Sinbad and product tanker Al Ruwais . Yanbu had only just returned to crude export operations after drone attacks forced Saudi Arabia to shut its East-West Pipeline on September 11. The pipeline restarted on September 22 and tanker loading resumed several days later, with crude exports from Yanbu estimated at about 2m barrels per day. Satellite imagery from September 27 showed almost 10m barrels being loaded across Yanbu and the nearby Al Muajjiz terminal as Saudi Arabia stepped up use of its Red Sea outlet to reduce reliance on Hormuz.

items.title: NYK plants flag in Silicon Valley
items.original_title: NYK plants flag in Silicon Valley
items.summary: Nippon Yusen Kaisha (NYK) is opening a new outpost in Silicon Valley as the Japanese shipping major looks to get closer to the startups, investors and research institutions shaping artificial intelligence, energy and digital technology. NYK Group Americas will establish a branch in Sunnyvale, California, this month, using it as a scouting and business development base for the wider Americas. The office will search for technologies and business models with potential applications across NYK’s shipping and logistics operations, with prospective ideas put through proof-of-concept projects, partnerships and, potentially, equity investments. The Japanese owner has previously invested in maritime technology venture fund theDOCK, AI company Ghelia and, earlier this year, unmanned surface vessel developer Oceanic Constellations. Silicon Valley and the wider San Francisco Bay Area already have some notable shipping connections. Its AI ship-performance technology has been deployed across more than 300 K Line vessels, while Mitsui OSK Lines has also worked with the company on fuel consumption and emissions optimisation. Across the bay in Alameda, Saildrone designs and builds autonomous surface vessels for ocean intelligence, mapping and defence. Its investors include shipping group Crowley, alongside a roster of Silicon Valley venture funds. Maersk Growth invested in Silicon Valley-based Prometheus Fuels in 2021, targeting its direct-air-capture technology as a potential route to low-carbon marine fuels.

items.title: South Africa advances landmark ports shake-up
items.original_title: South Africa advances landmark ports shake-up
items.summary: South Africa is pressing ahead with one of the most significant restructurings of its troubled ports sector in decades, with cabinet backing the separation of Transnet National Ports Authority (TNPA) from Transnet and its establishment as a standalone state-owned company. The move would see the country’s national port landlord owned directly by the state rather than sitting within the Transnet group. Cabinet has also approved a feasibility study into bringing in a minority equity partner from one of South Africa’s development finance institutions. South Africa’s ports have endured a prolonged period of congestion, equipment shortages, inadequate maintenance and declining productivity. Durban plunged back into heavy congestion in August, with vessels facing waits of eight to 12 days and some carriers reporting delays of up to 20 days following disruption around the terminal’s operating-system change. Private capital is increasingly central to Pretoria’s attempted ports revival. ICTSI began operating Durban’s flagship Pier 2 terminal this year under a 25-year partnership involving around R11bn ($638m) of investment after a lengthy legal battle delayed the concession. TNPA has also launched private-sector processes covering Cape Town’s multipurpose terminal, a new floating drydock there and the Richards Bay dry bulk terminal, while Transnet last week opened the qualification process for a private partner for the R30bn-R44bn Ngqura manganese corridor.

Announced at Gastech 2026, the MOU aims to combine computational fluid dynamics (CFD) analysis with digital twin technology to rapidly predict ammonia dispersion behavior in the event of a leak. This capability would assess a wide range of leakage and accident scenarios early in the vessel design process. “By pairing CFD analysis with digital twin technology, this project gives designers a faster, more rigorous way to understand leak behavior. ABS is proud to bring our technical authority to this collaboration with HD KSOE and Siemens,” said Patrick Ryan, ABS Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer. HD KSOE will develop ammonia safety systems and lead related experimental research, while Siemens will provide simulation analysis and digital twin technology. items.original_title: Oman’s Shinas port plans to start offering marine fuels to shippers
items.summary: Oman’s northernmost port, Shinas, is planning to start a marine fuel supply service as shipping companies seek alternatives to bunkering services during the conflict in the Middle East. The port, used by fishing boats and for boat repairs, has targeted first-phase capacity of 200,000 metric tons/month of marine fuels, or 2 million mt/year, the Oman Observer has reported, citing Oman’s ministry of transport. The port could not be immediately reached for comment. Germany’s Bilfinger has signed an agreement with Shinas Marine Fuels & Oil Terminals SPC for delivery of phase 1 of the project, the newspaper reported earlier this month. The UAE’s Port of Fujairah, just north of Shinas, is the most-used Middle East port for bunkering, although sales have declined amid severe shipping disruptions in the region since the start of the Iran war in late February. Sales in 2025 were 7.38 million mt, according to Port of Fujairah data. Volumes dropped to only about 88,000 mt in June, according to port data, although they have since rebounded. Earlier in September, Oman’s transportation ministry signed a 39-year agreement with QS Maritime LLC of Oman to manage, operate and develop the Shinas port, according to the Oman Observer. It took over port operations in January 2024, according to the newspaper report.

items.original_title: DNV Maritime Forecast to 2050: What The Latest Findings Mean For Greece And Cyprus?
items.summary: Lefteris Koukoulopoulos, Regional Decarbonization Specialist, Southeast Europe, DNV Maritime commented: “This is why I find the 10th edition of DNV’s Maritime Forecast to 2050 particularly relevant. It looks at how shipping can plan across different regulatory and fuel-market outcomes, with new analysis on energy efficiency, low-GHG fuels and fleet strategy. For me, one message stands out: energy efficiency is the most immediate and practical decarbonization solution available to shipowners today. It offers shipowners a way to reduce fuel consumption and emissions today, while managing costs and keeping their options open for the future. The report shows that energy use across the global fleet could be reduced by up to 28% by 2050 through fleet renewal, operational improvements and retrofits. I see the Maritime Forecast as a useful starting point for these conversations. Given the lifespan of newbuilds today, often beyond 2050, ships must be designed to meet future regulations, reducing risks and costs across fleets. For the world fleet, energy-efficiency measures and speed reductions can reduce energy use by up to 16% in 2030 compared to business-as-usual, and the potential towards 2050 is larger still. The corresponding number of vessels capable of using alternative fuels has grown more than six-fold from 213 to 1,329 (excluding LNG carriers), with significant variations across ship segments.

items.title: MABUX: October Bunker Prices Expected to Remain Volatile
items.original_title: MABUX: October Bunker Prices Expected to Remain Volatile
items.summary: • Middle East conflict and Strait of Hormuz. Supply and shipping disruptions kept the geopolitical risk premium elevated, driving bunker market volatility and briefly pushing Brent above USD 110/bbl. • Tight crude supply. The European gas benchmark TTF was virtually unchanged by the end of September, edging down by just EUR 0.004/MWh, from EUR 69.809/MWh at the end of August to EUR 69.805/MWh. However, the relatively stable month-end result masked significant intra-month volatility, with TTF quotations surging to as high as EUR 82.500/MWh during September. The price of LNG as bunker fuel in the port of Sines (Portugal) continued to rise in September, gaining USD 123 to USD 1,608/MT, compared with USD 1,485/MT at the end of August. At the same time, the price differential between LNG and conventional bunker fuel remained in favor of conventional fuel but narrowed significantly to USD 28, versus USD 80 in August. By the end of September, the MABUX Market Differential Index (MDI) — the correlation between market bunker prices (MBP) and the MABUX Digital Bunker Benchmark (DBP) — showed the following trends across the world’s four major bunkering hubs: Rotterdam, Singapore, Fujairah and Houston. In the 380 HSFO segment, Fujairah remained the only overvalued port, although its premium narrowed by 15 points, bringing the MDI closer to the 100% MBP/DBP correlation mark.

items.title: Suez Transits Are Up 59%, and Rates Are About to Fall
items.original_title: Suez Transits Are Up 59%, and Rates Are About to Fall
items.summary: Carriers Have Returned to Suez, and the Data Confirms It Maritime media sources state that container shipping is moving from a capacity shortage to a surplus as carriers return to Suez and shorter voyages free up ships. Suez containership transits rose 59% from March to September, from 139 to 221. The growth came from large ships, 300m and above, up to 24,000 TEU, the post-Panamax to ultra-large vessels used on main Asia-Europe services, which rose from 22 to 127 transits a month. Around 100 more large containerships now transit the Suez Canal instead of around Africa, compared to March, cutting one to two weeks off each round trip. Suez routing for Asia-Europe services has recovered to only about a quarter of pre-crisis levels, per Sea-Intelligence. Even a partial return matters, because carriers expanded Asia-Europe capacity by approximately 41% between May 2023 and May 2025 to cover the longer route around Africa, according to Alphaliner, meaning that every service that switches back to Suez frees ships the route no longer needs. Shorter voyages mean each liner service needs fewer ships to keep its schedule, freeing capacity just as Europe-bound demand softens after the summer and ahead of China’s Golden Week holiday (1-7 Oct), when factory closures halt much of China’s export production.

items.title: Fragmented trade drives dry bulk tonne-mile demand
items.original_title: Fragmented trade drives dry bulk tonne-mile demand
items.summary: Dry bulk shipping has entered the final quarter of 2026 in considerably better shape than most owners expected, with industry leaders at last week’s Splash Singapore conference arguing that increasingly fragmented trade could keep vessel demand elevated even without spectacular growth in cargo volumes. G2 Ocean chief executive Arthur English admitted the strength of the market had surprised him, particularly in minor bulks where underlying tonnes have barely grown. “All of the growth has come from geopolitical disruptions and delays in ports and so on,” English told the Dry Bulk Market Outlook panel. The executives were considerably less alarmed about the dry bulk orderbook than the contracting boom elsewhere in shipping. Norden has more than 30 newbuildings coming across its businesses but is now favouring modern secondhand dry tonnage over fresh orders. “That kind of reminds [me of] the period between 2007 and 2010.” Demand arguments extend well beyond traditional iron ore. Demand for new benchmarks and greater transparency is increasing around India and West Africa as cargo flows evolve. Asked at the end of the session whether today’s dry bulk market offered greater upside or downside risk, Rindbo gave perhaps the simplest summary of the panel’s stance.

items.title: Tankers enter the death zone
items.original_title: Tankers enter the death zone
items.summary: Like climbers entering the death zone above 8,000 metres en route to the summit of Everest, VLCCs have entered their own peak: the moment where prices for secondhand tonnage surpass newbuild prices, and sell signs flash hard. These moments tend to be fleeting and have historically been associated with the hottest stages of shipping cycles. The question is how often the market has reached this altitude before, and how long it can survive there. The previous maximum premium for a five-year-old VLCC over a newbuild was 21% in December 2007. Veson data shows a 15-year-old VLCC overtook the newbuild value for the first time on September 27. Danish Ship Finance takes a broader approach, using a monthly secondhand-to-newbuilding price ratio for tankers stretching back to January 2000. Its series identifies 11 distinct episodes, including the current one. “To stay with your analogy: the death zone usually punishes those who linger — but in 2003–08, the market camped up there for nearly six years,” Danish Ship Finance told Splash. The completed episodes have averaged around 12 months, although that number is heavily distorted by the extraordinary 2003-08 supercycle, which accounts for more than half of all the months its tanker index has spent above parity.

items.title: Nuclear-Powered LNG Carrier Would Cost 2.5 Times More to Build, Study Finds
items.original_title: Nuclear-Powered LNG Carrier Would Cost 2.5 Times More to Build, Study Finds
items.summary: A nuclear-powered LNG carrier could cost roughly 2.5 times as much to build as a conventional vessel, but lower fuel costs could significantly change the economics over the ship’s operating life, according to a new study supported by the American Bureau of Shipping. Presented at Gastech 2026, the study examined a 174,000-cubic-meter LNG carrier equipped with a 20-25 MWe high-temperature gas-cooled reactor, or HTGR, under development by Japan’s Blossom Energy. ABS, Blossom Energy and an unnamed global shipping company compared the nuclear design with a conventional LNG-fueled newbuild, assessing vessel arrangement, propulsion systems and operating conditions under a range of potential regulatory penalty scenarios. The study found that initial investment for the nuclear-powered vessel would be approximately 2.5 times that of a conventional LNG carrier. In 2024, ABS and Herbert Engineering Corporation studied the integration of an HTGR into a 145,000-cubic-meter LNG carrier , examining heat and energy management, shielding, weight distribution and other design challenges. In July, ABS awarded Approval in Principle for a nuclear-powered 15,000 TEU containership concept developed with the Korea Research Institute of Ships and Ocean Engineering and KAERI.

items.title: Turkey and UN Broker New Talks on Russia-Ukraine Black Sea Truce
items.original_title: Turkey and UN Broker New Talks on Russia-Ukraine Black Sea Truce
items.summary: Vessels are seen as they await inspection under the Black Sea Grain Initiative, brokered by the United Nations and Turkey, in the southern anchorage of the Bosphorus in Istanbul, Turkey December 11, 2022. REUTERS/Yoruk Isik/File Photo (Bloomberg) — Turkey and the United Nations have set up fresh talks in Russia and Ukraine to discuss a Black Sea ceasefire , trying to coalesce scattered efforts to protect grain shipments as global food prices surge. The meetings will take place in early October, according to a senior diplomat. The initiative, which launched in September with buy-in from other global powers, attempts to replicate a successful 2022 push to secure Black Sea grain shipping. The talks are picking up steam as Russia and Ukraine, which make up more than a quarter of the world’s wheat shipments, increase attacks on each other’s Black Sea port facilities, helping push wheat futures to a three-year high in August. Turkey and the UN bring credibility to the campaign, having also steered the 2022 ceasefire, which ensured the safe passage of grain, fertilizer and food from Ukrainian ports. Russia has set out tough conditions for resurrecting any Black Sea deal, including some sanctions relief and significant military concessions from Ukraine.

items.title: Four Of Europe’s Largest Quay Cranes Arrive At DP World’s UK Ports
items.original_title: Four Of Europe’s Largest Quay Cranes Arrive At DP World’s UK Ports
items.summary: DP World has welcomed four of Europe’s largest quay cranes to its UK ports, as part of its continued investment to expand capacity and support the growth of UK trade. The first pair of cranes, weighing more than 2,000 tonnes each and standing nearly 150 metres high, taller than world-famous London landmarks such as the London Eye and St Paul’s Cathedral, arrived fully assembled by sea at London Gateway on Friday 25 September, having completed their round the world journey from Shanghai. They will be installed at the new all-electric Berth 5, currently under construction as part of DP World’s £1 billion expansion of the port, which is due to become operational in 2027. The second pair are due to arrive at Southampton next week and follow the delivery of two new cranes in June, bringing the total number servicing the terminal to 16. Capable of consecutive ‘tandem lifts’ of two 40ft containers at once, the new cranes can service the largest container ships currently in operation, including 24,000 TEU megaships, enabling both terminals to accommodate growing trade volumes and the increasing size of vessels serving global shipping routes. • 46% share of UK containerised trade now handled by the combined DP World operations at London Gateway and Southampton.

items.title: Alternative-Fuel Ship Orders Surge to Two-Year High
items.original_title: Alternative-Fuel Ship Orders Surge to Two-Year High
items.summary: CMA CGM's LNG-powered CMA CGM Jacques Saadé under construction at China State Shipbuilding Corporation in 2020. Photo courtesy CMA CGM Alternative-fuel ship orders rebounded sharply in the third quarter, with September delivering the strongest monthly total in nearly two years as LNG remained the dominant choice for new vessels. Shipowners placed orders for 69 alternative-fuelled vessels in September, the highest monthly total since October 2024, according to new figures from DNV’s Alternative Fuels Insight platform. The September activity brought third-quarter orders to 168 vessels, making it the busiest quarter since the third quarter of 2024. “September capped the strongest quarter for alternative-fuelled vessel contracting in the past two years, bringing year-to-date orders comfortably above the level seen at the same point last year.” LNG accounted for 48 of September’s 69 orders, covering containerships, car carriers, bulk carriers and ro-ro cargo vessels. Another 12 orders were for ethanol-fuelled bulk carriers, while nine LPG-fuelled vessels were ordered during the month. DNV warned in its latest Maritime Forecast to 2050 that regulatory outcomes could significantly change the economics of alternative fuels over the operating lives of vessels ordered today. Alternative-fuel-capable tonnage has already grown from just 0.4% of the global fleet in 2020 to 5.2% in 2026, according to DNV, led primarily by LNG and methanol systems.

items.summary: CMA CGM announced today that it has completed its $1.4bn takeover of FedEx’s contract logistics business, FedEx Supply Chain, which is set to be folded into the shipping line’s contract logistics arm Ceva. The deal will see Ceva’s North American footprint almost treble in size, according to CMA CGM, with the addition of around 34m sqft of warehouse space offering combined operations across 150 warehouses in region and employing around 20,000 staff. “The completion of this acquisition marks an important step in the development of CMA CGM and CEVA Logistics in North America,” Rodolphe Saadé, chairman and chief executive of the CMA CGM group, said. “By significantly expanding our contract logistics capabilities, we are strengthening our ability to offer customers integrated, end-to-end supply chain solutions across ocean, air, land and logistics. “It also reinforces CMA CGM’s long-term commitment to investing in the United States, a strategic growth market for the group, and supporting the resilience and efficiency of its supply chain,” he added. The deal is central to Mr Saadé’s strategy of expanding CMA CGM’s less-cyclical logistics activities. An additional clause in the deal also sees FedEx “enter into multi-year commercial agreements” with CMA CGM’s ocean freight operations and CMA CGM Air Cargo.

items.title: Precious adds Asyad deal to ultramax fixing run
items.original_title: Precious adds Asyad deal to ultramax fixing run
items.summary: Thai dry bulk owner Precious Shipping has fixed its recently delivered ultramax Rossarin Naree to Asyad Shipping for up to 14 months in the latest index-linked deal for its larger bulker fleet. The Khalid Hashim-led company said the 63,500 dwt ship started a 12-to-14-month charter with Asyad on October 1 at a gross variable rate equivalent to 108% of the Baltic Exchange Supramax Index 63K weighted time-charter average over the preceding 15 days. Precious put the current equivalent rate at around $24,000 per day. The Rossarin Naree joined the fleet from China’s Taizhou Sanfu Ship Engineering at the end of May as the first in a four-ship ultramax series ordered in 2024 for a combined $133.46m, or about $33.36m apiece. Newly delivered sistership Ratima Naree went straight to Trafigura Maritime Logistics last month for 12 to 14 months at 107.5% of the BSI 63K, equivalent to around $22,800 per day when the charter started. A couple of weeks later, the 2016-built ultramax Sunisa Naree was fixed to Singapore’s PACC Line for 11 to 13 months at 103% of the same index, then equivalent to about $23,000 per day. The fixture comes as Precious continues to expand its ultramax exposure.

items.title: Torm cashes in on ageing MR
items.original_title: Torm cashes in on ageing MR
items.summary: Danish product tanker giant Torm has been linked to another fleet disposal, with brokers reporting the sale of one of its oldest MRs to China’s Seacon Shipping group for $22.5m. Splash understands the 2008-built Torm Laura has been picked up by Seacon Tankers Shipping. The 50,000 dwt scrubber-fitted vessel was built at Guangzhou Shipyard International. The 2008-built Torm Lene , from the same Guangzhou series, remains in the fleet and is now the oldest vessel listed by the company. Earlier this year, the company delivered the 2008-built LR2 Torm Maren to new owners while taking in two 2016-built LR2s and a 2018-built MR. Six MR resale newbuildings are due to arrive between 2027 and 2028, while the company confirmed in August that it had contracted another six MR newbuildings for delivery in 2029 with options on two more for 2030. Torm put the broker-assessed value of its fleet at $4.06bn at the end of June, up from $2.89bn a year earlier. At the end of March, the company said like-for-like fleet values had risen by $308m in just three months after adjusting for vessel purchases and sales.

items.title: Rio Tinto sell-down spreads to post-panamaxes
items.original_title: Rio Tinto sell-down spreads to post-panamaxes
items.summary: Rio Tinto’s owned-vessel sell-down appears to be extending beyond the newcastlemax fleet it cleared out this year, with a pair of 2013-built post-panamax bulkers reported sold en bloc for $42.8m. Broker reports list the 89,892 dwt RTM Dias and RTM Flinders , both built by Namura in Japan, at $21.4m each. The ships are part of Rio Tinto’s owned shipping operation. RTM Dias was delivered by Namura to Rio Tinto Shipping in 2013, while current fleet records list RTM Flinders under Rio Tinto Shipping Asia ownership and Rio Tinto Shipping management. The deal is separate from the newcastlemax sell-down Splash has tracked throughout 2026. Earlier this year, Rio Tinto moved the final two ships from its eight-strong owned newcastlemax fleet, with Yasa Shipping taking RTM Drake and RTM Tasman . That completed a disposal programme which had earlier seen six other 205,000 dwt-class vessels leave the miner’s fleet. Rio Tinto’s latest marine figures show the mining giant operates more than 230 chartered vessels, moving more than 300m tonnes of cargo across roughly 2,700 voyages a year.

items.title: Premier Alliance prepares for Asia-N Europe services return to Suez
items.original_title: Premier Alliance prepares for Asia-N Europe services return to Suez
items.summary: October will see almost all global ocean carriers make a tentative return to Suez transits on Asia-Europe sailings, after revised pro forma shipping schedules show the Premier Alliance is set to send one of its vessels on the route through the Red Sea and Egyptian waterway. The schedule of the 8,100 teu One Continuity, published by Japanese carrier ONE, shows the vessel departing Laem Chabang on 19 October, after being reassigned to the Premier Alliance’s FE1 Asia-North Europe service. According to Xeneta’s eeSea liner database, it has been deployed on ONE’s Asia-South America east coast SX1 service, operated in conjunction with Premier Alliance partners HMM and Yang Ming. According to the new FE1 pro forma, One Continuity will arrive at the Suez Canal on 9 November, and then at its first European port of call, Rotterdam, on 19 November. Other vessels in the FE1 service – the 9,000 teu NYK Venus , 8,200 teu ONE Hamburg , and 9,000 teu NYK Orion – are all also scheduled for Suez transits after leaving Asia in November and December. Meanwhile, Cosco vessels are also reportedly set to transit the Suez Canal, in the westbound direction, for the first time since the onset of the Red Sea Crisis, at the beginning of 2025.

items.original_title: Transpetrol trims aframax fleet in $73m deal
items.summary: Belgian tanker owner Transpetrol Maritime Services has offloaded its 2016-built aframax in a $73m deal with Turkish buyers. VesselsValue data identified Transpetrol as the seller of the Hyundai Samho-built 114,070 dwt TP Affinity and put the ship’s current market value at $80.72m. Transpetrol’s own fleet records show it was delivered in July 2016 and completed a scheduled drydock in Singapore in July. The reported disposal comes as Transpetrol pours capital into younger tonnage. Splash covered the company’s most recent order of two 75,000 dwt LR1 product tankers at Yangzijiang Shipbuilding for delivery in 2030, its first newbuildings in the segment. Earlier this year, it also booked two 90,000 cu m dual-fuel VLGCs at HD Hyundai Samho and has been taking delivery of a series of LR2s. Transpetrol currently lists TP Affinity and TP Spirit as its two aframaxes. Completion of the sale would therefore leave the company with a single ship in the segment while its LR1, LR2 and gas carrier fleets expand. The privately held outfit has also recently been linked to a sale of two 2011 Japanese-built MR2s, Turmoil and Luctor .
